srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), pp. 80–81

why: With the skeleton on the outside, a muscle has nothing internal to pull on, so the cuticle grows inwards instead: solid ingrowths are apodemes, hollow ones apophyses. The tentorium of the head and the furcae and pleural ridges of the thorax are all built this way. Because they are cuticle, they are shed with the rest of it at every moult and laid down again.
srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), p. 1

why: Thirty nanometres thick in a mosquito larva and four micrometres at the most anywhere: a hardened cuticulin lamina under a wax layer of paraffins and esters, secreted by oenocytes and pushed out through pore canals, with a cement layer over that in some groups. There is no chitin in it. It is the whole reason a land arthropod does not dry out.
srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), pp. 2–3

why: Paired appendages of the eleventh abdominal segment, or of the tenth where the eleventh has been lost. In cockroaches and crickets they are covered in filiform hairs light enough to be deflected by the air pushed ahead of a striking hand, and the turn away is under way before anything touches the animal. In earwigs the same appendages are hardened into forceps instead.
srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), pp. 59–60

why: Orthoptera — grasshoppers, locusts, crickets and katydids — is named for the tegmen, the straight leathery forewing laid flat along the back. The rest of the diagnosis is a saddle-shaped pronotum, four or fewer tarsal segments, and hind legs whose enlarged femora make the group’s jump. More than 20,000 species, distributed worldwide.
srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), p. 251

why: Tettigoniidae is the ensiferan family whose song apparatus is asymmetric — the toothed file carried on the left tegmen and the scraper on the right — so a katydid can only draw its wings one way round, where a cricket’s two tegmina are near mirror images and either could lead. The wings that sing are the same wings that hide it: held roof-like over the back, and veined like a leaf.
srcBook: Beutel RG, Friedrich F, Yang X-K & Ge S-Q, Insect Morphology and Phylogeny (De Gruyter, 2014), p. 253

why: Eusociality is defined by a division of labour into reproductive and non-reproductive groups, and those groups are the castes. In honeybees, ants and termites the difference is made after the egg is laid, by diet and by juvenile hormone during larval development, so full sisters end up as a layer or as a sterile worker — and in most species an individual of one caste can no longer perform the other’s work at all.

Every ant seen out of the nest is a female that will not reproduce. Workers forage, dig, nurse the brood, carry out the dead and fight, and they do all of it wingless, while the reproductives of the same colony grow wings and use them once. In many species the work is divided by age rather than by shape: a young worker nurses inside, an old one forages outside, where the dying is done.

In many ants the worker caste is not one shape but a size series, and the largest — majors, or soldiers — carry a head and mandibles enlarged out of all proportion to the body. Some crack seeds with them; some plug the nest entrance with the head itself. In army ants the mandibles are hooked so far towards fighting that the soldier has to be fed by smaller workers.

The reproductive caste of an ant or a termite colony, and the members of the colony that fly. They are reared as a batch, leave together, mate on the wing, and land — and the wings then break off along a preformed line of weakness, because a founding queen spends the rest of her life in a sealed chamber underground and wings would only be in the way.

A mature queen of the mound-building termites becomes physogastric: the abdomen distends with ovaries until the old plates of the body wall are separated by stretched pale membrane, and she is many times the length of her king. She cannot move herself. Workers feed and groom her in a royal cell, and a colony can run for decades on the eggs of one female.

The defensive caste: a dark, heavily sclerotised head carrying mandibles too large to eat with, so soldiers must be fed by workers. In the nasute termites the jaws are abandoned altogether and the head is drawn forward into a nozzle that squirts a sticky terpene at attackers. Both sexes serve, unlike ants, where every worker and every soldier is female.

Food swallowed by a forager into a social crop is brought back up and passed to a nestmate, who passes it on again, so a meal found by one animal spreads through the colony instead of staying in the finder. What travels with it is not only nutrition: hormones, the colony odour that tells nestmate from intruder, and in termites the gut symbionts a freshly moulted individual has just shed and must be given back.

Raised grain by grain from soil cemented with saliva and faeces, and in some African species reaching thirty metres across. The mound is mostly not living space: it is a ventilation structure standing over a nest dug below, its flues driven by the heat the colony and its fungus gardens give off. Mounds routinely outlast the colonies that built them.

Not an attack and not a migration — a colony dividing in two. The old queen leaves with a large part of the workforce and the swarm hangs in a cluster while scout bees argue over cavities; the comb, the stores and a daughter queen stay behind. Apis cerana swarms settle twenty to thirty metres from the nest they left and wait there for days before departing for the site the scouts agreed on.
Chewing and saliva do two different jobs: one breaks the food up, the other binds it into something a throat can grip. Dry food is hard to swallow because there is no bolus, only pieces.

The stomach churns for hours and then lets it through the pylorus in small squirts, because the duodenum can only neutralise so much acid at once. The rate of release is most of what controls how fast a meal is absorbed.
It is secreted as an inactive precursor and the stomach's own acid activates it. Outside that acid it does nothing, so an enzyme built to digest protein cannot digest the body that made it.
Saliva carries it, which is why bread held in the mouth turns sweet. Stomach acid stops it, and the pancreas sends far more of it into the intestine to finish the job.

The pancreas sends every one of its enzymes out inactive. Trypsin is activated at the gut wall and then activates the rest, so the cascade can only start where it is meant to — a pancreas that activates them early digests itself.

Fat and water do not mix, so an enzyme in water can only reach the surface of a fat globule. Bile emulsifies it into droplets and multiplies that surface enormously, and only then does lipase have anything to act on.
It makes albumin and clotting factors, stores glycogen, converts ammonia to urea, produces bile and breaks down most drugs. A dialysis machine replaces one kidney function; no machine does this.
Blood from the gut drains here and is delivered to the liver before it reaches the general circulation. That detour is why the liver sees every meal and every swallowed drug first.

The gut is a tube through the body, so its contents are topologically outside it. Nothing has entered until it crosses the wall — which is why fibre passing through is not food and why a swallowed marble is not absorbed.
It lays down the matrix around itself until it is trapped, and then becomes an osteocyte living in a little cavity. Building bone costs the builder its mobility.
The skeleton is laid down in cartilage and replaced from centres that spread outward, which is why growth happens at plates near the ends and why those plates closing ends your height.
Bone itself has few nerve endings; this wrapping has many, which is why a knock on the shin hurts so much. It also carries the blood supply and the cells that thicken a bone or mend it.
The coefficient of friction in a healthy joint is far below that of ice on ice. Cartilage releases fluid under load and takes it back when unloaded, which is why joints stiffen when you sit still.

Rising thyroid hormone suppresses the signal that called for it; rising blood sugar triggers the insulin that lowers it. It is the same loop as a thermostat, and it is why the word for the state is homeostasis.
It is made from testosterone by a single enzyme, in both sexes. Its withdrawal at menopause is why bone loss accelerates then, which is a skeletal consequence of a reproductive change.
Dopamine from the hypothalamus continuously suppresses it. Almost every other pituitary hormone waits for a signal to release; this one is released whenever the brake comes off.

It is the last step of the system that defends blood pressure when volume falls. Because water follows the salt, a hormone that regulates sodium is really a hormone that regulates how much blood you have.

When calcium falls they release a hormone that dissolves bone to raise it. The skeleton is the reserve, and it will be spent to keep the blood level right — because muscle and nerve need that number and bone can wait.

Every cell carries the same instructions and reads a different part of them. A liver cell is not missing the muscle genes; it has them silenced, which is why a specialised cell can sometimes be talked back into being general.
Lewis Wolpert's line is that it is not birth, marriage or death but gastrulation that is the truly important moment. Before it there are no layers and no body plan; after it, there is.

It closes within about four weeks, usually before a pregnancy is noticed, and folate is needed for that closure. That timing is the whole reason the advice is to take it before conceiving rather than after.
It runs from the back of the brain forward and is not finished until the mid-twenties, with the prefrontal cortex the last to complete. Judgement and impulse control mature on that schedule.
Cells that fire together wire together: repeated activity across a synapse makes it easier to cross next time. Memory is not stored in cells so much as in the changing strengths between them.
Both drain through one opening into the duodenum. A gallstone lodged there blocks the pancreatic duct as well, which is why gallstones are the commonest cause of pancreatitis.
It seals itself to the surface and pumps acid into the space underneath. Bone is rebuilt continuously, and osteoporosis is not a failure to build so much as this side winning.
An exocrine gland pipes its secretion somewhere specific. An endocrine one releases into the bloodstream, so the message goes everywhere and only cells with the matching receptor answer it.
Ectoderm becomes skin and nervous system; mesoderm muscle, bone and blood; endoderm the gut lining and its glands. Skin and brain sharing an origin is why so many conditions affect both.
It carries traffic between cerebrum and cerebellum, and during REM sleep it actively blocks motor signals to the body. Without that block, people act out their dreams.

Royal jelly is two thirds water and most of the rest protein and sugar, but the trace fraction is where this sits: it carries pantothenic acid and pyridoxine, and none of the fat-soluble vitamins at all.
Safflower and corn oil are both more than half linoleic acid by weight, which is as concentrated as a common food gets in a single fatty acid.
Seed oils are the richest sources of it — flaxseed, hempseed, chia, perilla, canola — and flax gave the molecule its name, from linon.

The insect head is enclosed in a hard, heavily sclerotised exoskeletal capsule made of six segments, each bearing one pair of head appendages. The thorax keeps its segments visibly apart; the head is the tagma where they have fused completely.

Hormonal oral contraceptives work by interacting with the hormonal changes of the menstrual cycle to prevent ovulation. Nothing is blocked mechanically — the cycle is held in a state where the release signal never comes, and the cervical mucus is altered as a second line.

The commonest loss it is fitted for is sensorineural, from damage to the hair cells and synapses of the cochlea. That is why simple amplification fails: the processing that matters is wide dynamic range compression, feedback management and directionality, not making everything louder.

A composite is a filler giving substance held in a binding matrix. In fibreglass the glass fibre is strong and stiff but brittle, and the polymer is ductile but weak and flexible — so the combination is stiff, strong, flexible and ductile at once, which neither component is.

Hardwood or softwood residuals are broken down to wood fibre in a defibrator, combined with wax and a resin binder, and formed into panels under high temperature and pressure. It is denser than plywood and stronger and denser than particle board.

Energy emitted or transmitted through space as waves or particles — photons on one side, particles with rest mass on the other. The division that matters is ionising against non-ionising: above roughly 10 electron volts a single quantum can ionise an atom and break a chemical bond, which is a property of frequency rather than of intensity.
The red of a cut tomato is a carotenoid with eleven conjugated double bonds, and the same pigment is sold as the food colouring E160d.
Gallotannins give it up to either acid or alkali: hydrolysis frees the gallic acid from the tannin it was bound into.
Olive oil is mainly this one fatty acid — up to 83% of it — with linoleic and palmitic acid making up most of the rest.
Of all the isoflavones, this is the one soybeans and soy products carry most of — it was first isolated from a dye plant, Genista tinctoria, which is where the name comes from.
A flavonol named after the oak forest, quercetum, and carried in quantity by capers, red onions and kale. It tastes bitter.
Named after rosemary, where Scarpatti and Oriente first isolated it in 1958, but it runs through the culinary Lamiaceae — sage, mint, basil and perilla alike.
Plants make it by hydrolysing their own tannins. The structure is two gallic acids joined head to tail, which is why the name is galle spelled backward.
The anthocyanidin behind red wine's colour. It decays to syringic acid, and finding that residue is how the Areni-1 winery was read as a winery at all.
Sesame oil's own lignan, isolated from the oil and, oddly, from the bark of Fagara plants as well.
The name records where it was first found rather than what it is: Beta vulgaris, the sugar beet. It is said beta-INE, because the beta is a plant and not a letter.
It is not in the plant until the plant is damaged: chewing or chopping lets the enzyme myrosinase meet glucoraphanin, and the two react into this.
The yellow of maize, and the name says so: Zea mays plus xanthos, Greek for yellow. Animals cannot make it and take it from plants — two carotenoids end up in the retina, and this is one.
The principal store of phosphorus in bran and seed. It binds calcium, iron and zinc tightly enough to block their absorption in the small intestine.
Plants make it in answer to injury or to attack by bacteria and fungi, which is why it turns up in grape skin, blueberries and peanuts rather than being stored.
The sterol in a fungal cell membrane, doing the job cholesterol does in an animal one. Named after ergot, the fungus it was first isolated from.
Ultraviolet light rearranges ergosterol into vitamin D2 — which is why a mushroom left in the sun has more of it than one that was not.
About 80% of the protein in cow's milk, named from the Latin for cheese. It is the half that sets; whey is the half that runs off.

Radon isotopes are the immediate decay products of radium isotopes: 222Rn, the most stable, has a half-life of 3.82 days and is a decay product of 226Ra, itself a decay product of 238U. It is a radioactive noble gas, colourless and odourless.

249Bk + 48Ca → 297Ts* → 294Ts + 3n (1 event), or 293Ts + 4n (5 events). The Dubna–Oak Ridge team reported it on 9 April 2010; the atoms lasted tens or hundreds of milliseconds, and IUPAC credited the Russian–American team in December 2015.

Californium-249 atoms hit by calcium-48 ions at Dubna: the first event took four months and a beam dose of 2.5×1019 calcium ions. Three, possibly four, nuclei of 294Og were detected in 2002 and 2005, and the half-life is 0.7 ms.

Inertia is the natural tendency of objects in motion to stay in motion and objects at rest to stay at rest, unless a force causes the velocity to change — one of the primary manifestations of mass. On Earth it is often masked by gravity, friction and air resistance, which tend to bring moving things to rest.

Torque is the rotational correspondent of linear force. Multiply the force applied perpendicularly to a lever by its distance from the fulcrum — the length of the lever arm — and that product is the torque.

Wavelength is the distance over which a wave's shape repeats, such as the gap between two adjacent crests. At a fixed wave speed it is inversely proportional to frequency: higher frequencies have shorter wavelengths, and lower frequencies longer ones.

Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion. It equals the work needed to accelerate the object from rest to its speed, and the same amount of work is done by the object when it decelerates to rest.

Potential energy is the energy of a system due to the position of its parts relative to other objects. Gravitational potential energy is the work of the gravitational force; elastic is the work of a deformed spring; electric is the work of the Coulomb force on a charge.

Absolute zero is the theoretically coldest temperature, where a system's internal energy reaches its minimum. The Kelvin scale puts it at 0 K, equivalent to −273.15 °C, and the third law of thermodynamics implies that no physical process can reach it in a finite number of steps.

Christian Doppler described it in 1842: the frequency of a wave changes for an observer who is moving relative to the source. A vehicle approaching an observer raises the pitch and receding lowers it, because each successive cycle is emitted from a position closer to — or farther from — the observer than the last.

Diffraction is the deviation of waves from straight-line propagation due to an obstacle or through an aperture. Francesco Maria Grimaldi coined the word from the Latin diffringere, "to break into pieces", for light breaking up into different directions.

In an ohmic conductor the electric current between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across them, and the constant of proportionality is the resistance: V=IR. Georg Ohm described it in a treatise published in 1827, from measurements on circuits of wire of various lengths.

Maxwell published an early form of the equations in 1861 and 1862. Their publication marked the unification of magnetism, electricity, light and associated radiation, and his addition was that magnetic fields also relate to changing electric fields — the displacement current.

The ideal gas law, pV=nRT, is the equation of state of a hypothetical ideal gas. Clapeyron stated it in 1834 as a combination of the empirical Boyle's, Charles's, Avogadro's and Gay-Lussac's laws, and the temperature in it must be absolute, in kelvins.

The total energy of an isolated system remains constant: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed or transferred. In thermodynamics it is the first law, and Noether's theorem derives it from the fact that the laws of physics do not change over time.

Software consists of computer programs that instruct the execution of a computer, and also includes design documents and specifications. High-level programming languages, introduced in 1958, allowed more human-readable instructions and made software more portable across computer architectures.

Email is a method of transmitting and receiving digital messages over a computer network, primarily the Internet. Mail servers accept, forward, deliver and store messages, so neither the users nor their computers need to be online at the same time.

Cryptography is the practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of adversarial behavior. Before the modern age it was effectively synonymous with encryption — turning readable plaintext into unintelligible ciphertext that only reversing the process can read.

A beach is a landform alongside a body of water, made of loose particles such as sand, gravel, shingle and pebbles, or of mollusc shells. Most beaches are on coasts, where wave or current action deposits and reworks the sediment.

Jet streams are fast flowing, narrow air currents in the atmosphere. The main terrestrial ones sit near the altitude of the tropopause and flow west to east; each hemisphere has a polar jet at around 9.1 km above sea level, typically travelling at around 180 km/h, and jet streams have been detected on Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

An ice sheet is a mass of glacial ice that covers surrounding terrain and is greater than 50,000 km². The two that exist are the Antarctic ice sheet, at 14 million km², and the Greenland ice sheet, at 1.7 million km², each with an average thickness of about 2 km.

Humidity is the concentration of water vapor present in the air. It depends on temperature and pressure: the same amount of water vapor gives a higher relative humidity in cool air than in warm air, because the amount needed for saturation rises with temperature.
A bog is a wetland that accumulates peat as a deposit of dead plant material, often mosses and typically sphagnum. Bogs occur where the water at the ground surface is acidic and low in nutrients.

An ester forms by substitution between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, the acid's hydroxyl hydrogen being replaced by the alcohol's organic group. Esters of carboxylic acids typically have a pleasant smell, and those of low molecular weight are used as fragrances.

A thiol is an organosulfur compound of the form R−SH, the sulfur analogue of an alcohol, and many have strong odors resembling garlic, cabbage or rotten eggs. The spray of skunks consists mainly of low-molecular-weight thiols and derivatives.
The chloride ion, Cl−, is the anion of chlorine — chlorine with an extra electron. Ionic chlorides include potassium chloride, calcium chloride and ammonium chloride.

A knot is an intentional complication in cordage which may be practical or decorative. Practical knots are classified by function: a hitch fastens a rope to another object, a bend fastens two ends of a rope to each other, and a loop knot creates a loop.

A scroll is a roll of papyrus, parchment or paper containing writing, usually partitioned into pages that are read by unrolling one page at a time. Scrolls were the first form of editable record-keeping texts, used in the Eastern Mediterranean and ancient Egyptian civilizations, before the codex came into popular use around the 1st century AD.

A central heating system provides warmth to a number of spaces within a building from one main source of heat. A furnace converts fuel or electricity to heat, which is circulated by forced air through ducts, by low-pressure steam to radiators, or by pumps carrying hot water through room radiators.

The tonsils are a set of lymphoid organs facing into the aerodigestive tract. Unqualified, the term usually means the palatine tonsils, two lymphoid organs at either side of the back of the throat, which tend to reach their largest size in puberty and then gradually atrophy.

The Kelvin scale is an absolute temperature scale that starts at the lowest possible temperature, absolute zero, taken to be 0 K. Its unit has the same magnitude as the Celsius degree, so a rise of one kelvin is a rise of 1 °C, and any Celsius temperature converts by adding 273.15.

The litre is a metric unit of volume equal to one cubic decimetre, a cube 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm. Because the kilogram was originally defined in 1795 as the mass of one cubic decimetre of water at melting-ice temperature, one litre of liquid water has a mass of almost exactly one kilogram.

An hour is a unit of time historically reckoned as 1/24 of a day and now defined as exactly 3,600 seconds. There are 24 hours in a day and 60 minutes in an hour, which is why a 24-hour clock reads out the hour of the day.

Struck with a harder material such as a steel edge, ferrocerium sheds hot fragments that oxidise rapidly in the oxygen of the air, producing sparks that can reach 3,315 °C. Rods of it are used in camping and survival kits as an emergency way to start a fire.
Legumes are plants in the pea family Fabaceae, or the fruit or seeds of such plants. Most of them have symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria, the rhizobia, living in structures called root nodules.

Water first enters rivers through precipitation, whether from rainfall, runoff down a slope, the melting of glaciers or snow, or seepage from aquifers. Rivers flow in channelled watercourses and merge in confluences to form drainage basins, areas where surface water eventually flows to a common outlet.

A sea is a very large body of salty water. One sense is the interconnected body of seawater spanning most of Earth, the ocean; the other is a named body of water, usually a marginal sea such as the Mediterranean, a section of the ocean, or a large, nearly landlocked body of water.

Ore is natural rock or sediment that contains one or more valuable minerals, typically including metals, concentrated above background levels and economically viable to mine and process. It is extracted from the earth through mining and then treated or refined, often by smelting, to extract the valuable metals or minerals.

Though sulfur is sometimes found in pure native form, on Earth it usually occurs as sulfide and sulfate minerals. Almost all elemental sulfur is now produced as a byproduct of removing sulfur-containing contaminants from natural gas and petroleum.

Malachite is a copper carbonate hydroxide mineral, and its Cu²⁺ gives it its green colour. Archaeological evidence indicates that it has been mined and smelted to obtain copper at Timna Valley, in present-day Israel, for more than 3,000 years.
Atoms are the basic particles of the chemical elements and the fundamental building blocks of matter. The chemical elements are distinguished from each other by the number of protons in their atoms.

In physical science, matter is anything that has mass and occupies space by having volume. All everyday objects that can be touched are ultimately composed of atoms, and DNA molecules, for example, are matter under this definition because they are made of atoms.

Time is the continuous progression of existence that occurs in an apparently irreversible succession from the past, through the present, and into the future. Practical, human-scale measurements of time are performed using clocks and calendars, reflecting a 24-hour day collected into a 365-day year linked to the astronomical motion of the Earth.

Light, or visible light, is electromagnetic radiation that can be perceived by the human eye. Single, massless elementary particles, or quanta, of light called photons can be detected with specialised equipment, although phenomena like interference are described by waves.

A rope is a group of yarns, plies, fibres or strands that are twisted or braided together into a larger and stronger form. It may be made of any long, fibrous material, but generally of natural or synthetic fibres; common natural fibres for rope are Manila hemp, hemp, linen, cotton, coir, jute, straw and sisal.

A gear, also called a toothed wheel or cog, is a rotating machine part typically used to transmit rotational motion or torque by means of a series of teeth that engage with compatible teeth of another gear. Gears can be used to trade torque for rotational speed between two axles, or to change the axis or sense of rotation.

The earliest inks from all civilisations are believed to have been made with lampblack, a kind of soot, easily collected as a by-product of fire. The earliest Chinese inks, similar to modern inksticks, date to around 256 BC and were made from soot and animal glue.
Bark is the outermost layer of the stems and roots of woody plants, including trees, woody vines and shrubs. It refers to all the tissues outside the vascular cambium.

A dune is a landform composed of wind- or water-driven sand. Dunes are most common in desert environments, where the lack of moisture hinders the growth of vegetation that would otherwise interfere with their development, though they are also found along sea shores and in areas of glacial outwash.

The Sahara is a desert spanning North Africa. With an area of 9,200,000 square kilometres, it is the largest hot desert in the world and the third-largest desert overall, smaller only than the deserts of Antarctica and the northern Arctic.

The Nile is a major north-flowing river in northeast Africa which empties into the Mediterranean Sea. At 7,088 kilometres long it is the longest river in the world, although the volume of water it carries is much smaller than other major rivers such as the Amazon or the Congo.

Earth's lithosphere, the rigid outer shell of the planet including the crust and upper mantle, is fractured into seven or eight major plates and many minor ones. Tectonic plates are composed of oceanic lithosphere and thicker continental lithosphere, each topped by its own kind of crust.

Natural gums are polysaccharides of natural origin, capable of causing a large increase in a solution's viscosity even at small concentrations. They are mostly botanical, found in the woody parts of plants or in seed coatings, and are used in food as thickening, gelling, emulsifying and stabilising agents and in industry as adhesives and binders.
Juice is a drink made from the extraction or pressing of the natural liquid contained in fruit and vegetables.

In biochemistry, a polymerase is an enzyme that synthesises long chains of polymers or nucleic acids. DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase are used to assemble DNA and RNA molecules by copying a DNA template strand using base-pairing interactions.

Canals, or artificial waterways, are waterways or engineered channels built for drainage management, such as flood control and irrigation, or for conveying water transport vehicles. They carry free, calm surface flow under atmospheric pressure and can be thought of as artificial rivers.

Cucurbita, Latin for 'gourd', is a genus native to the Andes and Mesoamerica of herbaceous fruits in the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae. They are variously known as squash, pumpkin or gourd, depending on species, variety and local parlance.

In physics, a fluid is a liquid, gas or other material that may continuously move and deform (flow) under an applied shear stress or external force. Fluids have zero shear modulus: they are substances that cannot resist any shear force applied to them.

Armour is a covering used to protect an object, individual or vehicle from physical injury or damage, especially from direct-contact weapons or projectiles during combat. Personal armour is used to protect soldiers and war animals, and has been used throughout recorded history.

Addition is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic, usually denoted with the plus sign. Besides counting items, it can be defined without referring to concrete objects, using abstractions called numbers instead, and repeated addition of 1 is the same as counting.

Subtraction is an operation that represents removal of objects from a collection. In a sense it is the inverse of addition: the difference of two numbers is the number that gives the first one when added to the second one, so the difference of 5 and 2 is 3.

The multiplication of whole numbers may be thought of as repeated addition: the multiplication of two numbers is equivalent to adding as many copies of one of them as the quantity of the other one. The expression 3×4 can be phrased as "three groups of four", and evaluated as 4+4+4.

Arithmetic is an elementary branch of mathematics that deals with numerical operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Ancient civilizations like the Egyptians and the Sumerians invented numeral systems to solve practical arithmetic problems in about 3000 BCE.

When n is a positive integer, exponentiation corresponds to repeated multiplication of the base: b to the n is the product of multiplying b by itself n times. The expression b squared is called "the square of b" because the area of a square with side-length b is b squared.

A square root of a number x is a number y such that y squared equals x; in other words, a number whose square, the result of multiplying the number by itself, is x. Every nonnegative real number x has a unique nonnegative square root, called the principal square root: the principal square root of 9 is 3.

As a single-variable function, the logarithm to base b is the inverse of exponentiation with base b. Logarithms were introduced by John Napier in 1614 as a means of simplifying calculations: using logarithm tables, tedious multi-digit multiplication steps can be replaced by table look-ups and simpler addition.

An integer is the number zero, a positive natural number (1, 2, 3, ...), or the negation of a positive natural number (−1, −2, −3, ...). The negations or additive inverses of the positive natural numbers are referred to as negative integers.

A negative number is the opposite of a positive real number; equivalently, a real number that is less than zero. A debt that is owed may be thought of as a negative asset, and Islamic mathematicians further developed the rules of subtracting and multiplying negative numbers.

A rational number is a number that can be expressed as the quotient or fraction of two integers, a numerator p and a nonzero denominator q. Every integer is a rational number, and the rationals are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational number.

Every real number can be almost uniquely represented by an infinite decimal expansion, and real numbers that are not rational are irrational. The real numbers are fundamental in calculus, in particular by their role in the classical definitions of limits, continuity and derivatives.

A complex number is a number of the form a+bi, where a and b are real numbers and i is the imaginary unit, which satisfies the equation i squared equals −1. Square roots of negative numbers were found helpful in the 16th century for determining the real solutions of cubic equations.

As zero-dimensional objects, points are usually taken to be the fundamental indivisible elements comprising the space. In classical Euclidean geometry, a point is a primitive notion, defined as "that which has no part".

In geometry, a straight line is an infinitely long object with no width, depth, or curvature. It is an idealisation of such physical objects as a straightedge, a taut string, or a ray of light, and a line segment is the part of a line delimited by two points.

One standard definition is that an angle is a figure consisting of two rays which lie in a plane and share a common endpoint. Each line is called a side of the angle and the point they share is its vertex, and the measurement of angles is intrinsically linked with circles and rotations.

A polygon is a plane figure made up of line segments connected to form a closed polygonal chain, and the segments are called its edges or sides. An n-gon is a polygon with n sides; for example, a triangle is a 3-gon.

A perimeter is the length of a closed boundary that encompasses, surrounds, or outlines a two-dimensional shape. The perimeter of a polygon equals the sum of the lengths of its sides, and a calculated perimeter is the length of fence required to surround a yard or garden.

Line m is in the same plane as line l but does not intersect l, recalling that lines extend to infinity in either direction. Parallel planes are likewise infinite flat planes in the same three-dimensional space that never meet.

The tangent line to a plane curve at a given point is, intuitively, the straight line that "just touches" the curve at that point. Euclid makes several references to the tangent to a circle in book III of the Elements.

Trigonometry, from Ancient Greek words for "triangle" and "measure", is a branch of mathematics concerned with relationships between angles and side lengths of triangles. Mathematicians in India created the earliest-known tables of trigonometric ratios such as sine.

The sine of an acute angle of a right triangle is the ratio of the length of the side opposite that angle to the length of the longest side of the triangle, the hypotenuse. The definitions of sine and cosine have been extended to any real value in terms of the lengths of certain line segments in a unit circle.

In solid geometry, a sphere is the set of points that are all at the same distance r from a given point in three-dimensional space. That given point is the center of the sphere, and the distance r is the sphere's radius; the word comes from the Ancient Greek for "ball".

Volume is a measure of regions in three-dimensional space. It is often quantified numerically using SI derived units, such as the cubic metre and litre, or by imperial or US customary units such as the gallon, quart and cubic inch.

The derivative of a function of a single variable at a chosen input value, when it exists, is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function at that point. It is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and is computed as the limit of a difference quotient.

Integration was initially used to solve problems in mathematics and physics, such as finding the area under a curve, or determining displacement from velocity. The fundamental theorem of calculus relates definite integration to differentiation: they are inverse operations.

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers or other mathematical objects with elements arranged in rows and columns, usually satisfying certain properties of addition and multiplication. Matrices can be used to compactly write and work with multiple linear equations, that is, systems of linear equations.

A sequence is a collection of objects, possibly with repetition, that come in a specified order. Unlike a set, the same elements can appear multiple times at different positions in a sequence, and the order does matter.

A series is, roughly speaking, an addition of infinitely many terms, one after the other. Among the Ancient Greeks, the idea that a potentially infinite summation could produce a finite result was considered paradoxical, most famously in Zeno's paradoxes.

A conjecture is a proposition that is proffered on a tentative basis without proof. Some conjectures, such as Fermat's conjecture, now a theorem, proven in 1995 by Andrew Wiles, have shaped much of mathematical history as new areas of mathematics are developed in order to prove them.

Mathematics is a field of knowledge concerned with abstract concepts such as numbers, geometric shapes, sets, functions, and probabilities. Its areas include number theory, the study of integers and their properties, and geometry, the study of shapes and the spaces that contain them.

A percentage, from Latin per centum "by a hundred", is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. It is a dimensionless number, primarily used for expressing proportions, though percent is nonetheless a unit of measurement in its orthography and usage.

Goods are the result of the secondary sector of the economy, which involves the transformation of raw materials or intermediate goods into goods. They are commonly considered to have diminishing marginal utility, which means that consuming more gives less utility per amount consumed.

A service is an act or use for which a consumer, company, or government is willing to pay. Services may be defined as intangible acts or performances whereby the service provider provides value to the customer.

A price in economics is the amount of money that buyers are willing and able to pay for a particular good or service, and that sellers are willing to accept. Prices are influenced by production costs, supply of the desired product, and demand for the product.

In microeconomics, supply and demand is an economic model of price determination in a market. It postulates that, holding all else equal, the unit price in a perfectly competitive market will vary until it settles at the market-clearing price, where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.

In economics, inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money, though it originally referred to the increase of the money supply that can cause such a universal shift. The increase is measured using a price index, typically a consumer price index.

The opposite of inflation is deflation, a decrease in the general price level of goods and services. It is an increase in the real value of the monetary unit of account, and a monetary phenomenon, explainable in terms of changes in money supply and velocity relative to spending on output.

In economics, profit is the difference between the revenue an economic entity has received from its outputs and the total costs of its inputs, also known as "surplus value". It is equal to total revenue minus total cost, including both explicit and implicit costs.

Business is the practice of making one's living or making money by producing or buying and selling products, such as goods and services. A business entity is not necessarily separate from the owner, and creditors can hold the owner liable for debts the business has acquired, except for a limited liability company.

A company is a legal entity representing an association of legal persons with a shared objective, such as generating profit or benefiting society. Companies are governed by company law, and incorporated companies are created through state registration, whereas unincorporated companies are not.

A corporation is an individual or other entity such as a company that has been authorized by the state to act as a single entity, recognized as such in law for certain purposes. One early advantage for investors over sole proprietorships and joint partnerships was limited liability.
A wage is the price of labor. Wages are part of the expenses involved in running a business, and wage payment is an obligation due to an employee regardless of the profitability of the company.

Employment is a relationship between two parties regulating the provision of paid labour services. Employing other people is often a significant step for a self-employed person whose work is developing into a small business.

Unemployment is the state of not being in paid employment or self-employment but currently available for work. It is measured by the unemployment rate, the number of people who are unemployed as a percentage of the labour force.

In finance, a loan is the tender of money by one party to another with an agreement to pay it back. Acting as a provider of loans is one of the main activities of financial institutions such as banks and credit card companies.

A mortgage is a loan used by purchasers of real property to raise funds to buy real estate, or by existing owners to raise funds for any purpose while putting a lien on the property. The word comes from a Law French term meaning "death pledge": the pledge dies when the obligation is fulfilled or the property is taken through foreclosure.

Insurance is a means of protection from financial loss in which, in exchange for a fee, a party agrees to compensate another party in the event of a certain loss, damage, or injury. The general average principle of marine insurance was established on the island of Rhodes in approximately 1000 to 800 BC.
Investment is traditionally defined as the "commitment of resources into something expected to gain value over time". When a low-risk investment is made, the return is also generally low.

Some view the founding of the Dutch East India Company in 1602 as the key event in the history of stock exchanges, while others point to earlier developments in Antwerp in 1531 and Lyon in 1548. Trade on an exchange is restricted to brokers who are members of the exchange.

The recording of financial transactions, so that summaries may be presented in financial reports, is known as bookkeeping, of which double-entry bookkeeping is the most common system. The double-entry system in use today was developed in medieval Europe, particularly in Venice, and is usually attributed to Luca Pacioli.

Gross domestic product is a monetary measure of the total market value of all the final goods and services produced during a specific period of time, usually a year, by a country or countries. It is often used to measure the economic activity of a country or region.

In economics, economic growth is an increase in the quantity and quality of the economic goods and services that a society produces. The rate of growth is typically calculated as the real GDP growth rate, real GDP per capita growth rate, GNI per capita growth or median income growth.

Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. Microeconomics analyses the basic elements of economies, including individual agents and markets, their interactions, and the outcomes of those interactions.

In economics, a monopoly is a single seller. It is characterized by a lack of economic competition to produce a particular thing, a lack of viable substitute goods, and the possibility of a high monopoly price well above the seller's marginal cost.

Employment or wage subsidies keep the employment relationship ongoing even during financial crisis, so workers are prevented from losing their jobs and associated benefits. Housing subsidies are designed to promote the construction industry and homeownership.

A sales tax is a tax paid to a governing body for the sales of certain goods and services. A purchaser who is not an end-user is usually issued a "resale certificate" by the taxing authority, to show that the item is for resale.

A property tax is an ad valorem tax on the value of a property, with its rate expressed as a percentage or per mille, also called millage. The tax is levied by the governing authority of the jurisdiction in which the property is located.

An income tax is a tax imposed on individuals or entities in respect of the income or profits earned by them, commonly called taxable income. It is generally computed as the product of a tax rate times the taxable income, and the tax on companies is usually known as corporate tax.

International trade is the exchange of capital, goods, and services across international borders or territories because there is a need or demand for goods or services. Cross-border trade typically incurs additional costs such as explicit tariffs, as well as non-tariff barriers such as time costs due to border delays, language and cultural differences.

In finance, an exchange rate is the rate at which one currency will be exchanged for another currency. Currencies are most commonly national currencies, but may be sub-national, as in the case of Hong Kong, or supra-national, as in the case of the euro.

A pension, from Latin pensiō "payment", is a fund or pay-as-you-go scheme into which amounts are paid regularly during an individual's working career, and from which periodic payments are made to support the person's retirement from work. Occupational pensions are a form of deferred compensation.

Bankruptcy is a legal process through which people or other entities who cannot repay debts to creditors may seek relief from some or all of their debts. Bankrupt is not the only legal status that an insolvent person may have, so the term bankruptcy is not a synonym for insolvency.

A black market is a clandestine market or series of transactions that has some aspect of illegality within a legal jurisdiction; it may also not be compliant with an institutional set of rules. Such activities are generally referred to using the definite article, as in "the black market in bush meat".

Protectionism is the economic policy of restricting imports from other countries through methods such as tariffs on imported goods, import quotas, and a variety of other government regulations. Tariffs and import quotas are the most common types of protectionist policies.

In economics, competition is a scenario where different economic firms are in contention to obtain goods that are limited by varying the elements of the marketing mix: price, product, promotion and place. The word competitiveness derives from the Latin competere, which refers to the rivalry found between entities in markets and industries.

Commerce is the organized system of activities, functions, procedures and institutions that directly or indirectly contribute to the smooth, unhindered large-scale exchange of goods, services, and other forms of value, predominantly through transactional processes.

Productivity is the efficiency of production of goods or services expressed by some measure. Measurements of productivity are often expressed as a ratio of an aggregate output to a single input or an aggregate input used in a production process.

Morality is a quality among social animals, including humans, through which communities and individuals evaluate actions, character, and social arrangements. It often refers to a set of standards, doctrines, or systems of conduct whose criteria vary across individuals, societies, religions, cultures, customs, and traditions.
Truth is commonly understood as conformity to reality or fact. It is typically treated as a property of sentences, propositions, or beliefs that describe things as they are.
In philosophy, ideas can also be mental representational images of some object. Our actions are based upon beliefs, and beliefs are patterns or organized sets of ideas.

A concept is a fundamental unit of cognition that classifies entities and encodes shared features. The classical theory holds that concepts are essentially definitions, each characterized by fixed rules determining to which entities the concept applies.

An argument is one or more premises — sentences, statements, or propositions — directed towards arriving at a logical conclusion. Its purpose is to give reasons for one's thinking and understanding via justification, explanation, or persuasion.

A fallacy is the use of invalid or otherwise faulty reasoning in the construction of an argument that may appear to be well-reasoned if unnoticed. An example is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

Inferences are steps in logical reasoning, moving from premises to logical consequences. Deduction is inference deriving logical conclusions from premises known or assumed to be true, with the laws of valid inference being studied in logic.

Deductive reasoning is the process of drawing valid inferences. An inference is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its premises, meaning that it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion to be false.

Inductive reasoning refers to a variety of methods of reasoning in which the conclusion of an argument is supported with some degree of probability, but not deductive certainty. An inductive generalization proceeds from premises about a sample to a conclusion about the population.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation for a phenomenon. If a hypothesis is repeatedly independently demonstrated by experiment to be true, it becomes a scientific theory.
A fact is a true datum about one or more aspects of a circumstance, or an occurrence in the real world. Standard reference works are often used to check facts.

Skepticism is a questioning attitude or doubt toward knowledge claims that are seen as mere belief or dogma. For example, a person who is skeptical about claims made by their government about an ongoing war doubts that these claims are accurate.

Empiricism is an epistemological view in philosophy which holds that true knowledge or justification comes either only or primarily from sensory experience and empirical evidence. It is one of several competing views within epistemology, along with rationalism and skepticism.

Rationalism is the epistemological view that regards reason as the chief source and test of knowledge, often in contrast to other possible sources such as faith, tradition, or sensory experience. More formally, it is a methodology in which the criterion of truth is not sensory but intellectual and deductive.

Free will is generally understood as the capacity of people to choose between different possible courses of action, or to exercise control over their actions in a way that is necessary for moral responsibility. It is closely linked to moral responsibility and to judgements that can logically apply only to actions that are freely chosen.

Determinism is the metaphysical view that all events within the universe can occur only in one possible way. It is often contrasted with free will, although some philosophers argue that the two are compatible.

Existentialism is a family of philosophical views that explore the human individual's struggle to lead an authentic life despite the apparent absurdity or incomprehensibility of existence. It often includes concepts such as angst, courage, and the curse and blessing of human freedom.

Nihilism is a family of philosophical views that reject the existence of any objectively meaningful purpose, moral value, truth, knowledge, or related concepts. It is also described as a broad cultural phenomenon or historical movement that pervades modernity in the Western world.

Utilitarianism is a family of theories in normative ethics that prescribe actions that maximize happiness and well-being for all affected individuals. It is a version of consequentialism, which states that the consequences of any action are the only standard of right and wrong.

Deontology, from the Ancient Greek for "duty, obligation", is the normative ethical theory that the morality of an action should be based on whether that action itself is right or wrong under a series of rules and principles, rather than on its consequences. It is commonly contrasted to utilitarianism and other consequentialist theories.

Relativism is a family of philosophical views which deny claims to absolute objectivity within a particular domain and assert that valuations in that domain are relative to the perspective of an observer or the context in which they are assessed. There are many different forms of relativism, with a great deal of variation in scope.

Humanism is a philosophical stance that emphasizes the agency, and the individual and social potential, of human beings, whom it considers the starting point for serious moral and philosophical inquiry. In contemporary usage it refers to a non-theistic view centered on human agency, and a reliance only on science and reason rather than revelation from a divine source.

Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that examines the basic nature or most fundamental structure of reality. It is traditionally seen as the study of mind-independent features of the world, but some theorists view it as an inquiry into the conceptual framework of human understanding.
Aesthetics is the branch of philosophy that studies beauty, taste, and related phenomena. Aesthetic properties are features that influence the appeal of objects.

Wisdom, also known as sapience, is defined by psychologists as a combination of wit and virtue: the ability to apply expert tacit and experiential knowledge, balancing intrapersonal, interpersonal and institutional interests, to deal with complex questions of life and attain a common good. Plato distinguished sophia, phronesis (practical wisdom) and episteme (formal or scientific knowledge).

A virtue is a trait of excellence, including traits that may be moral, social, or intellectual. The cultivation and refinement of virtue is held to be the "good of humanity" and thus is valued as an end purpose of life or a foundational principle of being.

A conscience is a cognitive process that elicits emotion and rational associations based on an individual's moral philosophy or value system. It is not an elicited emotion or thought produced by associations based on immediate sensory perceptions and reflexive responses.
A thought experiment is an imaginary scenario that is meant to elucidate or test an argument or theory. It is often an experiment that would be hard, impossible, or unethical to actually perform.

A deity is a supernatural being considered to have authority over some aspect of the universe and/or life, with many deities also regarded as sacred and as worthy of worship. Monotheism accepts only one deity, whereas polytheistic religions accept multiple deities.

Theology is the study of religious belief from a religious perspective, with a focus on the nature of divinity and the history behind religion. It is taught as an academic discipline, typically in universities and seminaries.

Sacrifice is an act or offering made to a deity. A sacrifice can serve as propitiation, or a sacrifice can be an offering of praise and thanksgiving, and varieties of ritual non-human sacrifices are practiced by numerous religions today.

In Christian belief, a saint is a person who is recognized as having an exceptional degree of holiness, likeness, or closeness to God. The saints are honored in the liturgical calendars of Evangelical Lutheranism and Anglicanism.

In religion, a relic is an object or article of religious significance from the past. It usually consists of the physical remains or personal effects of a saint or other person preserved for the purpose of veneration as a tangible memorial.

A monastery is a building or complex of buildings comprising the domestic quarters and workplaces of monastics, monks or nuns, whether living in communities (as cenobites) or alone (as hermits). In English usage, the term "monastery" is generally used to denote the buildings of a community of monks.

Heresy is any belief or theory that is strongly at variance with established beliefs or customs, particularly the accepted beliefs or religious law of a religious organization. A heretic is a proponent of a heresy.

Pantheism is a diverse family of philosophical and religious beliefs that equate reality with divinity. Most notably, it refers to the belief that the totality of being, called by names such as Nature, the universe or the cosmos, is a self-organizing unity that needs no distinct, supernatural creator.

Deism, from the Latin deus, "god", is the belief that a Supreme Being created the universe and that empirical reason and observation of the natural world are sufficient to determine the existence of a creator God. It is a philosophical position and rationalistic theology that rejects prophecies, revelations, and religious texts as reliable sources of divine knowledge.
In religion, salvation generally refers to the deliverance of the soul from a state of ignorance or perpetual harm. The academic study of salvation is called soteriology.

In religion and folklore, Hell is a location or state in the afterlife in which souls are subjected to punishment after death. Such places are sometimes equated with the English word hell, though a more correct translation would be "underworld" or "world of the dead".
Resurrection, or anastasis, is the concept of coming back to life after death. The English word derives from the Latin resurrectio, from surgere, "to rise".

Apocalyptic literature, from the Ancient Greek for "revelation, disclosure", is a literary genre originating in Judaism in the centuries following the Babylonian exile (597–587 BCE) but persisting in Christianity and Islam. Its means of mediation include dreams, visions and heavenly journeys.

A creation myth or cosmogonic myth is a type of cosmogony, a symbolic narrative of how the world began and how people first came to inhabit it. While in popular usage the term myth often refers to false or fanciful stories, members of cultures often ascribe varying degrees of truth to their creation myths.

A taboo is a social group's ban, prohibition or avoidance of something, usually an utterance or behavior, based on the group's sense that it is excessively repulsive, offensive, sacred or allowed only for certain people. Taboos may be prohibited explicitly, within a legal system or religion, or implicitly, by social norms or conventions.

Magic is the application of beliefs, rituals or actions employed with the intent to manipulate natural or supernatural beings and forces. It is a category into which various beliefs and practices have been placed, sometimes considered separate from both religion and science.

A superstition is any belief or practice considered by non-practitioners to be irrational or supernatural. It is commonly applied to beliefs and practices surrounding luck, fate, magic, amulets, astrology, fortune telling, spirits, and certain paranormal entities.

Astrology is a range of divinatory practices, recognized as pseudoscientific since the 18th century, that propose that information about human affairs and terrestrial events may be discerned by studying the apparent positions of celestial objects. Contemporary Western astrology is often associated with systems of horoscopes.

Divination is the attempt to gain insight into a question or situation by way of a magic ritual or practice. If a distinction is made between divination and fortune-telling, divination has a more formal or ritualistic element and often a more social character, usually in a religious context.
Folklore is the body of expressive culture shared by a particular group of people, culture or subculture. It is not something one typically gains from a formal school curriculum or fine arts study.

A funeral is a ceremony connected with the final disposition of a corpse, such as a burial, entombment or cremation with the attendant observances. A memorial service or celebration of life is a funerary ceremony performed without the remains of the deceased person.
Cremation is a method of final disposition of a corpse or animal carcass through burning. Starting in the 19th century, cremation was introduced or reintroduced into other parts of the world.

Fasting is the act of refraining from eating, and sometimes drinking. It may also be part of a religious ritual, often associated with specific scheduled fast days, as determined by the religion, or be applied as a public demonstration for a given cause, in a practice known as a hunger strike.

A totem is a spirit being, sacred object, or symbol that serves as an emblem of a group of people, such as a family, clan, lineage, or tribe, as in the Anishinaabe clan system. The word is an anglicisation of the Ojibwe term, and belief in tutelary spirits and deities is not limited to the Ojibwe people.

A curse is any expressed wish that some form of adversity or misfortune will befall or attach to one or more persons, a place, or an object. To reverse or eliminate a curse is sometimes called "removal" or "breaking", as the spell has to be dispelled, and often requires elaborate rituals or prayers.

Witchcraft is the use of magic by a person called a witch. Traditionally, witchcraft means the use of magic to inflict supernatural harm or misfortune on others, and this remains the most common and widespread meaning.

A monster is a type of imaginary or fictional creature found in literature, folklore, mythology, horror, fantasy, fiction and religion. They are very often depicted as dangerous and aggressive, with a strange or grotesque appearance that causes terror and fear, often in humans.

Popularly, mysticism is used synonymously with mystical experience, an ecstatic unitive experience of becoming one with God, the Absolute, or all that exists. Broadly defined, mysticism as a way of personal transformation can be found in a number of religious traditions, including Christianity, Judaism, Sufism, Buddhism and Hinduism.

Secularism is the principle of seeking to conduct human affairs based on naturalistic considerations, uninvolved with religion. It is most commonly thought of as the separation of religion from civil affairs and the state.

Education is the transmission of knowledge and skills and the development of character traits. Non-formal education is also structured but occurs outside the formal schooling system, while informal education is unstructured learning through daily experiences.

Teaching is the practice implemented by a teacher aimed at transmitting skills (knowledge, know-how, and interpersonal skills) to a learner, a student, or any other audience of an educational institution. It is closely related to learning, the student's activity of appropriating this knowledge.

A student is a person enrolled in a school or other educational institution, or more generally, a person who takes a special interest in a subject. Those in primary school are often referred to as pupils.

A university, from Latin universitas "a whole", is an institution of tertiary education and research which awards academic degrees in several academic disciplines. The word derives from the Latin phrase universitas magistrorum et scholarium, which roughly means "community of teachers and scholars".

The term curriculum often refers specifically to a planned sequence of instruction, or to a view of the student's experiences in terms of the educator's or school's instructional goals. Curricula are split into several categories: the explicit, the implicit (including the hidden), the excluded, and the extracurricular.

An examination (exam or evaluation), or test, is an educational assessment intended to measure a test-taker's knowledge, skill, aptitude, physical fitness, or classification in many other topics. There is no general consensus or invariable standard for test formats and difficulty.

An academic degree is a qualification awarded to a student upon successful completion of a course of study in higher education. Academic degrees are commonly structured in levels, most often categorized as undergraduate and postgraduate degrees.

A skill is the learned or innate ability to act with determined results and good execution often within a given amount of time, energy, or both. Although the arts are also skills, there are many skills that form an art but have no connection to the fine arts.

Pedagogy, taken as an academic discipline, is the study of how knowledge and skills are imparted in an educational context, and it considers the interactions that take place during learning. It is often described as the act of teaching.

Information is an abstract concept that refers to something which has the power to inform. Any natural process that is not completely random and any observable pattern in any medium can be said to convey some amount of information.

Data is a collection of discrete or continuous values that conveys information, describing the quantity, quality, fact, statistics, other basic units of meaning, or simply sequences of symbols that may be further interpreted formally. A datum, data value or data point is an individual value in a collection of data.

Communication is commonly defined as the transmission of information. Its precise definition is disputed, with disagreements about whether unintentional or failed transmissions are included and whether communication not only transmits meaning but also creates it.

Conversation is interactive communication between two or more people. Conversation analysis is a branch of sociology which studies the structure and organization of human interaction, with a more specific focus on conversational interaction.

Nonverbal communication is the transmission of messages through signals that don't involve spoken or written words. It often goes unnoticed but is used in communication everywhere, to aid in the message someone is intending to get across.

Body language is a type of nonverbal communication in which physical behaviors, as opposed to words, are used to express or convey information. Although it is an important part of communication, most of it happens without conscious awareness.

Culture is a concept that encompasses the social behavior, institutions, and norms found in human societies, as well as the knowledge, beliefs, arts, laws, customs, capabilities, attitudes, and habits of the individuals in these groups. It often originates from or is attributed to a specific region or location.

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.

Cultural anthropology is a branch of anthropology focused on the study of cultural variation among humans. It is in contrast to social anthropology, which perceives cultural variation as a subset of a posited anthropological constant.

Ethnography is a branch of anthropology and the systematic study of individual cultures. It is also a type of social research that involves examining the behavior of the participants in a given social situation and understanding the group members' own interpretation of such behavior.

An ethnicity or ethnic group is a group of humans who identify with each other on the basis of perceived shared attributes that distinguish them from other groups. These attributes may include language, culture, ancestry, traditions, society, religion, history, region, or social treatment.

Nomads are communities without fixed habitation who regularly move to and from areas. Nomadism is also a lifestyle adapted to infertile regions such as steppe, tundra, or ice and sand, where mobility is the most efficient strategy for exploiting scarce resources.
Cultural heritage is the tangible and intangible legacy of a group or society that is inherited from past generations. Not all legacies of past generations are "heritage".

Popular culture, also called pop culture or mass culture, is generally recognized by members of a society as a set of practices, beliefs, artistic output and objects that are dominant or prevalent in a society at a given point in time. Mass media, marketing, and the imperatives of mass appeal within capitalism constitute the primary engines of Western popular culture.

Oral tradition, or oral lore, is a form of human communication in which knowledge, art, beliefs, ideas and culture are received, preserved, and transmitted orally from one generation to another. The transmission is through speech or song and may include folktales, ballads, chants, prose or poetry.

Greeting is an act of communication in which human beings intentionally make their presence known to each other, to show attention to, and to suggest a type of relationship or social status between individuals or groups of people coming in contact with each other. Greetings are sometimes used just prior to a conversation or to greet in passing.

Body modification is the deliberate altering of the human anatomy or human physical appearance. It is performed for a large variety of reasons, including aesthetics, rites of passage, religious beliefs, and to display group membership or affiliation.

A tattoo is a form of body modification made by inserting tattoo ink, dyes, or pigments, either indelible or temporary, into the dermis layer of the skin to form a design. The etymology of the body modification term is not to be confused with the origins of the word for the military drumbeat or performance.

A birthday is the anniversary of the birth of a person or the figurative birth of an institution. Birthdays of people are celebrated in numerous cultures, often with birthday gifts, birthday cards, a birthday party, or a rite of passage.
A holiday is a day or other period of time set aside for festivals or recreation. Public holidays are set by public authorities and vary by state or region.

Carnival typically involves public celebrations, including events such as parades, public street parties and other entertainments, combining some elements of a circus. It is known as a time of great indulgence before Lent, which stresses the opposite, with drinking, overeating, and various other activities of indulgence.

Christmas is a religious and cultural celebration commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ, observed primarily on December 25 among billions of people around the world. Advent is followed by Christmastide, which historically in the West lasts twelve days and culminates on Twelfth Night.

Easter is the culmination of the Passion of Jesus, preceded by Lent (or Great Lent), a 40-day period of fasting, prayer, and penance. In Eastern Christianity, the same events are commemorated with the names of days all starting with "Holy" or "Holy and Great".

Halloween is at the beginning of the observance of Allhallowtide, the time in the Christian liturgical year dedicated to remembering the dead, including saints (hallows), Christian martyrs, and all the faithful departed. Thus, the name originates in Christianity, and means "Saints' eve(ning)".

Diwali is associated with the spiritual victory or triumph of Dharma over Adharma, light over darkness, good over evil, and knowledge over ignorance. It is celebrated during the Hindu lunisolar months of Ashvin and Kārtika, between around mid-October and mid-November.

New Year's Eve in the Gregorian calendar refers to the evening, or commonly the entire day, of the last day of the year: 31 December. In many countries it is celebrated with dancing, eating, drinking, and watching or lighting fireworks.

Marriage, also called matrimony or wedlock, is a culturally and often legally recognised union between people called spouses. It is nearly a cultural universal, but the definition of marriage varies between cultures and religions, and over time.
A wedding is a ceremony in which two people are united in marriage. Special wedding garments are often worn, and the ceremony is sometimes followed by a wedding reception.

Humanities are academic disciplines that study aspects of human society and culture, including certain fundamental questions asked by humans. The study of the humanities was a key part of the secular curriculum in universities at the time.

Social science is one of the branches of science, devoted to the study of societies and the relationships among members within those societies. The term was formerly used to refer to the field of sociology, the original "science of society", established in the 18th century.

Sociology is the scientific study of human society that focuses on human social behaviour, patterns of social relationships, social interaction, and aspects of culture associated with everyday life. The term sociology was coined in the late 18th century to describe the scientific study of society.

Linguistics is the scientific study of language. Theoretical linguistics is concerned with explaining the universal and fundamental nature of language and developing a general framework for describing it.

A museum is an institution dedicated to displaying and preserving culturally or scientifically significant objects. The word is originally from the Ancient Greek mouseion, which denotes a place or temple dedicated to the muses, the patron divinities in Greek mythology of the arts.

Civilizations are organized around densely populated settlements, divided into more or less rigid hierarchical social classes with a division of labour, often with a ruling elite. They are characterized by elaborate agriculture, architecture, infrastructure, technological advancement, currency, taxation, regulation, and specialization of labour.

An archive is an accumulation of historical records or materials, in any medium, or the physical facility in which they are located. They are distinguished from documents that have been consciously written or created to communicate a particular message to posterity.

Historical method is the collection of techniques and guidelines that historians use to research and write histories of the past. Some scholars of history have observed that there are no particular standards for historical fields such as religion, art, science, democracy, and social justice.

The Stone Age was a broad prehistoric period during which stone was widely used to make stone tools with an edge, a point, or a percussion surface. The period lasted for roughly 3.4 million years and ended between 4000 BC and 2000 BC, with the advent of metalworking.

The Paleolithic Age is characterized by the use of knapped stone tools, although at the time humans also used wood and bone tools. Other organic commodities were adapted for use as tools, including leather and vegetable fibers, but these have not survived to any great degree due to rapid decomposition.

The Mesolithic refers to the final period of hunter-gatherer cultures in Europe and the Middle East, between the end of the Last Glacial Maximum and the Neolithic Revolution. The term Epipaleolithic is often used synonymously, especially outside Northern Europe.

The Neolithic Revolution was humankind's first historically verifiable transition to agriculture. Other developments found very widely during this era are the domestication of animals, pottery, polished stone tools, and rectangular houses.

Ancient history is a time period from the beginning of writing and recorded human history through late antiquity. The span of recorded history is roughly 5,000 years, beginning with the development of Sumerian cuneiform script.
The Pharaoh was the monarch of ancient Egypt. Before this, "Pharaoh" was a term that referred more specifically to the king's administration rather than the king.
Serfdom was a condition of debt bondage. Serfs who occupied a plot of land were required to work for the lord of the manor who owned that land.
Nobility is a social class found in many societies that have an aristocracy. It is normally appointed by and ranked immediately below royalty.

Chivalry is an informal and varying code of conduct that developed in France between 1170 and 1220. It is associated with the medieval Christian institution of knighthood, with knights being members of various chivalric orders.

The Age of Discovery, also known as the Age of Exploration, was part of the early modern period and overlapped with the Age of Sail. It was a period from approximately the 15th to the 17th century, during which seafarers from European countries explored, colonized, and conquered regions across the globe.
Colonization is defined as "the act or process of sending people to live in and govern another country". The term is sometimes used synonymously with the word settlement.

The Columbian exchange is named after the Italian explorer Christopher Columbus and is related to the European colonization and global trade following his 1492 voyage. Some of the exchanges were deliberate while others were unintended.
The Atlantic slave trade was operated by slave ships from both Europe and the New World. Most of the people transported in the transatlantic trade were from Central and West Africa.
