Ontology is the philosophical study of being. It is traditionally understood as the subdiscipline of metaphysics focused on the most general features of reality.
Abstraction is the process of generalizing rules and concepts from specific examples, literal signifiers, first principles, or other methods.
Existence is the state of having being or reality in contrast to nonexistence and nonbeing.
The meaning of life is the concept of an individual's life, human life, or existence in general having an inherent significance or a philosophical point.

A mental representation, in philosophy of mind, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and cognitive science, is a hypothetical internal cognitive symbol that represents external reality or its abstractions.
Reality is the totality of existence or what all existing entities have in common. It is often contrasted with appearance, opposing what is with what seems to be.

Idealism in philosophy, also known as philosophical idealism or metaphysical idealism, is the set of metaphysical perspectives asserting that, most fundamentally, consciousness or spirit are equivalent to the highest type of reality.

In philosophy and metaphysics, materialism is a form of monism holding that matter is the fundamental substance of nature, so that all things, including mind and consciousness, arise from material interactions.
In philosophy of mind, mind-body dualism denotes either that mental phenomena are non-physical, or that the mind and body are distinct and separable.
Monism attributes oneness or singleness to a concept, such as existence. Primarily used in philosophy, the term sometimes overlaps with nondualism.
Philosophy of science is the branch of philosophy concerned with the foundations, methods, and implications of science.

Natural philosophy, philosophy of nature, or experimental philosophy, until the late modern period, was the systematic and research-based study of nature and the physical universe, while ignoring any supernatural influence.

In science and philosophy, a paradigm is a distinct set of concepts or thought patterns, including theories, research methods, postulates, and standards for what constitute legitimate contributions to a field.
Pseudoscience consists of statements, beliefs, or practices that claim to be scientific but are inherently incompatible with the scientific method.
Reductionism is any of several related philosophical ideas regarding the associations between phenomena which can be described in terms of simpler or more fundamental phenomena.
Philosophy of language, or sometimes linguistic philosophy, is the study of the nature of language. It investigates the relationship between language, language users, and the world.
Philosophy of mathematics is the branch of philosophy that deals with the nature of mathematics and its relationship to other areas of philosophy, particularly epistemology and metaphysics.
Philosophy of mind is a branch of philosophy that deals with the nature of the mind and its relation to the body and the external world.
Philosophy of religion is the philosophical examination of the central themes and concepts involved in religious traditions.

Political philosophy, also called political theory, is the study of the theoretical and conceptual foundations of politics. It examines the nature, scope, and legitimacy of political institutions, such as states.
Comparative religion is the branch of religious studies that systematically compares the doctrines, practices, themes and impacts of the world's religions.
Folk religion, traditional religion, or vernacular religion comprises various forms and expressions of religion that are distinct from the doctrines and practices of organized religion.
Religious studies, also known as religiology or the study of religion, is the study of religion from a historical or scientific perspective.
A goddess is a female deity. In some faiths, a sacred female figure holds a central place in religious prayer and worship.
The Lord's Prayer, also known by its incipit Our Father, is a central Christian prayer. It contains petitions to God focused on God's holiness, will, and kingdom, as well as human needs.

Apologetics is the defense of religious doctrines through systematic argumentation and discourse. Some sources identify apologetics as a separate branch of theology, especially when applied to Christianity.
Apostasy is the formal disaffiliation from, abandonment of, or renunciation of a religion by a person.
Celibacy is the state of voluntarily being unmarried, sexually abstinent, or both. It is often in association with the role of a religious official or devotee.
Iconoclasm is the belief in the importance of the destruction of icons and other images or monuments, often for religious or political reasons.
Idolatry is the worship of an idol as though it were a deity.
Liturgy is the customary public ritual of worship performed by a religious group.
In religion, mythology, and fiction, a prophecy is a message that has been communicated to a person, typically called a prophet, by a supernatural entity.
Religious conversion is the adoption of a set of beliefs identified with one particular religious denomination to the exclusion of others.
The veneration of the dead, including one's ancestors, is based on love and respect for the deceased. In some cultures, it is related to beliefs that the dead have a continued existence.
The meaning of spirituality has developed and expanded over time, and various meanings can be found alongside each other.
Eschatology concerns expectations of the end of the present age, human history, or the world itself. The end of the world or end times is predicted by several world religions.

The Mandate of Heaven is a Chinese political doctrine that was used in Ancient China and Imperial China to legitimize the rule of the king or emperor of China. According to this doctrine, Heaven bestows its mandate on a virtuous ruler.
A mystical or religious experience, also known as a spiritual experience or sacred experience, is a subjective experience which is interpreted within a religious framework.

Paranormal events are purported or imagined phenomena described in popular culture, folklore, and other non-scientific bodies of knowledge, whose existence within these contexts is described as being beyond the scope of normal scientific understanding.
Supernatural phenomena or entities are those beyond the laws of nature.
Sacred describes something that is dedicated or set apart for the service or worship of a deity; is considered worthy of spiritual respect or devotion; or inspires awe or reverence among believers.
Burial, also known as interment or inhumation, is a method of final disposition whereby a dead body is placed into the ground or in a structure such as a mausoleum, sometimes with objects.
A cemetery, burial ground, gravesite, or a green space called a memorial park or memorial garden, is a place where the remains of many dead people are buried or otherwise entombed.
Anti-clericalism is opposition to religious authority, typically in social or political matters.
A creed, also known as a confession of faith, a symbol, or a statement of faith, is a statement of the shared beliefs of a community, often a religious community, which summarizes its core tenets.

A cult is a social group that has unusual, and often extreme, religious, spiritual or philosophical beliefs and rituals. Extreme devotion to a particular person, object, or goal is another characteristic often ascribed to cults.

A schism is a division between people, usually belonging to an organization, movement, or religious denomination. The word is most frequently applied to a split in what had previously been a single religious body.
A sect is a subgroup of a religious, political, or philosophical belief system, typically emerging as an offshoot of a larger organization.
A state religion, also called official religion, is a religion or creed officially endorsed by a sovereign state.
Theism is belief in God or gods. In a narrow sense, it refers to belief in a single creator deity who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-benevolent.
Fundamentalism is a tendency among certain groups and individuals that is characterized by the application of a strict literal interpretation to scriptures, dogmas, or ideologies.
Orthodoxy is adherence to a purported correct or otherwise mainstream or classically accepted creed, especially in religion.

In early Christianity, paganism collectively referred to the diverse religious practices of all people who were polytheists. More specifically, it denoted anyone who did not adhere to an Abrahamic religion in the Roman Empire.
Panentheism is the belief that the divine intersects every part of the universe and also extends beyond space and time.
Freethought is a social movement espousing unorthodox attitudes and beliefs, formed independently from authority, tradition, revelation, or dogma.
Gnosticism is a collection of different religious and philosophical ideas and systems that fully developed among sects of early Christianity and other faiths.

The Old Testament is the first division of the Christian Bible. It is based primarily upon the books of the Hebrew Bible, or the Tanakh, a collection of ancient religious Hebrew and occasionally Aramaic writings by the Israelites.
The New Testament is the second division of the Christian Bible. It discusses the teachings and person of Jesus, as well as events relating to early Christianity.
The Holy Spirit, otherwise known as the Holy Ghost, is a concept within Abrahamic religions.
Predestination, in theology, is the doctrine that all events have been willed by God, usually with reference to the eventual fate of the individual soul.
Halakha is the collective body of Jewish religious laws that are derived from the Written and Oral Torah.
Kashrut is a set of dietary laws dealing with the foods that religiously observant Jews are permitted to eat and how those foods must be prepared according to Jewish religious law.
The Catholic Church, also called the Roman Catholic Church, is the largest Christian church.

The Eastern Catholic Churches or Oriental Catholic Churches, also known as the Eastern-Rite Catholic Churches, are Eastern Christian autonomous particular churches of the Catholic Church in full communion with the pope in Rome.

Eastern Christianity is one of two major classifications used to categorize church bodies with shared orientation within common historical root. Eastern Christianity is a category contrasted with Western Christianity.
The Eastern Orthodox Church, officially the Orthodox Catholic Church, also known as the Greek Orthodox Church is the second-largest Christian body in the world after the Roman Catholic Church.
The Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople is one of the autocephalous churches of the Eastern Orthodox Church. It is headed by the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople.
The Russian Orthodox Church, also officially known as the Moscow Patriarchate, is an autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church. It is the largest of the Eastern Orthodox churches by number of adherents.
The Oriental Orthodox Churches are a communion of Eastern Christian churches adhering to Miaphysite Christology.
The Coptic Orthodox Church, also known as the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria, is an Oriental Orthodox Christian church based in Egypt.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is the largest of the Oriental Orthodox Churches. It is the first indigenous Christian church from sub-Saharan Africa.

Nontrinitarianism is a form of Christianity that does not adhere to the Christian theology of the Trinity, the belief that God is three distinct persons who are coeternal, coequal, and indivisibly united in one being.
Unitarianism is a nontrinitarian movement of Christianity, which affirms the unitary nature of God as the singular and unique creator of the universe.

Protestantism is a form of Christianity that originated in the Protestant Reformation. It emphasizes justification of sinners through faith alone, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the sole infallible source of authority.
Arminianism is a theological tradition within Protestantism that is based on the ideas of a Dutch Reformed theologian and his followers, known as the Remonstrants.

Reformed Christianity, also called Calvinism, is a major branch of Protestantism that began during the Reformation. In the modern day, it is largely represented by the Continental Reformed, Presbyterian, and Congregational traditions.

Evangelicalism, also called evangelical Christianity or evangelical Protestantism, is a worldwide, interdenominational movement within Protestant Christianity that emphasizes evangelism, or the preaching and spreading of the Christian gospel.
Catholicity is a concept pertaining to beliefs and practices that are widely accepted by numerous Christian denominations.
Purgatory is a belief in Catholic theology. It is a passing intermediate state after physical death for purifying or purging a soul before entering Heaven.

Ecumenism is the concept and principle that Christians who belong to different Christian denominations and theological traditions should work together to develop closer relationships among their churches and promote Christian unity.
In Western Christian beliefs, grace is God's favor, and a share in the divine life of God. It is a spontaneous gift from God that cannot be earned.
The Second Coming, sometimes called the Second Advent or the Parousia, is the Christian and Islamic belief that Jesus Christ will return to Earth after his ascension to Heaven.
Islamic schools and branches have different understandings of Islam. There are many different sects or denominations, schools of Islamic jurisprudence, and schools of Islamic theology.
Fiqh is the term for Islamic jurisprudence.

Halal is an Arabic word that translates to permissible in English. Although the term halal is often associated with Islamic dietary laws, particularly meat that is slaughtered according to Islamic guidelines, it also governs ethical practices in business and finance.
Haram is an Arabic term meaning sinful or prohibited.
Imam is a Muslim spiritual act of leading daily prayers.

Manichaeism was a major world religion founded in the Sasanian Empire. It taught an elaborate dualistic cosmology describing the struggle between a good spiritual world of light, and an evil material world of darkness.
The Dhammapada is a collection of sayings in verse form and one of the most widely read and best known Buddhist scriptures.

In the Sinosphere and Chinese philosophy, qi is a vital force traditionally believed to be a part of all living entities. Literally meaning vapor, air, gas, or breath, the word qi is often translated as vital energy, vital force, material energy, or simply energy.
The swastika is an ancient cross-cultural geometrical symbol that has been used in many cultures and religions of Eurasia, as well as a few in Africa and the Americas, for thousands of years.
Tantra is an esoteric yogic tradition. It was developed in the Indian subcontinent; initially within Shaivism and Shaktism practices, and subsequently in Buddhism and Vaishnavism.

The Diamond Sutra is a Mahayana Buddhist sutra from the genre of perfection of wisdom sutras. Translated into a variety of languages over a broad geographic range, it is one of the most influential Mahayana sutras in East Asia.
The Pali Canon is the standard collection of scriptures in the Theravada Buddhist tradition, as preserved in the Pali language. It is the most complete extant early Buddhist canon.
There are several Buddhist canons, which refers to the various scriptural collections of Buddhist sacred scriptures.
Vajrayana, otherwise known as Mantrayana, Tantrayana, Indo-Tibetan Buddhism, Tantric Buddhism, and Esoteric Buddhism, is a vehicle of the Mahayana Buddhist tradition.
Kumbh Mela is a Hindu pilgrimage, celebrated every four or twelve years. These are held at four locations at varying time intervals.
The Ramayana is a Hindu epic poem from ancient India. It is one of the two important epics of Hinduism known as the Itihasas.
Vedanta is one of the orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy and textual exegesis. The word Vedanta means conclusion of the Vedas.
The Tao Te Ching, also known simply as the Laozi, is an ancient Chinese classic text. It is regarded as the foundational Taoist text alongside the Zhuangzi.
The Zhuangzi is an ancient Chinese text that is one of the two foundational texts of Taoism, alongside the Tao Te Ching. It was written during the late Warring States period.

The Kojiki is an early Japanese chronicle of myths, legends, hymns, genealogies, oral traditions, and semi-historical accounts concerning the origin of the Japanese archipelago, the kami, and the Japanese imperial line.
The Avesta is the corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism. All its texts are composed in the Avestan language and written in the Avestan alphabet.

Carrion begins to decay at the moment of the animal's death, and it can carry anthrax, botulinum toxin, rabies and West Nile virus. Apart from possibly some hagfish, the only vertebrates known to rely on it for survival are the vultures.

In humans, rigor mortis can occur as soon as one hour after death and peaks approximately 13 hours after it. ATP is required to separate the actin-myosin cross-bridges, and once the body's glycogen is depleted and ATP runs short, the body is unable to break those bridges. Meat chilled immediately to 15 °C can undergo cold shortening, its muscle sarcomeres shrinking to a third of their original length.

Putrefaction is caused by the decomposition of organic matter by bacterial or fungal digestion, and is the fifth stage of death, following pallor mortis, livor mortis, algor mortis and rigor mortis. Putrescine (from ornithine) and cadaverine (from lysine) carry the odor of rotten flesh.

A tombstone was originally the stone lid of a stone coffin, while a gravestone was a flat slab over a grave. Granite is one of the most durable stones used for gravestones. Zinc markers sold as white bronze were nearly all made by the Monumental Bronze Company of Bridgeport, CT, between 1874 and 1914.

Burying beetles have large club-like antennae with chemoreceptors capable of detecting a dead animal from a long distance. They usually bury a small vertebrate carcass to hide it from competitors, and they are unusual among insects in that both the male and female parents take care of the brood.

Blowflies are among the first insects to reach a body because they have the ability to smell death from up to ten miles (16 km) away, which is why forensic entomologists can estimate the time since death. Song Ci's handbook for coroners, written in 1247 AD, became the earliest recorded account of someone using forensic entomology for judicial means.

Chinese folk religion comprises a range of traditional religious practices of Han Chinese, including the veneration of spirits and ancestors, and worship devoted to deities and immortals, who can be deities of places or natural phenomena.

The beliefs and practices of African people are highly diverse and include various ethnic religions. Generally, these traditions are oral rather than scriptural and are passed down from one generation to another through narratives, songs, myths, and festivals.
The Yoruba religion, West African Orisha, or Isese, comprises the traditional religious and spiritual concepts and practice of the Yoruba people.
Prehistoric religion is the religious practice of prehistoric cultures. Prehistory, the period before written records, accounts for the bulk of human experience.

Ancient Celtic religion, also known as Celtic polytheism and Celtic paganism, was the religion of the ancient Celtic peoples of Europe. Because there are no extant native records of their beliefs, evidence about their religion is gleaned from archaeology, Greco-Roman accounts, and literature from the early Middle Ages.

Ancient Egyptian religion was a complex system of polytheistic beliefs and rituals that formed an integral part of ancient Egyptian culture. It centered on the Egyptians' interactions with many deities believed to be present and in control of the world.
Religious practices in ancient Greece were polytheistic, encompassing a collection of beliefs, rituals, and mythology, in the form of both popular public religion and cult practices.
Ancient Mesopotamian religion encompasses the religious beliefs and practices of the civilizations of ancient Mesopotamia, particularly Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia.

The Aztec religion is a polytheistic and monistic pantheism in which the Nahua concept of teotl was construed as the supreme god Ometeotl, as well as a diverse pantheon of lesser gods and manifestations of nature.

Germanic paganism or Germanic religion was the traditional, culturally significant religion of the Germanic peoples. It covered Scandinavia, the British Isles, modern Germany, the Netherlands, and at times other parts of Europe.
The traditional Maya religion of the extant Maya peoples of Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras, and parts of southern Mexico is part of the wider frame of Mesoamerican religion.

Old Norse religion, also known as Norse polytheism or Norse paganism, is a branch of Germanic religion which developed during the Proto-Norse period, when the North Germanic peoples separated into distinct branches. It was replaced by Christianity during the Christianisation of Scandinavia.

Religion in ancient Rome was polytheistic, consisted of varying imperial and provincial religious practices, which were followed both by the Roman people as well as those who were brought under its rule.

In pre-Islamic Arabia, the dominant religious practice was that of Arab polytheism, which was based on the veneration of various deities and spirits. Worship was centred on local shrines and temples, like the Kaaba in Mecca.
Slavic paganism encompasses the historical pre-Christian religious beliefs, mythologies, and ritual practices of the Slavic peoples before their gradual Christianization.

Western esotericism, also known as the Western mystery tradition, is a wide range of loosely related ideas and movements that developed within Western society. These ideas and currents are united in their distinctness both from orthodox Abrahamic religion and Age of Enlightenment rationalism.
Freemasonry consists of fraternal groups that trace their origins to medieval guilds of stonemasons. Freemasonry is considered the oldest existing secular fraternal organisation.

New Age is a range of spiritual or religious practices and beliefs that rapidly grew in Western society during the early seventies. Its highly eclectic and unsystematic structure makes a precise definition difficult.
A new religious movement, also known as a new religion or a modern religion, is a religious or spiritual group that has modern origins and is peripheral to its society's dominant religious culture.

Modern paganism, also known as neopaganism and contemporary paganism, is a range of new religious movements variously influenced by the indigenous beliefs of pre-modern peoples across Europe, North Africa, and the Near East.
Satanism is a group of religious, ideological, or philosophical beliefs based on Satan, particularly his worship or veneration.

A legendary creature is a type of supernatural entity that is described in folklore, including myths and legends, and may be featured in historical accounts before modernity, but has not been scientifically shown to exist.
Comparative mythology is the comparison of myths from different cultures in an attempt to identify shared themes and characteristics.
In religion and folklore, paradise is a place of everlasting happiness, delight, and bliss. Paradisiacal notions are often laden with pastoral imagery.

Adam and Eve, according to the creation myth of the Abrahamic religions, were the first man and woman. They are central to the belief that humanity is in essence a single family, with everyone descended from a single pair of original ancestors.
In the biblical Book of Genesis, Cain and Abel are the first two sons of Adam and Eve. Cain, the firstborn, was a farmer, and his brother Abel was a shepherd.
Daniel is the main character of the Book of Daniel. According to the Hebrew Bible, Daniel was a noble Jewish youth of Jerusalem taken into captivity by Babylon.
David was a leader of the Tribe of Judah who became the second king of the united Kingdom of Israel, according to the Hebrew Bible and Old Testament.
Elijah was a prophet and miracle worker who lived in the northern kingdom of Israel, according to the Books of Kings in the Hebrew Bible.
Ezra is the main character of the Book of Ezra. According to the Hebrew Bible, he was an important Jewish scribe and priest in the early Second Temple period.
Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions, including Samaritanism, Christianity, and Islam.
Isaiah was the Israelite prophet after whom the Book of Isaiah is named. The text of the Book of Isaiah refers to Isaiah as the prophet.
In the biblical Book of Genesis, Ishmael was the first son of Abraham. His mother was Hagar, the handmaiden of Abraham's wife Sarah.

Jacob, later given the name Israel, is the third Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions. He first appears in the Torah, where he is described in the Book of Genesis as a son of Isaac and Rebecca.
Joseph was a dream interpreter and considered an important Hebrew figure in the Bible's Book of Genesis. Joseph was the first of the two sons of Jacob and Rachel.
Noah appears as the last of the Antediluvian patriarchs in the traditions of Abrahamic religions. His story appears in the Hebrew Bible, the Quran and Baha'i writings, and extracanonically.

Solomon, also called Jedidiah, was a king of the Kingdom of Israel. The successor of his father David, he is described as the penultimate ruler of all Twelve Tribes of Israel under a united Israel and Judah.
Yahweh was an ancient Semitic deity in the southeastern ancient Levant that became the national god of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel-Samaria and Judah.

In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.
In Greek mythology, the Amazons were female warriors and hunters, known for their physical agility, strength, archery, riding skills, and the arts of combat.

In the myths and folk religion of Chinese culture, the Jade Emperor or Yudi is one of the representations of the primordial god. In Taoist theology, he is the assistant of Yuanshi Tianzun, who is one of the Three Pure Ones.
According to Chinese mythology and traditional Chinese historiography, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were a series of sage Chinese emperors, and the first Emperors of China.
The Yellow Emperor, also known as the Yellow Thearch or Huangdi, was a legendary Chinese leader of the Youxiong clan, a culture hero included among the legendary Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Yu the Great or Yu the Engineer was a legendary sage-king in ancient China who was credited with the first successful state efforts at flood control, and his establishment of the Xia dynasty.
Enki, also known as Ea, was the Mesopotamian god of wisdom, crafts, fresh subterranean waters, magic, and incantations. He was believed to rule the Abzu.
Enlil, later known as Elil and Ellil, is an ancient Mesopotamian god associated with wind, air, earth, and storms.
Inanna is the ancient Mesopotamian goddess of war, love, and sex. She is also associated with political power, divine law, sensuality, and procreation.

The Great Spirit is an omnipresent supreme life force, generally conceptualized as a supreme being or god, in the traditional religious beliefs of many, but not all, Indigenous cultures in Canada and the United States.
In Buddhism, Avalokitesvara, also known as Lokesvara and Chenrezig, is a Bodhisattva associated with Great Compassion.
Tengri is the all-encompassing God of Heaven in the traditional Turkic, Yeniseian, Mongolic, and various other nomadic religious beliefs.
A centaur, occasionally hippocentaur, is a creature from Greek mythology with the upper body of a human and the lower body and legs of a horse that was said to live in the mountains of Thessaly.

Personifications of death are found in many religions and mythologies. In more modern stories, a character known as the Grim Reaper, usually depicted as a robed skeleton wielding a scythe, causes the victim's death by coming to collect that person's soul.
A demon is an evil or malevolent supernatural entity. Historically, belief in demons, or stories about demons, occurs in folklore, mythology, religion, occultism, and literature.
Lilith is a feminine figure in late-antique Mesopotamian and Jewish mythology. Lilith does not appear in the Hebrew Bible or any other biblical source.
The devil is a mythical personification of evil as conceived in various cultures and religious traditions. It is seen as the objectification of a hostile and destructive force.
Satan, also known as the Devil, is an entity in Abrahamic religions who entices humans into sin or falsehood.

A fairy is a type of mythical being or legendary creature, generally described as anthropomorphic, found in the folklore of multiple European cultures, a form of spirit, often with magical, metaphysical, supernatural, or preternatural qualities.

A leprechaun is a diminutive supernatural being in Irish folklore, classed by some as a type of solitary fairy. They are usually depicted as little bearded men, wearing a coat and hat, who partake in mischief.
Jinn, also romanized as djinn or anglicized as genies, are supernatural beings in Islam, ancient Arabian religion and Arabic folklore and mythology.
A vampire is a mythical creature with a human-like appearance that subsists by feeding on the vital essence, usually the blood, of humans.
Yokai are a class of supernatural entities and spirits in Japanese folklore. Yokai are a vast range of beings, including shapeshifters, ghosts, demons, and tricksters.

A zombie is a legendary undead being created through the reanimation of a cadaver, a corporeal manifestation of the revenant type. In modern popular culture, zombies often appear in horror genre works.

El Dorado is a mythical city of gold supposedly located somewhere in South America. The legend originated in sixteenth-century Spanish accounts of a ruler known as El Dorado, or the Golden One, who was said to cover himself in gold dust before washing it off in a sacred lake.
The Holy Grail is a treasure that serves as an important motif in Arthurian literature. Various traditions describe the Holy Grail as a cup, dish, or stone with miraculous healing powers.

Australian Aboriginal religion and mythology is the sacred spirituality represented in the stories performed by Aboriginal Australians within each of the language groups across Australia in their ceremonies. Aboriginal spirituality includes the Dreamtime, songlines, and Aboriginal oral literature.

Chinese mythology is mythology that has been passed down in oral form or recorded in literature throughout the area now known as Greater China. Chinese mythology encompasses a diverse array of myths derived from regional and cultural traditions.

Egyptian mythology is the collection of myths from ancient Egypt, which describe the actions of the Egyptian gods as a means of understanding the world around them. The beliefs that these myths express are an important part of ancient Egyptian religion.

Greek mythology is the body of myths originally told by the ancient Greeks, and a genre of ancient Greek folklore, today absorbed alongside Roman mythology into the broader designation of classical mythology.

Japanese mythology is a collection of traditional stories, folktales, and beliefs that emerged in the islands of the Japanese archipelago. Shinto traditions are the cornerstones of Japanese mythology.

Korean mythology is the group of myths told by historical and modern Koreans. There are two types: the written, literary mythology in traditional histories, and the much larger and more diverse oral mythology.
The Indigenous peoples of the Americas comprise numerous different cultures. Each has its own mythologies, many of which share certain themes across cultural boundaries.

Norse, Nordic, or Scandinavian mythology, is the body of myths belonging to the North Germanic peoples, stemming from Old Norse religion and continuing after the Christianization of Scandinavia as the Nordic folklore of the modern period.
Iranian mythology, or Persian mythology in western term, is the body of the myths originally told by ancient Persians and other Iranian peoples and a genre of ancient Persian folklore.
Roman mythology is the body of myths of ancient Rome as represented in the literature and visual arts of the Romans, and is a form of Roman folklore.

An icon is a religious work of art, most commonly a painting, in the cultures of the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, and Lutheran churches. The most common subjects include Jesus, Mary, saints, and angels.

Faust is the protagonist of a classic German legend. The erudite Faust is highly successful yet dissatisfied with his life, which leads him to make a deal with the Devil at a crossroads, exchanging his soul for unlimited knowledge and worldly pleasures.
King Arthur was a legendary king of Britain. He is a folk hero and a central figure in the medieval literary tradition known as the Matter of Britain.

Robin Hood is a legendary heroic outlaw originally depicted in English folklore and subsequently featured in literature, theatre, and cinema. According to legend, he was a highly skilled archer and swordsman.

Santa Claus is a legendary figure originating in Western Christian culture who is said to bring gifts during the late evening and overnight hours on Christmas Eve. Christmas elves are said to make the gifts in Santa's workshop, while flying reindeer pull his sleigh through the air.
Hua Mulan is a legendary folk heroine from the Northern and Southern dynasties era of Chinese history.
Nezha or sometimes Nezha the Crown Prince is a protection deity in Taoism, Buddhism, Confucianism, and Chinese folk religion.
Sun Wukong, also known as the Monkey King, is a literary and religious figure best known as one of the main characters in the Chinese novel Journey to the West.
Aladdin is a Middle-Eastern folk tale. It is one of the best-known tales associated with One Thousand and One Nights, despite not being part of the original text.

"Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves" is a folk tale in Arabic added to the One Thousand and One Nights by its French translator. As one of the most popular Arabian Nights tales, it has been widely retold and performed in many media across the world.

Cinderella is a folk tale with thousands of variants that are told throughout the world. The protagonist is a young girl living in unfortunate circumstances who is suddenly blessed with remarkable fortune, ultimately ascending to the throne through marriage.
A utopia is an imagined community or society that possesses highly desirable or near-perfect qualities for its residents.

Sagas are prose stories and histories, composed in Iceland and to a lesser extent elsewhere in Scandinavia. The most famous saga-genre is the sagas of Icelanders, which feature Viking voyages, migration to Iceland, and feuds between Icelandic families.
Aesop's Fables, or the Aesopica, is a collection of fables credited to Aesop, a slave and storyteller who lived in ancient Greece.
Time travel is the hypothetical activity of traveling into the past or future. Time travel is a concept in philosophy, space, time and fiction, particularly science fiction.

The arts, or creative arts, are a vast range of human practices involving creative expression, storytelling, and cultural participation. The arts encompass diverse and plural modes of thought, deeds, and existence in an extensive range of media.

Religious architecture, also known as sacred architecture or sacral architecture, is a religious architectural practice concerned with the design and construction of places of worship or sacred or intentional space, such as churches, mosques, stupas, synagogues, and temples.
An architectural drawing or architect's drawing is a technical drawing of a building or building project that falls within the definition of architecture.
Architectural theory is the act of thinking, discussing, and writing about architecture. Architectural theory is taught in all architecture schools and is practiced by the world's leading architects.
Landscape architecture is the design of outdoor areas, landmarks, and structures to achieve environmental, social-behavioural, or aesthetic outcomes.

Spanning over three thousand years, ancient Egypt was not one stable civilization but subject to change and periods of great upheaval, commonly split into periods by historians. Likewise, ancient Egyptian architecture is not one style, but a set of styles differing over time but with some commonalities.
Ancient Greek architecture was made by the Greeks, or Hellenes, whose culture flourished on mainland Greece, the Peloponnese, Aegean Islands, and in colonies in Anatolia and Italy.

Ancient Roman architecture adopted the external language of classical ancient Greek architecture for the purposes of the ancient Romans, but was different from Greek buildings, becoming a new architectural style. The two styles are often considered one body of classical architecture.
Baroque architecture is a highly decorative and theatrical style which appeared in Italy in the late sixteenth century and gradually spread across Europe.

The architecture of the Byzantine Empire is usually dated from the establishment of a new Roman capital in Byzantium, which became Constantinople, until the fall of the Byzantine Empire. There was initially no hard line between the Byzantine and Roman Empires.

Chinese architecture is the embodiment of an architectural style that has developed over millennia in China and has influenced architecture throughout East Asia. Since its emergence during the early ancient era, the structural principles of its architecture have remained largely unchanged.
Indian architecture is rooted in the history, culture, and religion of India.
Iranian architecture or Persian architecture is the architecture of Iran and parts of the rest of West Asia, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

Islamic architecture comprises the architectural styles of buildings associated with Islamic civilization. It encompasses both secular and religious styles from the early history of Islam to the present day.

Mesoamerican architecture is the set of architectural traditions produced by pre-Columbian cultures and civilizations of Mesoamerica, traditions which are best known in the form of public, ceremonial and urban monumental buildings and structures.
The architecture of Mesopotamia is ancient architecture of the region of the Tigris-Euphrates river system, encompassing several distinct cultures.

Modern architecture, also called modernist architecture, or the modern movement, is an architectural movement and style that was prominent in the twentieth century, between the earlier Art Deco and later postmodern movements.

Neoclassical architecture, sometimes referred to as Classical Revival architecture, is an architectural style produced by the Neoclassical movement that began in the mid-eighteenth century in Italy, France and Germany. It became one of the most prominent architectural styles in the Western world.
Postmodern architecture is a style or movement that emerged in the nineteen sixties as a reaction against the austerity, formality, and lack of variety of modern architecture.

Renaissance architecture is the European architecture of the period between the early fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries in different regions, demonstrating a conscious revival and development of certain elements of ancient Greek and Roman thought and material culture.

Romanesque architecture is an architectural style of medieval Europe that was predominant in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The style eventually developed into the Gothic style with the shape of the arches providing a simple distinction: the Romanesque is characterized by semicircular arches, while the Gothic is marked by the pointed arches.

The Acropolis of Athens is an ancient citadel located on a rocky outcrop above the city of Athens, Greece, and contains the remains of several ancient buildings of great architectural and historical significance, the most famous being the Parthenon.
The Burj Khalifa is a megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. It is the world's tallest structure.
The Empire State Building is a supertall skyscraper in the Midtown South neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City, United States.
The Golden Temple is a gurdwara located in Amritsar, Punjab, India. It is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism and its holiest site.
Kinkaku-ji, officially named Rokuon-ji, is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan.

The Moscow Kremlin, commonly known as the Kremlin, is a fortified complex in Moscow, Russia that is one of the country's most recognizable landmarks. Located in the historic centre of the country's capital city, the Kremlin comprises five palaces, four cathedrals, and an enclosing wall along with numerous towers.

The Leaning Tower of Pisa, or simply the Tower of Pisa, is the campanile, or freestanding bell tower, of Pisa Cathedral. It is known for its nearly four-degree lean, the result of an unstable foundation.
Masjid al-Haram, also known as the Great Mosque of Mecca, is a mosque in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, serving as the holiest and most important mosque in Islam.

The Palace of Westminster is the meeting place of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and is located in London, England. It is colloquially known as the Houses of Parliament after the House of Commons and the House of Lords, the two legislative chambers which occupy the building.
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, also known as the Seven Wonders of the World or simply the Seven Wonders, is a list of seven notable structures present during classical antiquity.

The Papal Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican, or simply St. Peter's Basilica, is a church of the Italian Renaissance located in Vatican City, an independent microstate enclaved within the city of Rome, Italy.

The Temple Mount or al-Haram al-Sharif is an elevated plateau in the Old City of Jerusalem that comprises the Islamic religious compound known as al-Aqsa, which includes the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock.
A movie theater or cinema, also known as a movie house, cinema hall, picture house, or simply theater, is a business that contains auditoriums for viewing films.

The Museum of Egyptian Antiquities, commonly known as the Egyptian Museum and also called the Cairo Museum, is a national history museum in Cairo, Egypt. An Egyptological museum, it houses the largest collection of Egyptian antiquities in the world.

The American Museum of Natural History is a natural history museum on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City. Located in Theodore Roosevelt Park, across the street from Central Park, the museum complex comprises interconnected buildings housing permanent exhibition halls, in addition to a planetarium.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, colloquially referred to as the Met, is an encyclopedic art museum in New York City. By floor area, it is the fourth-largest museum in the world and the largest art museum in the Americas.
The Museum of Modern Art is an art museum located in Midtown Manhattan, New York City.
The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums, education and research centers, created by the United States federal government for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.
The National Museum of China is an art and history museum located on the eastern side of Tiananmen Square in Beijing.

The British Museum is a public museum dedicated to human history, art and culture located in the Bloomsbury area of London. Its permanent collection of eight million artefacts is the largest in the world.
The State Hermitage Museum is a museum of art and culture in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and holds the largest collection of paintings in the world.

The Louvre is a national art museum in Paris, France. It is located on the Right Bank of the Seine in the city's first arrondissement and home to some of the most canonical works of Western art, including the Mona Lisa, Venus de Milo, and Winged Victory.
The Musee d'Orsay is a museum in Paris, France, on the Left Bank of the Seine. One of the largest art museums in Europe, it is housed in the former Gare d'Orsay, a Beaux-Arts railway station.
The Museo del Prado, officially known as Museo Nacional del Prado, is the main Spanish national art museum, located in central Madrid.
The National Gallery is an art museum in Trafalgar Square in the City of Westminster, in Central London, England.
The Natural History Museum in London, England, is a museum that exhibits a vast range of specimens from various segments of natural history.

The Uffizi Gallery is an art museum adjacent to the Piazza della Signoria in the Historic Centre of Florence in the region of Tuscany, Italy. It is one of the most visited museums in Italy and among the most important worldwide for its Italian Renaissance art collection.

The Vatican Museums are the public museums of the Vatican City. They display works from the immense collection amassed by the Catholic Church and the papacy throughout the centuries, including several of the best-known Roman sculptures and most important masterpieces of Renaissance art in the world.
A character is a person or being in a narrative, such as a novel, play or film. The character may be entirely fictional or based on a real-life person.

A hero is a real person or fictional character who, in the face of danger, combats adversity through feats of ingenuity, courage, or strength. The original hero type of classical epics did such things for the sake of glory and honor.

A superhero or superheroine is a character who typically possesses superpowers or abilities beyond those of ordinary people, is frequently costumed, concealing their identity, and fits the role of the hero.

A genre of arts criticism, literary criticism or literary studies is the study, evaluation, and interpretation of literature. Modern literary criticism is often influenced by literary theory, which is the philosophical analysis of literature's goals and methods.

Fiction is any creative work, chiefly any narrative work, portraying individuals, events, or places that are imaginary or in ways that are imaginary. Fictional portrayals are thus inconsistent with fact, history, or plausibility.
Children's literature or juvenile literature includes stories, books, magazines, and poems that are created for children.
Detective fiction is a subtype of crime fiction and mystery fiction in which an investigator or a detective, whether professional, amateur or retired, investigates a crime, often murder.

A fictional universe, also known as an imagined universe, constructed universe, or diegetic world, is the internally consistent fictional setting used in a narrative or a work of art. This concept is most commonly associated with works of fantasy and science fiction.
Historical fiction is a literary genre in which a fictitious plot takes place in the setting of particular real historical events.

Romance, or romance fiction, is the genre of narrative fiction whose works focus on the budding emotional and loving relationship between two or more characters, often concluding with an emotionally satisfying or optimistic ending. Traditionally its most common format is the romance novel.

Satire is a genre of the visual, literary, and performing arts, usually in the form of fiction and less frequently non-fiction, in which vices, follies, abuses, and shortcomings are held up to ridicule.

Dark humor, also known as black comedy, black humor, bleak comedy, dark comedy, gallows humor or morbid humor is a style of comedy that makes light of subject matter that is generally considered taboo as a topic for humor or laughter.

Thriller is a genre of fiction with numerous, often overlapping, subgenres, including crime, horror, and detective fiction. Thrillers are characterized and defined by the moods they elicit, giving their audiences heightened feelings of suspense, excitement, surprise, anticipation and anxiety.
Non-fiction is any document or media content that attempts, in good faith, to convey information only about the real world, rather than being grounded in imagination.
Ghazal is a form of amatory poem or ode, originating in Arabic poetry and a predominant form in Persian Poetry, that often deals with topics of spiritual and romantic love.
Prose poetry is poetry written in prose form instead of verse form while otherwise deferring to poetic devices to make meaning.
African literature is literature from Africa, either oral or written in African and Afro-Asiatic languages.
Ancient Egyptian literature was written with the Egyptian language from ancient Egypt's pharaonic period until the end of Roman domination. It represents the oldest corpus of Egyptian literature.
Ancient Greek literature encompasses the literature written in the Ancient Greek language from the earliest texts until the time of the Byzantine Empire.
Arabic literature is the writing, both as prose and poetry, produced by writers in the Arabic language.

The history of Chinese literature extends thousands of years, and begins with the earliest recorded inscriptions, court archives, building to the major works of philosophy and history written during the Axial Age.
English literature is a form of literature written in the English language from the English-speaking world.
French literature generally speaking, is literature written in the French language, particularly by French citizens.
German literature comprises those literary texts written in the German language.
Indian literature refers to the literature produced on the Indian subcontinent until nineteen forty-seven and in the Republic of India thereafter.
Italian literature is written in the Italian language, particularly within Italy.
Japanese literature throughout most of its history has been influenced by cultural contact with neighboring Asian literatures, most notably China and its literature.
Jewish literature includes works written by Jews on Jewish themes, literary works written in Jewish languages on various themes, and literary works in any language written by Jewish writers.
Latin American literature consists of the oral and written literature of Latin America in several languages, particularly in Spanish, Portuguese, and the indigenous languages of Latin America.
Latin literature includes the essays, histories, poems, plays, and other writings written in the Latin language.
Persian literature comprises written texts in the Persian language and is one of the world's oldest literatures.
Russian literature is the literature of Russia, its emigres, and Russian-language literature.
Scandinavian literature, also referred to as Nordic literature, comprises literature written in the languages of the Nordic countries of Northern Europe.
Spanish literature is literature written in the Spanish language within the territory that presently constitutes the Kingdom of Spain.
The Bacchae is an ancient Greek tragedy, written by the Athenian playwright Euripides during his final years in Macedonia.
The Metamorphoses of Apuleius, which Augustine of Hippo referred to as The Golden Ass, is the only ancient Roman novel in Latin to survive in its entirety. The protagonist of the novel is Lucius.

The Investiture of the Gods, also known by its Chinese titles Fengshen Yanyi and Fengshen Bang, is a Chinese novel and one of the major vernacular Chinese works in the gods and demons genre written during the Ming dynasty.

Journey to the West is a Chinese novel published during the Ming dynasty. It is regarded as one of the great Chinese novels, and has been described as arguably the most popular literary work in East Asia.
The Kathasaritsagara is a famous collection of Indian legends and folk tales as retold in Sanskrit. It contains multiple layers of story within a story.
Lysistrata is an ancient Greek comedy, first staged in classical Athens. The play is a comic account of a woman's mission to end the Peloponnesian War between Greek city states.

The Oresteia is a trilogy of Greek tragedies concerning the murder of Agamemnon by Clytemnestra, the murder of Clytemnestra by Orestes, the trial of Orestes, the end of the curse on the House of Atreus and the pacification of the Furies.
Oedipus Rex, also known by its Greek title, Oedipus Tyrannus, or Oedipus the King, is an Athenian tragedy written by Sophocles.

One Thousand and One Nights or The Thousand and One Nights is a collection of Middle Eastern folktales compiled in the Arabic language during the Islamic Golden Age. It is often known in English as The Arabian Nights.
The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of interrelated animal fables in Sanskrit verse and prose, arranged within a frame story.
Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a Chinese historical novel. Its narrative covers events from the decline of the Han dynasty and the Yellow Turban Rebellion to the reunification of China.

Abhijnanashakuntalam, also known as Shakuntala, The Recognition of Shakuntala, The Sign of Shakuntala, is a Sanskrit play by the ancient Indian poet Kalidasa, dramatising the story of Shakuntala told in the epic Mahabharata.
The Tale of Genji is a classic work of Japanese literature. It is the first novel written by a woman to have won global recognition.

Water Margin, also called Outlaws of the Marsh or All Men Are Brothers, is a Chinese novel from the Ming dynasty. Regarded as one of the greatest Chinese novels, the novel is among the first works of Chinese fiction written entirely in vernacular Chinese.
Don Quixote is a novel written in Early Modern Spanish and published in two parts. It is considered a founding work of Western literature and the first modern novel.

Dream of the Red Chamber or The Story of the Stone is a Chinese novel, considered to be one of the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature. It is known for its psychological scope and its observation of the worldview, aesthetics, lifestyles, and social relations of High Qing China.

Faust is a tragic play in two parts, usually known in English as Faust, Part One and Faust, Part Two, based on the German folk legend Faust. Nearly all of Part One and the majority of Part Two are written in rhymed verse.
Gulliver's Travels is a satirical prose novel. It is one of the most famous classics of both English and world literature, and popularised the fictional island of Lilliput.
Hamlet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare. It is Shakespeare's longest play.

The Tragedy of King Lear, often shortened to King Lear, is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare. Set in pre-Roman Britain, the play depicts the consequences of King Lear's love-test, in which he divides his power and land according to the praise of his daughters.
The Tragedy of Macbeth, often shortened to Macbeth, is a tragedy by William Shakespeare. It dramatises the physically violent and damaging psychological effects of political ambitions and power.
A Midsummer Night's Dream is a comedy play written by William Shakespeare. The play is set in Athens, and consists of several subplots that revolve around the marriage of Theseus and Hippolyta.

The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice, often shortened to Othello, is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare. Set in Venice and Cyprus, the play depicts the Moorish military commander Othello as he is manipulated by his ensign, Iago, into suspecting his wife Desdemona of infidelity.

Robinson Crusoe is an English adventure novel by Daniel Defoe. It is often credited as marking the beginning of realistic fiction as a literary genre, and has been described as the first novel, or at least the first English novel.

Utopia is a work of fiction and socio-political satire by Thomas More, written in Latin. The book is a frame narrative primarily depicting a fictional island society and its religious, social and political customs.
Tartuffe, or The Impostor, or The Hypocrite, is a theatrical comedy and farce by Moliere, written in poetic verse.

The Tempest is a play by William Shakespeare, thought to be one of the last plays he wrote alone. After the first scene, which takes place on a ship at sea during a storm, the rest of the play is set on a remote island, where Prospero, a magician, lives with his daughter Miranda.
The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet, often shortened to Romeo and Juliet, is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare about the romance between two young Italians from feuding families.

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is a picaresque novel by an American author. It is commonly named among the Great American Novels, and it is among the first in major American literature to be written throughout in vernacular English.

Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, also known as Alice in Wonderland, is an English children's novel. It tells the story of a little girl named Alice who falls through a rabbit hole into a fantasy world of anthropomorphic creatures.
Anna Karenina is a novel by the Russian author Leo Tolstoy. Often considered to be among the greatest works of world literature, Tolstoy himself called it his first true novel.
Brave New World is a dystopian novel by an English author.
The Brothers Karamazov, also translated as The Karamazov Brothers, is the final novel by the Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky.
The Catcher in the Rye is an American coming-of-age novel by an American author.
A Christmas Carol, in prose, being a ghost story of Christmas, commonly known as A Christmas Carol, is a novella by Charles Dickens.
The Chronicles of Narnia is a series of seven portal fantasy novels by a British author, set in the fictional realm of Narnia, a fantasy world of magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals.
Crime and Punishment is a novel by the Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky. It was first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in twelve monthly installments.
Death of a Salesman is a stage play written by the American playwright Arthur Miller. The play premiered on Broadway.
A Doll's House is a three-act play written by the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen. It premiered at the Royal Danish Theatre in Copenhagen, Denmark.
Dracula is a Gothic horror novel by an Irish author. The narrative is related through letters, diary entries, and newspaper articles.
Eugene Onegin, A Novel in Verse is a novel in verse written by Alexander Pushkin. Onegin is considered a classic of Russian literature.
Ficciones is a collection of short stories by an Argentine writer and poet, originally written and published in Spanish.

Frankenstein, or The Modern Prometheus, is a Gothic novel written by an English author. It tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature from different body parts in an unorthodox scientific experiment.
The Grapes of Wrath is an American realist novel written by John Steinbeck. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction.
Grimms' Fairy Tales, originally known as the Children's and Household Tales, is a German collection of fairy tales by the Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm.

Harry Potter is a series of seven children's fantasy novels written by a British author. The novels chronicle the lives of a young wizard, Harry Potter, and his friends, all of whom are students at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.
Heart of Darkness is a novella by a Polish-British novelist, in which sailor Charles Marlow tells the story of his assignment as steamer captain for a Belgian company in the African interior.
The Hunchback of Notre-Dame is a French Gothic novel by Victor Hugo. The title refers to the Notre-Dame Cathedral, which features prominently throughout the novel.
The Picture of Dorian Gray is a philosophical fiction and Gothic horror novel by an Irish author.

In Search of Lost Time, first translated into English as Remembrance of Things Past, and sometimes referred to in French as La Recherche, is a novel in seven volumes by the French author Marcel Proust.
Jane Eyre, originally published as Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, is a novel by the English writer Charlotte Bronte.

Les Miserables is a French epic historical novel by Victor Hugo, that is considered one of the greatest novels of the nineteenth century. Les Miserables has been popularized through numerous adaptations for film, television, and the stage, including a musical.
The Little Prince is a novella written and illustrated by the French writer and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupery.

Little Women is a coming-of-age novel written by the American novelist Louisa May Alcott. The story follows the lives of the four March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy, and details their passage from childhood to womanhood.

The Lord of the Rings is an epic high fantasy novel written by the English author and scholar J. R. R. Tolkien. Set in Middle-earth, the story began as a sequel to Tolkien's children's book The Hobbit but eventually developed into a much larger work.

Madame Bovary: Provincial Manners, commonly known as simply Madame Bovary, is the debut novel of the French writer Gustave Flaubert. The eponymous character, Emma Bovary, lives beyond her means in order to escape the banalities and emptiness of provincial life.
The Master and Margarita is a novel by Mikhail Bulgakov, written in the Soviet Union.

The Metamorphosis, also translated as The Transformation, is a novella by Franz Kafka. It tells the story of the salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect and struggles to adjust to this condition, as does his family.
Middlemarch, A Study of Provincial Life is a novel by the English author George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans.

Midnight's Children is the second novel by the Indian-British writer Salman Rushdie, about India's transition from British colonial rule to independence and partition. It is a postcolonial, postmodern and magical realist story.

Moby-Dick, or The Whale, is an epic novel by the American writer Herman Melville. The book centers on the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the maniacal quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for vengeance against Moby Dick, the giant white sperm whale that bit off his leg on the ship's previous voyage.
Nineteen Eighty-Four is a dystopian and speculative fiction novel by the English writer George Orwell.
The Old Man and the Sea is a novella by the American author Ernest Hemingway. It was the last major fictional work Hemingway published during his lifetime.

One Hundred Years of Solitude is a novel by the Colombian author Gabriel Garcia Marquez that tells the multi-generational story of the Buendia family, whose patriarch, Jose Arcadio Buendia, founded the fictitious town of Macondo. The novel is often cited as one of the supreme achievements in world literature.
Pride and Prejudice is a novel by the English author Jane Austen.
Snow Country is a novel by the Japanese author Yasunari Kawabata. The novel is considered a classic work of Japanese literature.
The Sound and the Fury is a novel by the American author William Faulkner. Faulkner's fourth novel, it is the second to be set in Yoknapatawpha County and the first featuring the Compson family.

The Stranger, also published in English as The Outsider, is a novella written by the French author Albert Camus. The story follows Meursault, an indifferent man in French Algeria, who, weeks after his mother's funeral, kills an unnamed Arab man in Algiers.

Things Fall Apart is the debut novel by the Nigerian author Chinua Achebe. Set in Colonial Nigeria, it portrays the story of Okonkwo, a traditional and influential leader of the fictional Ibo clan of Umuofia, who opposes colonialism and early Christianity.
The Three Musketeers is a French historical adventure novel written and published by the French author Alexandre Dumas. It is the first of the author's three d'Artagnan Romances.
To Kill a Mockingbird is a Southern Gothic novel by the American author Harper Lee. It became instantly successful after its release.
To the Lighthouse is a novel by Virginia Woolf. The novel centres on the Ramsay family and their visits to the Isle of Skye in Scotland.
Ulysses is a modernist novel by the Irish writer James Joyce.
Uncle Tom's Cabin, or Life Among the Lowly, is an anti-slavery novel by the American author Harriet Beecher Stowe.
Waiting for Godot is a play by the Irish playwright and author Samuel Beckett. It was written, first published, and first performed in French as En attendant Godot.

War and Peace is an epic novel by the Russian author Leo Tolstoy. Set during the Napoleonic Wars, the work comprises both a fictional narrative and chapters in which Tolstoy discusses history and philosophy.

The War of the Worlds is a science fiction novel by the English author H. G. Wells about an attempted invasion of Earth by beings from the planet Mars with much greater intelligence and more advanced weapons than humans.

Wuthering Heights is the only novel by the English author Emily Bronte. It concerns two landowning families on the West Yorkshire moors, the Earnshaws and the Lintons, and their turbulent relationships with the Earnshaws' foster son, Heathcliff.

The Adventures of Tintin is a series of comic albums written and illustrated by the Belgian cartoonist Herge. One of the most popular European comics of the twentieth century, it has been published in many languages.

Asterix is a French comic album series about a Gaulish village which, thanks to a magic potion that enhances strength, resists the forces of Julius Caesar's Roman Republic Army in the time after the Gallic Wars. Many adventures take the titular hero Asterix and his friend Obelix to Rome and beyond.
Dragon Ball is a Japanese media franchise created by Akira Toriyama. The series follows the adventures of the protagonist Son Goku from his childhood through adulthood as he trains in martial arts.

One Piece is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Eiichiro Oda. It follows the adventures of Monkey D. Luffy and his crew, the Straw Hats, as he searches for the legendary treasure known as the One Piece to become the next King of the Pirates.
Peanuts is a syndicated daily and Sunday American comic strip written and illustrated by Charles M. Schulz, which eventually expanded into a media franchise.

The Concise Book of Calculation by Restoration and Balancing, commonly abbreviated Al-Jabr or Algebra, is an Arabic-language mathematical treatise on algebra written in Baghdad. It was a landmark work in the history of mathematics, with its title being the ultimate etymology of the word algebra itself.
The Apology of Socrates, written by Plato, is a Socratic dialogue of the speech of legal self-defence which Socrates spoke at his trial for impiety and corruption.
The Arthashastra is an Ancient Indian Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, politics, economic policy and military strategy.

The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise dating from the late Spring and Autumn period. The work, which is attributed to the ancient Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu, is composed of thirteen chapters.
The Book of Healing is a scientific and philosophical encyclopedia written by Abu Ali ibn Sina, also known as Avicenna.
On the Consolation of Philosophy, often titled as The Consolation of Philosophy or simply the Consolation, is a philosophical work by the Roman philosopher and Christian theologian Boethius.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, which mostly consist of the Qumran Caves Scrolls, are a set of ancient Jewish biblical manuscripts from the Second Temple period.
The Elements is a mathematical treatise written by the Ancient Greek mathematician Euclid. The Elements is the oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.
The Histories of Herodotus is considered the founding work of history in Western literature. Although it is not an impartial record, it remains one of the West's most important sources.
The History of the Peloponnesian War is a historical account of the Peloponnesian War, which was fought between the Peloponnesian League, led by Sparta, and the Delian League, led by Athens.

The I Ching or Yijing, usually translated as the Book of Changes or Classic of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text that is among the oldest of the Chinese classics. The I Ching was originally a divination manual in the Western Zhou period.

The Incoherence of the Philosophers is a landmark work by the Muslim polymath al-Ghazali, a student of the Asharite school of Islamic theology, criticizing the Avicennian school of early Islamic philosophy.

The Muqaddimah is an Arabic treatise on historiography, sociology, and the philosophy of history written by Ibn Khaldun. Some modern thinkers view it as the first work dealing with the social sciences of sociology, demography, and cultural history.
The Nicomachean Ethics is Aristotle's best-known work on ethics: the philosophical study of the good for human life, that which is the goal or end at which all our actions aim.
The Organon is the standard collection of Aristotle's six works on logical analysis and dialectic.

The Poetic Edda is the modern name for a collection of Old Norse anonymous narrative poems written in alliterative verse. It is distinct from the closely related Prose Edda, although both works are seminal to the study of Old Norse poetry.
The Septuagint, sometimes referred to as the Greek Old Testament or The Translation of the Seventy, is the earliest extant Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible from the original Biblical Hebrew.

The Summa Theologiae or Summa Theologica, often referred to simply as the Summa, is the best-known work of Thomas Aquinas, a scholastic theologian and Doctor of the Church. It is a compendium of all of the main theological teachings of the Catholic Church.
The Vulgate is a late fourth-century Latin translation of the Bible. It is largely the work of Saint Jerome.
The Critique of Pure Reason is a book by the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, in which he seeks to determine the limits and scope of metaphysics.
De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, is the seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences is a philosophical and autobiographical treatise by Rene Descartes.
The Encyclopaedia Britannica is a general-knowledge English-language encyclopaedia.
The Encyclopedie, ou dictionnaire raisonne des sciences, des arts et des metiers, better known as the Encyclopedie, was a general encyclopedia published in France.

The Gutenberg Bible, also known as the Mazarin Bible, is the earliest major book printed in Europe using mass-produced metal movable type. It marked the start of the Gutenberg Revolution and the age of printed books in the West.
The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, sometimes shortened to Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, is a six-volume work by the English historian Edward Gibbon.

Leviathan or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Commonwealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil, commonly referred to as Leviathan, is a work of social and political theory by the English empiricist philosopher and political theorist Thomas Hobbes.
Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, often called simply the Principia, is a book by Sir Isaac Newton that expounds Newton's laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation.
The Prince is a political treatise written by the Italian diplomat and political philosopher Niccolo Machiavelli in the form of an instruction guide for new princes.

A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: with Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects is an essay by the British philosopher and women's rights advocate Mary Wollstonecraft. It is considered a feminist or, more precisely, proto-feminist piece.

Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, also known as Das Kapital, is a foundational text in Marxist theory by Karl Marx. His magnum opus, the work is a critical analysis of political economy, meant to reveal the economic patterns underpinning the capitalist mode of production.

The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money is a book by the English economist John Maynard Keynes. It caused a profound shift in economic thought, giving macroeconomics a central place in economic theory.
The Oxford English Dictionary is the principal historical dictionary of the English language, published by Oxford University Press, a University of Oxford publishing house.

Quotations from Chairman Mao, colloquially referred to in the English-speaking world as the Little Red Book, is a compilation book of quotations from speeches and writings by Mao Zedong, the former chairman of the Chinese Communist Party.
Silent Spring is an environmental science book by Rachel Carson. The book documented the environmental harm caused by the indiscriminate use of DDT, a pesticide used by soldiers during World War II.

The Structure of Scientific Revolutions is a book about the history of science by the philosopher Thomas S. Kuhn. Its publication was a landmark event in the history, philosophy, and sociology of science.
The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem that tells the legendary story of Aeneas, a Trojan who fled the fall of Troy and travelled to Italy, where he became the ancestor of the Romans.
Beowulf is an Old English poem, an epic in the tradition of Germanic heroic legend. It is one of the most important and most often translated works of Old English literature.

The Canterbury Tales is an anthology of short stories written in Middle English. They are mostly in verse, and are presented as part of a fictional storytelling contest held by a group of pilgrims travelling from London to Canterbury.
The Divine Comedy is an Italian narrative poem by Dante Alighieri. It is widely considered the pre-eminent work in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of Western literature.

Divan-i Kabir, also known as Divan-i Shams and Divan-i Shams-i Tabrizi, is a collection of poems written by the Persian poet and Sufi mystic Rumi. A compilation of lyric poems written in the Persian language.
The Mahabharata is one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India revered in Hinduism, the other being the Ramayana.
The Masnavi is an extensive Persian masnavi, a poetic form, written by Rumi, and one of the most influential works in the history of Sufism. It is a series of six books of poetry.
The Metamorphoses is a Latin narrative poem by the Roman poet Ovid. It is considered his magnum opus.
The Nibelungenlied, translated as The Song of the Nibelungs, is an epic poem written in Middle High German. Its anonymous poet was likely from the region of Passau.
The Odyssey is one of two major epics of ancient Greek literature attributed to Homer. It is one of the oldest surviving works of literature and remains popular with modern audiences.
The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems, along with the Odyssey, attributed to Homer.
The Shahnameh is a long epic poem written by the Persian poet Ferdowsi and is the national epic of Greater Iran.

The Song of Roland is a chanson de geste based on the deeds of the Frankish military leader Roland at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass, during the reign of Charlemagne. It is the oldest surviving major work of French literature.

William Shakespeare wrote sonnets on a variety of themes. When discussing or referring to Shakespeare's sonnets, it is almost always a reference to the sonnets that were first published all together in a quarto.

Paradise Lost is an epic poem in blank verse by the English poet John Milton. The poem concerns the biblical story of the fall of man: the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan and their expulsion from the Garden of Eden.
The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam is a translation from Persian to English of a selection of quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, dubbed the Astronomer-Poet of Persia.
The Duino Elegies are a collection of ten elegies written by the Bohemian-Austrian poet Rainer Maria Rilke.
Gitanjali, meaning song offering, is a collection of poems by the Bengali poet Rabindranath Tagore.
Leaves of Grass is a poetry collection by the American poet Walt Whitman.
The Raven is a narrative poem by the American writer Edgar Allan Poe. The poem is often noted for its musicality, stylized language and supernatural atmosphere.
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, written by the English poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, is a poem that recounts the experiences of a sailor who has returned from a long sea voyage.
The Waste Land is a poem by T. S. Eliot, widely regarded as one of the most important English-language poems of the twentieth century and a central work of modernist poetry.
An album is a collection of audio recordings issued on a medium such as compact disc, vinyl, or audio tape, or in digital format.

In music theory, counterpoint is the relationship of two or more simultaneous musical lines that are harmonically dependent on each other, yet independent in rhythm and melodic contour. The term originates from the Latin punctus contra punctum meaning point against point.
Musicology is the academic, research-based study of music, as opposed to musical composition or performance.
A music video is a video that integrates a song or an album with imagery that is produced for promotional or musical artistic purposes.
An electronic musical instrument or electrophone is a musical instrument that produces sound using electronic circuitry.

A keyboard instrument is a musical instrument played using a keyboard, a row of levers that are pressed by the fingers. The most common of these are the piano, organ, and various electronic keyboards, including synthesizers and digital pianos.
A harpsichord is a keyboard instrument that makes its sound by plucking a set of strings.
The pipe organ is a musical instrument that produces sound by driving pressurised air, called wind, through the organ pipes selected from a keyboard.

A percussion instrument is a musical instrument that is sounded by being struck or scraped by a beater including attached or enclosed beaters or rattles struck, scraped or rubbed by hand or struck against another similar instrument.

In musical instrument classification, string instruments, or chordophones, are musical instruments that produce sound from vibrating strings when a performer strums, plucks, strikes or sounds the strings in varying manners.

The double bass, also known as the upright bass, the acoustic bass, the bull fiddle, the bass fiddle, the string bass, the contrabass, or simply the bass, is the largest and lowest-pitched chordophone in the modern symphony orchestra.

The bass guitar, also known as the electric bass, is the lowest-pitched member of the guitar family. It is similar in appearance and construction to an electric guitar but with a longer neck and scale length.
