The Kushan Empire was a syncretic empire formed by the Yuezhi in the early first century CE. Initially based in the Bactrian territories, it spread to encompass much of what is now Afghanistan, India, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
The Chola dynasty was a Tamil dynasty originating from Southern India. At its height, it ruled over the Chola Empire, an expansive maritime empire.

The Fertile Crescent is a crescent-shaped region in the Middle East, spanning modern-day Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, and Syria, together with northern Kuwait, south-eastern Turkey, and western Iran.

Assyria was a major ancient Mesopotamian civilization that existed from the twenty-first to the seventh century BC which conquered and administered most of West Asia from the Assyrian heartland in Upper Mesopotamia.
Babylonia was an ancient Akkadian-speaking state and cultural area based on the city of Babylon in central-southern Mesopotamia.

Chaldea refers to a region probably located in the marshy land of southern Mesopotamia. It is mentioned, with varying meaning, in Neo-Assyrian cuneiform, the Hebrew Bible, and in classical Greek texts.
The Amorites were an ancient Northwest Semitic-speaking Bronze Age people who originated in Western Mesopotamia. They expanded and ruled most of the Levant and Mesopotamia, and parts of Egypt.
Ebla was one of the earliest kingdoms in Syria. Ebla was an important center throughout the third millennium BC and in the first half of the second millennium BC.
Lydia was a powerful Iron Age civilization prominent in western Anatolia in the eighth to sixth centuries BCE. Its capital and only city was Sardis.
Mitanni or Mittani was a Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia with Indo-Aryan linguistic and political influences.
The Phoenicians were an ancient Semitic-speaking people who inhabited city-states in Canaan along the Levantine coast of the eastern Mediterranean, primarily in present-day Lebanon.
In classical antiquity, Phrygia was a civilization and kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia, in what is now Asian Turkey, centered on the Sangarios River.

The Seleucid Empire was a Greek state in West Asia during the Hellenistic period. It was founded by the Macedonian general Seleucus I Nicator in three hundred and twelve BC, following the division of Alexander the Great's Empire.
Sheba, or Saba, was an ancient South Arabian kingdom that existed in Yemen before two hundred and seventy-five CE.

The Trojan War was a legendary conflict in Greek mythology that took place around the thirteenth or early twelfth century BC. The war was waged by the Achaeans against the city of Troy after Paris of Troy took Helen from her husband Menelaus, king of Sparta.
Urartu was an ancient civilization and Iron Age kingdom centered on the Armenian highlands between Lake Van, Lake Urmia, and Lake Sevan.

Athens was a prominent polis of ancient Greece, located in the peninsula of Attica. Athenian democracy was established in five hundred and eight BC and remained in place for almost two centuries except for a few brief interruptions.

The Delian League was a confederacy of Greek city-states founded in four hundred and seventy-eight BC under the hegemony of Athens, whose purpose was to continue fighting the Persian Empire after the Greek victory in the Battle of Plataea.
Macedonia, also called Macedon, was an ancient kingdom on the periphery of Archaic and Classical Greece, which later became the dominant state of Hellenistic Greece.
The Etruscans created a civilization in Etruria, in ancient Italy, with a common language and culture, and formed a federation of city-states.
The Roman Kingdom, also known as the Roman monarchy and the regal period of ancient Rome, was the earliest period of Roman history, when the city and its territory were ruled by kings.
The Macedonian Wars were a series of conflicts fought by the Roman Republic and its Greek allies in the eastern Mediterranean against several different major Greek kingdoms.
The Gallic Wars were waged between fifty-eight and fifty BC by the Roman general Gaius Julius Caesar against the peoples of Gaul, Britain and Germania.
The Julio-Claudian dynasty comprised the first five Roman emperors: Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, and Nero.

The Crisis of the Third Century, also known as the Military Anarchy or the Imperial Crisis, was a period in Roman history during which the Roman Empire nearly collapsed under the combined pressure of repeated foreign invasions, civil wars and economic disintegration.

In modern historiography, the Western Roman Empire was the Roman Empire's western provinces collectively during any period in which they were administered separately from the eastern provinces by a separate, independent imperial court.
The Dacians were the ancient Indo-European speaking inhabitants of the cultural region of Dacia, located in the area near the Carpathian Mountains and west of the Black Sea.
The Goths were a Germanic people who played a major role in the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the emergence of medieval Europe.

The Saxons, sometimes called the Old Saxons or Continental Saxons, were a Germanic people of early medieval Old Saxony which became a Carolingian stem duchy in eight hundred and four, in what is now northern Germany.
The Vandals were a group of Germanic peoples who were first mentioned in passing by a small number of Roman writers in the first century.

The Migration Period, also known as the Barbarian Invasions, was a period in European history and late antiquity marked by large-scale migrations that saw the fall of the Western Roman Empire and subsequent settlement of its former territories by various tribes.
The Alans were an ancient and medieval Iranic nomadic pastoral people who migrated to what is today the North Caucasus; some continued on to Europe and later North Africa.

The Carolingian Empire was a Frankish-dominated empire in Western and Central Europe during the Early Middle Ages. It was ruled by the Carolingian dynasty, which had ruled as kings of the Franks since seven hundred and fifty-one and as kings of the Lombards in Italy from seven hundred and seventy-four.

The Merovingian dynasty was the ruling family of the Franks from around the middle of the fifth century until Pepin the Short in seven hundred and fifty-one. They first appear as Kings of the Franks in the Roman army of northern Gaul.

The First Crusade was the first of a series of religious wars, or Crusades, which were initiated, supported and at times directed by the Latin Church in the Middle Ages. Their aim was to return the Holy Land to Christian rule after its conquest by the Rashidun Caliphate in the seventh century.

The Fourth Crusade was a Latin Christian armed expedition called by Pope Innocent the Third. The stated intent of the expedition was to recapture the Muslim-controlled city of Jerusalem, by first defeating the powerful Egyptian Ayyubid Sultanate.

The Reconquista or the fall of al-Andalus was a series of military campaigns by northern Iberian Christian polities against Muslim-ruled al-Andalus, which had been part of the Visigothic Kingdom before the Muslim Conquest of seven hundred and eleven.

The Norman Conquest of England was an eleventh-century invasion by an army made up of thousands of Norman, French, Flemish, and Breton troops, all led by the Duke of Normandy, later styled William the Conqueror.

The Viking Age was the period during the Middle Ages when Norsemen, referred to as Vikings, undertook large-scale raiding, colonising, conquest, and trading throughout Europe and reached North America.

The Wars of the Roses, known at the time and in the following centuries as the Civil Wars, were a series of armed confrontations, machinations, battles and campaigns fought for control of the English throne from fourteen fifty-five to fourteen eighty-seven.
The Golden Horde, or Ulus of Jochi, was originally a Mongol and later Turkicized khanate established in the thirteenth century, originating from the northwestern part of the Mongol Empire.
The Rashidun Caliphate was the early Islamic polity led by the first four successive caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali, collectively known as the Rashidun, or Rightly Guided caliphs.

The Fatimid Caliphate, also known as the Fatimid Empire, was a caliphate that existed from the tenth to the twelfth centuries CE under the rule of the Fatimids, an Isma'ili Shi'a dynasty. Spanning a large area of North Africa and West Asia, it extended from the western Mediterranean in the west to the Red Sea in the east.

The Mamluk Sultanate, also known as Mamluk Egypt or the Mamluk Empire, was a state that ruled Egypt, the Levant and the Hejaz from the mid-thirteenth to early sixteenth centuries, with Cairo as its capital. It was ruled by a military caste of mamluks headed by a sultan.

The Almoravid dynasty was a Berber Muslim dynasty centered in the territory of present-day Morocco. It established an empire that stretched over the western Maghreb and al-Andalus, starting in the ten-fifties and lasting until its fall to the Almohads in eleven forty-seven.

The Almohad Caliphate or Almohad Empire was a North African Muslim empire ruled by a Berber dynasty from eleven thirty to twelve sixty-nine, which at its height controlled much of the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula.
The Ghana Empire, also known as simply Ghana, Ghanata, or Wagadu, was an ancient western-Sahelian empire based in the modern-day southeast of Mauritania and western Mali.
The Songhai Empire was a state located in the western part of the Sahel during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. At its peak, it was one of the largest African empires in history.

The Kingdom of Kongo was a kingdom in Central Africa. It was located in present-day northern Angola, the western portion of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, southern Gabon and the Republic of the Congo.
The Ethiopian Empire, historically known as Abyssinia or simply Ethiopia, was a country that encompassed the present-day territories of Ethiopia and Eritrea.

The Tang dynasty was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from six eighteen to nine oh seven, with an interregnum between six ninety and seven oh five. It was preceded by the Sui dynasty and followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The Song dynasty was an imperial dynasty of China that ruled from nine sixty to twelve seventy-nine. The dynasty was founded by Emperor Taizu of Song, who usurped the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty and went on to conquer the rest of the Ten Kingdoms, ending the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The Vijayanagara Empire, also known as the Karnata Empire, was a late medieval Hindu empire that ruled much of Southern India. It was established in thirteen thirty-six by the brothers Harihara the First and Bukka Raya the First of the Sangama dynasty.

Srivijaya, also spelled Sri Vijaya or Sriwijaya, was a Malay Buddhist thalassocratic empire based on the island of Sumatra that influenced much of Southeast Asia. Srivijaya was an important centre for the expansion of Buddhism from the seventh to eleventh century.
Majapahit, also known as Wilwatikta, was a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist thalassocratic empire in Southeast Asia based on the island of Java.

The Heian period is the last division of classical Japanese history, running from seven ninety-four to eleven eighty-five. It followed the Nara period, beginning when the fiftieth emperor, Emperor Kammu, moved the capital of Japan to Heian-kyo, modern Kyoto.

The Kamakura period is a period of Japanese history that marks the governance by the Kamakura shogunate, officially established in eleven ninety-two in Kamakura by the first shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo after the conclusion of the Genpei War, which saw the struggle between the Taira and Minamoto clans.
The Sengoku period was the period in Japanese history in which civil wars and social upheavals took place almost continuously in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

The Tokugawa shogunate, also known as the Edo shogunate, was the military government of Japan during the Edo period from sixteen oh three to eighteen sixty-eight. The Tokugawa shogunate was established by Tokugawa Ieyasu after victory at the Battle of Sekigahara, ending the civil wars of the Sengoku period following the collapse of the Ashikaga shogunate.
Kievan Rus, also known as Kyivan Rus, was the first East Slavic state and, later, an amalgam of principalities, in Eastern Europe from the late ninth to the mid-thirteenth century.
The Novgorod Republic, formally known as Lord Novgorod the Great, was a city-state that existed from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries in northwestern Russia. Its capital was Novgorod.

The Kingdom of England was a sovereign state on the island of Great Britain from nine twenty-seven, when all of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were united under the rule of Æthelstan, until seventeen oh seven, when it relinquished its sovereignty along with Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain.

The Kingdom of France is the historiographical name or umbrella term given to various political entities of France in the medieval and early modern period. It was one of the most powerful states in Europe from the High Middle Ages to eighteen forty-eight during its dissolution.

The Kingdom of Scotland was a sovereign state in northwest Europe, traditionally said to have been founded in eight forty-three. Its territories expanded and shrank, but it came to occupy the northern third of the island of Great Britain, sharing a land border to the south with the Kingdom of England.

The Counter-Reformation, also sometimes called the Catholic Revival or the Catholic Reformation, was the period of Catholic resurgence that was initiated in response to and as an alternative to, or from similar insights as, the Protestant Reformation.
The Thirty Years' War, fought primarily in Central Europe between sixteen eighteen and sixteen forty-eight, was one of the most destructive conflicts in European history.
Alfred the Great was King of the West Saxons from eight seventy-one to eight eighty-six, and King of the Anglo-Saxons from eight eighty-six until his death in eight ninety-nine.
Attila, frequently called Attila the Hun and also known by his nickname The Scourge of God, was the ruler of the Huns from four thirty-four until his death in early four fifty-three.

Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, commonly known as Saladin, was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. A Sunni Muslim ruler of Kurdish origin, Saladin was an important figure of the Third Crusade and spearheaded the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states in the Levant.

Richard the First, known as Richard the Lionheart or Richard Coeur de Lion because of his reputation as a great military leader and warrior, was King of England from eleven eighty-nine until his death in eleven ninety-nine.

Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese mariner, explorer and nobleman. His discovery of the first maritime route between Europe and India, around the Cape of Good Hope, opened up a direct sea link between Europe and Asia.

Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese explorer best known for planning and leading the Spanish expedition to the East Indies. During this expedition, he became the first European to encounter the Strait of Magellan and performed the first European crossing of the Pacific Ocean.

The Early Middle Ages, sometimes controversially referred to as the Dark Ages, is typically regarded by historians as lasting from the late fifth to the tenth century. They marked the start of the Middle Ages of European history, following the decline of the Western Roman Empire.

The High Middle Ages, or High Medieval Period, was the period of European history between about one thousand and thirteen hundred; it was preceded by the Early Middle Ages and followed by the Late Middle Ages.

The late Middle Ages or late medieval period was the period of European history lasting from thirteen hundred to fifteen hundred AD. The late Middle Ages followed the High Middle Ages and preceded Early modern Europe.

Constantinople, the modern Istanbul, was the capital of the Roman Empire and Byzantine Empire from three thirty until its takeover by the Ottoman Empire in fourteen fifty-three. After this, it continued to function as the Ottoman capital until the abolition of the Ottoman sultanate in nineteen twenty-two.

The Battle of Tours, also called the Battle of Poitiers, was an important battle during the Umayyad invasion of Gaul. It resulted in victory for the Frankish and Aquitanian forces, led by Charles Martel, over the invading Umayyad forces.
The Battle of Agincourt was an English victory in the Hundred Years' War. It took place near Azincourt, in northern France.

The Battle of Crecy took place in thirteen forty-six in northern France between a French army commanded by King Philip the Sixth and an English army led by King Edward the Third. The French attacked the English while they were traversing northern France during the Hundred Years' War, resulting in an English victory.

The Battle of Hattin took place in eleven eighty-seven, between the Crusader states of the Levant and the forces of the Ayyubid Sultanate of Egypt, led by Sultan Saladin. It is also known as the Battle of the Horns of Hattin, due to the shape of the nearby extinct volcano of that name.
From the twelve-twenties to the twelve-forties, the Mongols conquered the Turkic states of Volga Bulgaria, Cumania and Iranic state of Alania, and various principalities in Eastern Europe.
The East-West Schism, also known as the Great Schism or the Schism of ten fifty-four, is the break of communion between the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church since ten fifty-four.

The Investiture Controversy or Investiture Contest was a conflict between the Church and the state in medieval Europe over the ability to choose and install bishops, abbots of monasteries, and the Pope himself.

The Albigensian Crusade, also known as the Cathar Crusade, was a military and ideological campaign initiated by Pope Innocent the Third to eliminate Catharism in Languedoc, what is now southern France.

The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, mainly known as the Knights Templar, was a military order of the Catholic faith, and one of the most important military orders in Western Christianity.
Manorialism, also known as seigneurialism, the manor system or manorial system, was the method of land ownership in parts of Europe, notably France and later England, during the Middle Ages.
The pope is the bishop of Rome and the head of the worldwide Catholic Church. He is also known as the supreme pontiff, Roman pontiff, or sovereign pontiff.

The Peace of Westphalia is the collective name for two peace treaties signed in sixteen forty-eight in the Westphalian cities of Osnabruck and Munster. They ended the Thirty Years' War and brought peace to the Holy Roman Empire.
The Crusader states, or Outremer, were four Catholic polities established in the Levant region and southeastern Anatolia from ten ninety-eight to twelve ninety-one.
The Danelaw was the part of England between the late ninth century and the Norman Conquest under Anglo-Saxon rule in which Danish laws applied.

The Anglo-Saxons, in some contexts simply called Saxons or the English, were a cultural group who spoke Old English and inhabited much of what is now England and south-eastern Scotland in the Early Middle Ages.
The Normans were a population arising in the medieval Duchy of Normandy from the intermingling between Norse Viking settlers and locals of West Francia.

The Republic of Genoa was a medieval and early modern maritime republic from the years ten ninety-nine to seventeen ninety-seven in Liguria on the northwestern Italian coast. During the Late Middle Ages, it was a major commercial power in both the Mediterranean and Black Sea.

The Republic of Venice, officially the Most Serene Republic of Venice and traditionally known as La Serenissima, was a maritime republic with its capital in Venice, on the northeastern coast of Italy.

The Emirate of Granada, also known as the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, was an Islamic polity in the southern Iberian Peninsula during the Late Middle Ages, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty. It was the last independent Muslim state in Western Europe.

The Ayyubid dynasty, also known as the Ayyubid Sultanate, was a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin that founded the medieval Sultanate of Egypt, which was established by Saladin in eleven seventy-one, following his abolition of the Fatimid Caliphate.
The Ilkhanate or Il-khanate was a Mongol khanate founded in the southwestern territories of the Mongol Empire. It was ruled by the Il-Khans or Ilkhanids.
The Chagatai Khanate, also known as the Chagatai Ulus, was a Mongol khanate that comprised the lands ruled by Chagatai Khan, second son of Genghis Khan, and his descendants and successors.
The Timurid Empire was a late medieval Turco-Mongol, culturally Persianate, Muslim empire that dominated Greater Iran in the early fifteenth century.

The Guarded Domains of Iran, commonly called Safavid Iran, Safavid Persia or the Safavid Empire, was one of the largest and longest-lasting Iranian empires. It was ruled by the Safavid dynasty from fifteen oh one to seventeen thirty-six.

Shogun, officially sei-i taishogun, was the title of the military rulers of Japan during most of the period spanning from eleven eighty-five to eighteen sixty-eight. Nominally appointed by the Emperor, shoguns were usually the de facto rulers of the country.

Daimyo or daimio were powerful Japanese magnates, feudal lords who, from the fifteenth century to the early Meiji period in the middle nineteenth century, ruled most of Japan from their vast hereditary land holdings.
The Ashikaga shogunate, also known as the Muromachi shogunate, was the feudal military government of Japan during the Muromachi period from thirteen thirty-six to fifteen seventy-three.

The Russian Revolution was a period of political and social change in Russia starting in nineteen seventeen. This period saw Russia abolish its monarchy and adopt a socialist form of government following two successive revolutions and a civil war.

The Glorious Revolution was the deposition of King James the Second of England in November sixteen eighty-eight. He was replaced by his daughter Mary the Second and her Dutch husband, James's nephew William the Third of Orange.

The English Civil War or Great Rebellion was a series of civil wars and political machinations between Royalists and Parliamentarians in the Kingdom of England from sixteen forty-two to sixteen fifty-one.

The American Civil War was a civil war in the United States between the Union and the Confederacy, which was formed in eighteen sixty-one by Southern states that had seceded from the Union to preserve the institution of slavery.
The Vietnam War was an armed conflict in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia fought between North Vietnam and South Vietnam and their allies.
The Korean War was an armed conflict fought on the Korean Peninsula between North Korea and South Korea and their allies.
The Gulf War was an armed conflict between Iraq and a coalition led by the United States in response to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait on the second of August nineteen ninety.

The Iraq War, also referred to as the Second Gulf War, was a protracted armed conflict in Iraq from two thousand three to two thousand eleven. It began in March two thousand three with the invasion by a United States-led coalition, which resulted in the overthrow of the Ba'athist government of Saddam Hussein.

The war in Afghanistan was a prolonged armed conflict from two thousand one to two thousand twenty-one. It began with an invasion by a United States-led coalition under the name Operation Enduring Freedom in response to the September eleventh attacks carried out by the Taliban-allied and Afghanistan-based al-Qaeda.
The Spanish Civil War was fought in Spain from nineteen thirty-six to nineteen thirty-nine between the Republicans and the Nationalist rebels.

The Russian Civil War was a multi-party civil war in the former Russian Empire, lasting from nineteen seventeen to nineteen twenty-two, sparked by the overthrowing of the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution, as many factions vied to determine Russia's political future.
The Seven Years' War was a global conflict fought by numerous great powers, primarily in Europe, with significant subsidiary campaigns in North America and the Indian subcontinent.
The War of eighteen twelve was a conflict initiated by the United States against the United Kingdom and its allies fought mainly in North America and at sea during the wider Napoleonic Wars.
The Crimean War was fought between Russia and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, France, the United Kingdom, and Sardinia from October eighteen fifty-three to February eighteen fifty-six.
The Franco-Prussian War, occasionally known as the Franco-German War, was a conflict between France and the North German Confederation led by Prussia.

The Second Boer War was a conflict fought between eighteen ninety-nine and nineteen oh two between the British Empire and the Boer republics, triggered by the discovery of gold in the Transvaal, specifically the Witwatersrand gold fields.

The Opium Wars were two conflicts waged between the Qing dynasty and the Western powers during the mid-nineteenth century. The First Opium War was fought from eighteen thirty-nine to eighteen forty-two between China and the British Empire.

The Taiping Rebellion was a civil war in late imperial China fought between the ruling Qing dynasty and the rebelling Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. It was the deadliest civil war in history and the second-deadliest conflict in history overall.

The Boxer Rebellion, also known as the Boxer Uprising, Boxer Movement, Yihetuan Movement, or Boxer War, was an uprising in North China between eighteen ninety-nine and nineteen oh one, towards the end of the Qing dynasty, by the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists.
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored the Emperor of Japan's executive power in Japan in eighteen sixty-eight under Emperor Meiji and led to the Westernisation of Japan.
The First Sino-Japanese War was a conflict between the Qing dynasty of China and the Empire of Japan primarily for influence over Korea. In China it is commonly known as the Jiawu War.
The Russo-Japanese War was fought between the Russian Empire and the Empire of Japan over rival imperial ambitions in Manchuria and the Korean Empire.

The Balkan Wars were two conflicts that took place in the Balkan states in nineteen twelve and nineteen thirteen. In the First Balkan War, the four Balkan states of Greece, Serbia, Montenegro and Bulgaria declared war upon the Ottoman Empire and defeated it.

The Spanish-American War was an armed conflict fought between the United States and Spain in eighteen ninety-eight. It began with the sinking of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor in Cuba, and eventually resulted in the U.S. acquiring Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines, and establishing a protectorate over Cuba.
The Mexican-American War, also known in the United States as the Mexican War and in Mexico as the United States intervention in Mexico, was an invasion of Mexico by the United States.
The Texas Revolution was a rebellion by Anglo-American immigrants as well as Hispanic Texans against the centralist government of Mexico in the Mexican state of Coahuila y Tejas.

The War of the Spanish Succession was a European great power conflict. The death of Charles the Second of Spain in November seventeen hundred without children led to a succession crisis between Philip of Anjou, whose claim was supported by his grandfather, the King of France, and Archduke Charles of Austria.
In the Great Northern War, a coalition led by Russia successfully contested the supremacy of Sweden in Northern, Central and Eastern Europe.
The Berlin Wall was a guarded concrete barrier that encircled West Berlin from nineteen sixty-one to nineteen eighty-nine, separating it from East Berlin and the German Democratic Republic.

The Iron Curtain was the political and physical boundary that divided Europe from the end of World War Two in nineteen forty-five until the end of the Cold War in nineteen ninety. East of the Iron Curtain were many small states aligned with the Soviet Union, in nineteen fifty-five formally allied by the Warsaw Pact.

Nazi Germany, officially the German Reich and later the Greater German Reich, was the German state between nineteen thirty-three and nineteen forty-five, when Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party controlled the country, transforming it into a totalitarian dictatorship.

The Holocaust, known in Hebrew as the Shoah, was the genocide of European Jews during World War Two. From nineteen forty-one to nineteen forty-five, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews across German-occupied Europe, approximately two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population.

The Treaty of Versailles was a peace treaty signed on the twenty-eighth of June nineteen nineteen. As the most important treaty of World War One, it ended the state of war between Germany and most of the Allied Powers.

The Wall Street crash of nineteen twenty-nine, also known as the Great Crash, was a major stock market crash in the United States which began in October nineteen twenty-nine with a sharp decline in prices on the New York Stock Exchange.
The partition of India in nineteen forty-seven was the division of British India into two independent dominion states, the Union of India and Dominion of Pakistan.
The Chinese Civil War was fought between the government of the Republic of China, led by the Kuomintang, and the Chinese Communist Party.

The Cultural Revolution, formally known as the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, was a sociopolitical movement in the People's Republic of China. It was launched by Mao Zedong, chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, in nineteen sixty-six and lasted until his death in nineteen seventy-six.

The Great Leap Forward was an industrialization campaign within China from nineteen fifty-eight to nineteen sixty-two, initiated by Mao Zedong, chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, whose goal was to transform the country from an agrarian society to an industrialized society through the formation of people's communes.

The Long March was a military retreat by the Chinese Communist Party and Chinese Red Army from advancing Kuomintang National Revolutionary Army during the Chinese Civil War, occurring between October nineteen thirty-four and October nineteen thirty-five.
Mao Zedong was a Chinese revolutionary and political theorist who founded the People's Republic of China and was its paramount leader from nineteen forty-nine until his death in nineteen seventy-six.

Joseph Vissarionovich Stalin was a Soviet politician and revolutionary who led the Soviet Union from the late nineteen twenties until his death in nineteen fifty-three, holding the title of General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from nineteen twenty-two to nineteen fifty-two.

Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, better known as Vladimir Lenin, was a Russian revolutionary, politician, and political theorist. He served as the first and founding head of government of Soviet Russia from nineteen seventeen to nineteen twenty-four and of the Soviet Union from nineteen twenty-two to nineteen twenty-four.

Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician who was dictator of Germany in the Nazi era from nineteen thirty-three until nineteen forty-five. He rose to power as the leader of the Nazi Party, becoming the chancellor of Germany in nineteen thirty-three.

Sir Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill was a British statesman, military officer, and writer who was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from nineteen forty to nineteen forty-five, during the Second World War, and again from nineteen fifty-one to nineteen fifty-five.

Franklin Delano Roosevelt, also known as FDR, was the thirty-second president of the United States, serving from nineteen thirty-three until his death in nineteen forty-five. He is the longest-serving US president and the only one to have served more than two terms.

Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, politician, and philanthropist, who served as President of South Africa from nineteen ninety-four to nineteen ninety-nine. He was the country's first black head of state and the first elected in a fully representative democratic election.

Abraham Lincoln was the sixteenth president of the United States, from eighteen sixty-one until his assassination in eighteen sixty-five. He led the United States through the American Civil War, defeating the Confederacy and playing a major role in the abolition of slavery.
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from the twentieth of June eighteen thirty-seven until her death in nineteen oh one.

The Spanish Empire, sometimes referred to as the Hispanic Monarchy or the Catholic Monarchy, was a colonial empire that existed between fourteen ninety-two and nineteen seventy-six. In conjunction with the Portuguese Empire, it ushered in the European Age of Discovery.

The Portuguese Empire was the first and longest lasting of the European colonial empires. Initiated during the Age of Discovery, at one point territories included parts of the Americas and Africa, along with ports and trading posts throughout Asia and Oceania.
The Dutch colonial empire comprised overseas territories and trading posts under some form of Dutch control from the early seventeenth to late twentieth centuries.
The French colonial empire consisted of the overseas colonies, protectorates, and mandate territories that came under French rule from the sixteenth century onward.

In the history of the United Kingdom and the British Empire, the Victorian era was the reign of Queen Victoria, from the twentieth of June eighteen thirty-seven until her death on the twenty-second of January nineteen oh one, although slightly different definitions are sometimes used.
In the United Kingdom, the Edwardian era was a period in the early twentieth century that spanned the reign of King Edward the Seventh from nineteen oh one to nineteen ten.
In United States history, the Gilded Age is the period from about the late eighteen seventies to the late eighteen nineties, which occurred between the Reconstruction era and the Progressive Era.

The Roaring Twenties refers to the nineteen twenties decade in music and fashion, as it happened in Western society and Western culture. It was a period of economic prosperity with a distinctive cultural edge in the United States and internationally.

The Belle Époque was a period of French and European history that began after the end of the Franco-Prussian War in eighteen seventy-one and continued until the outbreak of World War One in nineteen fourteen.

The Edo period, also known as the Tokugawa period, is the period between sixteen hundred or sixteen oh three and eighteen sixty-eight in the history of Japan, when the country was under the rule of the Tokugawa shogunate and some three hundred regional daimyo, or feudal lords.
The California gold rush was a gold rush in California, which began in January eighteen forty-eight, when gold was found by James W. Marshall at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California.

The American frontier encompasses the geography, history, folklore, and culture associated with the forward wave of American expansion in mainland North America that began with European colonial settlements in the early seventeenth century.
The Oregon Trail was a large-wheeled wagon route and emigrant trail in North America that connected the Missouri River to valleys in Oregon Territory.

The Louisiana Purchase was the acquisition of the territory of Louisiana by the United States from the French First Republic in eighteen oh three. This consisted of most of the land in the Mississippi River's drainage basin west of the river.

Manifest destiny was the expansionist colonial belief in the nineteenth-century United States that American settlers were destined to expand westward across North America, and that this belief was both obvious and certain.

The Trail of Tears was the forced displacement and ethnic cleansing of about sixty thousand Native Americans of the Five Civilized Tribes, including their black slaves, between eighteen thirty and eighteen fifty by the United States government.

The Reconstruction era, often simply called Reconstruction, was a period in United States history that followed the American Civil War and was dominated by the legal, social, and political challenges of the abolition of slavery.
The Prohibition era was the period from nineteen twenty to nineteen thirty-three when the United States prohibited the production, importation, transportation, and sale of alcoholic beverages.

The labour movement is the collective organisation of working people to further their shared political and economic interests. It consists of the trade union or labour union movement, as well as political parties of labour.

The Armenian genocide was the systematic destruction of the Armenian people and identity in the Ottoman Empire during World War One. Spearheaded by the ruling Committee of Union and Progress, it was implemented primarily through the mass murder of around one million Armenians during death marches.

The Rwandan genocide, also known as the genocide against Tutsi, occurred from the seventh of April to the nineteenth of July nineteen ninety-four during the Rwandan Civil War. Over a span of approximately one hundred days, members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as some moderate Hutu and Twa, were systematically killed by Hutu militias.

On the seventh of December nineteen forty-one, the Empire of Japan launched a surprise military attack on the US Pacific Fleet at its naval base at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii. At the time, the US was a neutral country in World War Two.

The Normandy landings were the landing operations and associated airborne operations on the sixth of June nineteen forty-four of the Allied invasion of Normandy in Operation Overlord during the Second World War. Codenamed Operation Neptune and often referred to as D-Day, it is the largest seaborne invasion in history.

The Battle of Britain was a military campaign of the Second World War, in which the Royal Air Force and the Fleet Air Arm of the Royal Navy defended the United Kingdom against large-scale attacks by Nazi Germany's air force, the Luftwaffe.

The Battle of Stalingrad was a major battle on the Eastern Front of World War Two in which Nazi Germany and its Axis allies fought the Soviet Union for control of the city of Stalingrad in southern Russia.
The Battle of Midway was a major naval battle in the Pacific Theater of World War Two that took place in June nineteen forty-two, six months after Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor.

The Nuremberg trials were international criminal trials held by France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States against leaders of defeated Nazi Germany for plotting and carrying out invasions of several countries across Europe and committing atrocities against their citizens in the Second World War.
The Marshall Plan was an American initiative enacted in nineteen forty-eight to provide foreign aid to Western Europe.

The Yalta Conference, held in February nineteen forty-five, was the World War Two meeting of the heads of government of the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union to discuss the postwar reorganization of Germany and Europe.

The Potsdam Conference was held at Potsdam in the Soviet occupation zone from the seventeenth of July to the second of August nineteen forty-five, to allow the three leading Allies to plan the postwar peace.

The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday the eighteenth of June eighteen fifteen, near Waterloo, being the last engagement with Napoleon the First. The French Imperial Army under the command of Napoleon the First was defeated by two armies of the Seventh Coalition.

The Battle of Trafalgar was a fleet action fought on the twenty-first of October eighteen oh five off Cape Trafalgar between the Royal Navy and a combined fleet of the French and Spanish navies during the Trafalgar campaign of the War of the Third Coalition.

The Battle of Gettysburg was fought in the American Civil War between the Union and Confederate armies in and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The battle is widely considered the turning point of the war, leading to the preservation of the Union and freedom from slavery.
The Battle of the Somme, also known as the Somme offensive, was a battle of the First World War fought by the armies of the British Empire and the French Republic against the German Empire.

The Battle of Verdun was fought from the twenty-first of February to the eighteenth of December nineteen sixteen on the Western Front in France. The battle was the longest of the First World War and took place on the hills north of Verdun.
The Gallipoli campaign, the Dardanelles campaign, the Defence of Gallipoli or the Battle of Gallipoli was a military campaign in the First World War on the Gallipoli Peninsula.

The Blitz was a bombing campaign by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy against the United Kingdom during the Second World War. It lasted for eight months, from the seventh of September nineteen forty to the sixteenth of May nineteen forty-one.

Thebes, known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, was an ancient Egyptian city located along the Nile about eight hundred kilometers south of the Mediterranean. Its ruins lie within the modern Egyptian city of Luxor.
Memphis, or Men-nefer, was the ancient capital of Inebu-hedj, the first nome of Lower Egypt. Its ruins are located in the vicinity of the present-day village of Mit Rahina.
Meroë was an ancient city on the east bank of the Nile in Sudan, about two hundred kilometers north-east of Khartoum.

Ugarit was an ancient Levantine coastal city located in what is today northern Syria, at a site known in Arabic as Ras Shamra or Tell Shamra. Since its discovery in nineteen twenty-eight, the site has revealed the oldest known systematic use of an alphabet.
Ur was a major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia, located at the site of modern Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq.

Nineveh was an ancient Near Eastern city of Upper Mesopotamia, located in the modern-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq. It is located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River and was the capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and potentially the wealthiest city in the ancient world.

Babylon was an ancient city located on the lower Euphrates river in southern Mesopotamia, within modern-day Hillah, Iraq. Babylon functioned as the main cultural and political centre of the Akkadian-speaking region of Babylonia.
Antioch was a city located in northern Syria at the site of modern Antakya, Turkey. Founded in three hundred BC, Antioch became one of the most important cities of the ancient eastern Mediterranean.

Ctesiphon was an ancient city in modern Iraq, on the eastern bank of the Tigris. Ctesiphon served as a royal capital of the Iranian empires for over eight hundred years, in the Parthian and Sasanian periods.
Troy or Ilion was an ancient city located in present-day Çanakkale, Turkey. It is best known as the setting for the Greek myth of the Trojan War.
Corinth was a city-state on the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow stretch of land that joins the Peloponnese peninsula to mainland Greece, roughly halfway between Athens and Sparta.

Herculaneum is an ancient Roman town located in the modern-day comune of Ercolano, Campania, Italy. Herculaneum was buried under a massive pyroclastic flow in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in seventy-nine AD.
Lagash was an ancient city-state located northwest of the junction of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers and east of Uruk.
Nippur was an ancient Sumerian city. It was the special seat of the worship of the Sumerian god Enlil, the Lord Wind, ruler of the cosmos, subject to An alone.
Sidon, or Saida, is the third-largest city in Lebanon. It is located on the Mediterranean coast in the South Governorate, of which it is the capital.
Byblos, also known as Jbail, Jebeil, Jbeil or Jubayl, is an ancient city in the Keserwan-Jbeil Governorate of Lebanon.
Angkor, also known as Yasodharapura, was the capital city of the Khmer Empire, located in present-day Cambodia. The empire flourished from approximately the ninth to the fifteenth centuries.
Hammurabi, also spelled Hammurapi, was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon, reigning from about seventeen ninety-two BC to about seventeen fifty BC. He was preceded by his father, Sin-muballit.
Darius the First, commonly known as Darius the Great, was the third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, reigning from five twenty-two BCE until his death in four eighty-six BCE.

Xerxes the First was a Persian ruler who reigned as the fourth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, reigning from four eighty-six BC until his assassination in four sixty-five BC. He was the son of Darius the Great and Atossa.

Pericles was a Greek statesman and general during the Golden Age of Athens. He was prominent and influential in Ancient Athenian politics, particularly between the Greco-Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War.
Homer was an ancient Greek poet who is traditionally credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, two epic poems that are foundational works of ancient Greek literature.

Herodotus was a Greek historian and geographer from the Greek city of Halicarnassus, under Persian control in the fifth century BC. He wrote the Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars.
Thucydides was an Athenian historian and general. His History of the Peloponnesian War recounts the fifth-century BC war between Sparta and Athens.
Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus was Roman emperor from fifty-four AD until sixty-eight AD. He was the final emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, which comprised the first five emperors.

Constantine the First, also known as Constantine the Great, was a Roman emperor from three oh six to three thirty-seven AD. The first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity, Constantine played a pivotal role in elevating the religion's status in the Roman Empire.

Justinian the First, also known as Justinian the Great, was Roman emperor from five twenty-seven to five sixty-five. His reign was marked by the ambitious but only partly realized renovatio imperii, the restoration of the Empire.
Diocletian, nicknamed Jovius, was Roman emperor from two eighty-four until his abdication in three oh five. He was born Diocles to a family of low status in the Roman province of Dalmatia.
Trajan was the Roman emperor from ninety-eight to one seventeen, remembered as the second of the Five Good Emperors of the Nerva-Antonine dynasty.
Hadrian was the Roman emperor from one seventeen to one thirty-eight. His form of address as Roman emperor was Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from one sixty-one to one eighty and a Stoic philosopher. He was a member of the Nerva-Antonine dynasty, the last of the rulers later known as the Five Good Emperors.
Tutankhamun or Tutankhamen, was the third to last pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of ancient Egypt. His administration restored the traditional polytheistic form of ancient Egyptian religion.

Ramesses the Second, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Ramesses the Second is often regarded as the greatest, most celebrated, and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, which itself was the most powerful period of ancient Egypt.
Hatshepsut was the sixth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt, ruling first as regent, then as queen regnant. She was Egypt's second confirmed woman who ruled in her own right.
Akhenaten, also spelled Akhenaton, Echnaton, and Khuenaten, was an ancient Egyptian pharaoh. Originally named Amenhotep the Fourth, in the fifth year of his reign he changed his name to Akhenaten.
Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus was a Roman general and statesman who was one of the main architects of Rome's victory against Carthage in the Second Punic War.
Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who was one of the escaped slave leaders in the Third Servile War, a major slave uprising against the Roman Republic.
Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, also called Gaius or Caligula, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from thirty-seven AD until his assassination in forty-one AD.

Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, or simply Claudius, was a Roman emperor, ruling from forty-one AD until his death in fifty-four AD. The fourth ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, Claudius was born at Lugdunum in Roman Gaul.
Vespasian was Roman emperor from sixty-nine to seventy-nine. The last emperor to reign in the Year of the Four Emperors, he founded the Flavian dynasty.

Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor from fourteen AD until his death, reigning as the second ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. He succeeded his stepfather Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

Theodosius the First, also known as Theodosius the Great, was Roman emperor from three seventy-nine to three ninety-five. He won two civil wars and was instrumental in establishing the Nicene Creed as the orthodox doctrine for Nicene Christianity.
Alaric the First was the first king of the Visigoths, from three ninety-five to four ten. He rose to leadership of the Goths who came to occupy Moesia.

Romulus Augustus, nicknamed Augustulus, was Roman emperor of the West from four seventy-five until four seventy-six. Romulus was placed on the imperial throne while still a minor by his father Orestes.
Leonidas the First was Greek king of the Ancient Greek city-state of Sparta. He was the son of king Anaxandridas the Second and the seventeenth king of the Agiad dynasty.

Demosthenes was a Greek statesman and orator in ancient Athens. His orations constitute a significant expression of contemporary Athenian intellectual prowess and provide insight into the politics and culture of ancient Greece during the fourth century BC.
Philip the Second of Macedon was the king of Macedon from three fifty-nine BC until his death in three thirty-six BC.
Ptolemy Soter was a Macedonian Greek general, historian, and successor of Alexander the Great who went on to found the Ptolemaic Kingdom centered in Egypt.
Chandragupta Maurya was the founder and the first emperor of the Maurya Empire, based in Magadha in the Indian subcontinent.
Emperor Wu of Han, personal name Liu Che and courtesy name Tong, was the seventh emperor of the Han dynasty from one forty-one to eighty-seven BC.

The Battle of Salamis was a naval battle fought in four eighty BC, between an alliance of Greek city-states under Themistocles, and the Achaemenid Empire under King Xerxes. It resulted in a victory for the outnumbered Greeks.
The Battle of Cannae was a key engagement of the Second Punic War between the Roman Republic and Carthage, fought in two sixteen BC near the ancient village of Cannae in Apulia, southeast Italy.

The Battle of Actium was a naval battle fought between Octavian's maritime fleet, led by Marcus Agrippa, and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. The battle took place in thirty-one BC in the Ionian Sea, near the former Roman colony of Actium, Greece.

The Battle of Gaugamela, also called the Battle of Arbela, took place in three thirty-one BC between the forces of the Army of Macedon under Alexander the Great and the Persian Army under King Darius the Third.

The hilltop fortress of Masada, in present-day Israel, was successfully besieged and taken by Roman imperial forces during the final period of the First Jewish-Roman War. At the time, the fortress was held by members of the Sicarii rebel group.
The First Punic War was the first of three wars fought between Rome and Carthage, the two main powers of the western Mediterranean in the early third century BC.
The Great Fire of Rome began in the summer of sixty-four AD. The fire started in the merchant shops around Rome's chariot stadium, Circus Maximus.
The Year of the Four Emperors, sixty-nine AD, was the first civil war of the Roman Empire, during which four emperors ruled in succession, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian.
The Edict of Milan was the three thirteen AD agreement to treat Christians benevolently within the Roman Empire and allow religious freedom more broadly.
The First Council of Nicaea was a council of Christian bishops convened in the Bithynian city of Nicaea by the Roman Emperor Constantine the First, also known as the First Ecumenical Council.
The sack of Rome in four ten AD was undertaken by the Visigoths led by their king, Alaric. At that time, Rome was no longer the administrative capital of the Western Roman Empire.
The Roman Senate was the highest and constituting assembly of ancient Rome and its aristocracy.
The Roman Army served ancient Rome and the Roman people enduring through the Roman Kingdom, the Roman Republic, and the Roman Empire.
Roman law is the legal system of ancient Rome, including the legal developments spanning over a thousand years of jurisprudence.

The Pax Romana is a roughly two-hundred-year-long period of ancient Rome that is identified as a golden age of increased and sustained Roman imperialism, prosperous stability, hegemonic power, regional expansion, and relative peace and order.

A trireme was an ancient vessel and a type of galley that was used by the ancient maritime civilizations of the Mediterranean Sea, especially the Phoenicians, ancient Greeks and Romans. The trireme derives its name from its three rows of oars, manned with one man per oar.

Historiography is the study of the methods used by historians in developing history as an academic discipline. By extension, the term historiography is any body of historical work on a particular subject.
Chronology is the science of arranging events in their order of occurrence in time, such as in a timeline or other sequence of events.

Genealogy is the study of families, family history, and the tracing of their lineages. Genealogists use oral interviews, historical records, genetic analysis, and other records to obtain information about a family and to demonstrate kinship and pedigrees of its members.
Heraldry, also known as armory, is a discipline relating to the design, display, study and transmission of armorial bearings.
Vexillology is the study of the history, symbolism and usage of flags or, by extension, any interest in flags in general.
Numismatics is the study or collection of currency, including coins, tokens, paper money, medals, and related objects.
Palaeography or paleography is the study and academic discipline of historical writing systems.

Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions, or epigraphs, as writing; it is the science of identifying graphemes, clarifying their meanings, classifying their uses according to dates and cultural contexts, and drawing conclusions about the writing and the writers.
Sigillography, also known by its Greek-derived name, sphragistics, is the scholarly discipline that studies the wax, lead, clay, and other seals used to authenticate archival documents.
Philately is the study of postage stamps and postal history. It also refers to the collection and appreciation of stamps and other philatelic products.
A manuscript is any text written by hand as opposed to mechanically printed or reproduced using automated printing technologies. Texts that are mechanically printed and bound are called books.
A flag is a piece of fabric, most often rectangular, with distinctive colours and design, often flown from a pole and used for symbolic, signalling, or decorative purposes.
A coat of arms is a heraldic visual design on an escutcheon, surcoat, or tabard, originating in Europe. The coat of arms on an escutcheon forms the central element of the full heraldic achievement.
A timeline is a list of events displayed in chronological order. It is typically a graphic design showing a long bar labelled with dates paralleling it, and usually contemporaneous events.
A century is a numerical value of one hundred or more popularly period of one hundred years. Centuries are numbered ordinally in English and many other languages.
A millennium is a period of one thousand years.
A decade is a period of ten years. It may also be called a decennium.

Radiocarbon dating, also referred to as carbon dating or carbon-fourteen dating, is a method for determining the age of an object containing organic material by using the properties of radiocarbon, a radioactive isotope of carbon.
An artifact or artefact is a general term for an item made or given shape by humans, such as a tool or a work of art, especially an object of archaeological interest.
A monument is a type of structure created to commemorate a person or event, or which has become relevant to a social group as a part of their remembrance of historic times, or cultural heritage.
A memorial is an object or place which serves as a focus for the memory or the commemoration of something, usually an influential, deceased person or a historical, tragic event.
A shipwreck is the wreckage of a ship that is either beached on land or sunken to the bottom of a body of water.
Treasure is a concentration of wealth, often originating from ancient history, that is considered lost and forgotten until rediscovered.
A memoir is any nonfiction narrative writing based on the author's personal memories. The assertions made in the work are thus understood to be factual.
A chronicle is a historical account of events arranged in chronological order, as in a timeline.
Annals are a concise historical record in which events are arranged chronologically, year by year, although the term is also used loosely for any historical record.
A charter is the grant of authority or rights, stating that the granter formally recognizes the prerogative of the recipient to exercise the rights specified.

A bill of rights, sometimes called a declaration of rights or a charter of rights, is a list of the most important rights to the citizens of a country. The purpose is to protect those rights against infringement from public officials and private citizens.
The Voynich manuscript is an illustrated codex, hand-written in an undeciphered script referred to as Voynichese.

The Giza pyramid complex, also called the Giza necropolis, in Egypt is home to the Great Pyramid, the pyramid of Khafre, and the pyramid of Menkaure, along with their associated pyramid complexes and the Great Sphinx.

The history of art focuses on objects made by humans for any number of spiritual, narrative, philosophical, symbolic, conceptual, documentary, decorative, and even functional and other purposes, though focused on a primary emphasis on its aesthetic visual form.
The history of architecture traces the changes in architecture through various traditions, regions, overarching stylistic trends, and dates.

The history of literature is the historical development of writings in prose or poetry that attempt to provide entertainment or education to the reader, as well as the development of the literary techniques used in the communication of these pieces.

Although definitions of music vary wildly throughout the world, every known culture partakes in it, and it is thus considered a cultural universal. The origins of music remain highly contentious; commentators often relate it to the origin of language.
The history of science covers the development of science from ancient times to the present. It encompasses all three major branches of science: natural, social, and formal.

The history of medicine is both a study of medicine throughout history as well as a multidisciplinary field of study that seeks to explore and understand medical practices, both past and present, throughout human societies.
The history of mathematics deals with the origin of discoveries in mathematics and the mathematical methods and notation of the past.

The history of philosophy is the systematic study of the development of philosophical thought. It focuses on philosophy as rational inquiry based on argumentation, but some theorists also include myth, religious traditions, and proverbial lore.
The history of religion is the written record of human religious feelings, thoughts, and ideas.

Agriculture began independently in different parts of the globe, and included a diverse range of taxa. At least eleven separate regions of the Old and New World were involved as independent centers of origin.

The history of money is the development over time of systems for the exchange of goods and services. Money is a means of fulfilling these functions indirectly and in general rather than directly, as with barter.
The history of education extends at least as far back as the first written records recovered from ancient civilizations. Historical studies have included virtually every nation.
The history of sports extends back to the Ancient world. The physical activity that developed into sports had early links with warfare and entertainment.
The study of the history of clothing and textiles traces the development, use, and availability of clothing and textiles over human history.

The history of transport is largely one of technological innovation. Advances in technology have allowed people to travel farther, explore more territory, and expand their influence over increasingly larger areas.

Human history, or world history, is the record of humankind from prehistory to the present. Modern humans evolved in Africa around three hundred thousand years ago and initially lived as hunter-gatherers.

The early modern period is a historical period with divisions based primarily on the history of Europe and the broader concept of modernity. There is no exact date that marks the beginning or end of the period.

The modern era, or the modern period, is considered the current historical period of human history. It was originally applied to the history of Europe and Western history for events that came after classical antiquity and the Middle Ages.

The Age of Sail is the period in European history from the mid-fifteenth or sixteenth century to, at the latest, the mid-nineteenth century, in which the dominance of sailing ships in global trade and warfare culminated.

The spice trade involved historical civilizations in Asia, Northeast Africa and Europe. Spices, such as cinnamon, cassia, cardamom, ginger, pepper, nutmeg, star anise, clove, and turmeric, were known and used in antiquity and traded in the Eastern world.

Triangular trade or triangle trade is trade between three ports or regions. Triangular trade usually evolves when a region has export commodities that are not required in the region from which its major imports come.

Atropatene, also known as Atropatia or Atropatian Media, was an ancient Iranian kingdom established in about three twenty-three BC by the Persian satrap Atropates. The kingdom, mostly centered around the present-day Azerbaijan region in northwestern Iran.
Caucasian Albania is a modern exonym for a former state located in ancient times in the Caucasus, mostly overlapping the region of present-day Azerbaijan.

In Greco-Roman geography, Iberia was an exonym for the Georgian kingdom of Kartli, known after its core province. The kingdom existed during Classical Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, either as an independent state or as a dependent of larger empires.
The Tocharians or Tokharians were speakers of the Tocharian languages, a group of Indo-European languages found on the northern edge of the Tarim Basin, modern-day Xinjiang, China.

Old Chosŏn, also known as Gojoseon and its contemporary name Joseon, was the first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula. According to Korean mythology, the kingdom was established by the legendary king Tan'gun.
The Jin dynasty or the Jin Empire, officially Jin, sometimes distinguished as the Sima Jin or the Two Jins, was an imperial dynasty in China that existed from two sixty-six to four twenty CE.

The Northern and Southern dynasties was a period of political division in the history of China that lasted from four twenty to five eighty-nine AD, following the tumultuous era of the Sixteen Kingdoms and the Eastern Jin dynasty.

The Sixteen Kingdoms, less commonly the Sixteen States, was a period in Chinese history from AD three oh four to four thirty-nine when the political order of the Jin dynasty in northern China fragmented into a series of short-lived dynastic states.
The Three Kingdoms of Korea or Samhan of Korea, refers to the period in Korean history when the peninsula was divided into three major kingdoms: Goguryeo, Paekche, and Silla.
The official name of multiple Vietnamese monarchies in eastern Mainland Southeast Asia from the tenth century AD to the early nineteenth century, centered around the region of present-day Hanoi.
The Hong Bang period, also called the Hong Bang dynasty, was a legendary ancient period in Vietnamese historiography.
Nanyue was an ancient kingdom founded in two oh four BC by the Chinese general Zhao Tuo, whose family continued to rule until one eleven BC.
The Pyu city-states were a group of city-states that existed from about the second century BCE to the mid-eleventh century in present-day Upper Myanmar.

The Indo-Greek Kingdom, also known as the Yavana Kingdom, were Hellenistic-era Greek kingdoms in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent covering most of modern-day Pakistan, parts of northwestern India and some eastern parts of Afghanistan.

The Indo-Scythians, also known as Indo-Sakas, were a group of nomadic people of Iranic Scythian origin who migrated from Central Asia southward into the present-day regions of Afghanistan, eastern Iran and the northwestern Indian subcontinent.
The Satavahanas, also referred to as the Andhras in the Puranas, were an ancient Indian dynasty.

The Kingdom of Greater Armenia was a kingdom in the Ancient Near East from one eighty-nine BC to four twenty-eight AD, starting with the reign of Artaxias the First and ending with the abolition of the Arsacid dynasty by the Sasanians.

Ancient Israel and Judah were two Israelite kingdoms that existed in the Southern Levant during the Iron Age. Their history began with the early appearance of the Israelites in the central highlands of Samaria and Judea.

The Nerva-Antonine dynasty comprised seven Roman emperors who ruled from ninety-six AD to one ninety-two AD: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus, and Commodus. The first five of these are popularly known as the Five Good Emperors.
The Odrysian kingdom was an ancient Thracian state that thrived between the early fifth century BC and the early third or late first century BC.

In world history, post-classical history refers to the period from about five hundred CE to about fourteen fifty or fifteen hundred CE, roughly corresponding to the European Middle Ages following the decline of the Western Roman Empire.
The early Muslim conquests, or the early Islamic conquests, also known as the Arab conquests, were a series of wars initiated by the Islamic prophet Muhammad, and continued by the early Muslims.

A boyar or bolyar was a member of the highest rank of the feudal nobility in many Eastern European states, including Bulgaria, Kievan Rus (and later Russia), Moldavia and Wallachia, Lithuania and among Baltic Germans.
The Ajuran Sultanate, natively referred to as Ajuuraan, and often simply Ajuran or Ajur, was a Muslim empire in the Horn of Africa that thrived from the late medieval and early modern period.

The Kanem-Bornu Empire was an empire based around Lake Chad that once ruled areas which are now part of Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, Libya, Algeria, Sudan, and Chad. The empire was sustained by the prosperous trans-Saharan trade.

Trans-Saharan trade is trade between North Africa and the rest of Africa that requires travel across the Sahara. Though this trade began in prehistoric times, the peak of trade extended from the eighth century until the early seventeenth century.

The Aztecs were a Mesoamerican civilization that flourished in central Mexico from about thirteen hundred to fifteen twenty-one. The Aztec people included different ethnic groups of central Mexico, particularly those who spoke Nahuatl.
Chimor, also Kingdom of Chimor or Chimu Empire, was the political grouping of the Chimu culture. The culture arose about nine hundred CE, succeeding the Moche culture.

The Mississippian period is an archaeological cultural era in the history of the Southern United States and adjacent areas of the Eastern Woodlands spanning the end of the tenth century to the sixteenth century.
The Moche civilization flourished in northern Peru from about one hundred to eight hundred AD, during the Regional Development Epoch.

In the history of the Americas, pre-Columbian era, also known as pre-contact era or pre-Hispanic, spans from the initial peopling of the Americas in the Upper Paleolithic to the onset of European colonization.

The Wari were a Middle Horizon civilization that flourished in the south-central Andes and coastal area of modern-day Peru, from about five hundred to one thousand AD. At their height, they formed the Wari Empire.
The Islamic Golden Age was a period of cultural flourishing in the history of Islam, dated from the eighth century CE to the fourteenth century.
The Sultanate of Rum, or Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, was a culturally Turco-Persian, Sunni Muslim state established over conquered Byzantine territories and peoples of Anatolia by the Seljuk Turks.
Mamluk, mamaluk, or mameluke were non-Arab, ethnically diverse enslaved mercenaries, slave-soldiers, and freed slaves who were assigned military and administrative duties in the Muslim world.
The Aq Qoyunlu or the White Sheep Turkomans was a Turkoman, culturally Persianate, Sunni Muslim tribal confederation.
The Qara Qoyunlu or Kara Koyunlu, also known as the Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman, culturally Persianate, Muslim dynasty.
The Göktürks, also known as Türks, Celestial Turks or Blue Turks, were a Turkic people in medieval Inner Asia.

The Muslim conquest of Persia, also known as the Arab conquest of Iran, occurred between six thirty-three and six fifty-one CE, when the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire as part of the early Muslim conquests.
The Anushtegin dynasty or Anushteginids, also known as the Khwarazmian dynasty was a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Turkic mamluk origin from the Bekdili clan of the Oghuz Turks.
The Uyghur Khaganate, self defined as the Toquz Oghuz and known to the Tang Chinese as the Jiuxing was a Turkic empire that existed for about a century between the mid eighth and ninth centuries.

Champa was a collection of independent Cham polities that extended across the coast of what is present-day central and southern Vietnam from approximately the second century AD until eighteen thirty-two.
The Malacca Sultanate was a Malay sultanate based in the modern-day state of Malacca, Malaysia.
The Pagan Kingdom, also called Bagan Empire or the First Burmese Empire, was the first Burmese kingdom to unify the regions that would later constitute modern-day Myanmar.
The Tran dynasty was a Vietnamese dynasty that ruled from twelve twenty-five to fourteen hundred.
The Muslim conquests in the Indian subcontinent mainly took place between the thirteenth and the eighteenth centuries, as a part of the Indo-Muslim period.
The An Lushan rebellion was a civil war in China that lasted from seven fifty-five to seven sixty-three, at the approximate midpoint of the Tang dynasty.
The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period was an era of political upheaval and division in Imperial China from nine oh seven to nine seventy-nine CE.

Goryeo was a Korean state founded in nine eighteen, during a time of national division called the Later Three Kingdoms period, that unified and ruled the Korean Peninsula until the establishment of Joseon in thirteen ninety-two.
The Jin dynasty, officially the Great Jin, was a Jurchen-led imperial dynasty of China and empire ruled by the Wanyan clan that existed between eleven fifteen and twelve thirty-four.

The Liao dynasty, also known as the Khitan State, officially the Great Liao, was a Khitan-led imperial dynasty of China and empire ruled by the Yelü clan that existed between nine sixteen and eleven twenty-five.
The Mongol conquests took place during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, creating the largest contiguous empire in history, the Mongol Empire.
A ninja, shinobi no mono or shinobi was a spy and infiltrator in pre-modern Japan.

The Sui dynasty was a Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from five eighty-one to six eighteen AD. The re-unification of China proper under the Sui brought the Northern and Southern dynasties era to a close.
The Tibetan Empire was centered on the Tibetan Plateau and formed as a result of expansions under the Yarlung dynasty's thirty-third king, Songtsen Gampo, in the seventh century.
The Franks were a Western European people who began in the third century as a group of Germanic tribes near the Lower Rhine River, but gradually became a multilingual, Catholic Christian people.
The Lombards, Longobards or Langobards were a Germanic people who conquered most of the Italian Peninsula between five sixty-eight and seven seventy-four AD.
The Visigothic Kingdom, Visigothic Spain or Kingdom of the Goths was a barbarian kingdom that occupied what is now southwestern France and the Iberian Peninsula from the fifth to the eighth century.
Al-Andalus refers to the various Muslim ruled territories on the Iberian Peninsula that existed between seven eleven and fourteen ninety-two.
The Kingdom of Aragon was a medieval and early modern kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula, corresponding to the modern-day autonomous community of Aragon, in Spain.

The Kingdom of Castile was a polity in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages. It traces its origins to the ninth-century County of Castile, as an eastern frontier lordship of the Kingdom of León.
The Kingdom of Hungary was a monarchy in Central Europe that existed for nearly a millennium, from one thousand to nineteen forty-six.
The Kingdom of Bohemia, sometimes referenced in English literature as the Czech Kingdom, was a medieval and early modern monarchy in Central Europe.

The Kingdom of Sicily was a state that existed in Sicily and the southern Italian Peninsula as well as, for a time, in North Africa, from its founding by Roger the Second of Sicily in eleven thirty until eighteen sixteen.

In medieval history, the Kingdom of Germany was the original core of the Holy Roman Empire, which continued to be distinguished from other parts of the empire such as the Kingdom of Italy and the Kingdom of Burgundy.
The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was a sovereign state in northeastern Europe that existed from the thirteenth century, succeeding the Kingdom of Lithuania, to the late eighteenth century.
The Grand Principality of Moscow, also known by the exonym Muscovy, was a late medieval Russian monarchy. Its capital was the city of Moscow.
The House of Habsburg, also known as the House of Austria, was one of the most powerful dynasties in the history of Western civilization.

The House of Plantagenet was a royal house which originated in the French county of Anjou. The family held the English throne from eleven fifty-four, with the accession of Henry the Second, until fourteen eighty-five, when Richard the Third died in battle.
The Capetian dynasty, also known as the House of France, is a dynasty of Frankish origin. It is among the largest and oldest royal houses in Europe and the world.

The House of Medici was an Italian banking family and political dynasty that first consolidated power in the Republic of Florence under Cosimo de' Medici and his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent during the first half of the fifteenth century.

The Papal States, officially the State of the Church, were a conglomeration of territories on the Italian Peninsula under the direct sovereign rule of the pope from seven fifty-six to eighteen seventy.
The Guelphs and Ghibellines were factions supporting the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor in the Italian city-states of Central and Northern Italy during the Middle Ages.
The Cumans or Kumans were a Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia comprising the western branch of the Cuman-Kipchak confederation who spoke the Cuman language.

The Khazars were a semi-nomadic Turkic people who established a major commercial empire in the late sixth century CE spanning the south of modern European Russia, southern Ukraine, and western Kazakhstan.
The Pannonian Avars or Carpathian Avars were a confederation of Eurasian nomads.
The First Bulgarian Empire was a medieval state that existed in Southeastern and southeastern Central Europe between the seventh and eleventh centuries AD.
The Second Bulgarian Empire was a medieval Bulgarian state that existed from eleven eighty-five to thirteen ninety-six.
Great Moravia, or simply Moravia, was the first major state that was predominantly West Slavic to emerge in the area of Central Europe.

Wends is a historical name for the Polabian Slavs who inhabited the present-day northeast Germany and Poland. It refers not to a homogeneous people, but to various people, tribes, or groups depending on where and when it was used.
Ostsiedlung, lit. East settlement, is the term for the early medieval and high medieval migration of ethnic Germans and Germanization of the areas populated by Slavic, Baltic and Uralic peoples.
Vikings were a seafaring people originally from Scandinavia, who from the late eighth to the late eleventh centuries raided, pirated, traded, and settled throughout parts of Europe.
The Kingdom of the Franks, also known as the Frankish Kingdom or Francia, was the largest post-Roman kingdom in Western Europe. It was established by the Franks, one of the Germanic peoples.
The Duchy of Burgundy was a medieval and early modern feudal polity in north-western regions of historical Burgundy. It belonged to the Kingdom of France.

The Rurik dynasty, also known as the Rurikids, was the ruling dynasty of Kievan Rus and its successor principalities. According to tradition, it was founded by the Varangian prince Rurik, who established himself at Novgorod in eight sixty-two.
The Grand Principality of Vladimir, commonly known as Vladimir-Suzdal, or simply Suzdalia, was a Russian principality. Its capital was the city of Vladimir.
Volga Bulgaria or Volga-Kama Bulgaria was a historical Bulgar state that existed between the ninth and thirteenth centuries around the confluence of the Volga and Kama River.

The Hussite Wars, also called the Bohemian Wars or the Hussite Revolution, were a series of civil wars fought between the Hussites and the combined Catholic forces of Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund, the Papacy, and European monarchs loyal to the Catholic Church.

The Northern Crusades, or Baltic Crusades, were military campaigns conducted by several Catholic kingdoms and military orders in an effort to Christianize all the pagans around the southern and eastern shores of the Baltic Sea.
