The standard acceleration of gravity or standard acceleration of free fall, often called simply standard gravity, is the nominal gravitational acceleration of an object in a vacuum near the surface of the Earth.
The inverse second or reciprocal second, also called per second, is a unit defined as the multiplicative inverse of the second.
The radian per second is the unit of angular velocity in the International System of Units.
Revolutions per minute is a unit of rotational speed or rotational frequency for rotating machines.
The joule-second is the unit of action and of angular momentum in the International System of Units.

In chemistry, the mole fraction or molar fraction, also called mole proportion or molar proportion, is a quantity defined as the ratio between the amount of a constituent substance and the total amount of all constituents in a mixture.
In chemistry, the mass fraction of a substance within a mixture is the ratio of the mass of that substance to the total mass of the mixture.
The neper is a logarithmic unit for ratios of measurements of physical field and power quantities, such as gain and loss of electronic signals.
Relative density, also called specific gravity, is a dimensionless quantity defined as the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a given reference material.
In chemistry and fluid mechanics, the volume fraction is defined as the volume of a constituent divided by the volume of all constituents of the mixture prior to mixing.
The gram per cubic centimetre is a unit of density in the International System of Units, and is commonly used in chemistry.
The kilogram per cubic metre is the unit of density in the International System of Units.
Molar concentration, also called amount-of-substance concentration or molarity, is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution.
In chemistry, molality is a measure of the amount of solute in a solution relative to a given mass of solvent.
In science and engineering, parts-per notation is a set of pseudo-units to describe the small values of miscellaneous dimensionless quantities.
A shake is a metric unit of time which is equal to ten nanoseconds.
In chronology and periodization, an epoch or reference epoch is an instant in time chosen as the origin of a particular calendar era.
The word aeon, also spelled eon, originally meant life, vital force or being, generation or a period of time.
Eternity, also sempiternity or forever, or perpetuity, is time with no end, that is, infinite.
The jansky is a non-metric unit of spectral flux density, or spectral irradiance, used especially in radio astronomy.
An ampere-hour or amp-hour is a unit of electric charge, recommended for use in batteries and electrolytic devices.
The gauss is a unit of measurement of magnetic flux density, also known as magnetic induction or magnetic field.
The henry is the unit of electrical inductance in the International System of Units.
The Rankine scale is an absolute scale of thermodynamic temperature named after the University of Glasgow engineer and physicist William Rankine, who proposed it in the nineteenth century.
Candlepower is the unit of luminous intensity in the United States customary systems of measurement.
The lumen is the International System unit of luminous flux, which quantifies the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source.
The lux is the unit of illuminance, or luminous flux per unit area, in the International System of Units.
The curie is a non-metric unit of radioactivity originally defined in the early twentieth century.
The roentgen or röntgen is a legacy unit of measurement for the exposure of X-rays and gamma rays.
The rad is a unit of absorbed radiation dose.
The katal is a unit of the International System of Units used for quantifying the catalytic activity of enzymes and other catalysts.
The enzyme unit or international unit is a unit measuring an enzyme's catalytic activity.
In telecommunications and electronics, baud is a common unit of measurement of symbol rate, which is one of the components that determine the speed of communication over a data channel.
The natural unit of information, sometimes also nit or nepit, is a unit of information or information entropy, based on natural logarithms and powers of e.
The shannon is a unit of information named after Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory.
In quantum computing, a qubit or quantum bit is a basic unit of quantum information, the quantum version of the classic binary bit.
Dots per inch is a measure of spatial printing, video or image scanner dot density.

Pixels per inch and pixels per centimetre are measurements of the pixel density of an electronic image device, such as a computer monitor or a television set's display, or image digitizing device such as a camera or image scanner.
Alcohol by volume is a common measure of the amount of alcohol contained in a given alcoholic beverage.
An air quality index is an approximation of how polluted the air currently is or how polluted it is forecast to become.
The ultraviolet index is an international standard measurement of the strength of the sunburn-producing ultraviolet radiation at a particular place and time.

Appropriate technology is a movement encompassing technological choice and application that is small-scale, affordable by its users, labor-intensive, energy-efficient, environmentally sustainable, and locally autonomous.
Emerging technologies are technologies whose development, practical applications, or both are still largely unrealized.
The technical meaning of maintenance involves functional checks, servicing, repairing or replacing of necessary devices, equipment, machinery, building infrastructure and supporting utilities.

A heuristic or heuristic technique is any approach to problem solving that employs a pragmatic method that is not necessarily optimized, perfected, or rationalized, but is nevertheless sufficient for reaching an immediate, short-term goal.
Research and development is the set of innovative activities undertaken by corporations, wealthy industrialists, or governments in developing new services or products, or improving existing ones.
A scientific instrument is a device or tool used for scientific purposes, including the study of both natural phenomena and theoretical research.
A simulation is an imitative representation of a process or system that could exist in the real world.
Technological convergence is the tendency for technologies that were originally unrelated to become more closely integrated and even unified as they develop and advance.

Technological determinism is a reductionist theory in assuming that a society's technology progresses by following its own internal logic of efficiency, while determining the development of the social structure and cultural values.

The technology adoption lifecycle is a sociological model that describes the adoption or acceptance of a new product or innovation, according to the demographic and psychological characteristics of defined adopter groups.
Technology, society and life or technology and culture refers to the inter-dependency, co-dependence, co-influence, and co-production of technology and society upon one another.
Technology assessment is a practical process of determining the value of a new or emerging technology in and of itself or against existing technologies.
The technology life cycle describes the commercial gain of a product through the expense of research and development phase, and the financial return during its vital life.
Technology transfer, also called transfer of technology, is the process of transferring technology from the person or organization that owns or holds it to another person or organization.
Molecular machines are a class of molecules typically described as an assembly of a discrete number of molecular components intended to produce mechanical movements in response to specific stimuli.
Engineering ethics is the field concerned with the system of moral principles that apply to the practice of engineering.
Risk management is the identification, evaluation, and prioritization of risks, followed by the minimization, monitoring, and control of the impact or probability of those risks occurring.
Engineering management, also called management engineering, is the application of engineering methods, tools, and techniques to business management systems.
In systems engineering and software engineering, requirements analysis focuses on the tasks that determine the needs or conditions to meet the new or altered product or project.
Engineering economics is a subset of economics concerned with the use of economic principles in the analysis of engineering decisions.
Applied mechanics is the branch of science concerned with the motion of any substance that can be experienced or perceived by humans without the help of instruments.
Biochemical engineering, also known as bioprocess engineering, is a field of study with roots stemming from chemical engineering and biological engineering.

Pharmaceutical engineering is a branch of engineering focused on discovering, formulating, and manufacturing medication, analytical and quality control processes, and on designing, building, and improving manufacturing sites.

Molecular engineering is an emerging field of study concerned with the design and testing of molecular properties, behavior and interactions in order to assemble better materials, systems, and processes for specific functions.
Process engineering is a field of study focused on the development and optimization of industrial processes.
Polymer engineering is generally an engineering field that designs, analyses, and modifies polymer materials.

Construction engineering, also known as construction operations, is a professional sub-discipline of civil engineering that deals with the designing, planning, construction, and operations management of infrastructure.
Directional drilling, or slant drilling, is the practice of drilling non-vertical bores.
Highway engineering is a professional engineering discipline branching from the civil engineering subdiscipline of transportation engineering.
Computer engineering is a branch of engineering specialized in developing computer hardware and software.
Energy engineering is a multidisciplinary field of engineering that focuses on optimizing energy systems, developing renewable energy technologies, and improving energy efficiency.
Power engineering, also called power systems engineering, is a subfield of electrical engineering that deals with the generation, transmission, distribution, and utilization of electric power.

Radio-frequency engineering is a subset of electrical engineering involving the application of transmission line, waveguide, antenna, radar, and electromagnetic field principles to the design and application of devices.
Engineering physics is the field of study combining pure science disciplines and engineering disciplines.
Computer-aided engineering is the general usage of technology to aid in tasks related to engineering analysis.

Manufacturing engineering or production engineering is a branch of professional engineering that shares many common concepts and ideas with other fields of engineering such as mechanical, chemical, electrical, and industrial engineering.

Sanitary engineering or sanitation engineering, also known as public health engineering or wastewater engineering, is the application of engineering methods to improve sanitation of human communities.
Security engineering is the process of incorporating security controls into an information system so that the controls become an integral part of the system's operational capabilities.
Structural analysis is a branch of solid mechanics which uses simplified models for solids like bars, beams and shells for engineering decision making.
Energy development is the field of activities focused on obtaining sources of energy from natural resources.
A yakhchal is an ancient type of ice house, which produced ice and desserts associated with it, like faloodeh, or sorbets.
A jack-o'-lantern is a carved lantern, most commonly made from a pumpkin, or formerly a root vegetable such as a mangelwurzel, rutabaga or turnip.
Prism lighting is the use of prisms to improve the distribution of light in a space.
Light tubes, also known as solar pipes, tubular skylights or sun tunnels, are structures that transmit or distribute natural or artificial light for the purpose of illumination.
Microgeneration is the small-scale production of heat or electric power from a low carbon source, as an alternative or supplement to traditional centralized grid-connected power.
Micro combined heat and power is an extension of the idea of cogeneration to the single or multi family home or small office building.
A gas-fired power plant, sometimes referred to as gas-fired power station, is a thermal power station that burns natural gas to generate electricity.
Inertial confinement fusion is a fusion energy process that initiates nuclear fusion reactions by compressing and heating targets filled with fuel.
A pressurized heavy-water reactor is a nuclear reactor that uses heavy water as its coolant and neutron moderator.
Nuclear marine propulsion is propulsion of a ship or submarine with heat provided by a nuclear reactor.
Home energy storage refers to residential energy storage devices that store electrical energy locally for later consumption.
Power-to-X are electricity conversion, energy storage, and reconversion pathways from surplus renewable energy.
The availability factor of a power plant is the duration it achieves production of electricity divided by the duration that it was planned to produce electricity.
In an electric power system, automatic generation control is a system for adjusting the power output of multiple generators at different power plants, in response to changes in the load.
Backfeeding is the flow of electric power in the direction reverse to that of the generally understood or typical flow of power.
Droop speed control is a control mode used for alternating-current electrical power generators, whereby the power output of a generator reduces as the line frequency increases.
Efficient energy use, or energy efficiency, is the process of reducing the amount of energy required to provide products and services.

Energy demand management, also known as demand-side management or demand-side response, is the modification of consumer demand for energy through various methods including inducing behavioral changes through education and incentives.

In energy economics and ecological energetics, energy return on investment is the ratio of the amount of usable energy delivered from an energy resource to the amount of energy used to obtain that energy resource.

A grid code is a technical specification which defines the parameters a facility connected to a public electric grid has to meet to ensure safe, secure and economic proper functioning of the electric system.
In electrical engineering the load factor is defined as the average load divided by the peak load in a specified time period.

Nameplate capacity, also known as the rated capacity, nominal capacity, installed capacity, maximum effect or gross capacity, is the intended full-load sustained output of a facility such as a power station.
Electric power quality is the degree to which the voltage, frequency, and waveform of a power supply system conform to established specifications.
In power engineering, a power-flow study is a numerical analysis of the flow of electric power in an interconnected system.
Repowering is the process of replacing older power stations with newer ones that either have a greater nameplate capacity or more efficiency which results in a net increase of power generated.
Variable renewable energy or intermittent renewable energy sources are renewable energy sources that are not dispatchable due to their fluctuating nature, such as wind power and solar power.
Dynamic demand is the name of a semi-passive technology to support demand response by adjusting the load demand on an electrical power grid.

Load management, also known as demand-side management, is the process of balancing the supply of electricity on the network with the electrical load by adjusting or controlling the load rather than the power station output.
A transmission system operator is an entity entrusted with transporting energy in the form of natural gas or electrical power on a national or regional level, using fixed infrastructure.
An overhead cable is a cable for the transmission of information, laid on utility poles.
A wide area synchronous grid is a three-phase electric power grid that has regional scale or greater that operates at a synchronized utility frequency.
An arc-fault circuit interrupter is a circuit breaker that breaks the circuit when it detects the electric arcs that are a signature of loose connections in home wiring.
An earth-leakage circuit breaker is a safety device used in electrical installations to prevent shock.
Power system protection is a set of techniques and power grid equipment used to limit the damage caused by an electrical fault and safeguard other components of the grid.

In utility and industrial electric power transmission and distribution systems, a numerical relay is a computer-based system with software-based protection algorithms for the detection of electrical faults.
Sulfur hexafluoride circuit breakers protect electrical power stations and distribution systems by interrupting electric currents, when tripped by a protective relay.
The Continental Europe Synchronous Area is the second largest synchronous electrical grid in the world, primarily operating in Europe.
A conveyor system is a common piece of mechanical handling equipment that moves materials from one location to another.
Pelletizing is the process of compressing or molding a material into the shape of a pellet.
A disposable, also called disposable product, is a product designed for a single use after which it is recycled or is disposed as solid waste.
Food coloring, color additive or colorant is any dye, pigment, or substance that imparts color when it is added to food or beverages.
A sugar substitute or artificial sweetener is a food additive that provides a sweetness like that of sugar while containing significantly less food energy than sugar-based sweeteners.
Sewage, or domestic sewage, domestic wastewater, municipal wastewater, is a type of wastewater that is produced by a community of people.
Extractive metallurgy is a branch of metallurgical engineering studying the process and methods of extraction of metals from their natural mineral deposits.
A gold dredge is a placer mining machine that extracts gold from sand, gravel, and dirt using water and mechanical methods.
Mineral processing is the process of separating commercially valuable minerals from their ores in the field of extractive metallurgy.
Mechanical screening, often just called screening, is the practice of taking granulated or crushed material and separating it into multiple grades by particle size.
The term spiral separator can refer to either a device for sorting particles by density, or a device for sorting particles by shape.
A stamp mill, or stamp battery or stamping mill, is a type of mill machine that crushes material by pounding rather than grinding, either for further processing or for extraction of metallic ores.
A trommel screen, also known as a rotary screen, is a mechanical screening machine used to separate materials, mainly in the mineral and solid-waste processing industries.
Bending is a manufacturing process that produces a V-shape, U-shape, or channel shape along a straight axis in ductile materials, most commonly sheet metal.
Electrical discharge machining, also sometimes known as spark machining or spark eroding, is a metal cutting process whereby a desired shape is obtained by using electrical discharges.

Machining is a manufacturing process where a desired shape or part is created using the controlled removal of material, most often metal, plastic or rubber from a larger piece of raw material by cutting.
Metal fabrication is the creation of metal structures by cutting, bending and assembling processes.
Chino cloth is a twill fabric originally made from pure cotton.
A fire brick, firebrick, fireclay brick, or refractory brick is a block of ceramic material used in lining furnaces, kilns, fireboxes, and fireplaces.
A concrete slab is a common structural element of modern buildings, consisting of a flat, horizontal surface made of cast concrete.
Construction aggregate, or simply aggregate, is a broad category of coarse to medium-grained particulate material used in construction.
Siding or wall cladding is the protective material attached to the exterior side of a wall of a house or other building.
A stone slab is a big stone, flat and relatively thin, often of rectangular or almost rectangular form.
Tiles are usually thin, square rectangular coverings manufactured from hard-wearing material such as ceramic, stone, metal, baked clay, or even glass.

Engineered wood, also called mass timber, composite wood, man-made wood, or manufactured board, includes a range of derivative wood products which are manufactured by binding or fixing the strands, particles, fibres, veneers, or boards of wood, together with adhesives.
Wood drying, also seasoning lumber or wood seasoning, reduces the moisture content of wood before its use.

Environmental remediation is the cleanup of hazardous substances dealing with the removal, treatment and containment of pollution or contaminants from environmental media such as soil, groundwater, and sediment.
Bioaugmentation is a type of bioremediation commonly used in municipal wastewater treatment to restart activated sludge bioreactors.
Phytoremediation technologies use living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants.
Groundwater remediation is the process that is used to treat polluted groundwater by removing the pollutants or converting them into harmless products.
Soil vapor extraction is a physical treatment process for in situ remediation of volatile contaminants in vadose zone soils.
A marina is a dock or area of water with piers and moorings for securing and parking yachts and small boats.
A passenger terminal is a structure in a port which services passengers boarding and leaving water vessels such as ferries, cruise ships and ocean liners.
A container port, container terminal, or intermodal terminal is a facility where cargo containers are transshipped between different transport vehicles, for onward transportation.
A convention center is a large building that is designed to hold a convention, where individuals and groups gather to promote and share common interests.
A data center is a facility dedicated to housing computer equipment for the storage, manipulation, and transmission of digital information.
A military base is a facility directly owned and operated by or for the military or one of its branches that shelters military equipment and personnel, and facilitates training and operations.
Fire safety is the set of practices intended to reduce destruction caused by fire.
Flood control is an important issue for the Netherlands, as due to its low elevation, approximately two thirds of its area is vulnerable to flooding, while the country is densely populated.
The Bratsk Hydroelectric Power Station is a concrete gravity dam on the Angara River and adjacent hydroelectric power station.
The New Croton Dam is a masonry gravity dam forming the New Croton Reservoir, both parts of the New York City water supply system.
The Euphrates Dam, most commonly known as Tabqa Dam, is an embankment dam on the Euphrates, located upstream from the city of Raqqa in Raqqa Governorate, Syria.
The Gordon Dam, also known as the Gordon River Dam, is a major gated double-curvature concrete arch dam across the Gordon River, in the South West region of Tasmania, Australia.
The Enguri Dam is a hydroelectric dam on the Enguri River in Tsalenjikha, Georgia.
The Mangla Dam is a multipurpose dam situated on the Jhelum River in Pakistan, lying in the Mirpur District of Azad Kashmir and the Jhelum District of Punjab.
The Roghun Dam is an embankment dam under construction on the Vakhsh River in southern Tajikistan.
The Banpo Bridge is a major bridge for vehicular traffic over the Han River in central Seoul, South Korea.
The Bridge of the Americas is a road bridge in Panama which spans the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal.

The Confederation Bridge is a box girder bridge carrying the Trans-Canada Highway across the Abegweit Passage of the Northumberland Strait, linking the province of Prince Edward Island with the mainland province of New Brunswick.
The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge is a long viaduct on the Beijing–Shanghai High-Speed Railway.
The El Ferdan Railway Bridge is a swing bridge that spans the western shipping lane of the Suez Canal near Ismailia, Egypt.
The Kapellbrücke is a covered wooden footbridge spanning the river Reuss diagonally in the city of Lucerne in central Switzerland.
The Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge is a historic bridge over the Drina River in Višegrad, in the Republika Srpska region of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The Allahverdi Khan Bridge, popularly known as Si-o-se-pol, is the largest of the eleven historical bridges on the Zayanderud, the largest river of the Iranian Plateau, in Isfahan, Iran.
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel is a bridge–tunnel that crosses the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay between Delmarva and Hampton Roads in the commonwealth of Virginia.
The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge is a bridge–tunnel system consisting of a series of three cable-stayed bridges, an undersea tunnel, and four artificial islands.
The Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line, also known as the Trans-Tokyo Bay Expressway, is an expressway that is mainly made up of a bridge–tunnel combination across Tokyo Bay in Japan.
Micro-electromechanical systems is the technology of microscopic devices incorporating both electronic and moving parts.
Micromachines are mechanical objects that are fabricated in the same general manner as integrated circuits.
Nanoelectromechanical systems are a class of devices integrating electrical and mechanical functionality on the nanoscale.
A leg mechanism is a mechanical system designed to provide a propulsive force by intermittent frictional contact with the ground.
A user guide, user manual, owner's manual or instruction manual is intended to assist users in using a particular product, service or application.
A net comprises threads or yarns knotted and twisted into a grid-like structure which blocks the passage of large items, while letting small items and fluids pass.
The fisherman's knot is a knot—specifically a bend—that joins two lines.
A flexible shaft, often referred to as a flex shaft, is a device for transmitting rotary motion between two objects which are not fixed relative to one another.
A washer is a thin plate with a hole that is normally used to distribute the load of a threaded fastener, such as a bolt or nut.
An alarm is a mechanism that gives an audible, visual, combination, or other kind of alarm signal to alert someone to a problem or condition that requires urgent attention.
A disc tumbler or disc detainer lock is a lock composed of slotted rotating detainer discs.
A lever tumbler lock is a type of lock whose mechanism uses a set of levers to prevent the bolt from moving in the lock.
In classical mechanics, a kinematic pair is a connection between two physical objects that imposes constraints on their relative movement.
A tappet or valve lifter is a valve train component which converts rotational motion into linear motion in activating a valve.
A whippletree, or whiffletree, is a mechanism to distribute force evenly through linkages.
A capstan is a vertical-axled rotating machine developed for use on sailing ships to multiply the pulling force of sailors when hauling ropes, cables, and hawsers.
A pistonless rotary engine is an internal combustion engine that does not use reciprocating pistons in the way a reciprocating engine does.
A flat engine is a piston engine where the cylinders are located on either side of a central crankshaft.
A straight engine, or inline engine, is a configuration of multi-cylinder piston engine where all of the cylinders are arranged in a single row, rather than radially or in two or more cylinder banks.
Hydraulic machines use liquid fluid power to perform work.
A hydraulic manifold is a component that regulates fluid flow between pumps and actuators and other components in a hydraulic system.
A portable or mobile toilet is any type of toilet that can be moved around, some by one person, some by mechanical equipment such as a truck and crane.
A squat toilet is a toilet used by squatting, rather than sitting.
A toilet seat is a hinged unit consisting of a round or oval open seat, and usually a lid, which is bolted onto the bowl of a toilet used in a sitting position.
A urinal is a sanitary plumbing fixture similar to a toilet, but for urination only.
An inflatable is an object that can be inflated with a gas, usually with air, but hydrogen, helium, and nitrogen are also used.
A planter is a farm implement, usually towed behind a tractor, that sows seeds in rows throughout a field.
The reaper-binder, or binder, is a farm implement that improved upon the simple reaper.
A swather, or windrower, is a farm implement that cuts hay or small grain crops and forms them into a windrow for drying.
A transplanter is an agricultural machine used for transplanting seedlings to the field.
A major appliance is a non-portable or semi-portable machine used for routine housekeeping tasks such as cooking, washing laundry, or food preservation.
A water dispenser, sometimes referred to as a water cooler, is a machine that dispenses and often also cools or heats up water with a refrigeration unit.
Water heating is a heat transfer process that uses an energy source to heat water above its initial temperature.
A quern-stone is a stone tool for hand-grinding a wide variety of materials, especially for various types of grains.
Milling is the process of machining using rotary cutters by advancing a workpiece into the cutter.
A trip hammer, also known as a tilt hammer or helve hammer, is a massive powered hammer, usually raised by a cam and then released to fall under the force of gravity.
Lifting equipment, also known as lifting gear, is a general term for any equipment that can be used to lift and lower loads.
A hoist is a device used for lifting or lowering a load by means of a drum or lift-wheel around which rope or chain wraps.
A jack is a mechanical lifting device.
The roller is an agricultural tool used for flattening land or breaking up large clumps of soil, especially after ploughing or disc harrowing.
A scythe is an agricultural hand-tool for mowing grass or harvesting crops.

A drafting machine, also drafting arm, is a tool used in technical drawing, consisting of a pair of scales mounted to form a right angle on an articulated protractor head that allows an angular rotation.
Enamel paint is paint that air-dries to a hard, usually glossy, finish, used for coating surfaces that are outdoors or otherwise subject to hard wear or variations in temperature.
A cage is an enclosure often made of mesh, bars, or wires, used to confine, contain or protect something or someone.
A locker is a small, usually narrow storage compartment.
A pressure vessel is a container designed to hold gases or liquids at a pressure substantially different from the ambient pressure.
A safe, also called a strongbox or coffer, is a secure, lockable enclosure that protects objects against theft or fire.
A steel can, tin can, tin, or can is a container made of thin metal, for distribution or storage of goods.
A funnel is a tube or pipe that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, used for guiding liquid or powder into a small opening.
Clovis points are the characteristically fluted projectile points associated with the New World Clovis culture, a prehistoric Paleo-American culture.
In archaeology, ground stone is a category of stone tool formed by the grinding of a coarse-grained tool stone, either purposely or incidentally.
A microlith is a small stone tool usually made of flint or chert and typically several centimeters in length and half a centimetre wide.
In archaeology, a prismatic blade is a long, narrow, specialized stone flake tool with a sharp edge, like a small razor blade.
A breathalyzer or breathalyser, also called an alcohol meter, is a device for measuring breath alcohol content.
Electronic tagging is a form of surveillance that uses an electronic device affixed to a person to monitor their location or physiological state.
A feeler gauge is a tool used to measure gap widths.
A metre-stick, metrestick, or yardstick is either a straightedge or foldable ruler used to measure length, and is especially common in the construction industry.
An optical spectrometer is an instrument used to measure properties of light over a specific portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, typically used in spectroscopic analysis to identify materials.
A vernier scale, named after Pierre Vernier, is a visual aid to take an accurate measurement reading between two graduation markings on a linear scale by using mechanical interpolation.
The graphometer, semicircle or semicircumferentor is a surveying instrument used for angle measurements.
Gunter's chain, also known as Gunter's measurement, is a distance-measuring device used for surveying.
A laser rangefinder, also known as a laser telemeter or laser distance meter, is a rangefinder that uses a laser beam to determine the distance to an object.
A level is an optical instrument used to establish or verify points in the same horizontal plane in a process known as levelling.

A level staff, also called levelling rod, is a graduated wooden or aluminium rod, used with a levelling instrument to determine the difference in height between points or heights of points above a vertical datum.
A tiltmeter is a sensitive inclinometer designed to measure very small changes from the vertical level, either on the ground or in structures.

A plane table is a device used in surveying, site mapping, exploration mapping, coastal navigation mapping, and related disciplines to provide a solid and level surface on which to make field drawings, charts and maps.
A stadimeter is an optical device for estimating the range to an object of known height by measuring the angle between the top and bottom of the object as observed at the device.
A surveyor's wheel, also called a clickwheel, hodometer, waywiser, trundle wheel, measuring wheel or perambulator is a device for measuring distance.
A quill is a writing tool made from a moulted flight feather of a large bird.
Chemical laws are those laws of nature relevant to chemistry.
Chemical safety includes all safety policies, procedures and practices designed to minimize the risk of exposure to potentially hazardous chemicals.
Dangerous goods are substances that are a risk to health, safety, property or the environment during transport.
The regulation of chemicals is the legislative intent of a variety of national laws or international initiatives such as agreements, strategies or conventions.

A wet lab, or experimental lab, is a type of laboratory where it is necessary to handle various types of chemicals and potential wet hazards, so the room has to be carefully designed, constructed, and controlled to avoid spillage and contamination.
Molecular modelling encompasses all methods, theoretical and computational, used to model or mimic the behaviour of molecules.
In chemistry, electron counting is a formalism for assigning a number of valence electrons to individual atoms in a molecule.
In chemistry, the mass concentration is defined as the mass of a constituent divided by the volume of the mixture.
The number density is an intensive quantity used to describe the degree of concentration of countable objects such as particles, molecules, phonons, cells and galaxies in physical space.
A sol is a colloid made out of tiny solid particles in a continuous liquid medium.
In chemical nomenclature, the nomenclature of organic chemistry is a method of naming organic chemical compounds as recommended by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry.

In chemical nomenclature, the nomenclature of inorganic chemistry is a systematic method of naming inorganic chemical compounds, as recommended by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry.
The standard atomic weight of a chemical element is the weighted arithmetic mean of the relative isotopic masses of all isotopes of that element, weighted by each isotope's abundance on Earth.
In chemistry and atomic physics, the main group is the group of elements whose lightest members are represented by helium, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine.
In chemistry, periodic trends are specific patterns present in the periodic table that illustrate different aspects of certain elements when grouped by period and or group.
The van der Waals radius of an atom is the radius of an imaginary hard sphere representing the distance of closest approach for another atom.
In chemistry, reactivity is the impulse for which a chemical substance undergoes a chemical reaction, either by itself or with other materials, with an overall release of energy.

In chemistry, the law of multiple proportions states that in compounds which contain two particular chemical elements, the amount of one element per measure of the other will differ across these compounds by ratios of small whole numbers.
A natural product is a natural compound or substance produced by a living organism, that is, found in nature.
A chemical composition specifies the identity, arrangement, and ratio of the chemical elements making up a compound by way of chemical and atomic bonds.
In chemistry, tautomers are a subset of structural isomers of chemical compounds that readily interconvert.
The structural formula of a chemical compound is a graphic representation of the molecular structure, showing how the atoms are connected to one another.
A molecular model is a physical model of an atomistic system that represents molecules and their processes.
Molecular graphics is the discipline and philosophy of studying molecules and their properties through graphical representation.
A fragrance compound, or fragrance, is a chemical compound with a pleasant odor.
In chemistry, an open-chain compound or acyclic compound is a compound with a linear structure, rather than a cyclic one.
A hydrogen atom is an atom of the chemical element hydrogen.
Hydrogen has three naturally occurring isotopes, of which two are stable, while the third is radioactive.
Solid hydrogen is the solid state of the element hydrogen.
A helium atom is an atom of the chemical element helium.
Superfluid helium-four is the superfluid form of helium-four, the most common isotope of the element helium.
The boron group are the chemical elements in the thirteenth group of the periodic table, consisting of boron, aluminium, gallium, indium, thallium and nihonium.
The carbon group is a periodic table group consisting of carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, lead, and flerovium.
A pnictogen is any of the chemical elements in the fifteenth group of the periodic table.
The chalcogens are the chemical elements in the sixteenth group of the periodic table.
Octasulfur is an inorganic substance made of rings of eight sulfur atoms. It is an odourless and tasteless yellow solid, and is a major industrial chemical.
A base metal is a common and inexpensive metal, as opposed to a precious metal such as gold or silver.
A noble metal is a metallic chemical element that is resistant to corrosion and is usually found in nature in its raw form.
Precious metals are rare, naturally occurring metallic minerals of high economic value.
The rare-earth elements, also called rare-earth metals, or rare earths, are a set of nearly indistinguishable lustrous silvery-white soft heavy metals.
An extended periodic table theorizes about chemical elements beyond those currently known and proven.
Solid acids are acids that are insoluble in the reaction medium.
A base anhydride is an oxide of a chemical element from the first or second group, the alkali metals and alkaline earth metals.
A superbase is a compound that has a particularly high affinity for protons.

The Brønsted–Lowry theory, also called proton theory of acids and bases, is an acid–base reaction theory, developed independently in the early twentieth century by Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted and Thomas Martin Lowry.
In chemistry, an electrophile is a chemical species that forms bonds with nucleophiles by accepting an electron pair.
An acidity function is a measure of the acidity of a medium or solvent system, usually expressed in terms of its ability to donate protons to a solute.
Fluoroantimonic acid is a mixture of hydrogen fluoride and antimony pentafluoride, containing various cations and anions.
Magic acid is a superacid consisting of a mixture, most commonly in an equal molar ratio, of fluorosulfuric acid and antimony pentafluoride.
Non-stoichiometric compounds are chemical compounds, almost always solid inorganic compounds, having elemental composition whose proportions cannot be represented by a ratio of small natural numbers.
Mischmetal is an alloy of rare-earth elements. It is also called cerium mischmetal, or rare-earth mischmetal.
A ferrite is one of a family of iron-oxide-containing magnetic ceramic materials.
Cyanogen is a chemical compound of two cyano groups. The simplest stable carbon nitride, it is a colorless and highly toxic gas with a pungent odor.
Oxygen difluoride is a chemical compound of oxygen and fluorine. As predicted by valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, the molecule adopts a bent molecular geometry.
Diborane is an inorganic compound of boron and hydrogen. It is a highly toxic, colorless, and pyrophoric gas with a repulsively sweet odor.
Hydrogen selenide is an inorganic compound of hydrogen and selenium. This hydrogen chalcogenide is the simplest and most commonly encountered hydride of selenium.
In chemistry, hydrogen halides, called hydrohalic acids when in the aqueous phase, are diatomic, inorganic compounds that function as Arrhenius acids.
Tritiated water is a radioactive form of water in which the usual protium atoms are replaced with tritium atoms.
In polymer science, the polymer chain or simply backbone of a polymer is the main chain of a polymer.
In organic chemistry and biochemistry, a side chain or pendant chain is a chemical group that is attached to a core part of the molecule called the main chain or backbone.
Lipophilicity is the ability of a chemical compound to dissolve in fats, oils, lipids, and non-polar solvents such as hexane or toluene.
In organic chemistry, a substituent is one or a group of atoms that replaces one or more atoms, thereby becoming a moiety in the resultant new molecule.
In organic chemistry, enols are a type of functional group or intermediate in organic chemistry.
Tar is a dark brown or black viscous liquid of hydrocarbons and free carbon, obtained from a wide variety of organic materials through destructive distillation.
Aliphatic compounds are chemical compounds containing the element carbon that are not aromatic compounds.
In organic chemistry, an alicyclic compound contains one or more all-carbon rings which may be either saturated or unsaturated, but do not have aromatic character.
Cyclobutane is a cycloalkane and organic compound. Cyclobutane is a colourless gas and is commercially available as a liquefied gas.
Cyclopentane is a highly flammable alicyclic hydrocarbon consisting of a ring of five carbon atoms each bonded with two hydrogen atoms.
A polyyne is any organic compound with alternating single and triple bonds, that is, a series of consecutive alkynes.
Antiaromaticity is a chemical property of a cyclic molecule with a pi electron system that has higher energy, and is less stable, as opposed to aromaticity.
In organic chemistry, Hückel's rule predicts that a planar ring molecule will have aromatic properties if it has a particular number of pi electrons.
Fatty alcohols, or long-chain alcohols, are usually high-molecular mass, straight-chain primary alcohols derived from natural fats and oils.
Cetyl alcohol, also known as palmityl alcohol, is a fatty alcohol. At room temperature, cetyl alcohol takes the form of a waxy white solid or flakes.
A diol is a chemical compound containing two hydroxyl groups. An aliphatic diol may also be called a glycol.
Sugar alcohols, also called polyhydric alcohols, polyalcohols, alditols or glycitols, are organic compounds, typically derived from sugars, containing one hydroxyl group attached to each carbon atom.
Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid is an aminopolycarboxylic acid. This white, slightly water-soluble solid is widely used to bind to iron and calcium ions.
Dimethylformamide is an organic compound, the amide of formic acid with two methyl groups on the nitrogen.
Cadaverine is an organic compound classified as a diamine. It is a colorless liquid with an unpleasant odor.
Ethylenediamine is an organic compound. This colorless liquid with an ammonia-like odor is a basic amine.
Putrescine is an organic compound, a diamine. It is a colorless solid that melts near room temperature.
Propylene carbonate is an organic compound. It is a cyclic carbonate ester derived from propylene glycol.
Dioxane is a heterocyclic organic compound, classified as an ether. It is a colorless liquid with a faint sweet odor similar to that of diethyl ether.
Halocarbon compounds are chemical compounds in which one or more carbon atoms are linked by covalent bonds with one or more halogen atoms.
Dichlorodifluoromethane is a colorless gas popularly known by the genericized brand name Freon. It is a chlorofluorocarbon used as a refrigerant and aerosol spray propellant.
Organochlorine chemistry is concerned with the properties of organochlorine compounds, or organochlorides, organic compounds that contain one or more carbon–chlorine bonds.
Fluorocarbons are chemical compounds with carbon-fluorine bonds.
Hydrofluorocarbons are synthetic organic compounds that contain fluorine and hydrogen atoms, and are the most common type of organofluorine compounds.
Imidazole is an organic compound. It is a white or colourless solid that is soluble in water, producing a mildly alkaline solution.
Xanthine is a purine base found in most human body tissues and fluids, as well as in other organisms.
The phenylpropanoids are a diverse family of organic compounds that are biosynthesized by plants from the amino acids phenylalanine and tyrosine.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are a group of synthetic organofluorine chemical compounds that have multiple fluorine atoms attached to an alkyl chain.
Polypropylene glycol or polypropylene oxide is the polymer of propylene glycol. Chemically it is a polyether.
Polyvinyl acetate is commonly known as wood glue, white glue, carpenter's glue or school glue.
Anthoxanthins are a type of flavonoid pigments in plants.
Catechin is a flavanol, a type of secondary metabolite providing antioxidant roles in plants.
Humulene is a naturally occurring monocyclic sesquiterpene, containing an eleven-membered ring and consisting of three isoprene units.
Zingiberene is a monocyclic sesquiterpene that is the predominant constituent of the oil of ginger, from which it gets its name.
Terpenoids, also known as isoprenoids, are a class of naturally occurring organic chemicals derived from the five-carbon compound isoprene and its derivatives called terpenes, diterpenes, and so on.
Citronellal or rhodinal is a monoterpenoid aldehyde, the main component in the mixture of terpenoid chemical compounds that give citronella oil its distinctive lemon scent.
In organic chemistry, quaternary ammonium cations, also known as quats, are positively-charged polyatomic ions with four organic groups attached to a central nitrogen.
Acid salts are a class of salts that produce an acidic solution after being dissolved in a solvent.
Borohydride or tetrahydroborate refers to the anion made of boron and four hydrogen atoms, and its salts.
Sodium borohydride, also known as sodium tetrahydridoborate, is an inorganic compound. It is a white crystalline solid, usually encountered as an aqueous basic solution.
Lithium aluminium hydride is an inorganic compound of lithium, aluminium and hydrogen. It is a white solid, discovered by Finholt, Bond and Schlesinger in the late nineteen-forties.
Ferricyanide is the name of the anion made of iron and six cyanide groups. The most common salt of this anion is potassium ferricyanide, a red crystalline compound.
Potassium ferricyanide is the chemical compound of potassium and the ferricyanide ion. This bright red salt contains the octahedrally coordinated ferricyanide ion.
Boron trifluoride is the inorganic compound of boron and fluorine. This pungent, colourless, and toxic gas forms white fumes in moist air.
Silver nitride is an explosive chemical compound. It is a black, metallic-looking solid which is formed when silver oxide or silver nitrate is dissolved in concentrated solutions of ammonia.
In chemistry, azide is a linear, polyatomic anion made of three nitrogen atoms. It is the conjugate base of hydrazoic acid.
Lead azide is an inorganic compound. More so than other azides, it is explosive. It is used in detonators to initiate secondary explosives.
Silver azide is a chemical compound of silver and the azide ion. It is a silver salt of hydrazoic acid.
In chemistry, noble gas compounds are chemical compounds that include an element from the noble gases, the last group of the periodic table.

Helium is the smallest and the lightest noble gas and one of the most unreactive elements, so it was commonly assumed that helium compounds could not exist at all, or at least not under normal conditions.
Neon compounds are chemical compounds containing the element neon with other molecules or elements from the periodic table.
Argon compounds, the chemical compounds that contain the element argon, are rarely encountered due to the inertness of the argon atom.
Benzalkonium chloride, also known as alkyldimethylbenzylammonium chloride, is a type of cationic surfactant. It is an organic salt classified as a quaternary ammonium compound.
Merbromin, marketed as Mercurochrome, is an organomercuric disodium salt compound used as a topical antiseptic for minor cuts and scrapes.
Thiomersal, or thimerosal, also sold under the name merthiolate, is an organomercury compound. It is a well-established antiseptic and antifungal agent.
Chromium acetate hydrate, also known as chromous acetate, is a coordination compound of chromium and acetate.
Calcium citrate is the calcium salt of citric acid. It is commonly used as a food additive, usually as a preservative, but sometimes for flavor.
Ferric citrate describes any of several complexes formed upon binding any of the several conjugate bases derived from citric acid with ferric ions. Most of these complexes are orange or red-brown.
Magnesium citrates are metal-organic compounds formed from citrate and magnesium ions. They are salts.
Potassium citrate, also known as tripotassium citrate, is a potassium salt of citric acid. It is a white, hygroscopic crystalline powder.
Trisodium citrate is a chemical compound sometimes referred to simply as sodium citrate, though sodium citrate can refer to any of the three sodium salts of citric acid.
Zirconium dioxide, sometimes known as zirconia, is a white crystalline oxide of zirconium.
Potassium peroxide is an inorganic compound. It is formed as potassium reacts with oxygen in the air, along with potassium oxide and potassium superoxide.
In chemistry, a superoxide is a compound that contains the superoxide ion, a negatively charged oxygen molecule.
A borate is any of a range of boron oxyanions, anions containing boron and oxygen, or any salt of such anions, such as borax.
Sodium metaborate is a chemical compound of sodium, boron, and oxygen.
Ammonium carbonate is a chemical compound. It is an ammonium salt of carbonic acid.
The chlorite ion, or chlorine dioxide anion, is the halite made of one chlorine and two oxygen atoms. A chlorite is a compound that contains this group, with chlorine in a positive oxidation state.
Ammonium perchlorate is an inorganic compound. It is a colorless or white solid that is soluble in water.
Lead chromate is an inorganic compound. It is a bright yellow salt that is very poorly soluble in water.
In inorganic nomenclature, a manganate is any negatively charged molecular entity with manganese as the central atom.
Potassium manganate is an inorganic compound. This green-colored salt is an intermediate in the industrial synthesis of potassium permanganate.
Sodium permanganate is an inorganic compound closely related to the more commonly encountered potassium permanganate.
In chemistry, a vanadate is an anionic coordination complex of vanadium.
Ammonium metavanadate is an inorganic compound. It is a white salt, although samples are often yellow owing to impurities.
Sodium orthovanadate is an inorganic compound of sodium, vanadium and oxygen.
Lead nitrate is an inorganic compound. It commonly occurs as a colourless crystal or white powder and, unlike most other lead salts, is soluble in water.
Diammonium phosphate is one of a series of water-soluble ammonium phosphate salts that can be produced when ammonia reacts with phosphoric acid.
Trisodium phosphate is an inorganic compound. It is a white, granular or crystalline solid, highly soluble in water, producing an alkaline solution.
Sodium dithionite, also known as sodium hydrosulfite, is a white crystalline powder with a sulfurous odor.
Potassium alum, potash alum, or potassium aluminium sulfate is a chemical compound defined as the double sulfate of potassium and aluminium.

Calcium sulfate, or calcium sulphate, is an inorganic salt. It occurs in several hydrated forms; the anhydrous state, known as anhydrite, is a white crystalline solid often found in evaporite deposits.
Thiosulfate is an oxyanion of sulfur. Thiosulfate also refers to the compounds containing this anion, which are the salts of thiosulfuric acid.
Cadmium sulfide is an inorganic compound of cadmium and sulfur. Cadmium sulfide is a yellow salt.
Calcium sulfide is a chemical compound of calcium and sulfur. This white material crystallizes in cubes like rock salt.
Iron sulfide, or ferrous sulfide, is one of a family of chemical compounds and minerals of iron and sulfur. Iron sulfides are often iron-deficient non-stoichiometric.
Mercury sulfide is a chemical compound composed of the chemical elements mercury and sulfur.
Molybdenum disulfide, or moly, is an inorganic compound composed of molybdenum and sulfur.
In analytical chemistry, quantitative analysis is the determination of the absolute or relative abundance of one, several or all particular substances present in a sample.
Instrumental analysis is a field of analytical chemistry that investigates analytes using scientific instruments.
Electroanalytical methods are a class of techniques in analytical chemistry which study an analyte by measuring the potential and or current in an electrochemical cell containing the analyte.
Radioanalytical chemistry focuses on the analysis of samples for their radionuclide content.
In chemistry, a chemical test is a qualitative or quantitative procedure designed to identify, quantify, or characterise a chemical compound or chemical group.
A complexometric indicator is an ionochromic dye that undergoes a definite color change in presence of specific metal ions.

A pH indicator is a halochromic chemical compound added in small amounts to a solution so the acidity or basicity of the solution can be determined visually or spectroscopically by changes in absorption or emission.
A redox indicator, also called an oxidation-reduction indicator, is an indicator which undergoes a definite color change at a specific electrode potential.
Thermogravimetric analysis or thermal gravimetric analysis is a method of thermal analysis in which the mass of a sample is measured over time as the temperature changes.
In analytical electrochemistry, coulometry is the measure of charge transfer during an electrochemical redox reaction.
Voltammetry is a category of electroanalytical methods used in analytical chemistry and various industrial processes.
Polarography is a type of voltammetry where the working electrode is a dropping mercury electrode or a static mercury drop electrode.
Dielectric spectroscopy measures the dielectric properties of a medium as a function of frequency.
In physics, atomic spectroscopy is the study of the electromagnetic radiation absorbed and emitted by atoms.

Atomic emission spectroscopy is a method of chemical analysis that uses the intensity of light emitted from a flame, plasma, arc, or spark at a particular wavelength to determine the quantity of an element in a sample.
Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy is a statistical analysis, via time correlation, of stationary fluctuations of the fluorescence intensity.
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy is a technique used to obtain an infrared spectrum of absorption or emission of a solid, liquid, or gaseous material.
Microwave spectroscopy is the spectroscopy method that employs microwaves, that is, electromagnetic radiation at very high frequencies, for the study of matter.
Ultrafast laser spectroscopy is a category of spectroscopic techniques using ultrashort pulse lasers for the study of dynamics on extremely short time scales.

Dissociation in chemistry is a general process in which molecules, or ionic compounds such as salts, or complexes, separate or split into other things such as atoms, ions, or radicals, usually in a reversible manner.
Arrow pushing or electron pushing is a technique used to describe the progression of organic chemistry reaction mechanisms.
A reversible reaction is a reaction in which the conversion of reactants to products and the conversion of products to reactants occur simultaneously.
In organic chemistry, a leaving group typically means a molecular fragment that departs with an electron pair during a reaction step with heterolytic bond cleavage.
In organic chemistry, an addition reaction is an organic reaction in which two or more molecules combine to form a larger molecule called the adduct.
In organic chemistry, a cycloaddition is a chemical reaction in which two or more unsaturated molecules, or parts of the same molecule, combine with the formation of a cyclic adduct.

In organic chemistry, an electrophilic addition reaction is an addition reaction where a chemical compound containing a double or triple bond has a pi bond broken, with the formation of two new sigma bonds.
In organic chemistry, a nucleophilic addition reaction is an addition reaction where a chemical compound with an electrophilic double or triple bond reacts with a nucleophile.

An aldol condensation is a condensation reaction in organic chemistry in which two carbonyl moieties of aldehydes or ketones react to form a hydroxy aldehyde or hydroxy ketone, followed by loss of water.

In organic chemistry, the Diels–Alder reaction is a chemical reaction between a conjugated diene and a substituted alkene, commonly termed the dienophile, to form a substituted cyclohexene derivative.
An elimination reaction is a type of organic reaction in which two substituents are removed from a molecule in either a one- or two-step reaction mechanism.

The Grignard reaction is an organometallic chemical reaction in which, according to the classical definition, carbon alkyl, allyl, vinyl, or aryl magnesium halides are added to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone.
In chemistry, the haloform reaction is a chemical reaction in which a haloform is produced by the exhaustive halogenation of an acetyl group, in the presence of a base.
In organic chemistry, hydroformylation, also known as oxo synthesis or oxo process, is an industrial process for the production of aldehydes from alkenes.
In polymer chemistry, polymerization is a process of reacting monomer molecules together in a chemical reaction to form polymer chains or three-dimensional networks.

In polymer chemistry, step-growth polymerization is a type of polymerization mechanism in which bi-functional or multifunctional monomers react to form first dimers, then trimers, longer oligomers, and eventually long chain polymers.
Chain-growth polymerization is a polymerization technique where monomer molecules add onto the active site on a growing polymer chain one at a time.
In polymer chemistry, radical polymerization is a method of polymerization by which a polymer forms by the successive addition of a radical to building blocks.
In polymer chemistry, ring-opening polymerization is a form of chain-growth polymerization in which the terminus of a polymer chain attacks cyclic monomers to form a longer polymer.
In polymer chemistry, a chain transfer reaction is an event during a polymerization reaction by which the activity of a growing polymer chain is transferred to another molecule.
In polymer chemistry, emulsion polymerization is a type of radical polymerization that usually starts with an emulsion incorporating water, monomers, and surfactants.
In organic chemistry, a rearrangement reaction is a broad class of organic reactions that involves a change of connectivity.
An allylic rearrangement or allylic shift is an organic chemical reaction in which reaction at a center vicinal to a double bond causes the double bond to shift to an adjacent pair of atoms.

In organic chemistry, olefin metathesis or alkene metathesis is an organic reaction that entails the redistribution of fragments of alkenes by the breaking and regeneration of carbon-carbon double bonds.
In organic chemistry, a pericyclic reaction is the type of organic reaction wherein the transition state of the molecule has a cyclic geometry, the reaction progresses in a concerted fashion.
In chemistry, an acyl group is a moiety derived by the removal of one or more hydroxyl groups from an oxoacid, including inorganic acids.
A nucleophilic aromatic substitution is a substitution reaction in organic chemistry in which the nucleophile displaces a good leaving group, such as a halide, on an aromatic ring.
Electrophilic substitution reactions are chemical reactions in which an electrophile displaces a functional group in a compound, which is typically, but not always, aromatic.
The Wittig reaction or Wittig olefination is a chemical reaction of an aldehyde or ketone with a triphenyl phosphonium ylide called a Wittig reagent.
In chemistry, a half reaction, or half-cell reaction, is either the oxidation or reduction reaction component of a redox reaction.
In chemistry, the oxidation state, or oxidation number, is the hypothetical charge of an atom assuming all of its bonds to other atoms are fully ionic.
An oxidizing agent, also known as an oxidant, oxidizer, electron recipient, or electron acceptor, is a substance in a redox chemical reaction that gains or accepts an electron from a reducing agent.
A flame is the visible, gaseous part of a fire. It is caused by a highly exothermic chemical reaction made in a thin zone.

Galvanic corrosion, also called bimetallic corrosion or dissimilar metal corrosion, is an electrochemical process in which one metal corrodes when it is in electrical contact with another, different metal.
Passivation, in physical chemistry and engineering, refers to coating a material so it becomes passive, that is, less readily affected or corroded by the environment.

In chemistry, disproportionation, sometimes called dismutation, is a redox reaction in which one compound of intermediate oxidation state converts to two compounds, one of higher and one of lower oxidation state.
Chemical decomposition, or chemical breakdown, is the process or effect of simplifying a single chemical entity into two or more fragments.
Kipp's apparatus, also called a Kipp generator, is an apparatus designed for preparation of small volumes of gases.
Thermal decomposition, or thermolysis, is a chemical decomposition of a substance caused by heat.

In petrochemistry, petroleum geology and organic chemistry, cracking is the process whereby complex organic molecules such as kerogens or long-chain hydrocarbons are broken down into simpler molecules.
Destructive distillation is a chemical process in which decomposition of unprocessed material is achieved by heating it to a high temperature.

A salt metathesis reaction, also called a double displacement reaction, double replacement reaction, or double decomposition, is a type of chemical reaction in which two compounds exchange their component ions.
The water–gas shift reaction describes the reaction of carbon monoxide and water vapor to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
In chemistry a convergent synthesis is a strategy that aims to improve the efficiency of multistep synthesis, most often in organic synthesis.
In chemistry a divergent synthesis is a strategy with the aim to improve the efficiency of chemical synthesis.
In electrochemistry, electrosynthesis is the synthesis of chemical compounds in an electrochemical cell.
Enantioselective synthesis, also called asymmetric synthesis, is a form of chemical synthesis.
In chemistry a one-pot synthesis is a strategy to improve the efficiency of a chemical reaction in which a reactant is subjected to successive chemical reactions in just one reactor.
Organic synthesis is a branch of chemical synthesis concerned with the construction of organic compounds.
Retrosynthetic analysis is a technique for solving problems in the planning of organic syntheses.

Semisynthesis, or partial chemical synthesis, is a type of chemical synthesis that uses chemical compounds isolated from natural sources, such as microbial cell cultures or plant material, as the starting materials.
Total synthesis, a specialized area within organic chemistry, focuses on constructing complex organic compounds, especially those found in nature, using laboratory methods.
A separation process is a method that converts a mixture or a solution of chemical substances into two or more distinct product mixtures.
A theoretical plate in many separation processes is a hypothetical zone or stage in which two phases, such as the liquid and vapor phases of a substance, establish an equilibrium with each other.
Column chromatography is a chromatography method used in analytical chemistry to separate the individual components of a mixture.

High-performance liquid chromatography, formerly referred to as high-pressure liquid chromatography, is a chromatography technique in analytical chemistry used to separate, identify, and quantify specific components in mixtures.
Ion chromatography, or ion-exchange chromatography, is a form of chromatography that separates ions and ionizable polar molecules based on their affinity to the ion exchanger.
Gas chromatography is a common type of chromatography used in analytical chemistry for separating and analyzing compounds that can be vaporized without decomposition.
Gel permeation chromatography is a type of size-exclusion chromatography that separates high molecular weight or colloidal analytes on the basis of size or diameter.
Thin-layer chromatography is a chromatography technique that separates components in non-volatile mixtures.
An air separation plant separates atmospheric air into its primary components, typically nitrogen and oxygen, and sometimes also argon and other rare inert gases.
A desiccant is a hygroscopic substance that is used to induce or sustain a state of dryness in its vicinity; it is the opposite of a humectant.
Vacuum drying is the mass transfer operation in which the moisture present in a substance, usually a wet solid, is removed by means of creating a vacuum.
Spray drying is a method of forming a dry powder from a liquid or slurry by rapidly drying with a hot gas.

Flash evaporation, or partial evaporation, is the partial vapor that occurs when a saturated liquid stream undergoes a reduction in pressure by passing through a throttling valve or other throttling device.
In chemical engineering, a vapor–liquid separator is a device used to separate a vapor–liquid mixture into its constituent phases.
Fractional freezing is a process used in process engineering and chemistry to separate substances with different melting points.
A eutectic system or eutectic mixture is a type of a homogeneous mixture that has a melting point lower than those of the constituents.
An azeotrope or a constant heating point mixture is a mixture of two or more liquids whose proportions cannot be changed by simple distillation.
In chemistry, azeotropic distillation is any of a range of techniques used to break an azeotrope in distillation.

The Marcusson apparatus, Dean-Stark apparatus, Dean–Stark receiver, distilling trap, or Dean–Stark Head is a piece of laboratory glassware used in synthetic chemistry to collect water or occasionally other liquids.
Continuous distillation, a form of distillation, is an ongoing separation in which a mixture is continuously fed into the process and separated fractions are removed continuously as output streams.
Fractional distillation is the separation of a mixture into its component parts, or fractions.

A fractionating column or fractional column is equipment used in the distillation of liquid mixtures to separate the mixture into its component parts, or fractions, based on their differences in volatility.
Steam distillation is a separation process that consists of distilling water together with other volatile and non-volatile components.
Vacuum distillation or distillation under reduced pressure is a type of distillation performed under reduced pressure.
Adsorption is the adhesion of atoms, ions, or molecules from a gas, liquid, or dissolved solid to a surface.
Physisorption, also called physical adsorption, is a process in which the electronic structure of the atom or molecule is barely perturbed upon adsorption.
Chemisorption is a kind of adsorption which involves a chemical reaction between the surface and the adsorbate.
The Langmuir adsorption model explains adsorption by assuming an adsorbate behaves as an ideal gas at isothermal conditions.
The Freundlich equation or Freundlich adsorption isotherm, an adsorption isotherm, is an empirical relationship between the quantity of a gas adsorbed into a solid surface and the gas pressure.
Hygroscopy is the phenomenon of attracting and holding water molecules via either absorption or adsorption from the surrounding environment, which is usually at normal or room temperature.
Cyclonic separation is a method of removing particulates from an air, gas or liquid stream, without the use of filters, through vortex separation.
In chemistry, dialysis is the process of separating molecules in solution by the difference in their rates of diffusion through a semipermeable membrane, such as dialysis tubing.
Extraction in chemistry is a separation process consisting of the separation of a substance from a matrix.
Liquid–liquid extraction is a method to separate compounds based on their relative solubilities in two different immiscible liquids, often water and an appropriate organic solvent.
A Soxhlet extractor is a piece of laboratory apparatus invented in the late nineteenth century by Franz von Soxhlet. It was originally designed for the extraction of a lipid from a solid material.
In chemical engineering, biochemical engineering and protein purification, cross-flow filtration, also known as tangential flow filtration, is a type of filtration.

Microfiltration is a type of physical filtration process where a contaminated fluid is passed through a special pore-sized membrane filter to separate microorganisms and suspended particles from process liquid.
Ultrafiltration is a variety of membrane filtration in which forces such as pressure or concentration gradients lead to a separation through a semipermeable membrane.
Nanofiltration is a membrane filtration process that uses nanometer sized pores through which smaller particles pass through the membrane.
Reverse osmosis is a water purification process that uses a semi-permeable membrane to separate water molecules from other substances.

Recrystallization is a broad class of chemical purification techniques characterized by the dissolution of an impure sample in a solvent or solvent mixture, followed by some change in conditions that encourages crystallization.
In chemistry, fractional crystallization is a stage-wise separation technique that relies on the liquid–solid phase change.
Sedimentation is the deposition of sediments. It takes place when particles in suspension settle out of the fluid in which they are entrained and come to rest against a barrier.

In colloidal chemistry, flocculation is a process by which colloidal particles come out of suspension to sediment in the form of floc or flake, either spontaneously or due to the addition of a clarifying agent.
Settling is the process by which particulates move towards the bottom of a liquid and form a sediment.
Stripping is a physical separation process where one or more components are removed from a liquid stream by a vapor stream.
A chemical process is a means by which one or more substances undergoes a change in chemical identity.
A chemical reactor is an enclosed volume in which a chemical reaction takes place.
A batch reactor is a chemical reactor in which a non-continuous reaction is conducted, that is, one where the reactants, products and solvent do not flow in or out of the vessel during the reaction.
For both chemical and biological engineering, semibatch reactors operate much like batch reactors in that they take place in a single stirred tank with similar equipment.

The continuous stirred-tank reactor, also known as vat or backmix reactor, mixed flow reactor, or continuous-flow stirred-tank reactor, is a common model for a chemical reactor in chemical engineering and environmental engineering.
The plug flow reactor model, sometimes called continuous tubular reactor or piston flow reactor, is a model used to describe chemical reactions in continuous, flowing systems of cylindrical geometry.
A laminar flow reactor is a type of chemical reactor that uses laminar flow to control reaction rate, and or reaction distribution.
A microreactor or microstructured reactor or microchannel reactor is a device in which chemical reactions take place in a confinement with typical lateral dimensions below one millimetre.
In chemical engineering and related fields, a unit operation is a basic step in a process.
In industrial process engineering, mixing is a unit operation that involves manipulation of a heterogeneous physical system with the intent to make it more homogeneous.

A coordination complex is a chemical compound consisting of a central atom or ion, usually a metal, called the coordination centre, and a surrounding array of bound molecules or ions, known as ligands.
Chelation is a type of bonding and sequestration of metal atoms. It involves two or more separate dative covalent bonds between a ligand and a single metal atom, thereby forming a ring structure.
The coordination geometry of an atom is the geometrical pattern defined by the atoms around the central atom. The term is commonly applied in the field of inorganic chemistry.
In coordination chemistry, the first coordination sphere refers to the array of molecules and ions, the ligands, directly attached to the central metal atom.
In coordination chemistry, the ligand cone angle is a measure of the steric bulk of a ligand in a transition metal coordination complex.

In inorganic chemistry, crystal field theory describes the breaking of degeneracies of electron orbital states, usually d or f orbitals, due to a static electric field produced by a surrounding charge distribution.
In coordination chemistry, a ligand is an ion or molecule with a functional group that binds to a central metal atom to form a coordination complex.

Ligand field theory describes the bonding, orbital arrangement, and other characteristics of coordination complexes. It represents an application of molecular orbital theory to transition metal complexes.

Molecular geometry is the three-dimensional arrangement of the atoms that constitute a molecule. It includes the general shape of the molecule as well as bond lengths, bond angles, torsional angles and any other geometrical parameters that determine the position of each atom.
In chemistry, molecules with a non-collinear arrangement of two adjacent bonds have bent molecular geometry, also known as angular or V-shaped.
The linear molecular geometry describes the geometry around a central atom bonded to two other atoms, or ligands, placed at a bond angle of one hundred and eighty degrees.

In chemistry, octahedral molecular geometry, also called square bipyramidal, describes the shape of compounds with six atoms or groups of atoms or ligands symmetrically arranged around a central atom, defining the vertices of an octahedron.
In a tetrahedral molecular geometry, a central atom is located at the center with four substituents that are located at the corners of a tetrahedron.
In chemistry, trigonal planar is a molecular geometry model with one atom at the center and three atoms at the corners of an equilateral triangle, called peripheral atoms, all in one plane.
In chemistry, a trigonal pyramid is a molecular geometry with one atom at the apex and three atoms at the corners of a trigonal base.
Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory is a model used in chemistry to predict the geometry of individual molecules from the number of electron pairs surrounding their central atoms.
A linear combination of atomic orbitals is a quantum superposition of atomic orbitals and a technique for calculating molecular orbitals in quantum chemistry.
In chemistry, orbital hybridisation is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals with different energies and shapes than the component atomic orbitals.

In chemistry, pi bonds are covalent chemical bonds in which each of two lobes of an orbital on one atom overlap with two lobes of an orbital on another atom, and in which this overlap occurs laterally.
In chemistry, sigma bonds are the strongest type of covalent chemical bond. They are formed by head-on overlapping between atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis.

An electrochemical cell is a device that either generates electrical energy from chemical reactions in a so-called galvanic or voltaic cell, or induces chemical reactions by applying electrical energy, as in an electrolytic cell.
An electrolytic cell is an electrochemical cell that uses an external source of electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction, a process known as electrolysis.

A galvanic cell or voltaic cell, named after the scientists Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta, respectively, is an electrochemical cell in which an electric current is generated from spontaneous oxidation–reduction reactions.
In electrochemistry, a half-cell is a structure that contains a conductive electrode and a surrounding conductive electrolyte separated by a naturally occurring Helmholtz double layer.

In electrochemistry, a salt bridge or ion bridge is an essential laboratory device to minimize the liquid junction potential in an electrochemical cell. The salt bridge has been in use for more than one hundred years.
