Redox potential is a measure of the tendency of a chemical species to acquire electrons from, or lose electrons to, an electrode and thereby be reduced or oxidised respectively.
Absolute electrode potential, in electrochemistry, according to its official definition, is the electrode potential of a metal measured with respect to a universal reference system.
In electrochemistry, the standard hydrogen electrode is a redox electrode which forms the basis of the thermodynamic scale of oxidation-reduction potentials.

The Nernst equation is a chemical thermodynamical relationship in electrochemistry that permits the calculation of the reduction potential of a reaction from the standard electrode potential, absolute temperature, the number of electrons involved, and the activities of the species undergoing reduction and oxidation.
In electrochemistry, standard electrode potential is the electrode potential, a measure of the reducing power of any element or compound, under standard conditions.
The galvanic series determines the nobility of metals and semi-metals. When two metals are submerged in an electrolyte and electrically connected, the less noble one tends to corrode.
In chemistry, a reactivity series is an empirical, calculated, and structurally analytical progression of a series of metals, arranged by their reactivity from highest to lowest.

In chemistry, the rate equation, also known as the rate law, is an empirical differential mathematical expression for the reaction rate of a given reaction in terms of concentrations of chemical species and constant parameters.
In chemistry, the law of mass action is the proposition that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the activities or concentrations of the reactants.
In chemical kinetics, the overall rate of a reaction is often approximately determined by the slowest step, known as the rate-determining step or rate-limiting step.

The reaction rate or rate of reaction is the speed at which a chemical reaction takes place, defined as proportional to the increase in the concentration of a product per unit time or to the decrease in the concentration of a reactant per unit time.

In chemical kinetics, a reaction rate constant or reaction rate coefficient is a proportionality constant which quantifies the rate and direction of a chemical reaction by relating it with the concentration of reactants.

In chemistry, transition state theory explains the reaction rates of elementary chemical reactions. The theory assumes a special type of chemical equilibrium, quasi-equilibrium, between reactants and activated transition state complexes.
In chemistry, an activated complex represents a collection of intermediate structures in a chemical reaction when bonds are breaking and forming.
In the Arrhenius model of reaction rates, activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that must be available to reactants for a chemical reaction to occur.
Hammond's postulate is a hypothesis in physical organic chemistry which describes the geometric structure of the transition state in an organic chemical reaction.
In chemistry, a reaction coordinate is an abstract one-dimensional coordinate chosen to represent progress along a reaction pathway.

In chemistry, the transition state of a chemical reaction is a particular configuration along the reaction coordinate. It is defined as the state corresponding to the highest potential energy along this reaction coordinate.
In physical chemistry, the Arrhenius equation is a formula for the temperature dependence of reaction rates.
In chemical kinetics, the pre-exponential factor or A factor is the pre-exponential constant in the Arrhenius equation, an empirical relationship between temperature and rate coefficient.
Collision theory is a principle of chemistry used to predict the rates of chemical reactions.
Collision frequency describes the rate of collisions between two atomic or molecular species in a given volume, per unit time.

In chemical kinetics, the entropy of activation of a reaction is one of the two parameters, along with the enthalpy of activation, that are typically obtained from the temperature dependence of a reaction rate constant.

In materials science and molecular biology, thermostability is the ability of a substance to resist irreversible change in its chemical or physical structure, often by resisting decomposition or polymerization, at a high relative temperature.
Thermolabile refers to a substance which is subject to decomposition or change in response to heat. This term is often used to describe biochemical substances.
Stereochemistry, a subdiscipline of chemistry, studies the spatial arrangement of atoms that form the structure of molecules and their manipulation.

In stereochemistry, stereoisomerism, or spatial isomerism, is a form of isomerism in which molecules have the same molecular formula and sequence of bonded atoms, but differ in the three-dimensional orientations of their atoms in space.

In organic chemistry, the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog sequence rules, also called the priority convention, named after Robert Sidney Cahn, Christopher Kelk Ingold and Vladimir Prelog, are a standard process to completely and unequivocally name a stereoisomer of a molecule.
In chemistry, absolute configuration is the spatial arrangement of atoms within a molecular entity that is chiral, and its resultant stereochemical description.
In chemistry, an enantiomer, also known as an optical isomer, antipode, or optical antipode, is one of a pair of molecular entities which are mirror images of each other and non-superposable.
In chemistry, a racemic mixture or racemate is a mixture that has equal amounts of left- and right-handed enantiomers of a chiral molecule or salt.
In chemistry, racemization is a conversion, by heat or by chemical reaction, of an optically active compound into a racemic form.

In stereochemistry, a stereocenter of a molecule is an atom, axis or plane that is the focus of stereoisomerism; that is, when having at least three different groups bound to the stereocenter, interchanging any two different groups creates a new stereoisomer.
In chemistry, rotamers are chemical species that differ from one another primarily due to rotations about one single bond.

Atropisomers are a kind of stereoisomer arising because of hindered rotation about a single bond, where energy differences due to steric strain or other contributors create a barrier to rotation that is high enough to allow for isolation of individual conformers.

Cyclohexane conformations are any of several three-dimensional shapes adopted by cyclohexane. Because many compounds feature structurally similar six-membered rings, the structure and dynamics of cyclohexane are important prototypes of a wide range of compounds.

In organic chemistry, a ring flip, also known as a ring inversion or ring reversal, is the interconversion of cyclic conformers that have equivalent ring shapes, for example from one chair conformer to another.
In chemistry an eclipsed conformation is a conformation in which two substituents on adjacent atoms are in closest proximity, implying that the torsion angle is zero degrees.

In the study of conformational isomerism, the gauche effect is an atypical situation where a gauche conformation, groups separated by a torsion angle of approximately sixty degrees, is more stable than the anti conformation.

A Newman projection is a drawing that helps visualize the three-dimensional structure of a molecule. This projection most commonly sights down a carbon–carbon bond, making it a very useful way to visualize the stereochemistry of alkanes.

In organic chemistry, a staggered conformation is a chemical conformation of an ethane-like moiety in which the substituents on one atom are at the maximum distance from those on the neighbouring atom.
Steric effects arise from the spatial arrangement of atoms. When atoms come close together there is generally a rise in the energy of the molecule.
A-values are numerical values used in the determination of the most stable orientation of atoms in a molecule, known as conformational analysis, as well as a general representation of steric bulk.
In chemistry, a molecule experiences strain when its chemical structure undergoes some stress which raises its internal energy in comparison to a strain-free reference compound.
In stereochemistry, diastereomers are a type of stereoisomer. Diastereomers are defined as non-mirror image, non-identical stereoisomers.

Cis–trans isomerism, also known as geometric isomerism, describes certain arrangements of atoms within molecules. The prefixes cis and trans are from Latin, meaning on this side of and on the other side of.
E–Z configuration, or the E–Z convention, is the officially preferred method of describing the absolute stereochemistry of double bonds in organic chemistry.
Supramolecular chemistry is the branch of chemistry concerning chemical systems composed of discrete numbers of molecules.
In chemistry and materials science, molecular self-assembly is the process by which molecules adopt a defined arrangement without guidance or management from an outside source.

In supramolecular chemistry, host–guest chemistry describes complexes composed of two or more molecules or ions held together in unique structural relationships by forces other than those of full covalent bonds.
A clathrate or clathrate compound is a type of inclusion compound in which a guest atom, ion, or molecule is enclosed in a cage-like cavity formed by a host molecule or by an extended host lattice.
Endohedral fullerenes, also called endofullerenes, are fullerenes that have additional atoms, ions, or clusters enclosed within their inner spheres.
In chemistry, polarity is a separation of electric charge leading to a molecule or its chemical groups having an electric dipole moment, with a negatively charged end and a positively charged end.
In chemistry, an amphiphile, also referred to as an amphipath, is a chemical compound possessing both hydrophilic and lipophilic properties within the same molecule.

A hydrophile is a molecule or other molecular entity that is attracted to water molecules and tends to be dissolved by water. In contrast, hydrophobes are not attracted to water and may seem to be repelled by it.
In chemistry, hydrophobicity is the chemical property of a molecule, called a hydrophobe, that is seemingly repelled from a mass of water. By contrast, hydrophiles are attracted to water.

London dispersion forces are a type of intermolecular force acting between atoms and molecules that are normally electrically symmetric; that is, the electrons are symmetrically distributed with respect to the nucleus.
Chemical thermodynamics is the study of the interrelation of heat and work with chemical reactions or with physical changes of state within the confines of the laws of thermodynamics.
Thermochemistry is the study of the heat energy which is associated with chemical reactions and phase changes such as melting and boiling.

In chemistry, colligative properties are those properties of solutions that depend on the ratio of the number of solute particles to the number of solvent particles in a solution, and not on the nature of the chemical species present.

Boiling-point elevation is the phenomenon whereby the boiling point of a liquid, a solvent, will be higher when another compound is added, meaning that a solution has a higher boiling point than a pure solvent.
Osmotic pressure is the minimum pressure which needs to be applied to a solution to prevent the inward flow of its pure solvent across a semipermeable membrane.
Vapor pressure or equilibrium vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapor in thermodynamic equilibrium with its condensed phases, solid or liquid, at a given temperature in a closed system.
In chemistry, volatility is a material quality which describes how readily a substance vaporizes.

In chemical thermodynamics, the reaction quotient is a dimensionless quantity that provides a measurement of the relative amounts of products and reactants present in a reaction mixture for a reaction with well-defined overall stoichiometry at a particular point in time.

In thermodynamics, activity is a measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture, in the sense that the chemical potential of the species depends on its activity in a real solution just as it would depend on concentration in an ideal solution.
In thermodynamics, an activity coefficient is a factor used to account for deviation of a mixture of chemical substances from ideal behaviour.
The equilibrium constant of a chemical reaction is the value of its reaction quotient at chemical equilibrium, a state approached by a dynamic chemical system after sufficient time has elapsed.
Thermal runaway describes a process that is accelerated by increased temperature, in turn releasing energy that further increases temperature.

Flory–Huggins solution theory is a lattice model of the thermodynamics of polymer solutions which takes account of the great dissimilarity in molecular sizes in adapting the usual expression for the entropy of mixing.
Carbon has fourteen known isotopes, of which only carbon-twelve and carbon-thirteen are stable. The longest-lived radioisotope is carbon-fourteen, with a half-life of fifty-seven hundred years.
Natural nitrogen consists of two stable isotopes: the vast majority of naturally occurring nitrogen is nitrogen-fourteen, with the remainder being nitrogen-fifteen.
There are three known stable isotopes of oxygen: oxygen-sixteen, oxygen-seventeen and oxygen-eighteen.
Elemental phosphorus can exist in several allotropes, the most common of which are white and red solids. Solid violet and black allotropes are also known.
Uranium is a naturally occurring radioactive element with no stable isotopes. It has two primordial isotopes with long half-lives that are found in appreciable quantity in Earth's crust.
This isotope of technetium is a metastable nuclear isomer that is used in tens of millions of medical diagnostic procedures annually, making it the most commonly used medical radioisotope.
Group three is the first group of transition metals in the periodic table. This group is closely related to the rare-earth elements.
Group four is the second group of transition metals in the periodic table. It contains only the four elements titanium, zirconium, hafnium, and rutherfordium.
Group five is a group of elements in the periodic table. It contains vanadium, niobium, tantalum and dubnium.
Group six is a group of elements in the periodic table. Its members are chromium, molybdenum, tungsten, and seaborgium.
Group seven is a group of elements in the periodic table. It contains manganese, technetium, rhenium and bohrium.
Group eight is a group, or column, of chemical elements in the periodic table. It consists of iron, ruthenium, osmium and hassium.
Group nine is a group, or column, of chemical elements in the d-block of the periodic table. Members include cobalt, rhodium, iridium and meitnerium.
Group ten is the group of chemical elements in the periodic table that consists of nickel, palladium, platinum, and darmstadtium. All are d-block transition metals.
Group eleven is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table, consisting of copper, silver, gold, and roentgenium.
Group twelve is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc, cadmium, mercury, and copernicium.
A period one element is one of the chemical elements in the first row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.
A period two element is one of the chemical elements in the second row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.
A period three element is one of the chemical elements in the third row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.
A period four element is one of the chemical elements in the fourth row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.
A period five element is one of the chemical elements in the fifth row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.
A period six element is one of the chemical elements in the sixth row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements, including the lanthanides.
A period seven element is one of the chemical elements in the seventh row, or period, of the periodic table of the chemical elements.

A non-nucleophilic base is a sterically hindered organic base that is a poor nucleophile. Normal bases are also nucleophiles, but often chemists seek the proton-removing ability of a base without any other functions.
A conjugate acid is a chemical compound that is formed when an acid gives a proton to a base. A conjugate base is what remains after an acid has donated a proton during a chemical reaction.
Hard and soft acids and bases is a concept widely used in chemistry for explaining the stability of compounds, reaction mechanisms and pathways.
Carborane acids are a class of superacids, some of which are estimated to be at least one million times stronger than pure sulfuric acid in terms of their Hammett acidity function values.
Triflic acid, the short name for trifluoromethanesulfonic acid, is a sulfonic acid. It is one of the strongest known acids.
Copper alloys are metal alloys that have copper as their principal component. They have high resistance against corrosion.

Yttrium barium copper oxide is a family of crystalline chemical compounds that display high-temperature superconductivity; it includes the first material ever discovered to become superconducting above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
A borane is a compound of boron, hydrogen and sometimes other groups, and examples include multi-boron derivatives. Most of the known group thirteen hydrides belong to this class.
Carboranes are electron-delocalized clusters composed of boron, carbon and hydrogen atoms. Like many of the related boron hydrides, these clusters are polyhedra or fragments of polyhedra.
Pnictogen hydrides or hydrogen pnictides are binary compounds of hydrogen with pnictogen atoms, the elements of group fifteen: nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony, and bismuth.
Stibine is a chemical compound, a pnictogen hydride, that is a colourless, highly toxic gas and the principal covalent hydride of antimony, and a heavy analogue of ammonia.
Hydrogen chalcogenides are binary compounds of hydrogen with chalcogen atoms, the elements of group sixteen: oxygen, sulfur, selenium, tellurium, and polonium.
A polysulfane is a chemical compound of hydrogen with a chain of sulfur atoms.

In the analysis of the molecular formula of organic molecules, the degree of unsaturation, also known as the index of hydrogen deficiency, double bond equivalents, or unsaturation index, is a calculation that determines the total number of rings and pi bonds in a molecule.

A pendant group or side group is a group of atoms attached to a backbone chain of a long molecule, usually a polymer. Pendant groups are different from pendant chains, as they are neither oligomeric nor polymeric.
Arene substitution patterns are part of organic chemistry nomenclature and pinpoint the position of substituents other than hydrogen in relation to each other on an aromatic hydrocarbon.
Propanol, also called n-propyl alcohol, is a primary alcohol. It is a colourless liquid and an isomer of isopropyl alcohol.
Dodecanol, or lauryl alcohol, is an organic compound produced industrially from palm kernel oil or coconut oil. It is a fatty alcohol.
Stearyl alcohol, or octadecanol, is an organic compound classified as a saturated fatty alcohol. It takes the form of white granules or flakes, which are insoluble in water.

A geminal diol, or gem-diol for short, is any organic compound having two hydroxyl functional groups bound to the same carbon atom. Geminal diols are a subclass of the diols, which in turn are a special class of alcohols.
N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide, also called diethyltoluamide, is the oldest active ingredient, and one of the most effective and common, in commercial insect repellents.
Polymethyl methacrylate is a synthetic polymer derived from methyl methacrylate. It is a transparent thermoplastic used as an engineering plastic.
Alkali salts or base salts are salts that are the product of incomplete neutralization of a strong base and a weak acid.

Lithium borohydride is a borohydride known in organic synthesis as a reducing agent for esters. Although less common than the related sodium borohydride, the lithium salt offers some advantages, being a stronger reducing agent.
Aluminium carbide is a chemical compound of aluminium and carbon, a carbide of aluminium.

Disodium helide is an electride compound of helium and sodium that is stable only at very high pressures. It was first predicted using a crystal structure prediction algorithm and then synthesised in two thousand sixteen.
Argon fluorohydride, systematically named fluoridohydridoargon, or argon hydrofluoride, is an inorganic compound of hydrogen, argon and fluorine. It is a compound of the chemical element argon.
Xenon hexafluoroplatinate is the product of the reaction of platinum hexafluoride with xenon, in an experiment that proved the chemical reactivity of the noble gases.
Sodium calcium edetate, also known as edetate calcium disodium among other names, is a medication primarily used to treat lead poisoning, including both short-term and long-term lead poisoning.

The tetrasodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid results from the neutralization of the acid with four equivalents of sodium hydroxide, or an equivalent sodium base. It is a white solid that is highly soluble in water.
Aluminium triacetate, formally named aluminium acetate, is a chemical compound of aluminium with acetate.
Ammonium ferric citrate, also known as ferric ammonium citrate or ammoniacal ferrous citrate, is a compound of ammonium, iron and citrate. The iron in this compound is trivalent.
Monosodium citrate, more correctly sodium dihydrogen citrate, is an acid salt of citric acid. Disodium citrate and trisodium citrate are also known.
Disodium citrate, also known as disodium hydrogen citrate, is an acid salt of citric acid. It is used as an antioxidant in food and to improve the effects of other antioxidants.

Ammonium dihydrogen phosphate, also known as monoammonium phosphate, is a chemical compound of ammonium and phosphate. It is a major ingredient of agricultural fertilizers and dry chemical fire extinguishers.
A phosphite ion in inorganic chemistry usually refers to hydrogen phosphite, but includes dihydrogen phosphite. These anions are the conjugate bases of phosphorous acid.

In electrochemistry, cyclic voltammetry is a type of voltammetric measurement where the potential of the working electrode is ramped linearly versus time. Unlike in linear sweep voltammetry, after the set potential is reached the potential is ramped back in the opposite direction.

In organic chemistry, free-radical addition is an addition reaction which involves free radicals. These reactions can happen due to the free radicals having an unpaired electron in their valence shell, making them highly reactive.

The unimolecular conjugate base elimination reaction is a type of elimination reaction which occurs under basic conditions, where the hydrogen to be removed is relatively acidic, while the leaving group is a relatively poor one.

In organic chemistry, the Ei mechanism, also known as a thermal syn elimination or a pericyclic syn elimination, is a special type of elimination reaction in which two vicinal substituents on an alkane framework leave simultaneously via a cyclic transition state.

A one-two rearrangement, also called a one-two migration, one-two shift or Whitmore one-two shift, is an organic reaction where a substituent moves from one atom to another atom in a chemical compound.
The unimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction is a substitution reaction in organic chemistry.
The bimolecular nucleophilic substitution is a type of reaction mechanism that is common in organic chemistry.

Substitution nucleophilic internal refers to a specific, regio-selective but not often encountered reaction mechanism for nucleophilic aliphatic substitution. The name was introduced by Cowdrey and co-workers in nineteen thirty-seven.

The van Deemter equation in chromatography, named for Jan van Deemter, relates the variance per unit length of a separation column to the linear mobile phase velocity by considering physical, kinetic, and thermodynamic properties of a separation.

Random column packing is the practice of packing a distillation column with randomly fitting filtration material in order to optimize surface area over which reactants can interact while minimizing the complexity of construction of such columns.

Brunauer–Emmett–Teller theory aims to explain the physical adsorption of gas molecules on a solid surface and serves as the basis for an important analysis technique for the measurement of the specific surface area of materials.
An interstellar object is an astronomical object in interstellar space, not gravitationally bound to a star. The term is used for objects including some asteroids, some comets, and rogue planets.
A substellar object, sometimes called a substar, is an astronomical object, the mass of which is smaller than the smallest mass at which hydrogen fusion can be sustained.
Astrobiology is an interdisciplinary field of scientific study that aims to answer fundamental questions about the origin, distribution and evolution of life in the universe.
Extraterrestrial intelligence refers to hypothetical beings, extraterrestrial life or more artificial beings, having the intelligence to perform cognitive abilities similar to those of humans.
The search for extraterrestrial intelligence is the diverse efforts and scientific projects intended to detect extraterrestrial signals.
Astrochemistry is the interdisciplinary scientific study of the abundance and reactions of molecules in space and their interaction with radiation.
Cosmochemistry or chemical cosmology is the study of the chemical composition of matter in the universe and the processes that led to those compositions.
Cosmology is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
Space physics, also known as space plasma physics, is the study of naturally occurring plasmas within Earth's upper atmosphere and the rest of the Solar System.
Time-domain astronomy is the study of how astronomical objects change with time.
The night sky is the nighttime appearance of celestial objects like stars, planets, and the Moon, which are visible in a clear sky between sunset and sunrise, when the Sun is below the horizon.
Amateur astronomy is a hobby where participants enjoy observing, studying, or imaging celestial objects in the sky using the unaided eye, binoculars, telescopes, and other gadgets.
Astrophotography, also known as astronomical imaging, is the photography or imaging of astronomical objects, celestial events, or areas of the night sky.
A Bayer designation is a stellar designation in which a specific star is identified by a Greek or Latin letter followed by the genitive form of its parent constellation's Latin name.
The Messier objects are a set of astronomical objects catalogued by the French astronomer Charles Messier in his Catalogue des Nébuleuses et des Amas d'Étoiles.
Airglow is a faint emission of light by a planetary atmosphere. In the case of Earth's atmosphere, this optical phenomenon causes the night sky never to be completely dark.
The effective temperature of a body such as a star or planet is the temperature of a black body that would emit the same total energy as electromagnetic radiation.
In astronomy, a light curve is a graph of the light intensity of a celestial object or region as a function of time.
Proper motion is the angular speed of an astronomical object, such as a star, as it moves across the sky.
The radial velocity or line-of-sight velocity of a target with respect to an observer is the rate of change of the vector displacement between the two points.
The Fraunhofer lines are a set of spectral absorption lines. They are dark absorption lines, seen in the optical spectrum of the Sun.
Infrared astronomy is a sub-discipline of astronomy which specializes in the observation and analysis of astronomical objects using infrared radiation.
Neutrino astronomy is a branch of astronomy that gathers information about astronomical objects by observing and studying neutrinos emitted by them with the help of neutrino detectors.
Gravitational-wave astronomy is a subfield of astronomy concerned with the detection and study of gravitational waves emitted by astrophysical sources.

The first direct observation of gravitational waves was made in September two thousand fifteen and was announced by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo collaborations in February two thousand sixteen.
In astronomy, seeing is the degradation of the image of an astronomical object due to turbulence in the atmosphere of Earth that may become visible as blurring, twinkling or variable distortions.
Twinkling, also called scintillation, is a generic term for variations in apparent brightness, colour, or position of a distant luminous object viewed through a medium.
Luminosity distance is defined in terms of the relationship between the absolute magnitude and apparent magnitude of an astronomical object.
Recessional velocity is the rate at which an extragalactic astronomical object recedes from an observer as a result of the expansion of the universe.
A spectral energy distribution is a plot of energy versus frequency or wavelength of electromagnetic or mechanical radiation, most commonly light.
Angular resolution describes the ability of any image-forming device such as an optical or radio telescope, a microscope, a camera, or an eye, to distinguish small details of an object.
The angular diameter, angular width, angular size, apparent diameter, or apparent size is an angular separation describing how large a sphere or circle appears from a given point of view.
The Bortle dark-sky scale is a nine-level numeric scale that measures the night sky's brightness of a particular location.
Radio astronomy is a subfield of astronomy that studies celestial objects using radio waves.
Radio spectrum pollution is the straying of electromagnetic waves in the radio spectrum outside their allocations.
Submillimetre astronomy is the branch of observational astronomy that is conducted at submillimetre wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum.
An astronomical radio source is an object in outer space that emits strong radio waves. Radio emission comes from a wide variety of sources.
An astrophysical maser is a naturally occurring source of stimulated spectral line emission, typically in the microwave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Brightness temperature or radiance temperature is a measure of the intensity of electromagnetic energy coming from a source.
High-energy astrophysics or high-energy astronomy is the study of astronomical objects that release electromagnetic radiation of highly energetic wavelengths.
Ultraviolet astronomy is the observation of electromagnetic radiation at ultraviolet wavelengths.
X-ray astronomy is an observational branch of astronomy which deals with the study of X-ray observation and detection from astronomical objects.
Astrophysical X-ray sources are astronomical objects with physical properties which result in the emission of X-rays.
Gamma-ray astronomy is a subfield of astronomy where scientists observe and study celestial objects and phenomena in outer space which emit cosmic electromagnetic radiation in the form of gamma rays.
In astronomy, the Nice model is a scenario for the dynamical evolution of the Solar System.
The solar core is the hot, dense region at the center of the Sun where energy is generated by nuclear fusion.
A solar neutrino is a neutrino originating from nuclear fusion in the Sun's core, and is the most common type of neutrino passing through any source observed on Earth at any particular moment.
The interplanetary dust cloud, or zodiacal cloud, consists of cosmic dust that pervades the space between planets.
The geology of Mercury is the scientific study of the surface, crust, and interior of the planet Mercury.
The atmosphere of Venus is the very dense layer of gases surrounding the planet Venus.
The geology of Venus is the scientific study of the surface, crust, and interior of the planet Venus.
Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance of about one hundred and fifty million kilometres, in a counterclockwise direction as viewed from above the Northern Hemisphere.
Earth's shadow is the shadow that Earth itself casts through its atmosphere and into outer space, toward the antisolar point.
Earthlight is the diffuse reflection of sunlight reflected from Earth's surface and clouds.
The biological and geological future of Earth can be extrapolated based on the estimated effects of several long-term influences.
Knowledge of the location of Earth has been shaped by four hundred years of telescopic observations, and has expanded radically since the start of the twentieth century.
The geology of the Moon, sometimes called selenology, is the structure and composition of the Moon, which is quite different from that of Earth.
The Moon is a differentiated body, being composed of a geochemically distinct crust, mantle, and planetary core.
The orbit of the Moon is, while stable and known, highly complex, and as such still studied by lunar theory.
The origin of the Moon is usually explained by a Mars-sized body, known as Theia, striking Earth, creating a debris ring that eventually collected into a single natural satellite, the Moon.
Theia is a hypothetical planet in the early Solar System which, according to the giant-impact hypothesis, collided with the proto-Earth about four and a half billion years ago.
Selenography is the study of the surface and physical features of the Moon.
The near side of the Moon is the hemisphere of the Moon that is facing Earth.
The far side of the Moon, also called the dark side of the Moon, is the hemisphere of the Moon that faces away from Earth; the opposite hemisphere being the near side.
The lunar south pole is the southernmost point on the Moon. It is of interest to scientists because of the occurrence of water ice in permanently shadowed areas around it.
The geology of Mars is the scientific study of the surface, crust, and interior of the planet Mars.
The geological history of Mars follows the physical evolution of Mars as substantiated by observations, indirect and direct measurements, and various inference techniques.
The planet Mars has two permanent polar ice caps of water ice and some dry ice, frozen carbon dioxide.

The possibility of life on Mars is a subject of interest in astrobiology due to the planet's proximity and similarities to Earth. To date, no conclusive evidence of past or present life has been found on Mars.
A near-Earth object is by definition any small Solar System body orbiting the Sun whose closest approach to the Sun is less than one point three times the Earth–Sun distance.
Eros is a stony asteroid of the Amor group, and the first discovered, and second-largest near-Earth object. It has an elongated shape.
Vesta is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt. It was discovered by the German astronomer Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers.
Pallas is the third-largest asteroid in the Solar System by volume and mass. It is the second asteroid to have been discovered, after Ceres.
Juno is a large asteroid in the asteroid belt. Juno was the third asteroid discovered, in eighteen hundred and four, by the German astronomer Karl Harding.
Hygiea is a large asteroid in the outer region of the main asteroid belt, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Ida is an asteroid in the Koronis family of the asteroid belt.
The Jupiter trojans, commonly called trojan asteroids or simply trojans, are a large group of asteroids that share the planet Jupiter's orbit around the Sun.
The atmosphere of Jupiter is the largest planetary atmosphere in the Solar System. It is mostly made of molecular hydrogen and helium in roughly solar proportions.
The magnetosphere of Jupiter is the cavity created in the solar wind by Jupiter's magnetic field.
The rings of Jupiter are a system of faint planetary rings. The Jovian rings were the third ring system to be discovered in the Solar System, after those of Saturn and Uranus.
The magnetosphere of Saturn is the cavity created in the flow of the solar wind by the planet's internally generated magnetic field.
Saturn has hundreds of moons with confirmed orbits, the most of any planet in the Solar System.
Tethys is the fifth-largest moon of Saturn. It was discovered by Giovanni Domenico Cassini in sixteen eighty-four, and is named after the titan Tethys of Greek mythology.
Dione is the fourth-largest moon of Saturn.
Iapetus is the outermost of Saturn's large moons.
Lakes of liquid ethane and methane exist on the surface of Titan, Saturn's largest moon. This was confirmed by the Cassini–Huygens space probe, and had been suspected long before.
The atmosphere of Uranus is composed primarily of hydrogen and helium. At depth, it is significantly enriched in volatiles, dubbed ices, such as water, ammonia, and methane.

Uranus has twenty-nine known moons. The twenty-seven with names are named after characters that appear in, or are mentioned in, William Shakespeare's plays and Alexander Pope's poem The Rape of the Lock.
Ariel is the fourth-largest moon of Uranus. Ariel orbits and rotates in Uranus's equatorial plane, which is almost perpendicular to the planet's orbit, giving the moon an extreme seasonal cycle.
Umbriel is the third-largest moon of Uranus. It was discovered in eighteen fifty-one by William Lassell at the same time as neighboring moon Ariel.
The rings of Uranus consist of thirteen planetary rings. They are intermediate in complexity between the more extensive set around Saturn and the simpler systems around Jupiter and Neptune.
Neptune has sixteen known moons, fourteen of which are named after water deities and creatures in Greek mythology.
The rings of Neptune consist primarily of five principal rings.
The atmosphere of Pluto is the layer of gases that surround the dwarf planet Pluto. It consists mainly of nitrogen, with minor amounts of methane and carbon monoxide.
There are five known moons of the dwarf planet Pluto. In order of distance from Pluto, they are Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra.
The scattered disc is a distant circumstellar disc in the Solar System that is sparsely populated by icy small Solar System bodies.

Planet Nine is a hypothetical ninth planet in the outer region of the Solar System. Its gravitational effects could explain the peculiar clustering of orbits for a group of extreme trans-Neptunian objects.
This exoplanet orbits a Sun-like star within its habitable zone.
This candidate Earth-sized exoplanet orbits within the habitable zone of a red dwarf star, the outermost of five planets discovered around the star by NASA's Kepler space telescope.
This confirmed near-Earth-sized exoplanet, likely rocky, orbits within the habitable zone of a K-type main-sequence star.
This disputed super-Earth exoplanet candidate was initially reported to orbit within the inner edge of the habitable zone of a sun-like star.
Proxima Centauri b, also referred to as Proxima b, is an exoplanet orbiting within the habitable zone of the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri.
This exoplanet orbits a red dwarf star about one hundred and twenty-four light-years away from Earth.
This exoplanet in the constellation of Vulpecula is about sixty-four light-years away from the Solar System.
This exoplanet, specifically a hot Jupiter, orbits a solar analog in the constellation Pegasus.
The Double Cluster consists of two open clusters that are close together in the northern constellation Perseus.
The Trapezium Cluster is a tight open cluster of stars in the heart of the Orion Nebula, in the constellation of Orion.
Forty-seven Tucanae is a globular cluster located in the constellation of Tucana.
Messier four is a globular cluster in the constellation of Scorpius. It was discovered by Philippe Loys de Chéseaux in seventeen forty-five and catalogued by Charles Messier in seventeen sixty-four.
Messier thirteen is a globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars in the constellation of Hercules.
Messier fifteen is a globular cluster in the constellation Pegasus. It was discovered by Jean-Dominique Maraldi in seventeen forty-six.
Messier twenty-two, also known as the Great Sagittarius Cluster, is an elliptical globular cluster of stars in the constellation Sagittarius.
The supernova of one thousand and six is likely the brightest observed stellar event in recorded history, exceeding roughly sixteen times the brightness of Venus.
The Crab Supernova is a supernova that was first observed in July of ten fifty-four, and remained visible until April of ten fifty-six.
Tycho's Supernova was a supernova of Type Ia in the constellation Cassiopeia, one of eight supernovae visible to the naked eye in recorded history.
Supernova nineteen eighty-seven A was a Type II supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

This gravitational wave was observed by the LIGO and Virgo detectors in August two thousand seventeen, originating within a shell elliptical galaxy about one hundred and thirty million light-years from Earth.
This galaxy is the result of a collision between two galaxies which are now in the process of merging.
This supergiant lenticular galaxy lies at the center of a galaxy cluster.
Markarian four hundred and twenty-one is a blazar located in the constellation Ursa Major.
Markarian five hundred and one is an elliptical galaxy with a spectrum extending to the highest energy gamma rays.
This Seyfert galaxy, also known as Perseus A, lies about two hundred and twenty-five million light-years from Earth in the direction of the constellation of Perseus.
This intermediate spiral Seyfert galaxy with weak inner ring structure lies in the constellation Canes Venatici.
This galaxy, sometimes referred to as the Fireworks Galaxy, is a grand design, face-on intermediate spiral galaxy with a small bright nucleus.
The Sculptor Galaxy is an intermediate spiral galaxy in the constellation Sculptor. It is a starburst galaxy, which means that it is currently undergoing a period of intense star formation.
The Fornax Cluster is a cluster of galaxies lying about sixty-two million light-years away.
The Perseus Cluster is a cluster of galaxies in the constellation Perseus.
In astrodynamics, the orbital eccentricity of an astronomical object is a dimensionless parameter that determines the amount by which its orbit around another body deviates from a perfect circle.
Orbital elements are the parameters required to uniquely identify a specific orbit.
Orbital inclination measures the tilt of an object's orbit around a celestial body.
The orbital period is the amount of time a given astronomical object takes to complete one orbit around another object.
Eclipses may occur repeatedly, separated by certain intervals of time: these intervals are called eclipse cycles.
A transit of Mercury across the Sun takes place when the planet Mercury passes directly between the Sun and a superior planet.
A transit of Venus takes place when Venus passes directly between the Sun and the Earth, becoming visible against, and hence obscuring a small portion of, the solar disc.
In lunar astronomy, libration is the cyclic variation in the apparent position of the Moon that is perceived by observers on the Earth.
Sidereal time is a system of timekeeping used especially by astronomers.
A lunar phase or Moon phase is the apparent shape of the Moon's sunlit side as viewed from Earth.
The full moon is the lunar phase when the Moon appears fully illuminated from Earth's perspective.
In astronomy, the new moon is the first lunar phase, when the Moon and Sun have the same ecliptic longitude. At this phase, the lunar disk is not visible to the naked eye.
An apsis is one of the two extreme points in the orbit of a planetary body about its primary body, either the farthest point or the nearest point.
Gravitational collapse is the contraction of an astronomical object due to the influence of its own gravity, which tends to draw matter inward toward the center of gravity.
Tidal acceleration is an effect of the tidal forces between an orbiting natural satellite and the primary planet that it orbits.
Dawn is the time that marks the beginning of twilight before sunrise.
Dusk occurs at the darkest stage of twilight, or at the very end of astronomical twilight after sunset and just before nightfall.
Noon, also known as noontime or midday, is twelve o'clock in the daytime.
Midnight is the transition time from one day to the next, the moment when the date changes, on the local official clock time for any particular jurisdiction.

Midnight sun, also known as polar day, is a natural phenomenon that occurs in the summer months in places north of the Arctic Circle or south of the Antarctic Circle, when the Sun remains visible all day and night.
Polar night is a phenomenon that occurs in the northernmost and southernmost regions of Earth when the Sun remains below the horizon for more than twenty-four hours.
A space rendezvous is a set of orbital maneuvers during which two spacecraft, one of which is often a space station, arrive at the same orbit and approach to a very close distance.

In celestial mechanics, orbital resonance occurs when orbiting bodies exert regular, periodic gravitational influence on each other, usually because their orbital periods are related by a ratio of small integers.
A polar orbit is one in which a satellite passes above or nearly above both poles of the body being orbited.
In celestial mechanics, a horseshoe orbit is a type of co-orbital motion of a small orbiting body relative to a larger orbiting body.

Celestial cartography, uranography, astrography or star cartography is the aspect of astronomy and branch of cartography concerned with mapping stars, galaxies, and other astronomical objects on the celestial sphere.

An asterism is an observed pattern or group of stars in the sky. Asterisms can be any identified star pattern, and therefore are a more general concept than the eighty-eight formally defined constellations.

Spherical astronomy, or positional astronomy, is a branch of observational astronomy used to locate astronomical objects on the celestial sphere, as seen at a particular date, time, and location on Earth.

In astronomy, right ascension is the angular distance of a particular point measured eastward along the celestial equator from the Sun at the March equinox to the hour circle of the point in question.
In astronomy, declination is the angular distance from the celestial equator on the celestial sphere; when paired with right ascension, it forms the equatorial coordinate system.
In astrophysics, stellar nucleosynthesis is the creation of chemical elements by nuclear reactions within stars.
In astrophysics, the carbon nitrogen oxygen cycle is one of the two known sets of fusion reactions by which stars convert hydrogen to helium, the other being the proton proton chain reaction.
The slow neutron capture process is a series of reactions in nuclear astrophysics that occur in stars, particularly asymptotic giant branch stars.
A stellar core is the extremely hot, dense region at the center of a star.
A radiative zone is a layer of a star's interior where energy is primarily transported toward the exterior by means of radiative diffusion and thermal conduction, rather than by convection.
A convection zone of a star is a layer which is unstable due to convection.
The stellar atmosphere is the outer region of the volume of a star, lying above the stellar core, radiation zone and convection zone.
Stellar rotation is the angular motion of a star about its axis.
Stellar mass is a phrase that is used by astronomers to describe the mass of a star.
In astronomy, the initial mass function is an empirical function that describes the initial distribution of masses for a population of stars during star formation.
A stellar wind is a flow of gas ejected from the upper atmosphere of a star.
In astrophysics, chemically peculiar stars are stars with distinct patterns of metal and helium abundances, at least in their surface layers.
A circumstellar disc is a ring shaped accretion disk of matter composed of gas, dust, planetesimals, asteroids, or collision fragments in orbit around a star.
A debris disk is a circumstellar disk of dust and debris in orbit around a star.
A protoplanetary disk is a rotating circumstellar disc of dense gas and dust surrounding a young newly formed star.
A proplyd, short for ionized protoplanetary disk, is an externally illuminated photoevaporating protoplanetary disk around a young star.
A sub-brown dwarf or planetary mass brown dwarf is an astronomical object that formed in the same manner as stars and brown dwarfs but that has a planetary mass.
In observational astronomy, a double star or visual double is a pair of stars that appear close to each other as viewed from Earth, especially with the aid of optical telescopes.
In astronomy, the term compact object refers collectively to white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes.
A black dwarf is a theoretical stellar remnant, specifically a white dwarf that has cooled sufficiently to no longer emit significant heat or light.
The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf star.
X-ray pulsars are a class of astronomical objects that are X-ray sources displaying strict periodic variations in X-ray intensity.
A magnetar is a type of neutron star with an extremely powerful magnetic field.
A radio-quiet neutron star is a neutron star that does not seem to emit radio emissions, but is still visible to Earth through electromagnetic radiation at other parts of the spectrum.

An exotic star is a hypothetical compact star composed of exotic matter, something not made of electrons, protons, neutrons, or muons, and balanced against gravitational collapse by degeneracy pressure.
A quark star is a hypothetical type of compact, exotic star, where extremely high core temperature and pressure have forced nuclear particles to form quark matter.
An intergalactic star, also known as an intracluster star or a rogue star, is a star not gravitationally bound to any galaxy.
The red giant branch, sometimes called the first giant branch, is the portion of the giant branch before helium ignition occurs in the course of stellar evolution.
A helium flash is a very brief thermal runaway nuclear fusion of large quantities of helium into carbon through the triple alpha process in the core of low mass stars.
The asymptotic giant branch is a region of the Hertzsprung Russell diagram populated by evolved cool luminous stars.
A starburst region is a region of space that is undergoing a large amount of star formation.
The Jeans instability is a concept in astrophysics that describes an instability that leads to the gravitational collapse of a cloud of gas or dust.
Pre-stellar cores are the nurseries of new stars, and are an early phase in the formation of low mass stars, before gravitational collapse produces a central protostar.
The Hayashi track is a luminosity temperature relationship obeyed by infant stars in the pre-main-sequence phase of stellar evolution.
A pre-main-sequence star is a star in the stage when it has not yet reached the main sequence.
Young stellar object denotes a star in its early stage of evolution.
A binary pulsar is a pulsar with a binary companion, often a white dwarf or neutron star.
In astronomy, a common envelope is gas that contains a binary-star system.
X-ray binaries are a class of binary stars that are luminous in X-rays.
The Roche lobe is the region around a star in a binary system within which orbiting material is gravitationally bound to that star.
A stellar association is a very loose star cluster, looser than both open clusters and globular clusters.
An open cluster is a type of star cluster made of tens to a few thousand stars that were formed from the same giant molecular cloud and have roughly the same age.
A blue straggler is a type of star that is more luminous and bluer than expected.
A super star cluster is a very massive young open cluster that is thought to be the precursor of a globular cluster.
A hypernova is a very energetic supernova which is believed to result from an extreme core collapse scenario.
A Type two supernova results from the violent explosion of a massive star following the rapid collapse of its core.
A superluminous supernova is a type of stellar explosion with a luminosity far higher than that of standard supernovae.

A pair-instability supernova is a type of supernova predicted to occur when pair production, the production of free electrons and positrons in the collision between atomic nuclei and energetic gamma rays, reduces the pressure inside a star.
Supernova nucleosynthesis is the nucleosynthesis of chemical elements in supernova explosions.
In radio astronomy, a fast radio burst is a transient radio wave caused by a high energy astrophysical process that is not yet understood.
A kilonova is a transient astronomical event that occurs in a compact binary system when two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole collide.
Asteroseismology is the study of oscillations in stars.
In astrophysics, the mass luminosity relation is an empirical and theoretical relationship between a star's mass and its luminosity.
A subdwarf is a star with luminosity class six under the Yerkes spectral classification system.
A subgiant is a star that is brighter than a normal main-sequence star of the same spectral class, but not as bright as giant stars.
In astronomy, a blue giant is a hot star with a luminosity class of giant or bright giant.
A carbon star is typically an asymptotic giant branch star, a luminous red giant, whose atmosphere contains more carbon than oxygen.
A blue supergiant is a hot, luminous star, often referred to as an evolved massive supergiant.
Red supergiants are stars with a supergiant luminosity class and a stellar classification of type K or M.
A hypergiant is a very rare type of star that has an extremely high luminosity, mass, size and mass loss because of its extreme stellar winds.
Be stars are a heterogeneous set of stars with B spectral types and emission lines.
In astronomy, cataclysmic variable stars are stars which irregularly increase in brightness by a large factor, then drop back down to a quiescent state.
Classical Cepheids are a type of Cepheid variable star, young variable stars that exhibit regular radial pulsations.
Lyrae variables are periodic variable stars, commonly found in globular clusters and other old stellar populations in galaxies.
Type two Cepheids are variable stars which pulsate with regular periods.
Luminous blue variables are rare, massive, evolved stars that show unpredictable and sometimes dramatic variations in their spectra and brightness.
Mira variables are a class of pulsating stars characterized by very red colours, long pulsation periods, and large changes in brightness.
The unqualified term instability strip usually refers to a region of the Hertzsprung Russell diagram largely occupied by several related classes of pulsating variable stars.
Galactic astronomy is the study of the Milky Way galaxy and all its contents.
Extragalactic astronomy is the branch of astronomy concerned with objects outside the Milky Way galaxy.
An astrophysical jet is an astronomical phenomenon where ionised matter is expelled at high velocity from an astronomical object, in a pair of narrow streams in opposite directions.
An intermediate-mass black hole is a class of black hole with a mass significantly higher than stellar black holes but lower than the supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies.
Micro black holes, also known as mini black holes and quantum mechanical black holes, are hypothetical tiny black holes, for which quantum mechanical effects play an important role.

The Schwarzschild radius is a parameter in the Schwarzschild solution to Einstein's field equations that corresponds to the radius of a sphere which, if all the mass of an object were compressed within it, would become a black hole.
An interstellar cloud is an accumulation of gas, plasma, and cosmic dust in galaxies.
Interstellar ice consists of grains of volatiles in the ice phase that form in the interstellar medium.
In astronomy, reflection nebulae are clouds of interstellar dust which might reflect the light of a nearby star or stars.
An emission nebula is a nebula formed of ionized gases that emit light of various wavelengths.
In astronomy a superbubble or supershell is a cavity which is hundreds of light years across and is populated with hot gas atoms, less dense than the surrounding interstellar medium.
High-velocity clouds are large accumulations of gas with an unusually rapid motion relative to their surroundings.
In astroparticle physics, an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray is a cosmic ray with an energy far beyond that of any particle accelerator.
The galactic plane is the plane on which most of a disk-shaped galaxy's mass lies.
A thin disk is a structural component of spiral galaxies, composed of stars, gas and dust.
A thick disk is one of the structural components of about two thirds of all disk galaxies, including the Milky Way.
In astronomy, a galactic bulge is a tightly packed group of stars within a larger star formation.
The rotation curve of a disc galaxy is a plot of the orbital speeds of visible stars or gas in that galaxy versus their radial distance from that galaxy's centre.
A galactic halo is an extended, roughly spherical component of a galaxy which extends beyond the main, visible component.
In modern models of physical cosmology, a dark matter halo is a basic unit of cosmological structure.
Interacting galaxies, also known as colliding galaxies, are two or more galaxies whose gravitational fields result in a disturbance of one another.
Galaxy mergers can occur when two or more galaxies collide.
The Andromeda and Milky Way collision is a galactic collision that may occur between the two largest galaxies in the Local Group.
A galactic tide is a tidal force experienced by objects subject to the gravitational field of a galaxy such as the Milky Way.
A satellite galaxy is a smaller companion galaxy that travels on bound orbits within the gravitational potential of a more massive and luminous host galaxy.
In astronomy, weak gravitational lensing is a technique to map the mass distribution of astronomical objects.
Intergalactic dust is cosmic dust in between galaxies in intergalactic space.
In astronomy, the intracluster medium is the superheated plasma that permeates a galaxy cluster.
A field galaxy is a galaxy that does not belong to a larger galaxy group or cluster and hence is gravitationally alone.
In astrophysics, dark flow is a controversial hypothesis to explain certain non random measurements of peculiar velocity of galaxy clusters.
A wormhole is a hypothetical structure that connects disparate points in spacetime.
In cosmology, galaxy filaments are the largest known structures in the universe, consisting of walls of galactic superclusters.
A large quasar group is a collection of quasars that form what are thought to constitute the largest astronomical structures in the known universe.
The Hubble sequence is a morphological classification scheme for galaxies published by Edwin Hubble.
An unbarred spiral galaxy is a type of spiral galaxy without a central bar.
A grand design spiral galaxy is a spiral galaxy with prominent and well defined continuous spiral arms.
A flocculent spiral galaxy is a type of spiral galaxy whose arms are patchy and discontinuous rather than well defined.
A Magellanic spiral galaxy is a spiral galaxy with only one spiral arm.
Density wave theory is a theory proposed to explain the spiral arm structure of spiral galaxies.
In astronomy, the Tully Fisher relation is an empirical relationship between the mass or intrinsic luminosity of a spiral galaxy and its rotation velocity.
Dwarf elliptical galaxies are elliptical galaxies that are smaller than ordinary elliptical galaxies.
The Faber Jackson relation provided the first empirical power law relation between the luminosity and the central stellar velocity dispersion of elliptical galaxies.
A dark galaxy is a hypothesized galaxy with dark matter but no, or very few, stars.
A brightest cluster galaxy is defined as the brightest galaxy in a cluster of galaxies.
A ring galaxy is a type of galaxy that includes a large annular structure.
A peculiar galaxy is a galaxy of unusual size, shape, or composition.

The Eddington luminosity, also referred to as the Eddington limit, is the maximum luminosity a body such as a star can achieve when there is balance between the force of radiation acting outward and the gravitational force acting inward.
Luminous infrared galaxies are galaxies that emit most of their enormous output in the infrared.
In astronomical spectroscopy, the Lyman alpha forest is a series of absorption lines in the spectra of distant galaxies and quasars arising from neutral hydrogen.
A cosmological horizon is one of two boundaries in three dimensional space, the particle horizon or the event horizon.
The particle horizon is the maximum distance from which light from particles could have traveled to the observer in the age of the universe.
In physical cosmology, the shape of the universe refers to both its local geometry and cosmic topology.
The heat death of the universe is a scientific hypothesis regarding the ultimate fate of the universe which posits the universe will evolve to a state of no thermodynamic free energy.
In physical cosmology, the Big Rip is a hypothetical cosmological model concerning the ultimate fate of the universe, in which the matter of the universe is progressively torn apart.
The Big Crunch is a hypothetical scenario for the ultimate fate of the universe, in which the expansion of the universe eventually reverses and the universe recollapses.
A cyclic model is any of several cosmological models in which the universe follows infinite, or indefinite, self sustaining cycles.
The cosmic neutrino background is a proposed background particle radiation composed of neutrinos.
In physical cosmology, Big Bang nucleosynthesis is a model for the production of light nuclei during the early phases of the universe.
In cosmology, the missing baryon problem is an observed discrepancy between the amount of baryonic matter detected from shortly after the Big Bang and from more recent epochs.
In physical cosmology, baryogenesis is the physical process that is hypothesized to have taken place during the early universe to produce baryonic asymmetry.
The expansion of the universe is the increase in distance between gravitationally unbound parts of the observable universe with time.
Observations show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, such that the velocity at which a distant galaxy recedes from the observer is continuously increasing with time.
In cosmology, a Hubble volume is a spherical region of the observable universe surrounding an observer beyond which objects recede from that observer faster than the speed of light.
The expansion of the universe is parametrized by a dimensionless scale factor, also known as the cosmic scale factor.
In cosmology, baryon acoustic oscillations are fluctuations in the density of the visible baryonic matter of the universe, caused by acoustic density waves in the early universe.
Primordial fluctuations are density variations in the early universe which are considered the seeds of all structure in the universe.
The Lambda cold dark matter model is the standard form of the Big Bang theory of cosmology governing the chronology of the universe.
In physics, quintessence is a hypothetical form of dark energy, postulated as an explanation of the observation of an accelerating universe.
In standard cosmology, comoving distance and proper distance are two closely related distance measures used by cosmologists to define distances between objects.

In cosmology and philosophy of science, the anthropic principle is the proposition that the range of possible observations made about a universe is constrained by the fact that observation is only possible in a universe capable of developing observers.
The flatness problem is a cosmological fine tuning problem within the Big Bang model of the universe.
The horizon problem, also known as the homogeneity problem, is a cosmological fine tuning problem within the Big Bang model of the universe.
In cosmology, the steady-state model was an alternative to the Big Bang theory, in which the density of matter in the expanding universe remains unchanged.
In Big Bang models of physical cosmology, the age of the universe is the cosmological time back to the point when the scale factor of the universe extrapolates to zero.
In physical cosmology, the grand unification epoch is a poorly understood period in the evolution of the early universe following the Planck epoch and preceding inflation.

In physical cosmology, the electroweak epoch was the period in the evolution of the early universe when the temperature of the universe had fallen enough that the strong force separated from the electroweak interaction.

In physical cosmology, the quark epoch was the period in the evolution of the early universe when the four fundamental interactions had taken their present forms, but the temperature was still too high for quarks to bind together.
In physical cosmology, the photon epoch was the period in the evolution of the early universe in which photons dominated the energy of the universe.
In the fields of Big Bang theory and cosmology, reionization is the process that caused electrically neutral atoms in the primordial universe to reionize after the lapse of the dark ages.
Planetary science is the scientific study of celestial bodies such as planets, moons, asteroids and comets, and of planetary systems.
The definition of the term planet has changed several times since the word was coined by the ancient Greeks.
A carbon planet is a hypothetical type of planet that contains more carbon than oxygen.
An iron planet is a type of planet that consists primarily of an iron rich core with little or no mantle.
Chthonian planets are a hypothetical class of celestial objects resulting from the stripping away of a gas giant's hydrogen and helium atmosphere and outer layers.
An Earth analog, also called an Earth twin or second Earth, is a planet or moon with environmental conditions similar to those found on Earth.
An asteroid family is a population of asteroids that share similar proper orbital elements, such as semi major axis, eccentricity, and orbital inclination.
A satellite system is a set of gravitationally bound objects in orbit around a planetary mass object or minor planet.
An exomoon or extrasolar moon is a natural satellite that orbits an exoplanet or other non stellar extrasolar body.
A sungrazing comet is a comet that passes extremely close to the Sun at perihelion.
A bolide is normally taken to mean an exceptionally bright meteor.
In astronomy, axial tilt, also known as obliquity, is the angle between an object's rotational axis and its orbital axis.
In planetary science, planetary differentiation is the process by which the chemical elements of a planetary body accumulate in different areas of that body.
Planetary habitability is a measure used in astrobiology to characterize a planet's or a natural satellite's potential to develop and sustain an environment hospitable to life.
In astrobiology and planetary astrophysics, the galactic habitable zone is the region of a galaxy in which life is most likely to develop.
In astronomy, the geometric albedo of a celestial body is the ratio of its actual brightness as seen from the light source to that of an idealized flat, fully reflecting surface.
In astronomy, planetary mass is a measure of the mass of a planet-like astronomical object.
Antlia is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere. Its name means pump in Latin and Greek; it represents an air pump.
Apus is a small constellation in the southern sky. It represents a bird-of-paradise, and its name means without feet in Greek because the bird-of-paradise was once believed to lack feet.
Caelum is a faint constellation in the southern sky, introduced in the seventeen fifties by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille and counted among the modern constellations.
Camelopardalis is a large but faint constellation of the Northern Sky representing a giraffe.

Carina is a constellation in the southern sky. Its name is Latin for the keel of a ship, and it was the southern foundation of the larger constellation of Argo Navis until that constellation was divided.
Cetus is a constellation, sometimes called the whale in English. In Greek mythology, the Cetus was a large sea monster.
Chamaeleon is a small constellation in the deep southern sky. It is named after the chameleon, a kind of lizard.
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for compass, referring to the drafting tool.
Columba is a faint constellation designated in the late sixteenth century, remaining in official use. Its name is Latin for dove.
Coma Berenices is an ancient asterism in the northern sky, which has been defined as one of the modern constellations.
Corona Australis is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere. Its Latin name means southern crown, and it is the southern counterpart of Corona Borealis.
Delphinus is a small constellation in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere, close to the celestial equator. Its name is the Latin version for the Greek word for dolphin.
Dorado is a constellation in the Southern Sky. It was named in the late sixteenth century and is now one of the modern constellations.
Draco is a constellation in the far northern sky. Its name is derived from the Latin word for dragon.
Equuleus is a faint constellation located just north of the celestial equator. Its name is Latin for little horse, a foal.
Eridanus is a constellation which stretches along the southern celestial hemisphere. It is represented as a river.
Fornax is a constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, partly ringed by the celestial river Eridanus. Its name is Latin for furnace.
Grus is a constellation in the southern sky. Its name is Latin for the crane, a type of bird.
Hercules is a constellation named after Hercules, the Roman mythological hero adapted from the Greek hero Heracles.
Horologium is a faint constellation in the southern sky, named for the pendulum clock.
Hydrus is a small constellation in the deep southern sky. It was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Dutch navigators.
Indus is a constellation in the southern sky first professionally surveyed by Europeans in the fifteen nineties and mapped on a globe by Petrus Plancius.
Lacerta is one of the modern constellations defined by the International Astronomical Union. Its name is Latin for lizard.
Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere. Its name is Latin for the smaller lion, in contrast to Leo, the larger lion.
Lepus is a constellation lying just south of the celestial equator. Its name is Latin for hare.
Lupus is a constellation of the mid-Southern Sky. Its name is Latin for wolf.
Mensa is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere near the south celestial pole, one of fourteen constellations drawn up by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
Microscopium is a minor constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, one of twelve created by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
Monoceros is a faint constellation on the celestial equator. Its definition is attributed to the cartographer Petrus Plancius.
Musca is a small constellation in the deep southern sky. It was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Dutch navigators.
Norma is a small constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere between Ara and Lupus, one of twelve drawn up by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
Octans is a faint constellation located in the deep Southern Sky. Its name is Latin for the eighth part of a circle, but it is named after the octant, a navigational instrument.
Pavo is a constellation in the southern sky whose name is Latin for peacock.
Pictor is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere, located between the star Canopus and the Large Magellanic Cloud. Its name is Latin for painter.
Piscis Austrinus is a constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere. The name is Latin for the southern fish.
Puppis is a constellation in the southern sky. It was originally part of the traditional constellation of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts.
Pyxis is a small and faint constellation in the southern sky. Its name is Latin for a mariner's compass.
Sagitta is a dim but distinctive constellation in the northern sky. Its name is Latin for arrow.
Sculptor is a faint constellation in the southern sky. It represents a sculptor. It was introduced by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
Sextans is a faint, minor constellation on the celestial equator which was introduced by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius. Its name is Latin for the astronomical sextant.
Telescopium is a minor constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, one of twelve named by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
Triangulum is a small constellation in the northern sky. Its name is Latin for triangle, derived from its three brightest stars.
Triangulum Australe is a small constellation in the far Southern Celestial Hemisphere. Its name is Latin for the southern triangle, which distinguishes it from Triangulum.
Tucana is a constellation in the southern sky, named after the toucan, a South American bird.
Vela is a constellation in the southern sky. Its name is Latin for the sails of a ship, and it was originally part of a larger constellation.
Volans is a constellation in the southern sky. It represents a flying fish.
Vulpecula is a faint constellation in the Northern Sky. Its name is Latin for little fox.
Argo Navis, or simply Argo, is one of Ptolemy's constellations, now a grouping of three constellations. It was formerly a single large constellation in the Southern Sky.
Quadrans Muralis was a constellation created by the French astronomer Jerome Lalande. It depicted a wall-mounted quadrant with which he had made his observations.
The March equinox or northward equinox is the equinox on the Earth when the subsolar point appears to leave the Southern Hemisphere and cross the celestial equator, heading northward.
The September equinox or southward equinox is the moment when the Sun appears to cross the celestial equator, heading southward.
The summer solstice or estival solstice occurs when one of Earth's poles has its maximum tilt toward the Sun.
The winter solstice, or hibernal solstice, occurs when either of Earth's poles reaches its maximum tilt away from the Sun.
In astronomy and celestial navigation, the hour angle is the dihedral angle between the meridian plane and the hour circle containing a celestial body.
In astronomy, position angle is the convention for measuring angles on the sky.
In astronomy, the meridian is the great circle passing through the celestial poles, as well as the zenith and nadir of an observer's location.
The nadir is the direction pointing directly below a particular location.
The zenith is the imaginary point on the celestial sphere directly above a particular location.
The celestial equator is the great circle of the imaginary celestial sphere on the same plane as the equator of a planet, by convention generally Earth.
A tropical year, solar year, or tropical period is the time that the Sun takes to return to the same position in the sky.
The galactic coordinate system is a celestial coordinate system in spherical coordinates, with the Sun as its center and the primary direction aligned with the approximate center of the Milky Way.
Twilight is daylight illumination produced by diffuse sky radiation when the Sun is below the horizon as sunlight from the upper atmosphere is scattered.
Sunrise is the moment when the upper rim of the Sun appears on the horizon in the morning.
Morning is either the period from sunrise to noon, or the period from midnight to noon.
Daytime is the period of the day in which the Sun is above the local horizon in a given location.
Afternoon is the period from noon to sunset or evening.
Evening is the period of a day that begins at the end of afternoon and overlaps with the beginning of night.
The Belt of Venus, also called the antitwilight arch, is an atmospheric phenomenon visible shortly before dawn or after dusk, during twilight.
The blue hour is the period of twilight when the Sun is several degrees below the horizon, during which the remaining sunlight takes on a predominantly blue hue.
In photography, the golden hour is the period of daytime shortly after sunrise or before sunset, during which daylight is redder and softer than when the sun is higher in the sky.
In astronomy, the velocity dispersion is the statistical dispersion of velocities about the mean velocity for a group of astronomical objects.
The umbra, penumbra and antumbra are three distinct parts of a shadow, made by any light source after impinging on an opaque object of lesser size.
In astronomy, a transit is the passage of a celestial body directly between a larger body and the observer.
A supermoon is a full moon or a new moon that nearly coincides with perigee, the closest that the Moon comes to the Earth in its orbit.
In astronomy, axial precession is a gravity-induced, slow, and continuous change in the orientation of an astronomical body's rotational axis.
Observational astronomy is a division of astronomy that is concerned with recording data about the observable universe.
Sky brightness refers to the visual perception of the sky and how it scatters and diffuses light.
In astronomy, absolute magnitude is a measure of the luminosity of a celestial object on an inverse logarithmic astronomical magnitude scale.
The Zone of Avoidance is the area of the sky that is obscured by the Milky Way.
In astronomy, a photometric system is a set of well-defined passbands, with a known sensitivity to incident radiation.
Polarization of electromagnetic radiation is a useful tool for detecting various astronomical phenomena.
In spectroscopy, a forbidden mechanism is a spectral line associated with absorption or emission of photons by atoms or molecules which is not allowed by the usual selection rules.
Telluric contamination is contamination of the astronomical spectra by the Earth's atmosphere.
In astronomy, surface brightness quantifies the apparent brightness or flux density per unit angular area of a spatially extended object such as a galaxy or nebula.
A megamaser is a type of astrophysical maser, which is a naturally occurring source of stimulated spectral line emission.
In astronomy, the spectral index of a source is a measure of the dependence of radiative flux density on frequency.
