In astronomy, a corona is the outermost layer of a star's atmosphere, a region filled with relatively hot, tenuous plasma.
Orcus is a dwarf planet located in the Kuiper belt, with one large moon, Vanth.
Gonggong is a dwarf planet and a member of the scattered disc beyond Neptune. It has a highly eccentric and inclined orbit.
The dwarf planet Haumea has two known moons, named after Hawaiian goddesses.
Dysnomia is the only known moon of the dwarf planet Eris.
In astronomy, the Hills cloud, also called the inner Oort cloud, is a theoretical vast circumstellar disc, interior to the Oort cloud.
A sednoid is a trans-Neptunian object with a large semi-major axis, a distant perihelion and a highly eccentric orbit, similar to that of the dwarf planet Sedna.
Following the discovery of the planet Neptune, there was considerable speculation that another planet might exist beyond its orbit.
The Kreutz sungrazers are a family of sungrazing comets, characterized by orbits taking them extremely close to the Sun at perihelion.
Acrux is a multiple star system and the brightest star in the southern constellation of Crux.
Beta Centauri is a triple star system in the southern constellation of Centaurus. It is officially called Hadar.
CW Leonis is a variable carbon star that is embedded in a thick dust envelope.
Gamma Cassiopeiae is a multiple star system at the center of the distinctive asterism in the northern circumpolar constellation of Cassiopeia.
TW Hydrae is a young star in the constellation of Hydra, about eight tenths of the mass of the Sun.
Zeta Ophiuchi is a single star located in the constellation of Ophiuchus. It is the third brightest star in the constellation.
The Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is a complex of interstellar clouds with different nebulae, particularly a dark nebula.
Sagittarius B two is a giant molecular cloud of gas and dust that is located near the center of the Milky Way.
The Local Interstellar Cloud, also known as the Local Fluff, is an interstellar cloud roughly thirty light years across, through which the Solar System is moving.
The Perseus Arm is one of two major spiral arms of the Milky Way galaxy.
The Magellanic Stream is a stream of high-velocity clouds of gas extending behind the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
The Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is an elliptical loop-shaped satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
BL Lacertae is a highly variable, extragalactic active galactic nucleus.
The galaxy numbered five thousand five hundred and forty eight in the New General Catalogue is a Seyfert galaxy with a bright, active nucleus.
The Milky Way has several smaller galaxies gravitationally bound to it, as part of the Milky Way subgroup.
The group of galaxies around Messier eighty one is a galaxy group in the constellations Ursa Major and Camelopardalis.
The Shapley Supercluster is one of the largest concentrations of galaxies in the observable universe that forms a bound, gravitationally interacting system.
The South Pole Wall is a massive cosmic structure formed by a giant wall of galaxies that extends across a great stretch of sky.
The Great Wall found by the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey is a supercluster complex identified in the survey's redshift data.
The Local Hole, also known as the void named after Keenan, Barger and Cowie, is an immense, comparatively empty region of space.
The Giant Void is an extremely large region of space with an underdensity of galaxies located in the constellation Canes Venatici.
The dipole repeller is a center of effective repulsion in the large-scale flow of galaxies in the neighborhood of the Milky Way.
The cold spot of the cosmic microwave background is a region of the sky seen in microwaves that has been found to be unusually large and cold.
In astrodynamics, orbital station-keeping is keeping a spacecraft at a fixed distance from another spacecraft or celestial body.
In astronautics and aerospace engineering, the bi-elliptic transfer is an orbital maneuver that moves a spacecraft from one orbit to another.
In orbital mechanics, a frozen orbit is an orbit for an artificial satellite in which perturbations have been minimized by careful selection of the orbital parameters.
A halo orbit is a periodic, non-planar orbit associated with one of the Lagrange points in the three-body problem of orbital mechanics.
In orbital mechanics, a Lissajous orbit is a quasi-periodic orbital trajectory that an object can follow around a Lagrangian point.
A graveyard orbit, also called a junk orbit or disposal orbit, is an orbit that lies away from common operational orbits.
The Great Filter is the economist Robin Hanson's name for whatever step makes life that spreads across the stars so rare.
Computational astrophysics refers to the methods and computing tools developed and used in astrophysics research.
Present understanding in various scientific fields allows for the prediction of some far-future events.
The Astrophysics Data System is a digital library portal for researchers on astronomy and physics.
The Set of Identifications, Measurements and Bibliography for Astronomical Data is an astronomical database of objects beyond the Solar System.
The VizieR Catalogue Service is an astronomical catalog service provided by the Strasbourg Data Centre for astronomy.
The Henry Draper Catalogue is an astronomical star catalogue giving spectroscopic classifications for hundreds of thousands of stars.
The New General Catalogue of Nebulae and Clusters of Stars is an astronomical catalogue of deep-sky objects compiled by John Louis Emil Dreyer.
The Uppsala General Catalogue of Galaxies is a catalogue of galaxies visible from the northern hemisphere.
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey is a major imaging and spectroscopic redshift survey using a dedicated wide-angle optical telescope.
Methods of detecting exoplanets usually rely on indirect strategies, deducing a planet's existence rather than imaging it directly.
Several forms of biochemistry are agreed to be scientifically viable, but are not proven to exist at this time.
Geochemistry is the science that uses the tools and principles of chemistry to explain the mechanisms behind major geological systems such as the Earth's crust and its oceans.

Biogeochemistry is the scientific discipline that involves the study of the chemical, physical, geological, and biological processes and reactions that govern the composition of the natural environment.
Organic geochemistry is the study of the impacts and processes that organisms have had on the Earth. It is mainly concerned with the composition and mode of origin of organic matter in rocks.
In Earth science, a geochemical cycle is the pathway that chemical elements undergo to be able to interact with the reservoirs of chemicals in the surface and crust of the Earth.
The Goldschmidt classification, developed by Victor Goldschmidt, is a geochemical classification which groups the chemical elements within the Earth according to their preferred host phases.
In geology, igneous differentiation is an umbrella term for the various processes by which magmas undergo bulk chemical change during melting, cooling, emplacement, or eruption.
Isotope geochemistry is an aspect of geology based upon the study of natural variations in the relative abundances of isotopes of various elements.
In geochemistry, geophysics and nuclear physics, primordial nuclides are nuclides found on Earth that have existed in their current form since before the Earth was formed.
Natural hydrogen, also known as white hydrogen, is molecular hydrogen present on Earth that is formed by natural processes.
A trace element is a chemical element of a minute quantity, especially used in referring to a micronutrient, but also used to refer to minor elements in rocks.
Earth's internal heat budget is fundamental to the thermal history of the Earth, and describes the flow of heat from Earth's interior to the surface.
Geodynamics is a subfield of geophysics dealing with dynamics of the Earth. It applies physics, chemistry and mathematics to the understanding of how mantle convection leads to plate tectonics.
Geophysical fluid dynamics, in its broadest meaning, is the application of fluid dynamics to naturally occurring flows, such as lava, oceans, and atmospheres.
Gravimetry is the measurement of the strength of a gravitational field.
The gravity of Earth is the net acceleration that is imparted to objects due to the combined effect of gravitation and the centrifugal force.
Near-surface geophysics is the use of geophysical methods to investigate small-scale features in the shallow subsurface.
The geomagnetic poles are antipodal points where the axis of a best-fitting dipole intersects the surface of Earth.
In geophysics, a magnetic anomaly is a local variation in the magnetic field of a planetary body resulting from variations in the chemistry or magnetism of the rocks.
The north magnetic pole is a point on the surface of Earth's Northern Hemisphere at which the planet's magnetic field points vertically downward.
The south magnetic pole is the point on Earth's Southern Hemisphere where the geomagnetic field lines are directed perpendicular to the surface.
A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of the Earth's magnetosphere that is driven by interactions between the magnetosphere and the solar wind.
A seismic wave is a mechanical wave of acoustic energy that travels through the Earth or another planetary body.
In solid mechanics, shear waves are a type of elastic wave and are one of the two main types of elastic body waves.
Seismic intensity scales categorize the intensity or severity of ground shaking at a given location, such as resulting from an earthquake.
Seismic magnitude scales are used to describe the overall strength of an earthquake.
Seismic refraction is a geophysical principle governed by the law of refraction, using the bending of seismic waves by rock layers.
A seismic shadow zone is an area of the Earth's surface where seismographs cannot detect direct waves from an earthquake.
In geology, the elastic-rebound theory is an explanation for how energy is released during an earthquake.
Preparations for earthquakes can consist of survival measures that improve survival in the event of an earthquake, or mitigating measures taken beforehand.
An earthquake early warning system is a system of accelerometers, seismometers, communication, computers, and alarms devised for rapidly notifying people of ground shaking.
Earthquake prediction is an operational objective within the broader framework of earthquake forecasting, specifically a forecast with narrow bounds of time and place.
In seismology, the mainshock is the largest earthquake in a sequence, sometimes preceded by one or more foreshocks, and almost always followed by many aftershocks.
A foreshock is an earthquake that occurs before a larger seismic event, the mainshock, and is related to it in both time and space.
The epicenter in seismology is the point on the Earth's surface directly above a hypocenter or focus, the point where an earthquake begins.
The focal mechanism of an earthquake describes the deformation in the source region that generates the seismic waves.
A slow earthquake is a discontinuous, earthquake-like event that releases energy over a period of hours to months, rather than seconds.
An interplate earthquake occurs at the boundary between two tectonic plates.
A deep-focus earthquake in seismology is an earthquake with a hypocenter depth exceeding three hundred kilometres.
Historical geology is a discipline that uses the principles and methods of geology to reconstruct the geological history of Earth.
The age of Earth is estimated to be about four and a half thousand million years.
Potassium argon dating is a radiometric dating method used in geochronology and archaeology, based on the measurement of the product of the radioactive decay of an isotope of potassium.
The rubidium strontium dating method is a radiometric dating technique used to determine the age of rocks and minerals.
Monazite geochronology is a dating technique to study geological history using the mineral monazite.
Thermochronology is the study of the thermal evolution of a region of a planet.
Paleoclimatology is the scientific study of climates predating the invention of meteorological instruments.
Although oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, due to its high reactivity it mostly exists in compound forms such as water and carbon dioxide.
Paleotempestology is the study of past tropical cyclone activity by means of geological proxies as well as historical documentary records.
A paleothermometer is a methodology that provides an estimate of the ambient temperature at the time of formation of a natural material.
The Huronian glaciation refers to a series of ancient glacial periods, among the earliest known in Earth's history.
The Marinoan glaciation was a period of worldwide glaciation during the Cryogenian period.
The Hirnantian glaciation, also known as the Early Paleozoic Ice Age, was a glaciation at the end of the Ordovician.
The Late Paleozoic Icehouse was an ice age that began in the Late Devonian and ended in the Permian.
The Last Glacial Maximum was the most recent time during the Last Glacial Period when ice sheets were at their greatest extent.
The Late Pleistocene to the beginning of the Holocene saw the extinction of the majority of the world's megafauna.
Palaeogeography is the study of historical geography, generally physical landscapes.
The Paleo-Tethys Ocean was an ocean located along the northern margin of the paleocontinent Gondwana.
A paleocontinent is a distinct area of continental crust that existed as a major landmass in the geological past.
The Eoarchean is the first era of the Archean Eon of the geologic record.
The Paleoarchean, formerly known as the early Archean, is a geologic era within the Archean Eon.
The Neoarchean is the last geologic era in the Archean Eon, defined by dates rather than by any event in the rocks.
The Mesoproterozoic Era was the first era of Earth's history for which a fairly definite geological record survives.
The Neoproterozoic is the last of the three geologic eras of the Proterozoic eon, and the last era of the Precambrian.
The Andean orogeny is an ongoing process of orogeny that began in the Early Jurassic and is responsible for the rise of the Andes mountains.
The Cretaceous Paleogene boundary is a geological signature, usually a thin band of rock containing much more iridium than the layers around it.
The geology of the Appalachians dates back more than a thousand million years, to when two continental cratons collided.
The geology of the Himalayas is one of the most dramatic and visible creations of the immense mountain range formed by plate tectonic forces.
The Hawaii hotspot is a volcanic hotspot located near the namesake Hawaiian Islands, in the northern Pacific Ocean.
The Laramide orogeny was a time period of mountain building in western North America, beginning in the Late Cretaceous.
The Acasta Gneiss is a body of Archean basement rocks that form the northwestern edge of the Slave Craton.
The Yellowstone hotspot is a volcanic hotspot responsible for large scale volcanism in the northwestern United States.
Earth pigments are naturally occurring minerals that have been used since prehistoric times as pigments.
Mineral physics is the science of materials that compose the interior of planets, particularly the Earth.
Arsenate minerals usually refer to the naturally occurring orthoarsenates, possessing the arsenate anion group.
The borate minerals are minerals which contain a borate anion group.
Halide minerals are those minerals with a dominant halide anion.
Native element minerals are those elements that occur in nature in uncombined form with a distinct mineral structure.
A native metal is any metal that is found pure in its metallic form in nature.
Telluric iron, also called native iron, is iron that originated on Earth, and is found in a metallic form rather than as an ore.
The oxide mineral class includes those minerals in which the oxide anion is bonded to one or more metals.
Brookite is one of the natural forms of titanium dioxide, and it crystallises in the orthorhombic system.
In mineralogy, the spinels are any of a class of minerals which crystallise in the cubic crystal system.
Coltan is a dull black metallic ore from which the elements niobium and tantalum are extracted.
Thorianite is a rare thorium oxide mineral.
Silicate minerals are rock-forming minerals made up of silicate groups. They are the largest and most important class of minerals.
Aluminosilicate refers to materials containing linkages of silicon and aluminium through oxygen.
Amphibole is a group of inosilicate minerals, forming prism or needlelike crystals, composed of double chains of silicate units.
Diopside is a pyroxene mineral of calcium and magnesium.
Hedenbergite is the iron-rich end member of the pyroxene group.
Pigeonite is a mineral in the pyroxene group, containing calcium, magnesium and iron.
The chlorites are the group of phyllosilicate minerals common in low-grade metamorphic rocks and in altered igneous rocks.
Clay minerals are hydrous aluminium phyllosilicates, sometimes with variable amounts of iron, magnesium, alkali metals and alkaline earths.
Vermiculite is a hydrous phyllosilicate mineral which undergoes significant expansion when heated.
Plagioclase is a series of framework silicate minerals within the feldspar group.
Phosphate minerals are minerals that contain the tetrahedrally coordinated phosphate anion.
The sulfate minerals are a class of minerals that include the sulfate ion within their structure.
Within the field of geology, Bowen's reaction series describes the order in which minerals crystallise from a cooling magma.
Porosity or void fraction is a measure of the void spaces in a material, as a fraction of the total volume.
Iron ores are rocks and minerals from which metallic iron can be economically extracted.
Extrusive rock refers to the mode of igneous rock formation in which hot magma from inside the Earth flows out onto the surface as lava.
In geology, an igneous intrusion is a body of intrusive igneous rock that forms by crystallization of magma slowly cooling below the surface.
Intrusive rock is formed when magma penetrates existing rock, crystallizes, and solidifies underground.
Greisen is a highly altered granitic rock, usually composed predominantly of quartz and micas.
Porphyry copper deposits are copper ore bodies that are formed from hydrothermal fluids that originate from a magma chamber several kilometres below.
Volcanic rocks are rocks formed from lava erupted from a volcano.
Serpentinization is a hydration and metamorphic transformation of iron and magnesium minerals, such as olivine, in mantle rock.
Blueschist is a metavolcanic rock that forms by the metamorphism of basalt and similar rocks at relatively low temperatures but high pressure.
In structural geology, tectonites are metamorphic or tectonically-deformed rocks whose fabric reflects the history of their deformation.
Cataclasite is a cohesive granular fault rock, formed by the crushing and grinding of rock in a fault zone.
Ironstone is a sedimentary rock that contains a substantial proportion of an iron ore compound.
A geologist is a scientist who studies the structure, composition, and history of Earth.
Earth's rotation is the rotation of planet Earth around its own axis, as well as changes in the orientation of the rotation axis in space.
The Foucault pendulum is a simple device conceived as an experiment to demonstrate the Earth's rotation.
In geodesy, the figure of the Earth is the size and shape used to model planet Earth.
An equatorial bulge is a difference between the equatorial and polar diameters of a planet, due to the centrifugal force exerted by the rotation about the body's axis.
Flat Earth is an archaic and scientifically disproven conception of Earth's shape as a plane or disk.
Spherical Earth refers to the approximation of the figure of the Earth as a sphere.
The Gaia hypothesis proposes that living organisms interact with their inorganic surroundings on Earth to form a synergistic and self-regulating system.
Early Earth is loosely defined as Earth in the first thousand million years of its geological history.
Milankovitch cycles describe the collective effects of changes in the Earth's movements on its climate over thousands of years.
The calcium cycle is a transfer of calcium between dissolved and solid phases.
The oxygen cycle refers to the various movements of oxygen through the Earth's atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere.
The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that involves the movement of phosphorus through the lithosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere.
Carbon sequestration is a natural process of storing carbon in a carbon pool.
The geologic record is the entirety of the layers of rock strata, the deposits laid down by volcanism or by deposition of sediment.
A geologic hazard is an adverse geologic condition capable of causing widespread damage or loss of property and life.
Forensic geophysics is a branch of forensic science and is the study, the search, the localization and the mapping of buried objects beneath the soil.
Geomathematics is the application of mathematical methods to solve problems in geosciences.
In biogeochemistry, remineralisation refers to the breakdown or transformation of organic matter into its simplest inorganic forms.
Radium and radon are important contributors to environmental radioactivity.
Atmospheric chemistry is a branch of atmospheric science that studies the chemistry of the Earth's atmosphere and that of other planets.
Atmospheric escape is the loss of planetary atmospheric gases to outer space.
Earth's energy budget is the balance between the energy that Earth receives from the Sun and the energy the Earth loses back into outer space.
In climate science, longwave radiation is electromagnetic thermal radiation emitted by Earth's surface, atmosphere, and clouds.
Radiative forcing is a concept used to quantify a change to the balance of energy flowing through a planetary atmosphere.
Solar irradiance is the power per unit area received from the Sun in the form of electromagnetic radiation.
Ice albedo feedback is a climate change feedback, in which a change in the area of ice alters the albedo and surface temperature of a planet.
Climate sensitivity is a key measure in climate science and describes how much Earth's surface will warm in response to a doubling of the atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Numerical climate models are mathematical models that can simulate the interactions of important drivers of climate.
Earth's climate system is a complex system with five interacting components: the atmosphere, the hydrosphere, the cryosphere, the land surface and the biosphere.
A microclimate refers to localized atmospheric conditions in the near-surface layer.
Alpine climate is the typical climate for elevations above the tree line, where trees fail to grow due to cold.
Continental climates often have a significant annual variation in temperature, with warm to hot summers and cold winters.
A humid subtropical climate is a temperate climate type, characterized by long and hot summers, and cool to mild winters.
The polar climate regions are characterized by a lack of warm summers.
A semi-arid climate, or steppe climate, is a dry climate sub-type found in regions that receive less precipitation than they could evaporate.
The subarctic climate is a continental climate with long, cold winters, and short, warm to cool summers.
A Mediterranean climate, also called a dry summer climate, is a temperate climate type with dry summers and wet winters.
An area of tropical monsoon climate is a tropical climate with a pronounced wet season driven by the monsoon.
The tropical rainforest climate is a tropical climate sub-type that experiences high mean annual temperatures and heavy rainfall all year.
Tropical savanna climate is a tropical climate sub-type with a marked dry season.
Greenhouse gases are the gases in an atmosphere that trap heat, raising the surface temperature of astronomical bodies such as Earth.
Ocean acidification is the ongoing decrease in the acidity measure of the Earth's ocean.
Extreme weather includes unexpected, unusual, severe, or unseasonal weather, at the extremes of the historical distribution.
Global dimming is a decline in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, caused by atmospheric particulate matter.
Sea ice in the Arctic region has declined in recent decades in area and volume due to climate change.
Drylands are defined by a scarcity of water. Drylands are zones where precipitation is balanced by evaporation from surfaces and by evapotranspiration by plants.
Desertification is a type of gradual land degradation of fertile land into arid desert due to a combination of natural processes and human activities.
Deserts and xeric shrublands are a biome defined by the World Wide Fund for Nature, and form the largest terrestrial biome.
Chaparral is a shrubland plant community found primarily in California and northern Baja California.
A heath is a shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining infertile, acidic soils and is characterised by open, low-growing woody vegetation.
Mediterranean forests, woodlands and scrub is a biome generally characterized by dry summers and rainy winters.
Moorland or moor is a type of habitat found in upland areas, characterised by low-growing vegetation on acidic soils.
Montane ecosystems are found on the slopes of mountains, where the climate strongly affects what can live there.
Alpine tundra is a type of natural region or biome that does not contain trees because it is at high elevation, with an associated harsh climate.
Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests, also known as tropical moist forest, are forests of the warm wet tropics.
Temperate rainforests are rainforests with coniferous or broadleaf forests that occur in the temperate zone and receive heavy rain.
Temperate coniferous forest is a terrestrial biome found predominantly in areas with warm summers and cool winters, and adequate rainfall.
Temperate deciduous or temperate broadleaf forests are a variety of temperate forest mostly composed of deciduous trees that lose their leaves each winter.
Tropical forests are forested ecoregions with tropical climates, bounded roughly by the tropics.
Seasonal tropical forest, also known as monsoon forest, is a type of tropical forest that has a marked dry season.
The tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forest is a habitat type located at tropical latitudes with a long dry season.
Tropical and subtropical coniferous forests are a tropical forest habitat type defined by the World Wide Fund for Nature.
A woodland is land covered with woody plants, with a more open canopy than a closed forest.
A grove is a small group of trees with minimal or no undergrowth, or a small orchard planted for the cultivation of fruits or nuts.
Montane grasslands and shrublands are a biome of high-elevation grasslands and shrublands.
Temperate grasslands, savannas, and shrublands are terrestrial biomes whose predominant vegetation is grass.
Tropical and subtropical grasslands, savannas, and shrublands is a terrestrial biome of warm grasslands with scattered trees.
A fen is a type of peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water.
Flooded grasslands and savannas is a terrestrial biome consisting of large expanses of flooded grassland.
A peatland is a type of wetland whose soils consist of organic matter from decaying plants, forming layers of peat.
A riparian zone is the interface between land and a river or stream.
An aquatic ecosystem is an ecosystem found in and around a body of water, in contrast to land-based terrestrial ecosystems.
A deep-sea community is any community of organisms associated with a shared habitat in the deep sea.
Neuston are organisms that live at the surface of a body of water, such as an ocean, estuary, lake, river, wetland or pond.
Marine ecosystems are the largest of Earth's aquatic ecosystems and exist in waters that have a high salt content.
A marine coastal ecosystem is a marine ecosystem which occurs where the land meets the ocean.
Organisms that live freely at the ocean surface include keystone organisms like the golden seaweed that makes up the Sargasso Sea.
The sea surface microlayer is the boundary interface between the atmosphere and ocean, covering about seven tenths of Earth's surface.
A marine habitat is a habitat that supports marine life, which depends in some way on the saltwater that is in the sea.
The littoral zone is the part of an ocean, sea, lake, or river, that is close to the shore.
Mangrove forests are productive wetlands located in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones.
The neritic zone is the relatively shallow part of the ocean above the drop-off of the continental shelf.
A seagrass meadow is an underwater ecosystem formed by seagrasses, marine plants found in shallow coastal waters.
Freshwater ecosystems are a subset of Earth's aquatic ecosystems that include the biological communities inhabiting freshwater waterbodies.
A lake ecosystem includes plants, animals and micro-organisms, as well as physical and chemical interactions.
River ecosystems are flowing waters that drain the landscape, and include the interactions amongst plants, animals and micro-organisms.
A landscape is the visible features of an area of land, its landforms, and how they integrate with natural or human-made features.
Wilderness or wildlands are Earth's natural environments that have not been significantly modified by human activity.
Land use is a description of what happens on a parcel of land.
Planetary boundaries are a framework to describe limits to the impacts of human activities on the Earth system.
Human impact on the environment refers to changes to biophysical environments and to ecosystems caused by people.
Environmental degradation is the deterioration of the environment through depletion of resources such as quality of air, water and soil.
Environmental protection refers to the taking of measures to protect the natural environment, prevent pollution and maintain ecological balance.
Environmental science is an academic field that integrates the physical, biological, and mathematical sciences to study the environment.
Environmental studies is a multidisciplinary academic field which systematically studies human interaction with the environment.
Environmental policy is the pledge by governments or organizations to adopt laws, regulations, and other mechanisms concerning environmental issues.
Environmental resource management is the management of the interaction and impact of human societies on the environment.
Overexploitation refers to harvesting a renewable resource to the point of diminishing returns.
Overfishing is the removal of aquatic animals from a body of water at a rate greater than the species can replenish naturally.
Environmental issues are disruptions in the usual function of ecosystems.
Environmental justice is a social movement that addresses injustice which occurs when poor or marginalized communities are harmed by hazards.
The tragedy of the commons is the idea that when a resource is shared, it is rational for the individual to take more than their share, to the loss of all.
Human and wildlife conflict refers to the negative interactions between humans and wild animals, with undesirable consequences for both.
Disaster response refers to the actions taken directly before, during, or immediately after a disaster.
A weather station is a facility, either on land or sea, with instruments and equipment for measuring atmospheric conditions.
Surface weather observations are the fundamental data used for safety as well as climatological reasons to forecast weather and issue warnings.
Surface weather analysis is a special type of weather map that provides a view of weather elements over a geographical area at a specified time.
Marine weather forecasting is the process by which mariners and meteorological organizations attempt to forecast future weather conditions over the sea.
An Indian summer is a period of unseasonably warm, dry weather that sometimes occurs in autumn in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Cumulus humilis are cumuliform clouds with little vertical extent, common in the summer, often referred to as fair weather cumulus.
Cumulus mediocris is a low to middle level cloud with some vertical extent, taller than cumulus humilis.
Fractus clouds are small, ragged cloud fragments that are usually found under an ambient cloud base.
The altostratus undulatus is a type of altostratus cloud with signature undulations within it.
Rain and snow mixed, or sleet in Commonwealth English, is precipitation composed of a mixture of rain and partially melted snow.
Zonal and meridional flow are directions and regions of fluid flow on a globe, along the lines of latitude or across them.
A winter storm is an event in which wind coincides with varieties of precipitation that only occur at freezing temperatures.
Atmospheric electricity describes the electrical charges in the Earth's atmosphere.
A lightning strike is a lightning event in which an electric discharge takes place between the atmosphere and the ground.
Sprites are large-scale electric discharges that occur high above thunderstorm clouds.
An Atlantic hurricane is a type of tropical cyclone that forms in the Atlantic Ocean primarily between June and November.
Tropical cyclogenesis is the development and strengthening of a tropical cyclone in the atmosphere.
Tropical cyclone forecasting is the science of forecasting where a tropical cyclone's center, and its effects, are expected to be.
Tropical cyclone preparedness encompasses the actions and planning taken before a tropical cyclone strikes to mitigate damage and injury.
In meteorology, prevailing wind is a surface wind that blows predominantly from a particular direction.
In meteorology, vertical drafts are small-scale currents of rising or falling air, often within a cloud.
Climate change feedbacks are natural processes that impact how much global temperatures will increase for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
Arctic methane emissions contribute to a rise in methane concentrations in the atmosphere.
In climate science, a tipping point is a critical threshold that, when crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes.
Climate change mitigation, also called decarbonisation, is an action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change.
Climate change vulnerability is a measure of how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be affected by climate change.
Deforestation is a primary contributor to climate change, and climate change affects the health of forests.
The Amazon rainforest is the world's largest rainforest, and has lost a great deal of its area to clearing.
Effects of climate change are well documented and growing for Earth's natural environment and human societies.
There are numerous effects of climate change on agriculture, many of which are making it harder to provide global food security.
Climate change affects human health in many ways, including an increase in heat-related illnesses and deaths and worsened air quality.
One of the most important effects of climate change on oceans is an increase in ocean temperatures.
The effects of climate change, including sea level rise and tropical cyclones, threaten small island countries.
Greenhouse gas emissions from human activities intensify the greenhouse effect which contributes to climate change.
A carbon budget is a concept used to help set greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets in a fair and effective way.
Increasing methane emissions are a major contributor to the rising concentration of greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere.
The politics of climate change results from different perspectives on how to respond to climate change.
Climate change denial is a form of science denial characterized by rejecting or disputing the scientific consensus on climate change.
Patterns of solar irradiance and solar variation have been a main driver of climate change over very long timescales.
Economic analysis of climate change uses economic tools and models to calculate the scale and distribution of damages caused by climate change.
The East Asian monsoon is a monsoonal flow that carries moist air from the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean to East Asia.
The Monsoon of South Asia affects the Indian subcontinent, where it is one of the oldest and most anticipated weather phenomena.
The Harmattan is a season in West Africa characterized by a dry and dusty northeasterly trade wind.
The Atlantic hurricane season is the period in a year when tropical or subtropical cyclones are most likely to form in the Atlantic.
Climate change in Africa is a serious threat because the continent is one of the most vulnerable regions to the effects of climate change.
Despite its isolation, Antarctica has experienced warming and ice loss in recent decades, driven by greenhouse gas emissions.
Climate change has been a critical issue in Australia since the beginning of this century, as the country becomes hotter and more prone to extreme weather.
Climate change in Brazil is causing higher temperatures and longer-lasting heatwaves, changing precipitation patterns and more intense wildfires.
Climate change is greatly impacting Canada's environment and landscapes, and extreme weather has become more frequent and severe.
Climate change has resulted in a marked increase in temperature in Europe compared to pre-industrial levels.
Greenhouse gas emissions have contributed to changes in India's climate, including rising land temperatures and warming of the Indian Ocean.
Due to its geographical and natural diversity, Indonesia is one of the countries most susceptible to the impacts of climate change.
Climate change is impacting the human population and environment of Japan, which has observed notable changes in its climate patterns.
Conflict mineral laws require companies to report the use of specific minerals that may come from conflict zones.
Carbonate rocks are a class of sedimentary rocks composed primarily of carbonate minerals.
Clastic rocks are composed of fragments of pre-existing minerals and rock.
In geology, a nodule is a small, irregularly rounded mass or lump of a mineral or mineral aggregate.
Cementation is a process where minerals bond grains of sediment together by growing around them.
In geology, degradation refers to the lowering of a fluvial surface, such as a stream bed or floodplain, through erosional processes.
Grain size is the diameter of individual grains of sediment, or the lithified particles in clastic rocks.
Loam is soil composed mostly of sand, silt, and a smaller amount of clay.
Pelagic sediment is a fine-grained sediment that accumulates as the result of the settling of particles to the floor of the open ocean.
Siliceous ooze is a type of biogenic pelagic sediment located on the deep ocean floor.
Roundness is the degree of smoothing due to abrasion of sedimentary particles.
The term bed load describes particles in a flowing fluid that are transported along the stream bed.
Dissolved load is the portion of a stream's total sediment load that is carried in solution, especially ions from chemical weathering.
A sediment gravity flow is one of several types of sediment transport mechanisms driven by gravity acting on the sediment itself.
The suspended load of a flow of fluid is the portion of its sediment held up by the flow during transport.
Sedimentary structures include all kinds of features in sediments and sedimentary rocks, formed at the time of deposition.
A bedform is a geological feature that develops at the interface of fluid and a moveable bed.
Soft-sediment deformation structures develop at deposition or shortly after, during the first stages of the sediment's consolidation.
Edaphology is concerned with the influence of soils on living beings, particularly plants.
Pedology is a discipline within soil science which focuses on understanding and characterizing soil formation and evolution.
In pedology, leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone in soil to another via water movement.
Plant litter is dead plant material, such as leaves, bark, needles and twigs, that has fallen to the ground.
Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil.
Soil acidity is a measure of the acidity or basicity of a soil.
Soil classification deals with the systematic categorization of soils based on distinguishing characteristics.
Soil texture is the identifying quality of the upper layer of earth, which is composed of sand, silt and clay.
A soil type is a taxonomic unit in soil science, covering all soils that share a set of well-defined properties.
Soil health is a state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as appropriate to its environment.
Soil morphology is the branch of soil science dedicated to the technical description of soil, particularly its physical properties.
Soil physics is the study of soil's physical properties and processes.
Biostratigraphy is the branch of stratigraphy which focuses on correlating and assigning relative ages of rock strata by using the fossil assemblages contained within them.
Chronostratigraphy is the branch of stratigraphy that studies the ages of rock strata in relation to time.
Lithostratigraphy is a sub-discipline of stratigraphy associated with the study of strata or rock layers by their rock type.
Magnetostratigraphy is a geophysical correlation technique used to date sedimentary and volcanic sequences.
Sequence stratigraphy is a form of stratigraphy that subdivides and links sedimentary strata by the cycles of sea level that laid them down.
In geology, basement is the crystalline rock lying above the mantle and beneath all other rocks and sediments.
In biostratigraphy, biozones are intervals of geological strata that are defined on the basis of their characteristic fossil taxa.
In geology, a contact is a boundary that separates one rock body from another.
In geology, a facies is a body of rock with distinctive characteristics that reflect the conditions in which it formed.
Greenstone belts are zones of variably metamorphosed volcanic sequences with associated sedimentary rocks that occur within ancient continental cores.
A marine regression is a geological process occurring when areas of submerged seafloor are exposed during a drop in sea level.
A marine transgression is a geologic event where sea level rises relative to the land and the shoreline moves toward higher ground.
Global sea level has fluctuated significantly over Earth's history, driven by ice volume and by the shape of the ocean basins.
A stratigraphic section is a sequence of layers of rocks in the order they were deposited.
A stratigraphic unit is a volume of rock of identifiable origin and relative age range that can be mapped.
A diapir is a type of intrusion in which a more mobile and ductilely deformable material is forced into brittle overlying rocks.
In a geological context, crenulation is a fabric formed in metamorphic rocks by two or more stresses acting in turn.
Lineations in structural geology are linear structural features within rocks.
A detachment fault is a gently dipping normal fault associated with large-scale extensional tectonics.
In geology, a shear zone is a thin zone within the Earth's crust that has been strongly deformed.
In geology, a slickenside is a smoothly polished surface caused by frictional movement between rocks along a fault.
A structural basin is a large-scale formation of rock strata folded into a bowl shape.
A continental margin is the outer edge of continental crust abutting oceanic crust under coastal waters.
The continental rise is a low-relief zone of accumulated sediments that lies between the continental slope and the abyssal plain.
In geology, the slab is the part of the oceanic plate that descends into the mantle at a subduction zone.
A back-arc basin is a type of geologic basin found at some convergent plate boundaries, behind a volcanic arc.
A forearc is a region in a subduction zone between an oceanic trench and the associated volcanic arc.
A foreland basin is a structural basin that develops adjacent and parallel to a mountain belt.
A pull-apart basin is a structural basin where two strands of a strike-slip fault pull the crust open between them.
A geologic province is a spatial entity with common geologic attributes.
The Amur plate is a minor tectonic plate in the Eastern Hemisphere, covering much of northeast Asia.
The Okhotsk Plate is a minor tectonic plate covering Kamchatka, Sakhalin and parts of northern Japan.
The Somali plate is a minor tectonic plate which straddles the Equator in the Eastern Hemisphere.
The Sunda plate is a minor tectonic plate on which the majority of Southeast Asia is located.
The transition zone is the part of Earth's mantle located between the lower and the upper mantle.
Volcanology is the study of volcanoes, lava, magma, and related geological and geochemical phenomena.
Volcanism is the phenomenon where solids, liquids, gases, and their mixtures erupt to the surface of a planet.
Abrasion is a process of weathering that occurs when material being transported wears away at a surface over time.
Highlands or uplands are areas of high elevation such as a mountainous region, elevated plateau or high hills.
A coastal plain is an area of flat, low-lying land adjacent to a sea coast.
Isostatic depression is the sinking of large parts of the Earth's crust caused by a heavy weight placed on the surface.
An escarpment is a steep slope or long cliff that forms as a result of faulting or erosion and separates two relatively level areas.
Speleology is the scientific study of caves and other karst features.
A solutional cave is usually formed in a soluble rock like limestone.
A lava tube is a natural roofed conduit along which molten lava flows from a volcanic vent.
River morphology is used to describe the shapes of river channels and how they change over time.
A cut bank, also known as a river cliff, is the outside bank of a curve in a water channel, which is continually undergoing erosion.
A promontory is a raised mass of land that projects into a lowland or a body of water.
A streambed is the bottom of a stream or river and is confined within a channel or the banks of the waterway.
A gully is a landform created by running water which erodes soil to a sharp angle, typically on a hillside.
A ravine is a landform that is narrower than a canyon and is often the product of streambank erosion.
A wadi is a river valley or an ephemeral riverbed that typically contains water only when heavy rain occurs.
A cirque is an amphitheatre-like valley formed by glacial erosion.
An esker is a long, winding ridge of stratified sand and gravel formed by a stream flowing under a glacier.
Post-glacial rebound is the rise of land masses after the removal of the huge weight of ice sheets.
Valleys with a U-shaped profile, also called glacial troughs, are formed by the process of glaciation.
Mountain formation occurs due to a variety of geological processes associated with large-scale movements of Earth's crust.
Fault blocks are very large blocks of rock created by tectonic and localized stresses in Earth's crust.
Fold mountains are formed by the effects of folding on layers within the upper part of the Earth's crust.
An oceanic basin is anywhere on Earth that is covered by seawater, and geologically most are large structural basins.
A shingle beach is a commonly narrow beach that is composed of coarse, loose, well-rounded, and waterworn pebbles.
Coastal geography is the study of the constantly changing region between the ocean and the land.
Coastal management is defence against flooding and erosion, and techniques that stop erosion to claim lands.
At a flat coast the land descends gradually into the sea.
A headland is a coastal landform, a point of land usually high and often with a sheer drop, that extends into a body of water.
In geography, a cape is a headland, peninsula or promontory extending into a body of water.
A tidal island is a raised area of land within a body of water, connected to the mainland by a causeway exposed at low tide.
Barrier islands are a coastal landform where an area of sand off the coast has been formed by wave and tidal action.
A coral island is a type of island formed from coral detritus and associated organic material.
An islet is generally a small island, often unnamed, with little or no vegetation.
A lake island is any landmass within a lake.
A river island is any exposed landmass surrounded by river water.
In marine geology, a guyot is an isolated underwater volcanic mountain with a flat top well below the surface.
Mudflats are coastal wetlands that form in intertidal areas where sediments have been deposited by tides or rivers.
A shoal is a natural submerged ridge, bank, or bar that consists of sand or other unconsolidated material.
In geology, a hummock is a small knoll or mound above ground, typically appearing in groups.
A tor is a large, free-standing rock outcrop that rises abruptly from the surrounding smooth hillside.
A lava field is a large, mostly flat area of lava flows.
Volcanic cones are among the simplest volcanic landforms, built by ejecta piling up around a vent.
A flash flood is a rapid flooding of low-lying areas such as washes, rivers, dry lakes, and depressions.
Salinity is the saltiness or amount of salt dissolved in a body of water.
Fresh water is any naturally occurring liquid or frozen water containing low concentrations of dissolved salts.
Brackish water is water occurring in a natural environment that has more salinity than freshwater, but not as much as seawater.
Saline water is water that contains a high concentration of dissolved salts, mainly common salt.
A whirlpool is a body of rotating water produced by opposing currents or a current running into an obstacle.
Marine chemistry is the study of the chemical composition and processes of the world's oceans.
Ocean dynamics define and describe the flow of water within the oceans.
Ekman transport is part of Ekman motion theory, describing how wind-driven water moves at an angle to the wind.
A rip current is a specific type of water current that can occur near beaches where waves break.
Ocean surface topography are highs and lows on the ocean surface, similar to the hills and valleys of land.
The ocean temperature plays a crucial role in the global climate system, ocean currents and marine habitats.
Sea surface temperature is the temperature of ocean water close to the surface.
The abyssal zone is a layer of the pelagic zone of the ocean, lying in permanent darkness and near freezing.
Marine sediment are deposits of insoluble particles that have accumulated on the seafloor.
The sea level has generally been rising since the end of the Last Glacial Maximum, and the rise has accelerated in the past century.
Tidal range is the difference in height between high tide and low tide.
A megatsunami is an extremely large wave created by a substantial and sudden displacement of material into a body of water.
Glaciology is the scientific study of glaciers and of ice generally.
Basal sliding is the act of a glacier sliding over the bed due to meltwater under the ice acting as a lubricant.
A crevasse is a deep crack that forms in a glacier or ice sheet.
Methane clathrate, also called methane hydrate or fire ice, is a solid in which methane is trapped within a crystal structure of water.
In hydrology, discharge is the volumetric flow rate of a stream.
Streamflow is the flow of water in streams and other channels, and is a major element of the water cycle.
An artesian well is a well that brings groundwater to the surface without pumping because it is under pressure.
The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation, where the pores of the ground are filled with water.
An alpine lake is a high-altitude lake in a mountainous area, usually near or above the tree line.
Salt flats are flat, open expanses of ground covered with salt and other minerals.
A glacial lake is a body of water with origins from glacier activity.
A proglacial lake is a lake formed by the damming action of a moraine or ice during the retreat of a melting glacier.
A pluvial lake is a body of water that accumulated in a basin because of a greater moisture availability in the past.
A rift lake is a lake formed as a result of subsidence related to movement on faults within a rift zone.
Lake stratification is the tendency of lakes to form separate and distinct thermal layers during warm weather.
An underground lake is a lake underneath the surface of the Earth.
A volcanic crater lake is a lake in a crater formed by explosive activity or a collapse during a volcanic eruption.
An alluvial river is one in which the bed and stream banks are made up of mobile sediment or soil.
An arroyo is a dry watercourse that temporarily or seasonally fills and flows after sufficient rain.
In sedimentary geology, avulsion is the process by which flow is diverted out of an established river channel and into a new course.
A distributary is a stream channel that branches off and flows away from a main stream channel.
In geography, a confluence occurs where two or more watercourses join to form a single channel.
A river mouth is where a river flows into a larger body of water, such as a lake, a sea, or an ocean.
The source or headwater of a river is the geographical point of its beginning.
A mathematician is someone who uses an extensive knowledge of mathematics in their work, typically to solve mathematical problems.
Recreational mathematics is mathematics carried out for recreation rather than as a strictly research-based activity.
An approximation is anything that is intentionally similar but not exactly equal to something else.
Estimation is the process of finding an estimate, which is a value that is usable for some purpose even if the input data may be incomplete.
In mathematics, extrapolation is a type of estimation of the value of a variable beyond the original observation range.
Rounding is the process of adjusting a number to an approximate, more convenient value, often with a shorter or simpler representation.
In mathematics, the word constant conveys the idea of a quantity that does not change.
In mathematics, a monomial is, roughly speaking, a polynomial which has only one term.
In algebra, a binomial is a polynomial that is the sum of two terms, each of which is a monomial.
In elementary algebra, a trinomial is a polynomial consisting of three terms.
In mathematics, transfinite numbers are numbers that are infinite in the sense that they are larger than all finite numbers.
Mathematical notation consists of using symbols for representing operations, unspecified numbers, relations, and other mathematical objects.
A mathematical problem is a problem that can be represented, analyzed, and possibly solved, with the methods of mathematics.
Mathematical puzzles make up an integral part of recreational mathematics, with specific rules but no competition between players.
In mathematics and logic, a corollary is a proposition which can be readily deduced from a previous, already proven proposition.
In mathematics, a lemma is a generally minor proven proposition used to prove a larger statement.
In mathematics, an operation is a function that takes a fixed number of elements of a set and returns an element of the same set.
Recursion occurs when the definition of a concept or process depends on a simpler or previous version of itself.
In mathematics, the sign of a real number is its property of being either positive, negative, or zero.
In mathematics, a real number is said to be normal if its infinite sequence of digits is distributed uniformly.
In number theory, a Gaussian integer is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both integers.
In mathematics, a rate is the quotient of two quantities, often represented as a fraction.
A repeating decimal is a decimal representation of a number whose digits are eventually periodic.
In mathematics, an algebraic number is a number that is a root of a non-zero polynomial in one variable with integer coefficients.
In mathematics, a transcendental number is a real or complex number that is not the root of any non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients.
In geometry and algebra, a real number is constructible if a line segment of that length can be built with compass and straightedge.
In mathematics, computable numbers are the real numbers that can be computed to within any desired precision by a finite algorithm.
A decimal separator is a symbol that separates the integer part from the fractional part of a number written in decimal form.
Chinese numerals are words and characters used to denote numbers in written Chinese.
The system of ancient Egyptian numerals was used in Ancient Egypt for thousands of years.
In mathematics, a multiplicative inverse or reciprocal for a nonzero number is a number which when multiplied by it gives one.
In mathematics, a product is the result of multiplication, or an expression that identifies objects to be multiplied.
A divisibility rule is a shorthand way of determining whether a given integer is divisible by a fixed divisor without performing the division.
An Egyptian fraction is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions.
In mathematics and computing, modulo is the operation whose value is the remainder of a division of one number by another.
In mathematics, an algebraic function is a function that satisfies a polynomial equation.
In mathematics, a function of a real variable is a function whose domain is a subset of the real numbers.
A vector-valued function is a mathematical function of one or more variables whose values are vectors.
In number theory, an arithmetic function is generally any function whose domain is the positive integers.
In mathematics, an implicit equation is a relation in which the variables are not separated, and which may still define a function.
A parameter, generally, is any characteristic that can help in defining or classifying a particular system.
In mathematics, an even function is one unchanged by reflecting its input, and an odd function is one that changes sign.
In mathematics, a piecewise function is a function defined by different rules on different parts of its domain.
In mathematics, an injective function is a function that maps distinct elements of its domain to distinct elements.
In mathematics, a surjective function is a function that reaches every element of its codomain.
In mathematics, a bijection is a function between two sets such that each element of one is paired with exactly one element of the other.
In mathematics, the domain of a function is the set of inputs accepted by the function.
In mathematics, the range of a function may refer to the codomain of the function, or to the set of values it actually takes.
In mathematics, a zero of a function is a member of its domain at which the function takes the value zero.
In mathematics, a fixed point is a value that does not change under a given transformation.
In mathematics, a fixed-point theorem is a result saying that a function will have at least one fixed point under certain conditions.
In mathematics, a multivalued function is a function that has two or more values for some inputs.
In mathematics, a partial function from one set to another is a function defined only on a subset of the first.
In mathematics, a function is called bounded if the set of its values is bounded.
In mathematical analysis, an analytic function is a function that is locally represented by a convergent power series.
In complex analysis, an entire function is a complex-valued function that is well behaved on the whole complex plane.
In complex analysis, elliptic functions are special kinds of functions that repeat in two independent directions.
A periodic function is a function that repeats its values at regular intervals.
In mathematics, elementary functions are a class of functions built from powers, roots, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions.
In mathematics, a rational function is any function that can be defined by a ratio of two polynomials.
In calculus, a linear function from the real numbers to the real numbers is a function whose graph is a straight line.
In mathematics, an identity function is a function that always returns the value that was used as its argument.
In mathematics, a quadratic function of a single variable is a function whose highest power is the square.
In mathematics, a cubic function is a polynomial function of degree three.
Exponential growth occurs when a quantity grows at a rate directly proportional to its present size.
In mathematics, a Gaussian function is the function whose graph is the familiar symmetric bell shape.
In mathematics, the common logarithm is the logarithm with base ten.

In mathematics and classical mechanics, canonical coordinates are coordinates on phase space pairing each position with its momentum.
In physics, reduced mass is the effective mass of a two-body system when their motion is described relative to each other.
In classical mechanics, the two-body problem is to predict the motion of two massive bodies orbiting each other.
Flow measurement is the quantification of bulk fluid movement.
In continuum mechanics, finite strain theory deals with deformations in which the changes are too large for small-strain assumptions.
In materials science, fracture toughness describes how well a material resists the spreading of a crack.
Particle statistics is the description of how multiple identical particles are counted in statistical mechanics.
In particle physics, weak isospin is a quantum number relating to the weak interaction.
A pressure volume diagram describes corresponding changes in volume and pressure in a system.
In thermodynamics, thermal conductivity is a measure of a material's ability to conduct heat.
A thermodynamic potential is a quantity used to represent the state of a system.
In physics, Wien's displacement law states that the peak of a hot body's radiation shifts with its temperature.
In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is one that happens slowly enough for the system to stay in equilibrium throughout.
The relativistic Doppler effect is the change in frequency and wavelength of light caused by the relative motion of source and observer.
Optical path is the trajectory that a light ray follows as it propagates through a medium.
Snell's law is a formula describing the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction.
In optics, optical power is a measure of how strongly a lens converges or diverges light.
The Fresnel equations describe the reflection and transmission of light at the boundary between two media.
Fourier optics is the study of classical optics using Fourier transforms.
An audio engineer helps to produce a recording or a live performance, balancing and adjusting the sound.
Chemical reaction engineering is a specialty concerned with designing the vessels in which reactions are carried out.
Green chemistry is an area of chemistry focused on designing products and processes that reduce hazardous substances.
Precipitation hardening is a heat treatment technique used to increase the strength of alloys.
A scientist is an expert in one or more fields of science who uses scientific methods in their work.
In laboratory equipment, a beaker is a cylindrical container with a flat bottom and usually a lip for pouring.
In physics, the weber is the unit of magnetic flux in the International System of Units.
In geometry, the five cell is the convex four dimensional polytope bounded by five tetrahedral cells.
In geometry, the sixteen cell is the regular convex four dimensional polytope bounded by sixteen tetrahedral cells.
In four dimensional geometry, the twenty four cell is a convex regular four dimensional polytope, an analogue of a Platonic solid.
The modifiable temporal unit problem is a source of statistical bias that occurs in time series and spatial analysis when the data have been gathered into temporal units.
In mathematical optimisation, the push relabel algorithm is an algorithm for computing maximum flows in a flow network.
Numerical methods for partial differential equations is the branch of numerical analysis that studies the numerical solution of partial differential equations.
In game theory, a move, action or play is any one of the options a player can choose where the best outcome depends not only on their own actions but also on the actions of others.
In atomic physics, a magnetic quantum number is a quantum number used to tell apart the quantum states of an electron according to its angular momentum along a given axis in space.
In solid state physics, the valence band and the conduction band are the bands closest to the Fermi level, and so they settle the electrical conductivity of the solid.
Schwinger's quantum action principle is a variational approach to quantum mechanics and quantum field theory.
In continuum mechanics, shearing refers to a shear strain, a deformation of a material in which parallel internal surfaces slide past one another.

In statistical mechanics, an ensemble is an idealisation consisting of a large number of virtual copies of a system, considered all at once, each representing a possible state the real system might be in.
In the standard model of electroweak interactions, the weak hypercharge is a quantum number relating the electric charge and the third component of weak isospin.
The Diesel cycle is a combustion process of a reciprocating internal combustion engine.
In thermodynamics, the Redlich and Kwong equation of state is an empirical algebraic equation relating the temperature, pressure and volume of gases.
In physics and colour science, the Planckian locus is the path that the colour of a glowing black body takes in a chromaticity space as its temperature changes.
In optics, any instrument has a principal limit to its resolution owing to the physics of diffraction.
The Stokes parameters are a set of values that describe the polarisation state of electromagnetic radiation.
In the electrical power industry, the demand factor is the fractional amount of some quantity being used compared with the greatest amount the same system could use.
A load following power plant is a power plant that adjusts its output as the demand for electricity rises and falls through the day.
High fructose corn syrup is a sweetener made from maize, produced by the industrial use of enzymes.
The Supung Dam is a gravity dam on the Yalu River between Liaoning in China and North Pyongan in North Korea.
The Great Seto Bridge is a series of double deck bridges connecting Okayama and Kagawa in Japan across five small islands in the Seto Inland Sea.
The King Fahd Causeway is a long series of bridges and causeways connecting Khobar in Saudi Arabia and Al Jasra in Bahrain across the Gulf of Bahrain.
Physical restraint refers to means of limiting or obstructing the freedom of the bodily movement of a person or an animal.
A reticle, also known as a graticule, is a pattern of fine lines or markings built into the optical path of an optical device to give measurement references during visual inspections.
Fieldnotes are qualitative notes recorded by researchers in the course of field research, during or after their observation of the thing they are studying.
The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals is an internationally agreed standard managed by the United Nations.
Hazard pictograms form part of the international Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals.
The standard system for the identification of the hazards of materials for emergency response defines the safety square, or fire diamond, used to tell a firefighter at a glance what is inside.
In chemical nomenclature, a descriptor is a notational prefix placed before the systematic name of a substance, describing the configuration or the stereochemistry of the molecule.
A systematic element name is the temporary name assigned to an unknown or recently made chemical element.
In chemistry, a trivial name is a name for a substance that does not follow any formal system of nomenclature.
Conversion, with the related terms yield and selectivity, is a measure in chemical reaction engineering of how much of a reactant has reacted.
In chemistry, yield refers to the amount of product obtained in a chemical reaction.
The law of reciprocal proportions is one of the basic laws of stoichiometry, relating the proportions in which elements combine across a number of different elements.
In chemistry, the principle of Le Chatelier is used to predict the effect of a change in conditions on a chemical equilibrium.

The principle of microscopic reversibility states that the detailed dynamics of particles and fields is reversible in time, because the microscopic equations of motion are symmetric under inversion of time.
In chemistry, congeners are chemical substances related to each other by origin, structure or function.
Helium four is a stable isotope of the element helium, by far the more abundant of the two that occur in nature.
Potassium forty is the long lived radioactive isotope of potassium that occurs in nature, with a half life of more than a billion years.
Caesium of mass number one hundred and thirty seven is a radioactive isotope of caesium formed as one of the commoner products of the nuclear fission of uranium.
Carbon twelve is the most abundant of the two stable isotopes of carbon, making up almost all of the carbon on Earth.
Carbon fourteen, or radiocarbon, is a radioactive isotope of carbon whose nucleus holds six protons and eight neutrons.
Cobalt sixty is a synthetic radioactive isotope of cobalt with a half life of a little over five years.
Uranium of mass number two hundred and thirty eight is the most common isotope of uranium found in nature, above ninety nine parts in a hundred.
Uranium of mass number two hundred and thirty five is the isotope making up less than one part in a hundred of natural uranium.
Plutonium of mass number two hundred and thirty nine is the primary fissile isotope used for the production of nuclear weapons.
Unbinilium is a hypothetical chemical element with atomic number one hundred and twenty.
Unbibium is a hypothetical chemical element with atomic number one hundred and twenty two.
Unbiquadium is a hypothetical chemical element with atomic number one hundred and twenty four.
Unbihexium is a hypothetical chemical element with atomic number one hundred and twenty six.
Diphosphane is an inorganic compound of phosphorus and hydrogen.
In chemistry, the descriptor geminal refers to the relationship between two atoms or groups attached to the same atom.
In chemistry the descriptor vicinal identifies two functional groups as bonded to two adjacent carbon atoms.
In chemistry, an oligomer is a molecule that consists of a few repeating units derived from smaller molecules called monomers.
Per and polyfluoroalkyl substances are a group of synthetic organofluorine compounds with many fluorine atoms attached to an alkyl chain.
In chemistry, a hydride is formally the anion of hydrogen, a hydrogen ion with two electrons.
Glutamate flavouring is the generic name for flavour enhancing compounds based on glutamic acid and its salts.
In chemistry, a nucleophilic substitution is a class of reactions in which an electron rich species replaces a functional group within an electron poor molecule.
In chemistry, a reducing agent is a chemical species that donates an electron to an electron recipient called the oxidising agent.
Phase separation is the creation of two distinct phases from a single homogeneous mixture.
Mass transfer is the net movement of mass from one location to another.
Modern valence bond theory is the application of valence bond theory with computer programs that are competitive in accuracy and economy with the alternatives.
A meso compound is an optically inactive isomer in a set of stereoisomers, at least two of which are optically active.
Freezing point depression is a drop in the highest temperature at which a substance freezes, caused when a smaller amount of another substance is added.
In chemistry and pharmacology, a dissociation constant measures how readily a larger object separates reversibly into smaller components.
In thermochemistry, an exothermic reaction is a reaction whose overall standard enthalpy change is negative.
The law of constant heat summation, named for Germain Hess, states that the total enthalpy change over the course of a chemical reaction is the same whatever route the reaction takes.
An occultation is an event that occurs when one object is hidden from the observer by another object passing between them.
Arrokoth is a small icy Kuiper belt object orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune and Pluto.
Oumuamua is the first confirmed interstellar object detected passing through the Solar System.
Comet Borisov is the first observed rogue comet and the second observed interstellar interloper.
Epsilon Canis Majoris is a binary star system and the second brightest star in the constellation of Canis Major.
The Jewel Bug Nebula is a very young and dense planetary nebula lying about three thousand light years away in the constellation Cygnus.
The Ptolemy Cluster is an open cluster of stars in the constellation of Scorpius.
The supernova of Kepler was a supernova of the first type that appeared in the Milky Way, in the constellation Ophiuchus.
The galaxy of Bode is a grand design spiral galaxy about twelve million light years away in the constellation Ursa Major.
The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy is a barred spiral galaxy about fifteen million light years away on the border of Hydra and Centaurus.
The Local Sheet is a nearby galaxy filament, a region of space where the Milky Way, the members of the Local Group and other galaxies share a similar peculiar velocity.
Daylight is the combination of all direct and indirect sunlight during the daytime.
Scutum is a small constellation whose name is Latin for shield.
In astronomy, a trojan is a small celestial body that shares the orbit of a larger one, holding a stable place about sixty degrees ahead of or behind it.
A planetary core consists of the innermost layers of a planet.
The horizontal branch is a stage of stellar evolution that follows the red giant branch in stars of about the mass of the Sun.
A protoplanetary nebula is an astronomical object in the short lived episode of a rapid evolution between the late asymptotic giant branch and the planetary nebula that follows.
A low surface brightness galaxy is a diffuse galaxy whose surface brightness, seen from Earth, is fainter than the glow of the night sky itself.
A Lacertae object is a type of active galactic nucleus, named after its prototype in the constellation Lacerta.
Observational cosmology is the study of the structure, the evolution and the origin of the universe through observation, using instruments such as telescopes and detectors of cosmic rays.
The multiverse is the hypothetical set of all universes.
In physical cosmology, the paper of Alpher, Bethe and Gamow argued that the big bang would create hydrogen, helium and heavier elements in about the proportions observed.
The discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation was a major development in modern physical cosmology.
The warm to hot intergalactic medium is the sparse plasma that cosmologists believe fills the spaces between galaxies and holds a large share of the ordinary matter of the universe.
Visible light astronomy is astronomical observation through telescopes that are sensitive to the range of light the eye can see.
The photometric system of Johnson is a system for classifying stars by their colours, measured through ultraviolet, blue and visual filters.
The Pisces and Cetus Supercluster Complex is a galaxy supercluster complex that counts the Virgo Supercluster among its outlying members.
An extraterrestrial vortex is a vortex that occurs on planets and moons other than Earth that have enough atmosphere to carry one.
Supernovae of types one b and one c are caused by the collapse of the core of massive stars that have shed or been stripped of their outer envelope of hydrogen.
The G cloud is an interstellar cloud lying next to the Local Interstellar Cloud, within the Local Bubble.
Westerhout forty is a star forming region in the Milky Way, in the constellation Serpens.
A world is a totality of entities, customarily viewed in philosophy as all of existence or the whole of reality.
A low ionisation nuclear emission line region is a type of galactic nucleus defined by the spectral lines it emits.
Artificial life is a field of study in which researchers examine systems related to natural life, its processes and its evolution, through simulations with computer models, robotics and biochemistry.
Carbon based life is the idea that carbon is the core element of all known forms of life and a core component of all complex biological molecules.
Non cellular life is life that exists without a cellular structure for at least part of its life cycle.
Human biology is an area of study that examines humans through the interplay of genetics, evolution, physiology, anatomy, ecology, nutrition and the influences of society.
The earliest known life forms on Earth may be as old as the possible microfossils found in the Nuvvuagittuq belt in Quebec.
A neural network is an interconnected population of neurons, typically containing many neural circuits.
Organic matter is the large source of carbon based compounds found in natural and engineered environments, on land and in water.
Computational biology is the study of biological systems through computer science, data analysis, mathematical modelling and simulation.
Ethnobiology is the study of the relationships among peoples, living things and environments, drawing on the social, biological and medical sciences.
A trace fossil is a fossil record of the activity of a living thing rather than the preserved remains of the organism itself.
Micropaleontology is the branch of paleontology that studies microfossils, fossils that need a microscope to see the organism and its details.
Paleobotany is the branch of botany and paleontology dealing with the recovery and identification of plant fossils and their use in reconstructing past environments.
Paleoecology is the study of the interactions between organisms, and between organisms and their environments, across geological timescales.
Incertae sedis, Latin for of uncertain placement, is a term used for a taxonomic group whose broader relationships are unknown or undefined.
In biological taxonomy, a synonym is one of two or more scientific names that apply to the same taxon.
In biological taxonomy, a taxonomic rank is the level a group of organisms occupies in a hierarchical system of classification.
Order is one of the major hierarchical taxonomic ranks in Linnaean taxonomy, classified between family and class.
In biological taxonomy, the type genus is the genus that defines a biological family and gives the family its name.
A type species is the species permanently associated with the name of a genus, used to identify it and tell it from others.
In botany, an infraspecific name is the scientific name for any taxon below the rank of species.
