A disc herniation, also known as a spinal disc herniation, is a condition affecting the intervertebral disc between two vertebrae, usually caused by excessive strain or trauma to the spine.
Heat illness is a spectrum of disorders due to increased body temperature.
Hyperthermia, also known as overheating, is a condition in which an individual's body temperature is elevated beyond normal due to failed thermoregulation.
A joint dislocation, also called luxation, occurs when there is an abnormal separation in a joint where two or more bones meet.
A mouth ulcer, or aphtha, sometimes called a canker sore or salt blister, is an ulcer that occurs on the mucous membrane of the oral cavity.
Penetrating trauma is an open wound injury that occurs when an object pierces the skin and enters a tissue of the body, creating a deep but relatively narrow entry wound.
A gunshot wound is a penetrating injury caused by a projectile, for example a bullet, shot from a gun.
A stab wound is a specific form of penetrating trauma to the skin that results from a knife or a similar pointed object.
A repetitive strain injury is an injury to part of the musculoskeletal or nervous system caused by repetitive use, vibrations, compression or long periods in a fixed position.
A splinter, also known as a sliver, is a fragment of a larger object, or a foreign body that becomes embedded in a body.
Tendinopathy is a type of tendon disorder that results in pain, swelling and impaired function.
A toxic injury is a type of injury resulting from exposure to a toxin.
A drug overdose is the ingestion or application of a drug or other substance in quantities much greater than are recommended.
Botulinum toxin, botulinum neurotoxin, or botox is a neurotoxic protein produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum and related species.
Metal toxicity or metal poisoning is toxicity affecting plants, animals or humans due to excessive concentration of metals.
Mercury poisoning is a type of metal poisoning due to exposure to mercury.
An ingrown nail, also known as onychocryptosis, is a common form of nail disease.
Conjoined twins, popularly referred to as Siamese twins, are twins joined in utero.
Dwarfism is a condition marked by the unusually small size or short stature of individual animals.
Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.
Amusia, also called being tone deaf, is a musical disorder that appears mainly as a defect in processing pitch but also encompasses musical memory and recognition.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders are a group of conditions that can occur in a person who is exposed to alcohol during gestation.

Dyscalculia is a learning disorder, resulting in difficulty learning or comprehending arithmetic, such as difficulty in understanding numbers, numeracy, learning how to manipulate numbers, performing mathematical calculations and learning facts in mathematics.
Dysgraphia is a neurological disorder and learning disability that concerns impairments in written expression, which affects the ability to write, primarily handwriting, but also coherence.
Aphasia, also known as dysphasia, is an impairment in a person's ability to comprehend or formulate language because of dysfunction in specific brain regions.
In human development, muteness or mutism is defined as an absence of speech, with or without an ability to hear the speech of others.
Speech disorders, impairments or impediments are a type of communication disorder in which normal speech is disrupted.

Stuttering, also known as stammering, is a speech disorder characterized externally by involuntary repetitions and prolongations of sounds, syllables, words or phrases as well as involuntary silent pauses called blocks.
A benign tumor is a mass of cells that does not invade neighboring tissue or spread throughout the body.
A bone tumor is an abnormal growth of tissue in bone.
Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the cervix, the lower narrow part of the uterus.
Head and neck cancer is a general term encompassing multiple cancers that can develop in the head and neck region.
Liver cancer, also known as hepatic cancer, primary hepatic cancer or primary hepatic malignancy, is cancer that starts in the liver.
Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer where multinucleated Reed Sternberg cells are present in the lymph nodes.
Oral cancer, also known as oral cavity cancer, tongue cancer or mouth cancer, is a cancer of the lining of the lips, mouth or upper throat.
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.
Pancreatic cancer is any cancer with a primary location in the pancreas, a glandular organ lying behind the stomach.
A sarcoma is a rare type of cancer that arises from cells of mesenchymal origin, meaning that sarcomas are cancers of connective tissues such as bone, cartilage, muscle, fat or vascular tissues.
Stomach cancer, also known as gastric cancer, is a malignant tumor of the stomach.
A parasitic disease, also known as parasitosis, is an infectious disease caused by parasites.
Helminthiasis, also known as worm infection, is any macroparasitic disease of humans and other animals in which a part of the body is infected with parasitic worms, known as helminths.
Immunization is the process by which an individual's immune system becomes fortified against an infectious agent, known as the immunogen.
Neglected tropical diseases are a diverse group of tropical infections that are common in low income populations in developing regions of Africa, Asia and the Americas.
In medicine, public health and biology, transmission is the passing of a pathogen causing communicable disease from an infected host individual or group to a particular individual or group.
Mosquito borne diseases or mosquito borne illnesses are diseases caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites transmitted by mosquitoes.

In infectious disease ecology and epidemiology, a natural reservoir, also known as a disease reservoir or a reservoir of infection, is the population of organisms or the specific environment in which an infectious pathogen naturally lives, persists and reproduces.
Waterborne diseases are diseases caused by pathogenic micro organisms, such as bacteria, viruses, protozoa and parasitic worms, that are transmitted through contaminated water.
The fecal oral route describes a particular route of transmission of a disease wherein pathogens in fecal particles pass from one person to the mouth of another person.
A reverse zoonosis, also known as a zooanthroponosis or anthroponosis, is a pathogen reservoired in humans that is capable of being transmitted to non human animals.
Conjunctivitis, also known as pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
Keratitis is a condition in which the eye's cornea, the clear dome on the front surface of the eye, becomes inflamed.
Otitis externa, also called swimmer's ear, is inflammation of the ear canal.
Otitis media is a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear.
Respiratory tract infections are infectious diseases involving the lower or upper respiratory tract.
A skin infection is an infection of the skin in humans and other animals, that can also affect the associated soft tissues such as loose connective tissue and mucous membranes.

Glanders is a contagious, zoonotic infectious disease caused by the bacterium Burkholderia mallei, which primarily occurs in horses, mules and donkeys, but can also be contracted by dogs, cats, pigs, goats and humans.
Bubonic plague is one of three types of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Streptococcal pharyngitis, also known as streptococcal sore throat or strep throat, is pharyngitis, an infection of the pharynx, the back of the throat, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.
Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory disease that can involve the heart, joints, skin and brain.
Long COVID or long haul COVID is a group of health problems persisting or developing after an initial period of COVID from coronavirus infection.
Croup, also known as croupy cough, is a type of respiratory infection that is usually caused by a virus.
Hepatitis D is a type of viral hepatitis caused by the hepatitis delta virus.
A cold sore is a type of herpes infection caused by the herpes simplex virus that affects primarily the lip.
Japanese encephalitis is an infection of the brain caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus.
Mpox, originally known as monkeypox, is an infectious viral disease that can occur in humans and other animals.
Rift Valley fever is a viral disease of humans and livestock that can cause mild to severe symptoms.
Severe acute respiratory syndrome is a viral respiratory disease of zoonotic origin caused by a coronavirus.
Zika fever, also known as Zika virus disease or simply Zika, is an infectious disease caused by the Zika virus.
Athlete's foot, known medically as tinea pedis, is a common skin infection of the feet caused by a fungus.
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida.
Onychomycosis, also known as tinea unguium, is a fungal infection of the nail.
Head lice infestation, also known as pediculosis capitis, is the infection of the head hair and scalp by the head louse.
Myiasis, also known as flystrike or fly strike, is the parasitic infestation of the body of a live animal by fly larvae, called maggots, that grow inside the host while feeding on its tissue.
Toxocariasis is an illness of humans caused by the dog roundworm and, less frequently, the cat roundworm.
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, commonly known as mad cow disease, is an incurable and fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle.
Infestation is the state of being invaded or overrun by pests or parasites.
Signs and symptoms are diagnostic indications of an illness, injury or condition.
Abdominal pain, also known as a stomach ache, is a symptom associated with both non serious and serious medical issues.
Ageusia is the loss of taste functions of the tongue, particularly the inability to detect sweetness, sourness, bitterness, saltiness and umami.
Dysgeusia, also known as parageusia, is a distortion of the sense of taste.
Hyposmia, or microsmia, is a reduced ability to smell and to detect odors.
Ataxia is a neurological sign consisting of lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements that can include gait abnormality, speech changes and abnormalities in eye movements.
Atrophy is the partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body.
Bad breath, also known as halitosis, is a symptom in which a noticeably unpleasant breath odour is present.
Chest pain is pain or discomfort in the chest, typically the front of the chest.
Constipation is a bowel dysfunction that makes bowel movements infrequent or hard to pass.
A cough is a sudden expulsion of air through the large breathing passages which can help clear them of fluids, irritants, foreign particles and microbes.
Cyanosis is the change of tissue color to a bluish purple hue, as a result of decrease in the amount of oxygen bound to the hemoglobin in the red blood cells of the capillary bed.
Delirium tremens is a rapid onset of confusion caused by withdrawal from alcohol.
Dizziness is an imprecise term that can refer to a sense of disorientation in space, vertigo or lightheadedness.
A headache, also known as cephalalgia, is the symptom of pain in the face, head or neck.
Heartburn is a burning sensation felt behind the breastbone.
Heart rate is the frequency of the heartbeat measured by the number of contractions of the heart per minute.
Tachycardia, also called tachyarrhythmia, is a heart rate that exceeds the normal resting rate.
Hives, also known as urticaria, is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh colored, raised, itchy bumps.
Hypoglycemia, sometimes called low blood sugar, is a fall in blood sugar to levels below normal.
An itch, also known as pruritus, is a sensation that causes a strong desire or reflex to scratch.
Jaundice, also known as icterus, is a yellowish or, less frequently, greenish pigmentation of the skin and conjunctivae due to high bilirubin levels.
Myoclonus is a brief, involuntary, irregular twitching of a muscle, a joint or a group of muscles, different from clonus, which is rhythmic or regular.
A hiccup, from the Latin word for sob, is an involuntary contraction of the diaphragm that may repeat several times per minute.
Nausea is a diffuse sensation of unease and discomfort, sometimes perceived as an urge to vomit.
Nevus or naevus is a nonspecific medical term for a visible, circumscribed, chronic lesion of the skin or mucosa.
Photophobia is a medical symptom of abnormal intolerance to visual perception of light.
A running nose, or runny nose, also known as rhinorrhea, is the free discharge of a thin mucus fluid from the nose.
Post nasal drip, also known as upper airway cough syndrome or catarrh, occurs when excessive mucus is produced by the nasal mucosa.
Shortness of breath, known as dyspnea, is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough.
Sleep deprivation, also known as sleep insufficiency or sleeplessness, is the health condition of not having adequate duration or quality of sleep to support proper alertness, performance and health.
Sore throat, also known as throat pain, is pain or irritation of the throat.
Tinnitus is a condition when a person hears a ringing sound or a different variety of sounds when no corresponding external sound is present and that other people cannot hear.
A toothache, also known as dental pain or tooth pain, is pain in the teeth or their supporting structures, caused by dental diseases or pain referred to the teeth by non dental diseases.
Weakness is a symptom of many different medical conditions.

Dissociative disorders are a range of mental disorders characterized by significant disruptions or fragmentation in the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception and behavior.
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.

Conduct disorder is a mental disorder diagnosed in childhood or adolescence that is characterized by a repetitive and persistent pattern of antisocial behavior involving the violation of the basic rights of others or major age appropriate norms.

Anorexia nervosa, commonly referred to as anorexia, is an eating disorder characterized by predominant food restriction, body image disturbance, fear of gaining weight and an overwhelming desire to be thin.
Bulimia nervosa, also known simply as bulimia, is an eating disorder characterized by binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors.
Pica is the psychologically compulsive craving or consumption of objects that are not normally intended to be consumed.
Body image disturbance is a common symptom in patients with eating disorders and is characterized by an altered perception of one's own body.

Hoarding disorder is a mental disorder characterized by persistent difficulty in parting with possessions and engaging in excessive acquisition of items that are not needed or for which no space is available.
Kleptomania is the inability to resist the urge to steal items, usually for reasons other than personal use or financial gain.

Mass psychogenic illness, also called mass sociogenic illness or mass hysteria, involves the spread of illness symptoms through a population where there is no infectious agent responsible for the outbreak.
Body dysmorphic disorder, also known as dysmorphophobia or simply dysmorphia, is a mental disorder defined by an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in one's physical appearance.

Oppositional defiant disorder is listed among the disruptive, impulse control and conduct disorders and defined as a pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behavior, or vindictiveness.
In psychiatry, paranoia is a wrong perception in which a person thinks others are planning to harm them.
Pyromania is an impulse control disorder in which individuals repeatedly fail to resist impulses to deliberately start fires.
Somatic symptom disorder is a mental disorder characterized by an excessive focus on physical symptoms, such as pain or shortness of breath, that cause significant distress or impairment.
Tourette syndrome, or simply Tourette's, is a motor disorder that begins in childhood or adolescence.
Acrophobia, also known as hypsophobia, is an extreme or irrational fear or phobia of heights, especially when one is not particularly high up.
Arachnophobia is the fear of spiders and other arachnids, such as scorpions and ticks.
Claustrophobia is a fear or anxiety of confined spaces.
Fear of flying is the fear of being on an aircraft, such as an airplane or helicopter, while it is in flight.

Social anxiety disorder, previously known as social phobia, is an anxiety disorder characterized by high levels of anxiety and self consciousness in social situations, resulting in significant distress and an impaired ability to function.
Hypochondriasis or hypochondria is a condition in which a person is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness.
Panic attacks are sudden periods of intense fear and discomfort that may include palpitations, sweating, chest pain, shortness of breath, trembling, dizziness, numbness and confusion.
Bipolar I disorder is a type of bipolar spectrum disorder characterized by the occurrence of at least one manic episode.
Bipolar II disorder is a mood disorder on the bipolar spectrum, characterized by at least one episode of hypomania and at least one episode of major depression.
Hypomania is a psychiatric condition of abnormally heightened mood and increased energy that is less severe than mania.

Dysthymia, known as persistent depressive disorder, is a psychiatric condition marked by symptoms that are similar to those of major depressive disorder, but which persist for at least two years in adults.
Postpartum depression, from the Latin for after birth, also known as perinatal depression, is a mood disorder which may be experienced by pregnant or postpartum women.
Bruxism is excessive teeth grinding or jaw clenching.
Sleep paralysis is a state, during waking up or falling asleep, in which a person is conscious but in a complete state of paralysis.
Sleepwalking, also known as somnambulism, is a phenomenon of combined sleep and wakefulness.
Substance use, also known as drug use or substance abuse, is the use of a drug in amounts or by methods that are harmful to the individual or others.

Asperger syndrome, also known as Asperger's, is a formerly used diagnostic category for a condition characterized by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior and interests.
Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.
Neurosis is a term mainly used today by followers of Freudian psychoanalytic theory to describe mental disorders caused by past anxiety, often anxieties that have undergone repression.
Frailty or frailty syndrome refers to a state of health in which older adults gradually lose their bodies' in built reserves and functioning.
Hair loss, also known as alopecia or baldness, refers to a loss of hair from part of the head or body.
Alopecia areata, also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
Pattern hair loss, also known as androgenetic alopecia, is a hair loss condition that primarily affects the top and front of the scalp.
Telogen effluvium is a scalp disorder characterized by the thinning or shedding of hair resulting from the early entry of hair in the resting phase of the hair follicle.
Breast milk, or mother's milk, is milk produced by the mammary glands in the breasts of humans.
A wet nurse is a woman who breastfeeds and cares for another's child.
A hazard is a potential source of harm.
Being overweight is having more body fat than is considered healthy.
Psychological trauma, also known as mental trauma, psychiatric trauma or emotional damage, is an emotional response caused by severe, distressing events.

Quality of life is defined by the World Health Organization as an individual's perception of their position in life in the context of the culture and value systems in which they live and in relation to their goals, expectations, standards and concerns.
Activities of daily living is a term used in healthcare to refer to an individual's daily self care activities.
Underweight is a term describing a person whose body weight is considered too low to be healthy.
Appetite is the desire to eat food items, usually due to hunger.

A healthy diet is a diet that maintains or improves overall health, providing the body with essential nutrition: water, macronutrients such as protein, micronutrients such as vitamins, and adequate fibre and food energy.
Human nutrition deals with the provision of essential nutrients in food that are necessary to support human life and good health.
Lactose intolerance is a lessened ability or a complete inability to digest lactose, a sugar found in dairy products.
A nutrient is a substance used by an organism to survive, grow and reproduce.
B vitamins are a class of water soluble vitamins that play important roles in cell metabolism and synthesis of red blood cells.
Vitamin B three, colloquially referred to as niacin, is a vitamin family that includes three forms, or vitamers: nicotinic acid, nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside.
Nicotinic acid, or niacin, is an organic compound and a vitamer of vitamin B three, an essential human nutrient.
Pyridoxine is a form of vitamin B six found commonly in food and used as a dietary supplement.

A health club, also known as a fitness club, fitness center, health spa, weight room and commonly referred to as a gym, is a place that houses, and usually an organization that maintains, exercise equipment for the purpose of physical exercise.
Physical activity is defined as any movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure.
Aerobic exercise, also known as cardio, is physical exercise of low to high intensity that depends primarily on the aerobic energy generating process.
Anaerobic exercise is a type of exercise that breaks down glucose in the body without using oxygen.
Aerobics is a form of physical exercise that combines rhythmic aerobic exercise with stretching and strength training routines with the goal of improving all elements of fitness.
Calisthenics, also known as bodyweight exercises, is a form of strength training that utilizes an individual's body weight as resistance to perform multi joint, compound movements.
The crunch or curl up is an abdominal exercise that works the rectus abdominis muscle.
A pull up is an upper body strength exercise.
The push up, called a press up in British English, is a calisthenics exercise beginning from the prone position.
The sit up is an abdominal endurance training exercise to strengthen, tighten and tone the abdominal muscles.
High intensity interval training is a training protocol alternating short periods of intense or explosive anaerobic exercise with brief recovery periods until the point of exhaustion.
A jumping jack, also known as a star jump, is a physical jumping exercise performed by jumping to a position with the legs spread wide.
Pilates is a type of mind body exercise developed in the early twentieth century by Joseph Pilates, after whom it was named.
Strength training, also known as weight training or resistance training, is exercise designed to improve physical strength.
The bench press or chest press is a weight training exercise where a person presses a weight upwards while lying horizontally on a weight training bench.
A squat is a strength exercise in which the trainee lowers their hips from a standing position and then stands back up.

Yoga as exercise is a physical activity consisting mainly of postures, often connected by flowing sequences, sometimes accompanied by breathing exercises, and frequently ending with relaxation lying down or meditation.
Body odor or body odour is the unique odor secreted by an animal or produced by microorganisms on an animal's outermost surfaces.
Hair care or haircare is an overall term for hygiene and cosmetology involving the hair which grows from the human scalp, and to a lesser extent facial and other body hair.
Skin care or skincare is the practice and process of maintaining and improving the health and appearance of the skin.

Dental floss is a cord of thin filaments, typically made of nylon or silk, used in interdental cleaning to remove food and dental plaque from between teeth or places a toothbrush has difficulty reaching.
Facial tissue and paper handkerchief refers to a class of soft, absorbent, disposable papers that are intended for using on the face.
A hairbrush is a brush with rigid or light and soft spokes used in hair care for smoothing, styling and detangling human hair, or for grooming an animal's fur.
Hair conditioner is a hair care cosmetic product used to improve the feel, texture, appearance and manageability of hair.
Hand sanitizer, also known as hand antiseptic, hand disinfectant or hand rub, is a liquid, gel or foam used to kill viruses, bacteria and other microorganisms on the hands.
Lip balm or lip salve is a wax like substance applied to the lips to moisturize and relieve chapped or dry lips, angular cheilitis, stomatitis or cold sores.
Medical gloves are disposable gloves used during medical examinations and procedures to help prevent cross contamination between caregivers and patients.

Mouthwash, mouth rinse, oral rinse or mouth bath is a liquid which is held in the mouth passively or swirled around the mouth by contraction of the perioral muscles or movement of the head, and may be gargled.
A napkin, serviette or face towelette is a square of cloth or paper tissue used at the table for wiping of the mouth and fingers while eating.
A safety razor is a shaving implement with a protective device positioned between the edge of the blade and the skin.
Shaving cream or shave cream is a category of cream cosmetics used for shaving preparation.
Shower gel, also called body wash, is a specialized liquid product used for cleaning the body during showers.
A straight razor is a razor with a blade that can fold into its handle.

A toothpick is a small thin stick of wood, plastic, bamboo, metal, bone or other substance with at least one and sometimes two pointed ends to insert between teeth to remove detritus, usually after a meal.
A paper towel is an absorbent, disposable towel made from paper.
A wet wipe, also known as a moist towelette, disposable wipe or baby wipe, is a moistened, generally biodegradable wipe made from non woven fabric.
Developmental disability is a diverse group of chronic conditions, comprising mental or physical impairments that arise before adulthood.
Low back pain or lumbago is a common disorder involving the muscles, nerves and bones of the back, in between the lower edge of the ribs and the lower fold of the buttocks.
Paralysis, also known as plegia, is a loss of motor function in one or more muscles.
Medulloblastoma is a common type of primary brain cancer in children.
Multiple myeloma, also known as plasma cell myeloma and simply myeloma, is a cancer of plasma cells, a type of white blood cell that normally produces antibodies.
A viral disease, or viral infection, occurs when an organism's body is invaded by pathogenic viruses, and infectious virus particles attach to and enter susceptible cells.
Inoculation is the act of implanting a pathogen or other microbe or virus into a person or other organism.
Tick borne diseases, which afflict humans and other animals, are caused by infectious agents transmitted by tick bites.
Bloodstream infections are infections of blood caused by blood borne pathogens.

Erysipelas is a relatively common bacterial infection of the superficial layer of the skin, extending to the superficial lymphatic vessels within the skin, characterized by a raised, well defined, tender, bright red rash.
Shingles, also known as herpes zoster or zona, is a viral disease characterized by a painful skin rash with blisters in a localized area.
Hepatitis E is inflammation of the liver caused by infection with the hepatitis E virus; it is a type of viral hepatitis.
Creutzfeldt Jakob disease is an incurable, terminal, neurodegenerative disease belonging to the transmissible spongiform encephalopathy group, also known as prion diseases.
A cramp is a sudden, involuntary, painful contraction of one or more skeletal muscles, or an overshortening of such associated with electrical activity.
Indigestion, also known as dyspepsia or upset stomach, is a condition of impaired digestion.
Myalgia or muscle pain is a painful sensation evolving from muscle tissue.
Syncope, commonly known as fainting or passing out, is a loss of consciousness and muscle strength characterized by a fast onset, short duration and spontaneous recovery.
Vomiting, scientifically known as emesis, and otherwise known as puking and throwing up, is the forceful expulsion of the contents of one's stomach through the mouth and sometimes the nose.
Complex post traumatic stress disorder is a stress related mental disorder generally occurring in response to complex traumas.
Mania is a psychiatric behavioral syndrome defined as a state of abnormally elevated mood with hyperactivity and risky behavior.
Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that impairs the ability to regulate sleep wake cycles, and specifically impacts rapid eye movement sleep.
The deadlift is a strength training exercise in which a weight is lifted off the ground to hip level and then returned to the floor.
Dental plaque is a biofilm of microorganisms, mostly bacteria but also fungi, that grows on surfaces within the mouth.
Hair removal is the deliberate removal of body hair or head hair.
A residential treatment center, or residential treatment facility, is a live in health care facility providing therapy for substance use disorders, mental illness, or other behavioral problems.
The human musculoskeletal system, also known as the human locomotor system, is an organ system that gives humans the ability to move using their muscular and skeletal systems.
Hemorrhoids, also known as piles, are vascular cushions that help with stool control.
Infectious diseases, also known as infectiology, is a medical specialty dealing with the diagnosis and treatment of infections.
A blood donation occurs when a person voluntarily has blood drawn and used for transfusions or made into blood products and biopharmaceutical medications by a process called fractionation.

The Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical Classification System is a drug classification system that classifies the active ingredients of drugs according to the organ or system on which they act and their therapeutic, pharmacological and chemical properties.
The World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines contains the medications considered to be most effective and safe to meet the most important needs in a health system.
Antisense therapy is a form of treatment that uses antisense oligonucleotides to target messenger RNA.
Salmeterol is a long acting adrenergic receptor agonist used in the treatment and prevention of asthma symptoms and control of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease symptoms.

Glucagon like peptide receptor agonists, also known as GLP agonists, are a class of medications that activate the GLP receptor, causing reduced blood sugar, reduced appetite and reduced energy intake.
Methylphenidate, sold under the brand names Ritalin and Concerta, among others, is a central nervous system stimulant used in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy.
Ranitidine, sold under the brand name Zantac among others, is a medication used to decrease stomach acid production.
Alcohols, in various forms, are used medically as an antiseptic, disinfectant and antidote.
Cefazolin, also known as cefazoline and cephazolin, is a cephalosporin antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.

Neomycin, polymyxin B and bacitracin, also known as triple antibiotic ointment, and sold under the brand name Neosporin, among others, is an antibiotic medication used to reduce the risk of infections following minor skin injuries.
Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
Fluphenazine, sold under the brand name Prolixin among others, is a high potency typical antipsychotic medication of the phenothiazine class.
Clomipramine, sold under the brand name Anafranil among others, is a tricyclic antidepressant.
Imipramine, sold under the brand name Tofranil, among others, is a tricyclic antidepressant mainly used in the treatment of depression.

Sertraline, sold under the brand name Zoloft among others, is an antidepressant medication of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor class used to treat major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.
A comedo is a clogged hair follicle in the skin.
A pimple or zit is a kind of comedo that results from excess sebum and dead skin cells getting trapped in the pores of the skin.
Impacted wisdom teeth is a condition where the third molars are prevented from erupting into the mouth.
Sudden infant death syndrome, sometimes known as cot death or crib death, is the sudden, unexplained death of a child of less than one year of age.

A congenital heart defect, also known as a congenital heart anomaly, congenital cardiovascular malformation, and congenital heart disease, is a defect in the structure of the heart or great vessels that is present at birth.
An embolism is the lodging of an embolus, a blockage causing piece of material, inside a blood vessel.
Peripheral artery disease is a vascular disorder that causes abnormal narrowing of arteries other than those that supply the heart or brain.
Distributive shock is a medical condition in which abnormal distribution of blood flow in the smallest blood vessels results in inadequate supply of blood to the body's tissues and organs.
Obstructive shock is a type of shock caused by a physical obstruction in the flow of blood.
Acromegaly is a disorder that results in excess growth of certain parts of the human body.
Gigantism, also known as giantism, is a condition characterized by excessive growth and height significantly above average.
Gastrointestinal diseases refer to diseases involving the gastrointestinal tract, namely the esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
Ehlers Danlos syndromes are a group of genetic connective tissue disorders.
Stunted growth, also known as stunting, refers to impaired growth and development in children, which results in a lower than average height for the child's age.
Thiamine deficiency is a medical condition of low levels of thiamine, also known as vitamin B one.
Motion sickness occurs due to a difference between actual and expected motion.
Myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome, is a disabling chronic illness.
Dysmenorrhea, also known as period pain, painful periods or menstrual cramps, is pain during menstruation.
Ectopic pregnancy is a complication of pregnancy in which the embryo attaches outside the uterus.
Endometriosis is a disease in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows elsewhere in the body.
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, previously called polycystic ovary syndrome, is a hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age.
In medicine, an avulsion is an injury in which a body structure is torn off by either trauma or surgery.

Perinatal asphyxia, also known as neonatal asphyxia or birth asphyxia, is the medical condition resulting from deprivation of oxygen to a newborn infant that lasts long enough during the birth process to cause physical harm, usually to the brain.
Developmental coordination disorder, also known as developmental motor coordination disorder, developmental dyspraxia, or simply dyspraxia, is a neurodevelopmental disorder.

Speech language pathology, also known as speech and language pathology or logopedics, is a healthcare and academic discipline concerning the evaluation, treatment and prevention of communication disorders.
Escherichia coli is a gram negative, rod shaped bacterium that is commonly found in the lower intestine of warm blooded organisms.
Classical swine fever or hog cholera, also sometimes called pig plague, is a highly contagious disease of swine.
Herpes simplex encephalitis, or simply herpes encephalitis, is a rare form of encephalitis caused by the herpes simplex virus.
Herpes esophagitis is a viral infection of the esophagus caused by herpes simplex virus.
Herpetic simplex keratitis is a form of keratitis caused by recurrent herpes simplex virus infection in the cornea.
Gingivostomatitis is a combination of gingivitis and stomatitis, or an inflammation of the oral mucosa and gingiva.
A herpetic whitlow is a herpes lesion, typically on a finger or thumb, caused by the herpes simplex virus.
Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, also known as naegleriasis, is an infection of the brain by the free living protozoan Naegleria fowleri.
Variant Creutzfeldt Jakob disease, colloquially called mad cow disease or human mad cow disease, is a prion disease of humans.
Neurodevelopmental disorders are a diverse group of complex psychiatric conditions caused by the abnormal or disrupted development of the brain, or by injury or infection during early childhood.
Dissociative identity disorder, previously known as multiple personality disorder, is a dissociative disorder characterized by the presence of at least two personality states or alters.
Dissociative amnesia or psychogenic amnesia is a dissociative disorder characterized by retrospectively reported memory gaps.
Depersonalization derealization disorder is a dissociative disorder in which the person experiences persistent or recurrent feelings of depersonalization or derealization.
Depressive personality disorder, also known as melancholic personality disorder, is a former psychiatric diagnosis that denotes a personality disorder with depressive features.
Hypogeusia can be defined as the reduced ability to taste things.
Amenorrhea or amenorrhoea is the absence of a menstrual period in a female organism which has reached reproductive age.
Lightheadedness, also known as pre syncope, is a common and typically unpleasant sensation of dizziness or a feeling that one may faint.
A balance disorder is a disturbance that causes an individual to feel unsteady, for example when standing or walking.
Hirsutism is excessive body hair on parts of the body where hair is normally absent or minimal.
Hypoesthesia or numbness is a common side effect of various medical conditions that manifests as a reduced sense of touch or sensation, or a partial loss of sensitivity to sensory stimuli.
Phonophobia, also called ligyrophobia or sonophobia, is a fear of or aversion to specific sounds.
Men's health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well being as experienced by men, and not merely the absence of disease.

Women's health is an example of population health, where health is defined by the World Health Organization as a state of complete physical, mental and social well being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

Stretching is a form of physical exercise in which a specific muscle or tendon, or muscle group, is deliberately expanded and flexed in order to improve the muscle's felt elasticity and achieve comfortable muscle tone.
A cigar is a rolled bundle of dried and fermented tobacco leaves made to be smoked.
An electronic cigarette or vape is a device that simulates tobacco smoking.
Passive smoking is the inhalation of tobacco smoke by individuals who are not actively smoking.
A smoking pipe, often simply referred to as a pipe, is used to inhale or taste the smoke of a burning substance.
A hookah, shisha, or waterpipe is a single or multi stemmed instrument for heating or vaporizing and then smoking tobacco.
Betel nut chewing, also called betel quid chewing or areca nut chewing, is a practice in which areca nuts are chewed together with slaked lime and betel leaves.
Smoking tobacco has serious negative effects on human health.
Blood alcohol content, also known as blood alcohol concentration or blood alcohol level, is the concentration of alcohol in a person's blood, measured for legal or medical purposes.
Atopic dermatitis, also known as atopic eczema, is a chronic type of inflammation of the skin.

Coronary artery disease, also called coronary heart disease or ischemic heart disease, is a type of heart disease involving the reduction of blood flow to the cardiac muscle due to the presence of atheromatous plaques in the arteries of the heart.
Hypertensive heart disease includes a number of complications of high blood pressure that affect the heart.
Cardiogenic shock is a medical emergency resulting from inadequate blood flow to the body's organs due to the dysfunction of the heart.
A metabolic disorder is a disorder that negatively alters the body's processing and distribution of macronutrients, such as proteins, fats and carbohydrates.
Vitiligo is a chronic autoimmune disorder that causes skin to lose pigment in patches that vary in size and can appear anywhere on the body.
A neurological disorder is any disorder of the nervous system.

Polytrauma and multiple trauma are medical terms describing the condition of a person who has been subjected to multiple traumatic injuries, such as a serious head injury in addition to a serious burn.
A staphylococcal infection or staph infection is an infection caused by members of the Staphylococcus genus of bacteria.

Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, or prion diseases, are a group of rare, progressive, incurable conditions that cause degeneration of the nervous system in humans and other animals, such as cattle and sheep.
An aura is a perceptual disturbance experienced by some with epilepsy or migraine.
Abies balsamea or balsam fir is a North American fir, native to eastern and central Canada and the northeastern United States.
Abies nordmanniana, the Nordmann fir or Caucasian fir, is a fir indigenous to the mountains south and east of the Black Sea, in Turkey, Georgia and the Russian Caucasus.
Abies fraseri, commonly known as Fraser's fir, or Fraser fir, is a species of fir in the order Pinales native to the Appalachian Mountains of the southeastern United States.
Pinus halepensis, commonly known as the Aleppo pine, also known as the Jerusalem pine, is a species of conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine native to the Mediterranean region.
The longleaf pine is a species of conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine native to the Southeastern United States, found along the coastal plain.
Pinus lambertiana, commonly known as the sugar pine, is a tall and massive pine tree and has among the longest cones of any conifer.
Pinus taeda, commonly known as loblolly pine, is a species of conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine native to the Southeastern United States.
The blue spruce, also commonly known as Colorado spruce or Colorado blue spruce, is a species of spruce tree native to North America.
Picea glauca, the white spruce, is a species of spruce native to the northern temperate and boreal forests in Canada and United States, North America.
Nymphaea lotus, the white Egyptian lotus, tiger lotus, white lotus, or Egyptian water lily, is a flowering plant of the family Nymphaeaceae.
Oryza glaberrima, commonly known as African rice, is one of the two domesticated rice species.
Zoysia is a genus of creeping grasses widespread across much of Asia and Australia, as well as various islands in the Pacific.
Matoke, locally also known as matooke, is a cooking banana dish from the Great Lakes region of Africa.
The Blue Java, also known as the blue banana or ice cream banana, is a hardy, cold tolerant banana cultivar known for its sweet aromatic fruit.
Dianthus caryophyllus, commonly known as carnation or clove pink, is a species of Dianthus native to the Mediterranean region.
Kabocha is a type of winter squash, a Japanese variety of the species Cucurbita maxima.
Summer squash can either refer to a squash plant with fruit that is harvested when immature, or the fruit itself.
Vaccinium is a common and widespread genus of shrubs or dwarf shrubs in the heath family.
Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry and whortleberry.
Primula is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants in the family Primulaceae.

Kudzu, also called Japanese arrowroot or Chinese arrowroot, is a group of climbing, coiling and trailing deciduous perennial vines native to much of East Asia, Southeast Asia and some Pacific islands.
The pigeon pea is a perennial legume from the family Fabaceae native to the Eastern Hemisphere.
Vigna angularis, also known as the adzuki bean, azuki bean, aduki bean, red bean, or red mung bean, is an annual vine widely cultivated throughout East Asia for its small bean.
Wisteria is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, Fabaceae.

Alnus glutinosa, the common alder, black alder, European alder, European black alder, or just alder, is a species of tree in the family Betulaceae, native to much of Europe, southwest Asia and northern Africa.
Betula papyrifera, the paper birch, also known as white birch and canoe birch, is a short lived species of birch native to northern North America.
Betula pendula, the silver birch, is a species of tree in the flowering plant family Betulaceae.
Hornbeams are hardwood trees in the plant genus Carpinus in the family Betulaceae.
Fagus sylvatica, the European beech or common beech, is a species of tree in the flowering plant family Fagaceae.
Quercus alba, the white oak, is one of the preeminent hardwoods of eastern and central North America.
Quercus robur, pedunculate oak, European oak, or English oak, is a species of flowering plant in the beech and oak family, Fagaceae.
Quercus rubra, the northern red oak or common red oak, is an oak tree in the red oak group.
Quercus virginiana, also known as the southern live oak, is a semi evergreen oak tree native to the Southeastern United States coastal plain.
The acorn is the nut of the oaks and their close relatives in the family Fagaceae, alternatively known as glans.
Carya ovata, the shagbark hickory, is a common hickory native to eastern North America.
Nothofagus, also known as the southern beeches, is a genus of trees and shrubs native to the Southern Hemisphere.
Asclepias is a genus of herbaceous, perennial, flowering plants known as milkweeds, named for their latex, a milky substance containing cardiac glycosides.
Ocimum tenuiflorum, commonly known as tulasi, tulsi, or holy basil, is an aromatic perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Thai basil is a type of basil native to and widely used throughout Southeast Asia, that has been cultivated to provide distinctive traits.
Hyssopus officinalis or hyssop is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
Jasminum officinale, known as the common jasmine or simply jasmine, is a species of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae.
Osmanthus fragrans is a species of flowering plant in the family Oleaceae.
Syringa is a genus of currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family known colloquially as lilacs.
Populus tremula, commonly called aspen, common aspen, Eurasian aspen, European aspen, or quaking aspen, is a species of poplar native to cool temperate regions of the Old World.
Salix alba, the white willow, is a species of willow native to Europe and western and Central Asia.
Salix babylonica is a species of willow native to dry areas of northern China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and Siberia.
Salix nigra, or the black willow, is a species of willow native to a large portion of North America.
Gossypium hirsutum, also known as upland cotton or Mexican cotton, is a widely planted species of cotton in the world.
Hibiscus is a genus of plants in the family Malvaceae native to the tropics and subtropics.

The common bream, also known as the freshwater bream, bream, bronze bream, carp bream or sweaty bream, is a European species of freshwater fish in the family Leuciscidae.
The zebrafish is a species of danionin belonging to the genus Danio in the suborder Cyprinoidei.
The grass carp is a species of large herbivorous freshwater fish in the family Cyprinidae, native to the Pacific Far East.
The silver carp or silverfin is a species of freshwater cyprinid fish, a variety of Asian carp native to China and eastern Siberia.
The tench or doctor fish is a fresh and brackish water fish of the order Cypriniformes found throughout Eurasia from Western Europe including Britain and Ireland east into Asia.
Minnow is the common name for a number of species of small freshwater fish, belonging to several genera of the family Cyprinidae and in particular the subfamily Leuciscinae.
The banded knifefish is a species of gymnotiform knifefish native to a wide range of freshwater habitats in South America.
Gars are an ancient group of ray finned fish in the family Lepisosteidae.
The ruddy bowfin is a ray finned fish native to North America.
Barreleyes, also known as spookfish, are small deep sea argentiniform fish comprising the family Opisthoproctidae found in tropical to temperate waters of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans.
The Antarctic toothfish, also known as the Antarctic cod, is a large, black or brown fish found in very cold waters of the Southern Ocean near Antarctica.
Needlefish, family Belonidae, or long toms are piscivorous fishes primarily associated with very shallow marine habitats or the surface of the open sea.
The Pacific saury is species of fish in the family Scomberesocidae.
The black swallower is a species of deep sea fish in the family Chiasmodontidae.
The butterflyfish are a group of conspicuous tropical marine fish of the family Chaetodontidae.
The four eyed fishes are a genus, Anableps, of fishes in the family Anablepidae.
A killifish is any of various oviparous, egg laying, cyprinodontiform fish, including families Aplocheilidae, Pantanodontidae, Cyprinodontidae, Fundulidae and others.
Pupfish are a group of small killifish belonging to ten genera of the family Cyprinodontidae of ray finned fish.
Damselfish are fish within the subfamilies Abudefdufinae, Chrominae, Lepidozyginae, Pomacentrinae, and Stegastinae within the family Pomacentridae.

The burbot, also known as bubbot, mariah, loche, cusk, freshwater cod, freshwater ling, freshwater cusk, the lawyer, coney fish, lingcod, or eelpout, is a species of coldwater ray finned fish native to the subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Hake is the common name for fish in the Merlucciidae family of the northern and southern oceans and the Phycidae family of the northern oceans.
Pollock or pollack is the common name used for either of the two species of North Atlantic marine fish in the genus Pollachius.
The three spined stickleback is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of thirty degrees north.
Mudskippers are extant species of amphibious fish from the subfamily Oxudercinae of the goby family Oxudercidae.
Gouramis, or gouramies, are a group of freshwater anabantiform fish that comprise the family Osphronemidae.
John Dory, St Pierre, or Peter's fish are names which refers to fish of the genus Zeus, especially Zeus faber, which is a demersal coastal marine fish.
The giant oarfish is a species of oarfish of the family Regalecidae.
The opah, also commonly known as moonfish, sunfish, cowfish, kingfish, and redfin ocean pan are large, colorful, deep bodied pelagic lampriform fishes comprising the genus Lampris.
Frogfishes are any member of the anglerfish family Antennariidae, of the order Lophiiformes.
Handfish or warty frogfish are marine, ray finned fishes belonging to the subfamily Brachionichthyinae.
The footballfish form a family, Himantolophidae, of globose, deep sea anglerfishes found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
Goosefishes, sometimes called anglers or monkfishes, form the family Lophiidae of marine ray finned fishes belonging to the order Lophiiformes, the anglerfishes.
The Murray cod is a large Australian predatory freshwater fish of the genus Maccullochella in the family Percichthyidae.
Pearlfish are marine fish in the ray finned fish family Carapidae.
Parrotfish, named because their mouths resemble a parrot's beak, are a clade of fish placed in the subfamily Scarinae of the wrasse family Labridae.

The European perch, also known as the common perch, redfin perch, big scaled redfin, English perch, Euro perch, Eurasian perch, Eurasian river perch, Hatch, poor man's rockfish or in Anglophone parts of Europe, simply perch, is a predatory species of freshwater fish.
Pomfrets are scombriform fish belonging to the family Bramidae.
Bonitos are a tribe of medium sized, ray finned, predatory fish in the family Scombridae, which it shares with the mackerel, tuna, and Spanish mackerel tribes.
Scomberomorini is a tribe of ray finned, saltwater, bony fishes that is commonly known as Spanish mackerels, seerfishes, or seer fish.
The Pacific bluefin tuna is a predatory species of tuna found widely in the northern Pacific Ocean, but it is migratory and also recorded as a visitor to the south Pacific.
The skipjack tuna is a perciform fish in the tuna family, Scombridae.
Lionfish are venomous marine ray finned fish of the genus Pterois, native to coral reefs of the Indo Pacific.
The common seadragon or weedy seadragon is a marine fish of the order Syngnathiformes, which also includes the similar pipefishes, seahorses, and trumpetfishes.
The leafy seadragon or Glauert's seadragon, is a marine fish.
The trumpetfishes are three species of highly specialized, tubularly elongated marine fishes in the genus Aulostomus, of the monogeneric family Aulostomidae.
The filefish are a diverse family of tropical to subtropical tetraodontiform marine fish, which are also known as foolfish, leatherjackets, or shingles.
Porcupinefishes are medium to large fish belonging to the family Diodontidae from the order Tetraodontiformes which are also commonly called blowfishes and, sometimes, balloonfishes and globefishes.
Triggerfish are marine, ray finned fishes belonging to the family Balistidae.
The humphead wrasse is a large species of wrasse mainly found on coral reefs in the Indo Pacific region.
The Moorish idol is a species of marine ray finned fish belonging to the family Zanclidae.
The emperor angelfish is a species of marine angelfish.
The barramundi, Asian sea bass, Asian sea lates, giant sea lates, or giant sea perch is a species of catadromous fish in the family Latidae of the order Carangiformes.
The sailfish is one or two species of marine fish in the genus Istiophorus, which belong to the family Istiophoridae, the marlins.
Flounders are a group of flatfish species.
Halibut is the common name for three species of flatfish in the family of right eye flounders.
The muskellunge, often shortened to muskie, musky, ski, or lunge, is a species of large freshwater predatory fish native to North America.
A viperfish is any species of the genus Chauliodus, marine fish inhabiting the twilight or mesopelagic zone.
Helicoprion is an extinct genus of large shark like cartilaginous fish that lived from the Early to the Middle Permian.
Xiphactinus is an extinct genus of large predatory marine ray finned fish that lived during the late Albian to the late Maastrichtian.
Leedsichthys is an extinct genus of pachycormid fish that lived in the oceans of the Middle to Late Jurassic.
The sea lamprey is a parasitic lamprey native to the Northern Hemisphere.
Artemia is a genus of aquatic crustaceans also known as brine shrimp.

The red king crab, also called Kamchatka crab or Alaskan king crab, is a species of king crab native to cold waters in the North Pacific Ocean and adjacent seas, but also introduced to the Barents Sea.
The Japanese giant spider crab is a species of marine crab and is a large crab found in the waters around Japan.
The Christmas Island red crab is a species of land crab that is endemic to Christmas Island and Cocos Islands in the Indian Ocean.
The American lobster is a species of lobster found on the Atlantic coast of North America, chiefly from Labrador to New Jersey.
Slipper lobsters are a family, Scyllaridae, of about ninety species of achelate crustaceans, in the Decapoda clade Reptantia, found in all warm oceans and seas.
Hyneria is a genus of large prehistoric predatory lobe finned fish which lived in fresh water during the Famennian stage of the Devonian period.
Cretoxyrhina is an extinct genus of large mackerel shark that lived during the late Albian to late Campanian of the Late Cretaceous.
The Arizona bark scorpion, Centruroides sculpturatus, is a small light brown scorpion common to the Sonoran Desert in the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico.
The deathstalker, Leiurus quinquestriatus, is a species of scorpion in the family Buthidae, also known as the Palestine yellow scorpion, the Omdurman scorpion and the Naqab desert scorpion.
The emperor scorpion, Pandinus imperator, is a species of scorpion native to rainforests and savannas in West Africa, and it lives for six to eight years.
Fattail scorpion is the common name given to scorpions of the genus Androctonus, a group counted among the more dangerous scorpions worldwide.
Atracidae is a family of mygalomorph spiders, commonly known as Australian funnel-web spiders or atracids, now recognised as a separate family.
The brown recluse, Loxosceles reclusa, is a recluse spider with necrotic venom, and its bites sometimes require medical attention.
The diving bell spider or water spider, Argyroneta aquatica, is a species of spider known to live almost entirely under water.
Huntsman spiders, members of the family Sparassidae, catch their prey by hunting rather than in webs, and are also called giant crab spiders because of their size and appearance.

The redback spider, Latrodectus hasselti, also known as the Australian black widow, is a species of highly venomous spider believed to originate in Australia and now found in Southeast Asia, Japan and New Zealand.
Orb-weaver spiders are members of the spider family Araneidae, common builders of spiral wheel-shaped webs often found in gardens, fields and forests.
Wolf spiders are members of the family Lycosidae, named for their robust and agile hunting skills and excellent eyesight; they live mostly in solitude, hunt alone and usually do not spin webs.
The Goliath birdeater, Theraphosa blondi, is a large spider of the tarantula family Theraphosidae, found in northern South America.
A tarantula hawk is a spider wasp of the family Pompilidae that preys on tarantulas, belonging to the genera Pepsis and Hemipepsis.

The Asian giant hornet, Vespa mandarinia, also known as the northern giant hornet, is native to temperate and tropical East Asia, South Asia, mainland Southeast Asia and parts of the Russian Far East.
Yellowjacket is the common name in North America for predatory social wasps of the genera Vespula and Dolichovespula, which are known simply as wasps in other English-speaking countries.
Fig wasps are wasps of the superfamily Chalcidoidea which spend their larval stage inside fig syconia; some are pollinators but others simply feed off the plant.
The Argentine ant, Linepithema humile, is an ant native to northern Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia and southern Brazil.
The name army ant is applied to more than two hundred ant species in different lineages, known for aggressive predatory foraging groups called raids.
Harvester ant is a common name for any of the species or genera of ants that collect seeds, which are stored in the colony in communal chambers.
Leafcutter ants are several species of fungus-growing ants that share the behaviour of cutting leaves, which they carry back to their colonies to farm fungus.
Weaver ants or green ants are eusocial insects of the ant family Formicidae, belonging to the tribe Oecophyllini; they live in trees and are known for their unique building behaviour.
The pharaoh ant, Monomorium pharaonis, is a small yellow or light brown, almost transparent ant notorious as a major indoor nuisance pest, especially in hospitals.
Carpenter bees are species in the genus Xylocopa of the subfamily Xylocopinae, a genus that includes some five hundred bees in thirty-one subgenera.
The term cuckoo bee is used for a variety of bee lineages that have evolved the kleptoparasitic behaviour of laying their eggs in the nests of other bees, reminiscent of cuckoo birds.
Stingless bees, sometimes called stingless honey bees or meliponines, are a large group of bees comprising the tribe Meliponini.
The European dark bee, Apis mellifera mellifera, is a subspecies of the western honey bee that spread into eastern and western Europe from a proposed origin in the Tien Shan Mountains.
The luna moth, Actias luna, also called the American moon moth, is a Nearctic moth of the family Saturniidae, a group commonly named the giant silk moths, with lime-green wings and a white body.
Clothes moth or clothing moth is the common name for several species of moth considered to be pests, whose larvae eat animal fibres such as hairs and fabrics.
The hummingbird hawk-moth, Macroglossum stellatarum, is a hawk moth found across temperate regions of Eurasia, named for its similarity to hummingbirds as it feeds on the nectar of flowers.
The monarch butterfly, Danaus plexippus, is a milkweed butterfly of the subfamily Danainae in the family Nymphalidae, also called the milkweed butterfly, common tiger or wanderer.
The morpho butterflies comprise many species of Neotropical butterfly under the genus Morpho, found mostly in South America, Mexico and Central America.
Vanessa cardui, commonly called the painted lady, is a butterfly found across much of the world, formerly called the cosmopolitan butterfly in North America.
Gonepteryx rhamni, commonly named the Common Brimstone, is a butterfly of the family Pieridae that lives throughout the Palearctic zone and is found across Europe, Asia and North Africa.
Flower mantises are mantises that use a form of camouflage called aggressive mimicry, both to attract prey and to avoid predators, with colorations and behaviors that mimic flowers.
Dead leaf mantis is a common name given to various species of praying mantises that mimic dead leaves, often used for species of the genus Deroplatys.
The emperor dragonfly or blue emperor, Anax imperator, is a large species of hawker dragonfly of the family Aeshnidae.
Giant wētā are several species of wētā in the genus Deinacrida of the family Anostostomatidae, endemic to New Zealand and protected by law because they are considered at risk.
The common walkingstick or northern walkingstick, Diapheromera femorata, is a species of phasmid or stick insect found across North America.
The crab louse, Pthirus pubis, is an insect that is an obligate ectoparasite of humans, feeding exclusively on blood.

The cat flea, Ctenocephalides felis, is an extremely common parasitic insect whose principal host is the domestic cat, although a high proportion of the fleas found on dogs also belong to this species.
The Oriental rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis, also known as the tropical rat flea, is a parasite of rodents, primarily of the genus Rattus, and a primary vector for plague and murine typhus.
The firebrat, Thermobia domestica, is a small insect in the order Zygentoma, distinguished from the related silverfishes by its habit of living in warm regions of homes.
The antlions are a group of about two thousand species of insect in the neuropteran family Myrmeleontidae, known for larvae that mostly dig pits to trap passing ants or other prey.
Blister beetles are beetles of the family Meloidae, so called for their defensive secretion of a blistering agent, cantharidin.
The Colorado potato beetle, Leptinotarsa decemlineata, also known as the ten-striped spearman, is a beetle known for being a major pest of potato crops.
The longhorn beetles, Cerambycidae, also known as longicorns, are a large family of beetles with tens of thousands of species described, whose larvae are often called roundheaded borers.
Mealworms are the larval form of the yellow mealworm beetle, Tenebrio molitor, a species of darkling beetle.
The common cockchafer, Melolontha melolontha, known colloquially as the Maybug, Maybeetle or doodlebug, is a species of scarab beetle belonging to the genus Melolontha.
The Goliath beetles, named after the biblical giant Goliath, are any of the six species belonging to the genus Goliathus.
The Hercules beetle, Dynastes hercules, is a species of rhinoceros beetle native to the tropical forests of southern Mexico, Central America, South America and the Lesser Antilles.
The Japanese rhinoceros beetle, Trypoxylus dichotomus, also known as the Japanese horned beetle or by its Japanese name kabutomushi, is a species of rhinoceros beetle.
Stag beetles compose the family Lucanidae, with about twelve hundred species of beetles in four subfamilies.
The whirligig beetles are water beetles of the family Gyrinidae that usually swim on the surface of the water if undisturbed, though they swim underwater when threatened.
The giraffe weevil, Trachelophorus giraffa, is a species of small weevil endemic to Madagascar.
The American cockroach, Periplaneta americana, is a species of cockroach routinely found in homes and often considered a pest, colloquially known in parts of the United States as the waterbug.
The German cockroach, Blattella germanica, colloquially known as the croton bug, is a species of small cockroach.
The Madagascar hissing cockroach, Gromphadorhina portentosa, also known as the hisser, is a large species of cockroach from Madagascar.
The Formosan termite, Coptotermes formosanus, is a species of termite local to southern China and introduced to Taiwan, Japan, South Africa and Sri Lanka, taking its name from Formosa.
Aedes aegypti, sometimes called the yellow fever mosquito, is a mosquito that spreads diseases such as dengue fever, yellow fever and chikungunya.
Anopheles is a genus of mosquito known as nail mosquitoes and marsh mosquitoes, many of which are vectors of the parasite genus Plasmodium.
Culex, or typical mosquitoes, is a genus of mosquitoes, several species of which serve as vectors of important diseases of birds, humans and other animals.
Hoverflies, also called flower flies or syrphids, make up the insect family Syrphidae and are often seen hovering, maintaining a spot in the air as part of their display behavior.
Nairobi fly is the common name for two species of rove beetle in the genus Paederus, native to East Africa, which contain a corrosive substance known as pederin.
The Gerridae are a family of insects in the order Hemiptera, commonly known as water striders, water skeeters, pond skaters, water skippers and puddle flies.

A periodical cicada is any of the seven species of the genus Magicicada of eastern North America, the thirteen- and seventeen-year cicadas, so called because nearly all individuals in a local population emerge together.
Treehoppers and thorn bugs are members of the family Membracidae, a group of insects related to the cicadas and the leafhoppers.
Sawflies are wasp-like insects in the suborder Symphyta of the order Hymenoptera, named for the saw-like appearance of the ovipositor that females use to cut into plants where they lay their eggs.
The common blue butterfly or European common blue, Polyommatus icarus, is a butterfly in the family Lycaenidae and subfamily Polyommatinae, found throughout the Palearctic.
The fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, is a species in the order Lepidoptera, one of the fall armyworm moths distinguished by their larval life stage.
Lymantria dispar, also known as the gypsy moth and in the United States the spongy moth, is a species of moth in the family Erebidae native to Europe and Asia.
Acherontia lachesis, the greater death's head hawkmoth or bee robber, is a large sphingid moth found in India, Sri Lanka and much of the East Asian region.
Scolopendra gigantea, also known as the Peruvian giant yellow-leg centipede or Amazonian giant centipede, is a centipede in the genus Scolopendra.
Scutigera coleoptrata, the house centipede, is a species of centipede that is typically yellowish-gray with up to fifteen pairs of long legs, originating in the Mediterranean region.
Archispirostreptus gigas, known as the giant African millipede, shongololo or Bongololo, is a very large extant species of millipede.
Pill millipedes are any members of two living orders of millipedes, often grouped together into a single superorder, Oniscomorpha.
Arthropleura is an extinct genus of massive myriapod that lived in modern-day Europe and North America, its name meaning joint and rib.
Anomalocaris is an extinct genus of radiodont, an order of early-diverging stem-group marine arthropods, known from the Burgess Shale.
Eurypterus is an extinct genus of eurypterid, a group of organisms commonly called sea scorpions, that lived during the Silurian period.
Meganeura is a genus of extinct insects from the Late Carboniferous, about three hundred million years ago, belonging to the extinct order Meganisoptera.
Opabinia regalis is an extinct stem group marine arthropod found in the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, a soft-bodied animal from the Middle Cambrian.
Tridacna gigas, the giant clam, is a species of the giant clam genus Tridacna and a very large living bivalve mollusc.
The zebra mussel, Dreissena polymorpha, is a small freshwater mussel, an aquatic bivalve mollusc in the family Dreissenidae, originating from the lakes of southwestern Russia and southeastern Europe.
The Pacific geoduck is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae, its common name derived from the Lushootseed name.
The freshwater pearl mussel, Margaritifera margaritifera, is an endangered species of freshwater mussel, an aquatic bivalve mollusc in the family Margaritiferidae.
Pecten maximus, common names the great scallop, king scallop, St James shell or escallop, is a northeast Atlantic species of scallop, an edible saltwater clam in the family Pectinidae.
Shipworms, teredo worms or simply teredo are a group of xylophagic marine bivalve molluscs in the family Teredinidae that consume wood submerged in saltwater.
The common octopus, Octopus vulgaris, is a mollusc of the class Cephalopoda, and is one of the intensively studied octopus species.
Umbrella octopuses, the Opisthoteuthidae, are a group of pelagic octopuses.
The colossal squid, Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni, is a species of very large squid in the family Cranchiidae, sometimes called the Antarctic cranch squid or giant cranch squid.
The argonauts, genus Argonauta, are a group of pelagic octopuses, also called paper nautili after the paper-thin eggcase that females secrete.
Ammonoids are extinct, typically coiled-shelled cephalopods composing the subclass Ammonoidea, more closely related to octopuses, squid and cuttlefish than to nautiluses.
Belemnites are an extinct order of squid-like cephalopods that existed from the Late Triassic to Late Cretaceous, with a mineralized internal skeleton unlike that of squid.
Orthoceras is a genus of extinct nautiloid cephalopod, its name from Ancient Greek meaning straight horn, restricted to Middle Ordovician marine limestones.
Banana slugs, genus Ariolimax, are air-breathing, terrestrial gastropod slugs in the family Ariolimacidae, often yellow in color with an elongated shape that can resemble a banana.
Sea slug is a common name for some marine invertebrates with varying levels of resemblance to terrestrial slugs, mostly gastropods that are sea snails.
The Spanish dancer, Hexabranchus sanguineus, is a dorid nudibranch, a very large and colorful sea slug in the family Hexabranchidae.
Glaucus atlanticus, the blue sea dragon, is a species of sea slug in the family Glaucidae, also called the sea swallow, blue angel or blue glaucus.
Lissachatina fulica, the giant African land snail, is a species of large land snail in the subfamily Achatininae of the family Achatinidae.
Helix pomatia, known as the Roman snail or Burgundy snail, is a species of large, air-breathing land snail of the family Helicidae, native to Europe, with a globular brown shell.
Cone snails are highly venomous sea snails that constitute the family Conidae, predatory marine gastropod molluscs.
Cowrie is the common name for a group of small to large sea snails in the family Cypraeidae, whose shells have held cultural, economic and ornamental significance in various cultures.
Abalone are sea snails in the genus Haliotis, with distinctive flattened, ear-like shells that have a nacreous interior.
Pycnopodia helianthoides, the sunflower sea star, is a large sea star found in the northeastern Pacific Ocean.
The Euryalida, commonly known as basket stars, are an order of echinoderms in the class Ophiuroidea, a type of brittle star with branching or long curling arms.
Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the purple sea urchin, is a species of sea urchin in the family Strongylocentrotidae that lives along the eastern edge of the Pacific Ocean.
Sea apple is the common name for the colorful and somewhat round sea cucumbers of the genus Pseudocolochirus, found in Indo-Pacific waters.
Brain coral is a common name given to various corals in the families Mussidae and Merulinidae, so called for their spheroid shape and grooved surface that resembles a brain.
Precious coral, or red coral, is the common name given to a genus of marine corals, Corallium, with a durable and intensely colored red or pink-orange skeleton.
Sea pens are marine cnidarians of the superfamily Pennatuloidea, fleshy colonial organisms anchored to the seabed, with tiny polyps embedded in a soft matrix.
Siphonophores are cnidarian animals of the hydrozoan order Siphonophorae.
Turritopsis dohrnii, commonly known as the immortal jellyfish, is a species of small, biologically immortal jellyfish found worldwide in temperate to tropical waters.
Aurelia is a genus of jellyfish commonly called moon jellies, in the class Scyphozoa.
Spongia officinalis, better known as a bath sponge, is a commercially used sea sponge that grows in large lobes with small openings, formed by a mesh of primary and secondary fibres.
The giant Gippsland earthworm, Megascolides australis, is one of the native earthworm species of Australia.
The gyrfalcon, Falco rusticolus, also abbreviated as gyr, is a bird of prey and a very large species in the falcon family, Falconidae, breeding on the Arctic coasts and tundra.
The bearded vulture, Gypaetus barbatus, also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the genus Gypaetus.

Haast's eagle, Hieraaetus moorei, sometimes known as Fuller's eagle, is an extinct species of eagle that lived in the South Island of New Zealand, commonly accepted to be the pouākai of Māori mythology.
The harpy eagle, Harpia harpyja, is a large neotropical species of eagle, also called the American harpy eagle to distinguish it from the Papuan eagle.
The Philippine eagle, Pithecophaga jefferyi, also known as the monkey-eating eagle, is a critically endangered species of eagle of the family Accipitridae, endemic to forests in the Philippines.
The steppe eagle, Aquila nipalensis, is a large bird of prey that, like all eagles, belongs to the family Accipitridae.
The wedge-tailed eagle, Aquila audax, is a very large bird of prey of the continent of Australia, also found in southern New Guinea and as far south as Tasmania.
The Andean condor, Vultur gryphus, is a South American New World vulture, found in the Andes mountains and adjacent Pacific coasts of western South America.

The California condor, Gymnogyps californianus, is a New World vulture and a very large North American land bird, which became extinct in the wild when all remaining wild individuals were captured, but has been reintroduced.

The cinereous vulture, Aegypius monachus, also known as the black vulture, Eurasian black vulture and monk vulture, is a very large raptor in the family Accipitridae distributed through much of temperate Eurasia.

The Egyptian vulture, Neophron percnopterus, also called the white scavenger vulture or pharaoh's chicken, is a small Old World vulture, widely distributed from the Iberian Peninsula and northern Africa to India.
The common eider, Somateria mollissima, also called St. Cuthbert's duck or Cuddy's duck, is a large sea-duck distributed over the northern coasts of Europe, North America and eastern Siberia.
The harlequin duck, Histrionicus histrionicus, is a small sea duck that takes its name from Harlequin, the colourfully dressed character in the commedia dell'arte theatre of Italy.

The long-tailed duck, Clangula hyemalis, is a medium-sized sea duck that breeds in the tundra and taiga regions of the arctic and winters along the northern coastlines of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
The pintail or northern pintail, Anas acuta, is a duck species with wide geographic distribution that breeds in the northern areas of Europe and across the Palearctic and North America.

The northern shoveler, often known simply as the shoveler where other related species do not occur, is a common and widespread duck that breeds in northern areas of Europe and throughout the Palearctic and across North America.
The snow goose, Anser caerulescens, is a species of goose native to North America, with both white and dark morphs, the latter often known as the blue goose.

The Canada goose, Branta canadensis, is a large species of goose with a black head and neck, white cheeks, white under its chin and a brown body, native to the Arctic and temperate regions of North America.
The nene, Branta sandvicensis, also known as the nēnē or the Hawaiian goose, is a species of bird endemic to the Hawaiian Islands.
The magpie goose, Anseranas semipalmata, is the sole living representative of the family Anseranatidae, a waterbird found in northern Australia and southern New Guinea.
The Muscovy duck, Cairina moschata, is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay, and has been domesticated.
The black swan, Cygnus atratus, is a large waterbird, a species of swan that breeds mainly in the southeast and southwest regions of Australia.
The great auk, Pinguinus impennis, also known as the penguin or garefowl, is an extinct species of flightless alcid driven to extinction by human exploitation.
Puffins are any of three species of small alcids, or auks, in the bird genus Fratercula, pelagic seabirds that feed primarily by diving in the water.
The oystercatchers are a group of waders forming the family Haematopodidae, which has a single genus, Haematopus, found on coasts worldwide, apart from the polar regions and some tropical regions.

Godwits are a group of four large, long-billed, long-legged and strongly migratory waders of the bird genus Limosa, whose long bills allow them to probe deeply in the sand for aquatic worms and molluscs.
